Prau.ma.- *kṛtaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46). The term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti; by virtue of that, there is an application of the rule to what ends with these [suffixes]. For in the case of a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, the *kṛt* suffixes [do not apply].

Furthermore, the meaning of taddhita suffixes does not exist [independently]; rather, it is obtained through the understanding of what previously occurred (*bhūtapūrvagati*), but that is not the primary sense. Even in the case of the *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning) view, the meaning is not fully established by the suffix alone. With this intention, he says: "Those ending in kṛt and taddhita suffixes."

In cases such as *liṭ* and *dhuk*, since the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) [of suffixes] would apply by the rule "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*), and in cases such as *kartṛ* the exclusion "not ending in a suffix" (*apratyayāntam*) would apply, this is a positive injunction (*vidhi*). As for the phrase "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*): one should not suspect that this is for the purpose of a positive injunction in view of the exclusion based on ending in a suffix.

Because the word *vākya* does not end in an affix (*pratyaya*), and because when an affix is mentioned [in a rule], only that which begins with the element immediately preceding that affix is included. If it is argued: "But is it not the case that the restriction regarding 'beginning with that' (*tadādiniyama*) is prohibited in the case of feminine affixes?
Therefore, let this [rule] exist for the sake of the injunction in cases such as *rājakumārīm*"?—it is not so.

Even though the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (and so on) is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, it does not apply in the domain of *luk* elision; therefore, the compound is formed only when the case-ending (*sup*) is actually heard.

Furthermore, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies there because the item does not end in a suffix (*apratyayānta*), that designation remains easily available even when the case-ending is elided by *luk*, according to the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). For this very reason...

In examples such as *gomatpriya*, the augment *num* and others do not occur; however, they would certainly occur if the internal (*antaraṅga*) operation were to take effect prior to the elision (*luk*). If it is argued: "Even so, let this [rule] be for the purpose of an injunction regarding meaningless compounds in cases of 'unconnected' composition (*asamarthasamāsa*), such as *daśadāḍima*," we reply: No, because it has already been stated that the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

If it is asked, "How then can this be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) within an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound)?"—understand that it is so because of the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). For by the rule "asūryalalāṭayoḥ—" (*Pāṇini 3.2.36*), the suffix *khaś* is prescribed when the word *asūrya* is used as an *upapada*.
And a word uttered in proximity is an *upapada*; furthermore, a word is defined as that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

He states the body of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) with the words "in which aggregate," and so forth. The phrase "the preceding portion" is an illustration; it should be understood that the subsequent suffix is not [included]. Otherwise, in cases such as *janmavān*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply, because the mention of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) [in the definition] is intended for instances like *aupagava*.

Because its purpose has been fulfilled. Why is it stated that "the preceding portion is a *pada*"? So that the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may apply to that which is qualified by the suffix *bahuc*. By means of this, in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, when the initial *jas* is elided, the word *bahupaṭu-* receives the accent of a *cit* suffix; then, when *jas* is added again, the penultimate vowel's acute accent (*udātta*) is established. Or else:

Let it be that the rule concerns a composite [word] that has not entered into the relationship of base and suffix. Nor should it be argued that, under the first view, in cases such as *rājapuruṣau* (the king’s two men), the designation [of "subanta"] would apply to *puruṣau* and so forth;
for this is prevented precisely by the condition of being meaningful (*arthavattva*). For the meaning of the suffix connects only with the qualified [meaning], and not...
[Otherwise], the term *puruṣau* would have its meaningfulness [only] in the mere sense of the second member of the compound.

He states the result of the restriction with the words "by that," etc. But even so, in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, the designation of the sentence (*vākya*) would be unavoidable; for when there is the mention of a *kṛt*-affix, [the rule applies] even to that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka.

If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the mention [of the word], do not say so; for it is sublated by the subsequent restriction established by the mention of *samāsa*. And thus, in the rule *kṛttaddhita-*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of *kṛt* does not apply at all, as it would be fruitless—this is the truth. As for what they say—that the mention of *samāsa*...

This is not for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), but rather for the sake of injunction (*vidhyartha*) alone. For "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) consists in having a function (*vṛttimatva*). And function is twofold: primary denotation (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Now, that [function] does not exist in a compound (*samāsa*). To this, it must be said: according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted, there is no such thing as a "function" [in the compound].
This is indeed refuted. For even in the Mīmāṃsā system, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) certainly exists. As they say:
"It is established that in every case, the sentence-meaning is indeed what is indicated.
Now, if it were argued according to the Naiyāyika method, that too is not correct, because [examples such as] *bahupaṭavaḥ* ("very many cloths") would remain unestablished.

If it is argued that the mention of *taddhita* refers to that which is qualified by it, [we reply: no, because this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pacatakī*. Furthermore, in this way, by the maxim regarding the mention of *kṛt* suffixes, the over-extension in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam* would be unavoidable; let us leave that matter for now.

The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this, the statement "the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) should be prescribed for a meaningless particle" becomes redundant; this [present rule] is intended for those cases where even a suggested meaning (*dyotya*) does not exist. For example: *avadyati*. However, in the case of imitations (*anukaraṇa*), [the status of the imitation is determined] by that which is being imitated (*anukārya*).

When there is no intention to express a distinction [between the base and the suffix], it does not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) precisely because it lacks meaning, just as in the case of *bhū* in the sense of "existence. However, when a distinction is intended to be expressed, it would certainly be a nominal stem, just as in the case of *bhuvaḥ* in the rule *bhuvo vuk*. [The phrase] "of that which is qualified by gender" [is used].
The meaning is: "even that which is qualified by a suffix indicating gender. The purpose of this *paribhāṣā* is as follows:

in the word *ayaskumbhī*, there is the substitution of *s* [for *k*] according to the rule "ataḥ kṛkami-". For that [substitution] is prescribed when words such as *kaṃsa* follow as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, from the verb *kumārayati* (derived from *kumārīm ācaṣṭe*), [the form *kumāri* arises] by the rule "ṇāviṣṭavat".

There is elision of the *ṭi*. Thus, in the example *yāminayantyahāni*, the result is obtained even when the suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*). Regarding the rule "before the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *ā*" (*ṅyābhyāṃ prāk*): by this, forms such as *lohinikā* and *āryakā* are established. For instance, because it is an affix applied in its own meaning (*svārthika*), the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule "after *lohita*, [the suffix *kan* is added] when referring to a gem" (*lohitānmaṇau*) is both internal (*antaraṅga*) and subsequent (*para*) to the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
[If it were not so,] it would subvert [the rule]; consequently, there would only be *lohitikā*. However, both forms are desired.

By virtue of the inclusion of the term *ṅīp*, two forms are established from a stem ending in *ṅī* when the suffix *kan* is added, because the rule "from a non-udātta vowel... is optional. But from the word *ārya*, [the form *āryakā* does not arise] because of the prohibition "na... [etc.]...
In the rule *sāmivacane*, even the suffix *kan*— which will be taught as being used in its absolute primary sense (*atyantasvārthika*)—

does not apply prior [to the application of *āp*], due to the force of the inclusion of the term *āp*. Consequently, the optional substitution of *it* (shortening) by the rule *udīcāmātaḥ sthāne yatapūrvāyāḥ* is established.

It might be argued: "If this were the case, *bahugomatkaḥ* would not be established, because the suffix *ṅīp*—conditioned by the presence of a *u*-vowel or an *it*-marker—would apply prior to the addition of the *kap* suffix. This is not so. For the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) attaches as a constituent part of the final member (*uttarapada*) precisely within the non-worldly (alaukika) analytical statement (*prakriyāvākya*), while the compound itself has not yet been formed.
This is because it will be stated [later] that "it proceeds. Regarding this, some hold that it occurs before the case-ending (*vibhakti*);

however, according to the view that it occurs after, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since it ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, and the compound is formed only when the case-ending has not yet been reapplied. Therefore, even due to the interruption by the intermediate [suffix], [the rule applies] prior to the *taddhita*.
It is established that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the sake of [ensuring] the application [of the rule].
As for what some have said—that the mention of *āp* is for the sake of clarity—that is refuted by this very point.
In reality, however, let there be no mention of *ṅī* and *āp*; for the formation of secondary (*taddhita*) derivatives occurs from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The conclusion is as follows: it should be noted that the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* operate even prior to the case endings (*sup*), because it is accepted that the operations triggered by their respective meanings (such as gender and number) occur sequentially.
Regarding the term *suṅsyoh*: the letter *u* in *su* is for the purpose of distinguishing it in the rule "arvaṇastrasau."

For if [the sūtra] were stated simply as *asi*, the meaning would be "when [the suffix] begins with the letter *a*"; and in that case, the form *vāja arvatsu paya usriyāsu* would not be established. Furthermore, the vowel *i* in *ṅsi* is for the purpose of preventing its inclusion in the rule *yuṣmadasmabhyāṃ ṅsoś*. However, if [the rule] were *ekavacanasya ca*...

If it is argued that, because the word *pañcamyāḥ* (of the fifth [case-ending]) is understood by anuvṛtti, the remaining [suffix] *ṅsi* will be understood here, then the purpose [of the rule] is "ṭā-ṅsi-ṅsām— " [to provide the *ṭā* augment]. As for the letters *ja* and *śa* in *jas* and *śas*, [they serve respectively in the rules] "jasaḥ śī" and "tasmāc chaso naḥ."

Thus, these two [suffixes] are for the purpose of distinguishing their respective domains. If it is argued that one of them may simply be without an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), we say no; for if the *jakāra* were absent from *jas*, then for *āṬ* there would be *āv*, and consequently, the suffix would also be considered to end in *v*. Similarly, if the *śakāra* were absent from *śas*, then *āṬṭaḥ* would possess the quality of being *ṅit*.

It might be so suspected; therefore, for the sake of removing doubt, it is appropriate to include that [ṭ]. The letter ṭ in *auṭ* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra *suṭ*. The letter ṭ in *ṭā* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*ṭāṅsi*.
The letter ṅ in *ReĀ* and the following [cases] is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*gherṅiti*. As for the letter *p*, however...

The purpose is for the sake of brevity (*pratyāhāra*). Thus, even though all [the rules] are fruitful, the statement of the ancient authors that "they are for the sake of technical names" (*saṃjñārtha*) is indeed inconsistent. Even if one were to offer an interpretation by breaking down the compound as *saṃjñā* meaning "correct knowledge" and explaining that they are "for the sake of that"—i.e., for the sake of specification—that too is merely laborious and has therefore been disregarded.

Regarding the rule *supaḥ*: he explains that the word *trīṇi trīṇi* from the sūtra *tiṅstrīṇi trīṇi* and the entire sūtra *tāny ekavacana-* etc. are carried over [into this rule] by saying *supas trīṇi trīṇi* and so forth. As for *ekaśaḥ*, it means one by one (*ekaikam*).

Regarding the rule *saṅkhaikavacanācca*, the suffix *śas* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case when expressing repetition (*vīpsā*). As for what the ancient grammarians stated—that the form is *ekaikaśaḥ*—that is incorrect; because repetition is already expressed by the suffix *śas* itself, reduplication (dvirvacana) is not applicable. By the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable," the suffix *śas* is an exception (*apavāda*) to reduplication.
This follows from the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for what they say— that both [forms] are correct because of the usage *ekaikaśo dadāti* in the *bhāṣya* on the rule "sarvasya dve," and because of the author of the sūtras' own designation *ekaśaḥ* in the sūtra "tāny eka..."— that is not so.

That is not so, because the cited Bhāṣya has a different subject matter. For, having begun with the statement, "Where the distributive sense (vīpsā) is not expressed by a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), there occurs reduplication," the Bhāṣya provides the example, "He gives one by one" (*ekaikaśo dadāti*). And Kaiyaṭa explains: "There is also an *ekaśeṣa* [compound] in the sense of 'a small amount'."

Regarding the word *tasya*, when it is doubled for the sake of repetition (*vīpsā*), the suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule "from words meaning 'much' or 'few'... However, this meaning is not possible in the present context, so let us leave it at that. As for *rāma*:

on the view that this is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*) that is not etymologically derived (*avyutpanna*), its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established by the rule "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat-sūtra*).

The distinction is as follows: under the governing rule "karaṇādhikaraṇayośca," the suffix *ghañ* (applied by the exception to *gha*) is used to derive the form in the sense of "they delight in this" (*ramante 'smin*), whereas the suffix is applied by the rule "kṛttaddhita-samāsāśca."

Prau.ma.: *Sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). Regarding the phrase "those which [occur] in a single case-ending": the case-ending (*vibhakti*) serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for similarity of form; it is not, however, the cause (*nimitta*) for the retention of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Thus...

Furthermore, because it is not occasioned by a specific condition (*anaimittika*), the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) operation is internal and applies even prior to the generation of case-endings (*sub*).
If this were not commenced, then a case-ending would apply to each individual word, and a *dvandva* compound would consequently take effect.
However, once the *ekaśeṣa* has been commenced, since there is an absence of multiple *sub*-ending words, the *dvandva* simply does not apply.
The sense is that [the word] becomes *phalitā* (fruit-bearing). "Only those that are similar" (*sarūpāṇyeva*):

this is obtained by the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the particle *eva* from the subsequent sūtra. Consequently, there is no single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) between the two words *mātṛ*, one denoting a biological mother and the other denoting a measurer.

In cases such as *mātṛbhyām*, although there is similarity (*sārūpya*) [in the base], there is dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) in forms like *āṬ* and *jas*. "Only one" means that this [rule] operates only when there is a desire to express [the items] together; that is to say, within the domain of the *itaretarayoga* (copulative) *dvandva*. For where several meanings, joined together, have a connection with another [word], it is of that nature.
The scope [of this rule] is understood from the indicator (*liṅga*) in the sūtra "idito num dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.58) and from reasoning as well. To explain:
once it is established that "that which remains expresses the meaning of what is elided," [the meaning] presented by the single heard word [is expressed].

Everything ought to be construed with a single uniform form, without distinction. Alternatively, one should explain it by carrying over the word "dvandve" from the preceding sūtra, such that it means "when a dvandva compound is applicable.
It might be argued: let the meaning be "when a dvandva has been formed. This is not so; [for instance, in the case of] *panthānau*.

Otherwise, in examples such as *pathānaḥ*, there would be the unwanted application of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*); in *karau* and *karāḥ*, there would be the unwanted application of singular concord (*ekavadbhāva*); and in *sarve* and *sarveṣām*, there would be the unwanted application of the rules "dvandve ca" and "vibhāṣā jasi. This is the general direction [of the argument]. As for what was stated by the ancients—namely, *rāma-rāma-au*—...

It has been stated [in Pāṇini 1.4.1] that "when [an item] stands," and also "when followed by a case-ending. In this regard, the following explanation is possible: in the expression *rāma rāma*, the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) applies not only to the individual members but also to the whole, because the whole possesses meaning when combined. Nor does the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) [in the definition of *prātipadika*] prevent this.

It should not be argued that this is not so because [the rule] serves as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*). For it has been stated that the restriction applies to those cases where the preceding portion of a composite is a word (*pada*); furthermore, it is more appropriate that the restriction concerns members of the same class, in accordance with forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*. Thus, by the logic of the "doubling of a single vowel" (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*),...

The dual and other case endings arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the aggregate itself; for even by that much, it is possible to support the application of number to the meanings of the individual members. If it is objected: "In that case, would not case endings also arise from the aggregate in *rāmakṛṣṇau* and similar compounds, even without a *dvandva* [compound]?"—do not say so.

In the formulation of *dvandva*, because the phrase "multiple inflected words" (*aneka-subanta*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the maxim regarding the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvivacana-nyāya*) is set aside; such is the direction [of the argument]. If it is asked: "Even though such an explanation is possible, for what reason was the alternative view—that [the compound is formed] when a single case-ending follows the whole aggregate—rejected? Listen: in this view...

In cases such as *mātṛ-mātarau* ("mother and mother"), there would also have to be a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*). Now, one might argue that by repeating the phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) and drawing forward the word "only" (*eva*), the rule should be explained as: "those which have the same form [occur] in a single case-ending. But this is not so, because there is no evidence for such a repetition. Furthermore, if the case-ending were the qualifier of the single-remainder formation...

And because there would be no result [for the rule]. Nor can the exclusion of cases such as "milk digests milk" be the result, because the requirement of "intended co-reference" (*sahavivakṣā*) is indispensable; otherwise, in the case of "he carries milk [to the cow]," there would be the undesirable consequence of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) between the secondary and primary objects. Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "God of gods."

On the contrary, if both were qualifiers by way of *āvṛtti* (repetition), the formation of the word *bhaikṣam*— meaning "a collection of alms"— would not be established. For instance, when the sequence *bhikṣā bhikṣā bhikṣā ām a* is reached,
the rule "an external operation [supersedes] even internal operations" (*antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgaḥ*) would cause the elision (*luk*) to take effect.

Because of the absence of being followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule would not apply; for when the suffix has been elided, there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treatment as if the suffix were present). Furthermore, in forms such as *rāmāu*, since the substitution of *vṛddhi* [for the first vowel] by the rule "vṛddhireci" applies because it is both subsequent and obligatory, the *ekaśeṣa* would not occur due to the absence of being followed by a case-ending once that partial modification has taken place. On both counts...

The point is that when [the remaining form] becomes the basis [of grammatical operations], the treatment as being like the end or the beginning does not apply; this is the direction of the argument. As for the alternative view proposed by the ancient commentator—that there is *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of forms accompanied by their case-endings—that is incorrect. For even if the disappearing forms were to cease together with their case-endings, [the rule would still fail] regarding the form that remains...
Because it would follow that only the singular number would be heard.

Now, if it were argued that when there is simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatā*), there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for those ending in dual or plural numbers— and that a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is likewise— then indeed:

In a non-abandoning (*ajahatsvārthā*) function, each individual word denotes multiple meanings due to their mutual co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*). Thus, in the non-worldly (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) for a *dvandva* or *ekaśeṣa* compound,
only the dual and plural case-endings are introduced.
"The position that there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of words ending in case-suffixes is indeed unassailable. That too is not correct;

for it is incompatible with the theory of *jahatsvārthā* (the word losing its own meaning) in the formation of a compound. Even in the alternative view (*ajahatsvārthā*), it is impossible to abandon the singular number that was applied first. Otherwise, [the rule would fail].

[Otherwise] there would result the undesirable consequence of [the compound being analyzed as] a genitive *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and so forth; for even in that case, since the first member is absorbed into the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*), it cannot be connected with the genitive case ending and the like. And thus says the Bhāṣya: "This simultaneous expression of the substratum (*yugapad-adhikaraṇavacanatā*) is both difficult and hard to justify."

As for what they have explained— that under the view of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), since the use of each respective word would apply to as many individuals as exist, this *sūtra* is intended so that only one [word] may be used; whereas under the view of the generic form (*ākṛtipakṣa*),
it is useless because a single [word] already conveys the many individuals that constitute the manifestation of that form— that is not correct.

Even in the view that [the word] refers to an individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), in the case of the injunction "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," it is easily explained through *tantra* (simultaneous application) that the single word "Brāhmaṇa" denotes many individuals. Otherwise, even in the view that it refers to a genus (*jātipakṣa*), the sūtra would have to be [interpreted] in accordance with various meanings, such as "by means of dwelling, and properly in patience toward him," and so forth.

Because it cannot be maintained otherwise. Therefore, although the application [of the term] can be sustained through *tantra* (simultaneous reference) in both the view that the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are denoted, there is no restrictive rule that it must always be understood through *tantra* alone;
consequently, an optional *dvandva* compound would be unavoidable in the absence of the Sūtra. For example: "This is a jar."

This is because we observe the use of various words such as "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam*); likewise, the formation of the copulative compound *ghaṭau ghaṭau* is established by logical rule. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of forming the compound *ghaṭakalaśau*, because of the Vārttika rule: "Even for words that have different forms, if they have the same meaning [they may form a copulative compound]. That which is formed (*rūpyate*) is that which is understood (*bodhyate*).
Thus, by relying on the fact that the word *rūpa* denotes the meaning through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*),

and because the meaning of the Vārttika is also encompassed by the Sūtra itself, [the rule must apply] in both cases in order to prevent undesirable optional forms such as *ghaṭa-ghaṭau* or *ghaṭa-kalaśau*.
It should be understood that the Sūtra is indeed necessary.

This being the case, those who have explained this [Sūtra]—thinking the Sūtra to be useless—have said such things as, "By this, the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* compound is not prescribed," and so forth; and furthermore, regarding that which [arises] from the whole...

Having rejected the position that the rule applies when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, they state again: "When *rāma*, *rāma*, and *au* stand [in sequence]. This is an inferred non-standard (*alaukika*) procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), not a standard (*laukika*) one; and in a non-standard context, operations such as the substitution of a single substitute for case-endings do not take effect.

"Because [grammar] provides the grammatical description (anvākhyāna) only of those forms that are actually used," and so forth—all of this is contrary to the context and contrary to logic. For it is precisely in order to describe those forms that are actually used that the "extraordinary" (alaukika) form is postulated. Furthermore, all grammatical operations apply only to these extraordinary forms, and not to the final, established (pariniṣṭhita) form.

This is because the final established form cannot be obtained without the application of rules such as "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ," and because it is difficult to justify the application of those rules once the form has already been finalized; let this matter rest for now.
*Prau.ma.*: *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107). Regarding *ami aci*: it means "in that *ac* which is part of *am*"—that is to say, in the *ac* that is a constituent of *am*.
Consequently, there is no single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* for the [final vowel] together with the letter *m*. Thus...
In cases such as *akṣādūhinyām* and so forth, it should be understood that [the rule applies] when there is an *ac* (vowel) in *ūhinī*, and so on;

for there is no dispute regarding the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *ac* from the rule *iko yaṇaci*. Furthermore, the indications (*liṅga*) in rules such as *padāsvairibāhyā-* serve as evidence here.

Prau.ma.: *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.1.28). Regarding the phrase *tasmāc chasaḥ*: the word *tat* refers back to the preceding *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the homogeneous vowel).
The term *śasaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and that part [of the word] follows [the preceding element].

It is specified as "of the *śas* following a long vowel resulting from the substitution of a homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). This is what [the author] expresses by saying: "the *s* which follows the *śas*. However, it is not stated as "the *śas* which follows," because that is impossible; for once the substitution of a homogeneous vowel has taken place, a subsequent *śas* cannot exist.

Prau.ma.: *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2). Regarding *aṭkupvāṅ*: since the rule *raṣābhyām* (8.4.1) employs a fifth-case (ablative) designation, this present rule is stated because [the operation] would otherwise not apply when there is an intervention. Here, an intervention by all [of these] together is impossible; rather, it refers to an intervention by each one individually.
It is not necessary [to state this separately], because of the force of the inclusion of the word *kṣubhna* in the list of *kṣubhnādi* words, and because of the mention in rules such as "sarūpāṇām.
With this intention, he says: "by separate [words] or by combined [words], as the case may be.
But if this were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ādarśena*. Nor can it be argued that [the rule applies] only with *aṭ* and the like.

The rule [that the augment *ṇ* occurs] when there is an intervention is a restriction (*niyama*). Since it has been stated that this is an injunction (*vidhi*) where [the rule] was not previously established, this is true;
however, a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) should be understood here: one yoga—"even when there is an intervention" (*vyavāye 'pi*)—is for the purpose of an injunction;
another yoga—"after *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, or *num*" (*aṭkupvāṅnum*)—is for the purpose of a restriction. The elision of the case-ending *bhis* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

"In order to prevent the prohibition [of the rule]. The intention is that by this, the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *paryāṇaddham* is established according to the rule "upasargādasamāse'pi. Regarding the mention of *num*:

the meaning is that it is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both the *anusvāra* in place of *num* and for the natural (*svābhāvika*) *anusvāra*. By this, [the form] from the root *bṛh* "to increase" [is accounted for].

After [a root ending in] *id*, there is *num*. For that [root], there is *anusvāra*. In the case of *tṛṃh* in the sense of "injuring," the *anusvāra* here is inherent. [Examples are] *bṛṃhaṇam* and *tṛṃhaṇam*; in both cases, the substitution of *ṇ* is established. In the case of *iv* in the sense of "pleasing," [the form is] *prenvanam*. Here, [the rule] "after a *kṛt* suffix ending in a vowel or *c*, and after a root beginning with *i* or *ī* that has *num*" applies.

Thus, there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. For example, in the injunction, "Having seen a star, one should release speech," the sight of a star serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a specific time; therefore, even if stars are seen during the day, speech is not released, because the specific time indicated by them is absent. At night, however...
Even when the asterism is not visible, [the offering] is released because it exists; so too should it be understood here.

But if this is so, the inclusion of *num* is redundant, since the *anusvāra* is already included by virtue of being an *aṭ*. For in cases such as *uraḥ keṇa*, where there is an intervention by the visarga or the jihvāmūlīya, this same principle applies.

If this is true, he says: "And that... This might be so: according to the method stated, the mention of *num* in the rule "anum visarjanīyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.58) would also have to be abandoned, because there too the *anusvāra* is what is to be indicated, as otherwise it would be impossible; for at the time when the substitution of *ṣ* is about to take effect...

In examples such as *sapaṣi*, the augment *num* is obtained because the substitution of *ṣ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the *anusvāra* occurs prior to that. Although this is indeed possible in the case of *suhinsu*, nevertheless,
in order to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that very instance, [the rule applies] to the *anusvāra* in place of *num*, in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).

If it is argued that a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must indeed be resorted to because of the explanation [of the rule], and that since that [num] is a vowel (*svara*), the substitution of *ṣ* is established even when there is an intervention by it— do not say so. For although, according to the method stated,
the inclusion of the visarga in that [rule] can be rejected, the mention of *num* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

For instance, if *ṣatva* were to occur when there is an intervention by an *anusvāra*, it would then be restricted solely to that which stands in the place of *num*. Consequently, in forms such as *puṃsu*, it would not occur; this is the general direction. Pariśiṣṭa-prakāśa: That from which a suffix is prescribed, beginning with that [element], is the *aṅga* (base) with respect to that suffix (Pāṇini 1.4.13).

Regarding the rule *yasmātpratyayavidhiḥ*, the ancient [commentators] stated: "from whatever [stem], whether a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). That is not correct, because even forms ending in *tiṅ* (finite verbs) and so forth serve as bases (*aṅga*) for suffixes such as *tarap*. Furthermore, there is no basis for such a restriction; for instance, in the case of *āmuṣyāyaṇa* and similar forms...

Furthermore, it would result in the absence of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*); for this secondary suffix (*taddhita*) does not follow a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather follows that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*). This is the general direction of the argument.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9). Now, one might object: let it simply be "ais. [The opponent asks: Is there not the risk of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule "ato guṇe" applying? [We reply: No, because that would render the pronunciation of the letter *e* redundant. Otherwise, [the sūtra] would have simply said "is."

If it is argued that [the rule] should be formulated as *vidadhyāt*? True; however, because there is no difference between *e* and *ai* in terms of having two morae (*dvimātra*), and thus no increase in complexity (*gaurava*), *ai* was employed. In this way, there is no suspicion of the application of the *pararūpa* rule at all, which results in great economy (*lāghava*). As for what they say—that the formation of *ai* is for the sake of hearing the sound *ai* in the word *nirjarasaiḥ*—[that is not the case].

That contradicts the Bhāṣya; for, according to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the substitution of *jaras* would result [in an undesired form], and thus it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya that [the form] should be *nirjaraiḥ*.
(Prau.ma.-nāmi, Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.3)

Regarding the phrase "due to contradiction with the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*)," this is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rules "śnam after *rudh*-class roots" and "elision of *n* after [a root ending in] *śna*.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the force of its formulation," the rule "and before a *sup* suffix" lacks such force.

The intention is that [the rule] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* has scope in examples such as *rāmābhyām*. Thus, the claim made by some—that the citation of the rule *nāmi* in the word *rāma* is due to a scribal error—is to be considered doubtful.
Prakriyākaumudī: *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59).

Regarding the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*: with the intention that even a single genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is divided according to the difference in its objects, he explains it as "the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the constituent part of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). However, if the "substitute" were taken to mean a constituent part of a substitute, then there would be a fault in forms such as *tisṛṇām*. And if the "affix" were taken to mean whatever *s*-sound [occurs in an affix], then...

In cases such as *rāmeṣu* and so forth, [the rule] would not apply. Although, if explained in this way with such a discrepancy (*vairūpya*), a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is not appropriate due to the absence of the intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), nevertheless, it should be understood as being based on the authority of Pāṇini’s sūtra (*sautratvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "of the non-aspirated and voiced" (*vivṛtāghoṣasya*): as for what they say—that [it applies] to the letter *s*.

"The closest internal [substitute] for a voiceless aspirated [consonant] is the palatal *ṣ* itself"—this is insufficient, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the letter *ṭh*. Thus, the Prātiśākhya states:
"In each class (*varga*), the first two are voiceless; the pair [the second and third] are aspirated (*soṣman*); the other is nasal."

If it is argued: "In examples such as *dadhi-secaḥ*, the Bhāṣya states that the compound *padādādiḥ padādiḥ*—a genitive compound—is employed to prevent the application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) prior to the generation of case endings (*sup*). Consequently, would there not also be a prohibition here by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*? Do not say so; for [the word *pada* in that context] refers to those [elements] beginning with *sva*.

The prohibition stated [in Pāṇini 8.3.11] does not apply with reference to that which is designated as a *pada*, because this is indicated by the inclusion of the word *sāti* [in the rule 8.3.106]. As for what some say—that it is indicated that this prohibition does not apply in the domain of suffixes—that is not correct, because [otherwise] *ṣatva* would undesirably apply in forms such as *vyatise*. Now, regarding the alternative view that [a *pada*] is "the beginning of a word" (*padasyādi*):

In the case of *ṭhvyatiṣe*, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) would be unavoidable. Nor should it be suspected that *se* also possesses the status of a word (*padatva*) by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), since it too is a *tiṅ*-ending; for when there is a reference to a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is understood. Otherwise, [the fault would apply] even in cases such as *rāmeṣu*.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, [we reply: true. We do not claim that the status of being "ending in that" (*tadanta*) applies to the suffix alone; rather, we extend by the maxim of "substitution of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) the designation of "word" (*pada*), which applies to the entire aggregate of stem and suffix, even to a suffix whose stem has been elided.

For even in cases such as *rāmau* and *rāmāḥ*, the status of being a word (*padatva*) occurs precisely by the maxim of "that which undergoes modification in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), because the designation of a word applies prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). However, once the single-substitute has been applied, the rule "that which ends in a sup or tiṅ affix is a word" (*suptiṅantam*) does not apply. This is because of the principle: "when both sides are relied upon, [the resulting form] is neither like the final element of the preceding nor like the initial element of the following."
From the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for what they say— that in the presence of a *prakṛti*, the suffix lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*) because of such indications as "in mantras" and "of all"— that is weak, because [the status of being a word] would be absent according to the reasoning already stated.
Since it is impossible to indicate [a meaning] when [the status of being a *sarvanāman*] is already established by logic, and because it would be useless [to do so], [the rule] is not required.
Prakriyākaumudī: *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27).
The term *sarvādīni* is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*.

It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as indicated by the rule "hali sarveṣām. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of a *dvandva*": it will be explained that this prohibition applies to the whole aggregate (*samudāya*), and not to its individual parts (*avayava*). The point is that, without the application of the rule for suffixes denoting "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*), there would be no possibility of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applying to the aggregate. Now, what is the purpose of this designation for that which ends in [the specified element]?
The result [of the rule] is not that *smāy* and so on occur after *paramasarva* and the like;

for under the heading governing the *aṅga*, this is already established by the rule of "extension to what ends with [the specified element]. Therefore, he says: "by that" (*tena*). Nor does the same apply here, because of the continued application of the term "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), which serves as a qualifier for the pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

It should be stated that the rule regarding the final element applies, because of the statement: "There is a prohibition [of the application of suffixes] in the case of rules for compounds and suffixes. This is the intended meaning. Regarding *akac*: by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *tasil* occurs in the form *paramasarvataḥ*. [The next rule is: *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17).

Regarding the rule *jasaḥ śī*: the intention is that [the substitution occurs] because [the suffix *jas*] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), and not because it is marked with the *ś* indicatory letter (*śit*). Regarding the phrase "after a stem ending in an *a*-vowel": this means "after a member (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel. Therefore, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yeṣām*, *keṣām*, and *teṣām*. [The expression] "of *ām* prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)" refers to [the *ām*] following a pronoun.
However, the word *parasya* ("of the subsequent") was not stated [in the rule], because otherwise there would be the unwanted application of *suṭ* in the case of *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.

For the prohibition by the rule "dvandve ca" applies to the whole compound (*samudāya*), not to its individual parts (*avayava*). Nor is this *ām* derived from that [part], but rather from the whole compound itself; therefore, *suṭ* does not occur.
The authority for resorting to the qualification of the prior member (*vihitaviśeṣaṇatva*) is precisely the usage in the Bhāṣya: "of the south, north, and east.
As for *pañcatriṃśat*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "five and thirty"; that is, thirty with five added.

Or rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the statement made by those explaining the ancient text that "the *pratyāhāras* are forty"— namely, that this is not a *tatpuruṣa* with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*)— if that were the case,
[the rules] prescribed by the sūtras "in the case of *rājanya*, plural *dvandva*s, and among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis" and "in the case of a numeral" would [be contradicted].
The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would not apply; therefore, this must indeed be a collective dvandva compound.

As for the neuter gender in cases such as *ekaviṃśatiḥ*, it does not occur because gender is dependent upon worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāl liṅgasya*). However, that [explanation] is to be reconsidered, since there is a difference in accent depending on the specific type of compound.

This is because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Accordingly, while explaining the Vārttika on the sūtra "bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye" (Pāṇini 2.2.25)—which states, "The addition [of the feminine suffix] for a *tatpuruṣa* compound of a numeral is for the sake of forms such as *nistriṃśā*, since elsewhere there is the elision of the additional member"—the author of the Bhāṣya says: "one plus one."
"Twenty-one" (*ekaviṃśati*) [is derived from] twenty (*viṃśati*) and one; "twenty-two" (*dvāviṃśati*) likewise.

"For this very reason" means that it is only logical for the dual number to apply to two things. [Objection: If this is so, then the inclusion [of these numerals] among the *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) is useless, since the functions of pronouns (*sarvanāma*), such as *smāy* and so forth, would not apply.

Because [the form] does not exist in the dual number; nor is it correct to argue that the result is the optional third case (tṛtīyā) in the phrase *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām ubhayor hetvoḥ* by the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*, since the Vārttika states:
"In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all case endings are generally observed."

Because the meaning has already been established. Nor should it be said that this *vārttika* depends upon the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*), on the grounds that the author of the *Vṛtti* read it under the rule "sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca";
for it is read in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule "hetau". Precisely for this reason, [one says]: "He dwells because of food" (*annena kāraṇena vasati*).

Anticipating the objection that Haradatta has stated this to be the cause for [the application of] *ann*, he says: "But its reading here is... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "due to the contingency of *ayaC*": the intended meaning is as follows—in the rule "ubhādudāto nityam," the constituent "ubhādudātaḥ" is separated [as a distinct rule]. This is because [the word *ubha*] denotes a number when functioning as a part-whole (*avayava-vṛtti*).

The suffix *ayac* shall be applied after the word *ubha* when expressing the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). For example: *ubhayoḥ maṇiḥ* (a jewel belonging to both). Then [the rule] "always" (*nityam*):
in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), the suffix *ayac* shall always be applied after the word *ubha* in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Therefore, just as *ayac* is necessarily applied in such cases as *ubhayapakṣavinītanidrāḥ* (those whose sleep has been dispelled by both wings), so too [is it applied here].

[The objection: "It would also occur when the suffix *kap* is applied. [The response: "But even if *akac* is applied, *ayaj* remains unavoidable; therefore, this is not so. For the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of achieving a desired result, and because of the mention in the form "both [the initial and final consonants] of the reduplicated base," it is explained that this [rule applies] only where the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is not heard.

And so says the Vārttika: "The absence of the other [suffixes] is because [the word *ubhaya*] is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. For when the suffix *akac* is present, the status of the word *ubhaya* as being within the domain of the dual number is not obstructed by the maxim "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing"; however, when the suffix *kap* is present, it is indeed obstructed.
Regarding the phrase "it has been so stated": the words "by the author of the Vārttika" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Although the suffix *ṭāp* was also mentioned in the preceding Vārttika, it is not intended here; for Kaiyaṭa and others have explained that even the applicability of *ṭāp* must be understood as occurring only when followed by a dual ending. With this intention, he explains [the text] as follows:

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of being followed by a dual ending": the intention is that even in the case of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) [of *ṭā* and *ā*], there is the status of being followed by a dual ending because it is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*). Although in cases such as *ubhau*, the status of being followed by a dual ending is difficult to establish—since the application of the *antādivadbhāva* rule is precluded when both sides are relied upon—[the present case is different].

Nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that the dual suffix produced from the word *ubha* has not been elided by *luk*— that is, in cases other than those [where elision occurs]. Even though, according to the Bhāṣya, the suffix *kap* is also considered *svārthika* (having its own inherent meaning), [it applies] after the word *ubha*.

The reading of the word *ubha* has been rejected on the grounds that it possesses the status of a dual number; nevertheless, that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because here it is appropriate to understand only a technical (*kṛtrima*) dual number. Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasakta*) to suffixes such as *tratasil* and others. Now, [one might object]:

If it is argued that the suffixes *trā* and *til* (forming *tatra* and *tatraiva*), when prescribed after a case-inflected word (*kārakavibhaktyanta*), do not denote anything more than duality (*dvitvamātra*) even though they are *svārthika* (suffixes expressing their own meaning), we say no; for the suffix *kap* also conveys the sense of being unknown (*ajñātārtha*), and in the view that [the suffix] expresses five meanings (*pañcakapakṣa*), it necessarily conveys even more. This is the direction of the argument.

"It does not exist"—the meaning is that it is because it is not so designated. And thus, since the word *ubhaya* lacks a dual suffix and is therefore not a term ending in all case-endings (*asarvavibhaktika*), it would follow that it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

However, regarding the rule "A taddhita suffix that does not end in all case-endings [is an indeclinable]," there is the principle: "The inclusion of kṛt and taddhita formations occurs through their recitation [in the Gaṇapāṭha]."

Thus the *Bhāṣya* was introduced by Kaiyaṭa. Regarding the word "asti": the sense is that since the recitation [of the rule] has been exhausted by the exclusion of forms such as *pacatikalpam* and *pacatirūpam*, there is no evidence for its non-mention. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in the suffix *tayap*": the sense is "of the word *ubhaya*."
"Always [so]," etc. However, the statement "the higher, the lower, both, and enemies" should be understood as being due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*).
"Underived," etc.; this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Paspaśā* section.

"Some"—namely, the authors of the *Kāśikā*. Regarding the udātta [accent] of "I consider this to be the essence" (*etattvaṃ manye*), [there is the reading] "seeing this repeatedly" (*etattvaḥ paśyan*).

The meaning is that this is because an unaccented vowel is also observed [in such cases]. "Ekaḥ" means "the first. Even though the state of ending in "-ta" is not clearly manifest in the *saṃhitā* recitation, the word ending in "-ta" must be separated; otherwise, one would recite it only once with a single tone (*ekaśruti*). Nor should one contradict the rule: "The words *tva*, *tvasma*, *si*, and *me* are unaccented."
This is from the *Phiṭ-sūtras*. Likewise, there is a Rigvedic mantra: "At one time you are barren, at another you have given birth.

The commentators on the Vedas have explained it thus: "The word *tvat* is listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāma*) and is unaccented; it is a synonym for 'another' (*anya*). Jayadeva also employed it [in this sense]:

Regarding the phrase "drinking the honey-sweet nectar of your lower lip": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the lower lip of another woman than you," and not "your own lower lip. This is because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the preceding sentence, "He sees you in secret in every direction. Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture]: nema... (and so forth) [as cited in the source].

"In this breath, Soma was seen"—thus [it is said]. Regarding the word *sama*: likewise, it is heard in the Veda: "May all others perish, *same*"; "Not for the wolf, nor for the she-wolf, *samasmai*"; "Protecting us from the one who intends evil, *samasmāt*"; and "Also, in this *samasmim*"—and so forth.

"The word *sima* occurs in the senses of 'entirety' (*kṛtsna*) and 'capacity' (*śakta*), as well as in the senses of 'boundary' (*maryādā*) and 'understanding' (*buddhi*). And it is heard [in the Veda]: 'The night spreads her garment for him entirely (*simasmai*),' and 'He has risen up from everything (*simasmāt*). In both instances, the word *sima* is a synonym for 'all' (*sarva*); such is the Vedabhāṣya."

Regarding the term *gaṇasūtra*: although the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra located in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* reads the vārttika "it should be stated that [the rule applies] except for *puru*" (*apuri iti vaktavyam*), nevertheless, this is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the *gaṇasūtra*, and not to the rule prescribing the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of the *jas* ending. This is because the substitution of *śī* for *jas* is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "*ataḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.1.14).

Because there is no possibility [of the application] from a form ending in *ṭā*. Regarding the term *antarāyām*: the meaning is "in that which is outside the enclosure wall" or "within it. Alternatively, the possibility of its application should be understood through the inclusion of the *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*), by virtue of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning forms qualified by gender). These two are *tyad* and *tad*.

These two [words] have been explained as *parāmarśaka* (referents). Regarding this, the author of the *Gaṇaratna* states that the first is Vedic (*chāndasa*). That is not correct, because it would render the mention of "Vedic" (*cchandasi*) in the rule *syaś chandasi bahulam* redundant. Furthermore: "The word *eka* has the sense of 'another,' 'principal,' 'first,' and likewise 'alone.'"
The word *sādhāraṇa* is employed in the senses of common, equal, small, and number.

The phrase *svābhidheya* means that there is a restriction (*niyama*) of the limit (*avadhi*) required by the denotation (*abhidheya*) of the word itself, such as "east" and so forth. Even in examples such as "be the rival of the southern direction," a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*) certainly exists; however, it is not mentioned because it is well-known (*prasiddhatvāt*).

A word denoting a limit (*avadhi*) is not employed [here]. Nor is there a prohibition based on it being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), for a *saṃjñā* is indeed a recent convention (*ādhunikasaṃketa*). And such a convention does not exist regarding the directions (*diś*), according to Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others in the section on the suffix *astāti*. In this context, [the usage] regarding the directions is ancient (*cirantana*), whereas that regarding the Kurus is recent (*ādhunika*).

Regarding the term *saṃketa*, the word of the commentator alone is the authority. By this, the phrase "of all the gods" (*viśveṣāṃ devānām*) is explained, because it is well-known in the Veda. The sense is that although there is a possibility of connecting it to a specific limit—such as "skilled in this or that"—there is no such restriction here. *Adhare*...

One should also provide counter-examples such as *tāmbūlarāgaḥ* (the red dye of betel) and *pratyuttare ca śaktaḥ* (capable of replying). How then are we to understand Kālidāsa’s usage in "tathā pareṣāṃ yudhi ca" (and likewise against others in battle) and "apare pratyavatiṣṭhante" (others stand opposed), and so forth? On this point, they say: [these are instances] where the word *para* refers to a place (*deśa*) and thus pertains specifically to the domain of spatial distinction.

The terms *parā* and *apara* are used metaphorically (*upacāra*) for the adversary and the respondent, respectively; yet this does not constitute their status as subordinate members (*upasarjanatā*). For being derivative (*lākṣaṇikatva*) is not the same as being subordinate; rather, subordination consists in the transfer of one's own meaning to another object qualified by that meaning. And such transfer occurs only in compound formations (*samāsa*) and the like. Therefore...

The statement of Kaiyaṭa in the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"‘These also’ means these things to be explained"—is thus consistent. In reality, however, the meaning of the words ‘para’ and ‘apara’ is simply their being situated in a different location and so forth; whereas enmity and the like—

The meaning is "according to the sense. Why say "not when it is a name"? [Consider] "the Northern Kurus" (*uttarāḥ kuravaḥ*). With reference to Mount Sumeru as a limit, the word "northern" (*uttara*) applies to the Kurus; thus there is a fixed determination here. However, they say that this is merely a modern convention.

Prau.ma.: "svamajñātidhanākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.1.35). The word *sva* denotes self (*ātman*), what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). Since kinsmen and wealth are excluded here, the intention is that the self and what belongs to the self remain as the referents.

He explains: the meaning is "one's own," or "oneself. As for what they say—that the word *sva* is neuter when it refers to the self (*ātman*), and therefore an example such as *sve* or *svāḥ* is not possible there—that is to be considered, because the word *sva* is masculine even when referring to the self, according to the rule "vibhāṣā jasi."

In this context, since the author of the Sūtras himself provides the authoritative evidence by employing a cumbersome designation when he could have simply said "sva means one's own," [we accept his word]. Furthermore, as support for his own statement:
"Sva means a kinsman; in the masculine, it means the self; in the three genders, it means one's own; and in the neuter, it means wealth."

Thus they cite the statement of Amarasiṃha. That too is to be considered. For in the lexicon, "ātmani" (in the self) connects with the preceding [verse], while "svam" (one's own) connects with the following. And so Hemacandra says: "Dyauḥ (heaven) refers to heaven and the sky; svaḥ (own) refers to kinsmen and the self; svaṃ (one's own) refers to what is one's own and to wealth."
Medinīkāra also states:
"The word *svaḥ* may be masculine when meaning 'self' or 'known'; it is used in three genders for 'one's own,' and in the feminine for 'wealth.
Therefore, it is established that the gloss *ātmānaḥ* (selves) for *sve svāḥ* is indeed correct."

Regarding the phrase "jñātidhanavāci tu": by using the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*), it is implied that even for words denoting "kinsmen" (*jñāti*) and "wealth" (*dhana*), the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) indeed exists when they function by prioritizing their own inherent nature (*ātmīyatva*).
It is precisely for this purpose that the term *ākhyā* ("designation") was included in the rule.

Prau.ma.- *antaraṃ bahiryogopasaṃvyānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.36). The term *antara* [is used] in the sense of being connected with the exterior (*bahiryoga*) and in the sense of an undergarment (*upasaṃvyāna*). "Exterior" (*bahiḥ*) refers to an uncovered space and also to that which is external. Taking the first meaning, he says: "the meaning is 'external'. But in the second [meaning],...
The meaning to be understood is "internal" (ābhyantara). For there is indeed a connection of the internal with the external.

Furthermore, both [the internal and the external] reside in the letter *a*. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* also refers to that which is external (*bāhya*) when derived through the *karaṇa* (instrumental) analysis, but refers to that which is internal (*antarīya*) when derived through the *karman* (objective) analysis.

Prau.sū.—*pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.16). Here, this should be noted: this sūtra is to be explained by carrying it over (*anuvartana*) to the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17) and treating it as a separate sentence; furthermore, the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.39) [is to be carried over] to the rule *āmi*.

As in the case of [the rule] *pūrvaḥ* (A 1.1.34); and thus, in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the three rules beginning with *pūrvapara-* (A 1.1.34–36) have their purpose already served, which results in great economy of expression (*mahallāghava*). Eight meanings of the word *eka* have been stated;
regarding that, he states the distinction: "in the sense of number. But in the other seven [meanings], there is also another [grammatical] designation (*vacanāntara*).
The sense is that it would indeed be so for some [grammarians], according to the view of some; thus [the sūtra] says:

*prau.ma.*—*na bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.29). Once a *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] is redundant, because [the word] has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

Since it will be stated later that "not [words] beginning with *sarva*," he says: "in the case of what is intended to be formed" (*cikīrṣite*) and "even before the compound" (*samāsāt prāg eva*). He uses the term "derivation" (*prakriyā*). Nor should it be argued that the designation cannot occur even earlier because the cause—the status of being a non-subordinate (*anapasarjanatva*)—is on the verge of being destroyed.

Because the prohibition regarding *akṛtavyūha* is not universal (*anitya*), and because this very sūtra serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that case. The sense is that the very result of this indication is [the form] *atibhavakān*. Regarding the phrase "having accepted the desired conclusion": [it refers to] the inclusion of the augment *t* (as in *satuk*) in the rule *cchÂavoḥ śūḍ*.
Alternatively, the fact that the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are not explicitly stated [in every rule] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for their non-eternality;
the sense is that the application is determined according to the requirements of the specific linguistic forms (*lakṣya*). As for the phrase "according to what follows" (*yathottaram*):
the sense is that, in the present day, the determination is made precisely on the basis of the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

As for what was stated previously: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) would not apply to words beginning with *sarva-*; as in *priyasarvāya*. According to the view of the author of the *Sūtras*, there is no status of being a pronoun in a *bahuvrīhi*; according to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, it applies only when [the meaning] is figurative (*gauṇa*); as in *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*."

Regarding this, the opinion of the author of the *Nyāsa* is that this sūtra exists for the purpose that, since the members of the compound *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are pronominals (*sarvanāman*), the augment *akac*—which is not an operation pertaining to a word-base (*anaṅgaka*)—might apply; otherwise, only the suffix *kap* would apply. On this point, the following must be said:
Is it intended that the designation [of *sarvanāman*] does not apply to the *bahuvrīhi* compound as a whole, or rather to its constituent parts,
namely those beginning with *sarva*? It cannot be the first case,
because that would contradict the subsequent text which states "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are constituents of a compound," since [the prohibition] applies to the whole.

And because of the absence of application [of the rule]. Nor is there application by means of the *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule extending an operation to that which ends with a specified element), because since the members of a *bahuvrīhi* compound are *upasarjana*s (subordinate elements), they fall outside the scope of the *sarva-* group; thus, application to that which ends [with such a member] is effectively ruled out. For this very reason, the second [alternative] is also not tenable. Nor [is it possible] for subordinate elements...

It should not be said that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* based on the wording [of the *Mahābhāṣya*] but is not established within the words of the *sūtra* itself;

for that is obtained from the very syllables of the *sūtra* through the force of its etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). By this, the view that "in the opinion of the author of the *sūtra*, the term 'pronominal' (*sarvanāman*) does not apply to a *bahuvrīhi*" is also refuted. [The rule applies] only to the *bahuvrīhi*.

The meaning of that is as follows: even the statement beginning with "In the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya" and so forth is not [correct]. For by the specific mention [of the Bhāṣyakāra], it is understood that the opinions of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Vārttika are otherwise;
just as when it is said, "Devadatta sees with his left eye," it is implied that he does not see with his right. And that is not the case.

Even according to the view of the *Sīravārtika*, the exclusion of the secondary sense (*gauṇaparyudāsa*) is accepted. As for the example "tvatkapitṛka" and so forth, it was explained by the ancients as follows: having analyzed [the compound] as "one whose father is you" (*tvaṃ pitā yasya*) and "one whose father is I" (*ahaṃ pitā yasya*), and having formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the rule applies] to the two members of that compound.

Since the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when occurring within a compound, denote all things and thus possess the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronominal), the suffix *akac* would undesirably apply to them when there is an intention to express meanings such as "unknown," according to the rule "avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ. To prevent this—

This is because, unlike [the elements] beginning with *sma*, they lack the status of being prescribed under the heading of "limbs" (*aṅga*), and thus do not depend upon the technical designation of "limb" (*aṅgasaṃjñā*). Consequently, undesirable forms such as *tvakat-pitṛka* would result. Even the author of the *Nyāsa*, having rejected the designation on the strength of its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), raised the objection that *akac* would therefore not occur; he then stated: "For the aggregate [the whole word] functions in a specific sense, whereas the prior member has not yet departed from its universal reference. All of this is merely a product of oversight.

For instance: in the *jahatsvārthā* theory of meaning, the individual meanings of the constituent parts of a compound simply do not exist. Even in the *ajahatsvārthā* theory, since the word functions with respect to another referent qualified by its own meaning, its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is quite evident. Consequently, the passage beginning with "because the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which fall within the compound, denote all things," as well as the section in the *Nyāsa* commentary beginning with "for the aggregate," are contradicted under both theories.

Furthermore, in this way, the substitution of *smāy* [for *te*] in the case of *atisarvāya* would be unavoidable, because under the governing rule for the "base" (*aṅga*), there is the inclusion of that which ends with it; and according to the method you have stated, the quality of denoting the whole (*sarvārthatā*) of the word *sarva* does not disappear. For it is not logical to claim that the quality of denoting the whole exists in the first member of a compound but not in the second. Moreover, if this were so, then when the words beginning with *sarva* are used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*), they would lack the quality of denoting the whole, which would result in a contradiction with your own statement. Thus, this argument is trivial. As for what others have explained—that in a case such as *tvaṃ pitā yasya*, the technical designation [of *sarvanāman*] applies to the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—[that too is incorrect].

"It is prohibited"—that too is not correct. For is the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) intended to be worldly (*laukika*) or non-worldly (*alaukika*)? Not the first [option], because that would contradict Kaiyaṭa’s statement: "This prohibition applies to the sentence used in formal derivation (*prakriyāvākya*), but not to the worldly [sentence]."

Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the preceding and following passages within the author's own work concerning the original forms *san* and *darbha*. Nor is the second alternative tenable;
for since that [form] consists of *yuṣmad-su* and *pitṛ-su*, it is impossible for it to take the form *tvaṃ pitā*.

Regarding what they have explained—namely, "But surely a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to 'atisarva' and the like, whereas it does apply to 'tvatkapitṛka' and the like; what is the determining factor here?"—he says: "Because it is not an operation dependent on a stem (*anaṅgakāryatvena*). The word *aṅga* refers to the entire complex (*samudāya*).
Therefore, in the rule *atisarva*, the designation of a stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) is required because the suffixes *smāy* and so forth are prescribed after a stem that is a pronoun;

for there is no fault even if the individual component alone possesses the status of a pronoun, since the entire complex (*samudāya*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) with respect to its own referent, and thus the suffix cannot apply to the complex as a whole. As for the form ending in that [complex], [the same logic applies].

It is logical that [the name] "saṃjñā" does not apply [to the whole]. However, in this case, it is intended for the individual constituent alone and not for the aggregate; and since the constituent has its own primary meaning as its principal referent, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would follow.

This is the underlying intention regarding the difference [between the two cases]. But even that is not correct, because of the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) under the heading of *aṅga*.

This is because the statement that "there is no fault even when it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) provided it exists merely as a constituent part due to being universally accepted" is contradicted; furthermore, it would conflict with your own text which states "it should be *smai*" by means of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) governing the context of "a member of a compound" (*aṅga*). Now, if the intention is this: "even though the designation (*saṃjñā*) has already been applied..."
"If it has already occurred when there is a transition to another meaning, then let *akac* also go [by that same rule]. If you object:

"Under the view that grammatical operations take place at the time of their application (*kāryakālapakṣa*), a new technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is required for the sake of forms such as *smāi*, and that is difficult to obtain"—let it be so; however, this is not the intended meaning of the present text.

This is because it contradicts the supplementary statement: "The stability [of the ritual] is the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa, due to the lack of inconsistency with the Nyāsa texts. The Nyāsa text will be cited immediately below. Furthermore, as for what they have explained: "That which is primary, whether a limb (aṅga) or the principal (pradhāna), is to be set aside; that which is contrary to it is not a limb (anaṅga)."

The meaning is that it is an obstructor (*bādhaka*). And thus, the meaning is that *akac* would occur because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kap*. That too is strained and redundant, and moreover, it is not accepted by the author of the *Nyāsa*. For instance, having explained the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the passage "tvatkapitṛkaḥ, matkapitṛkaḥ," the author of the *Nyāsa* [states as follows].

He raised this objection: "But surely, since the designation [of 'sarvanāman'] is made according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), the application of the suffix *akac* will not occur here once the designation has been excluded; for in this case, the status of being a 'universal term' (*sarvārthatā*) is impossible, because it refers to a specific [limited] scope. This is not so. For while the composite whole (*samudāya*) functions with respect to a specific [limited] object, the first member of the compound...

It is indeed not devoid of the quality of being applicable to all purposes. Let it be, then, that these two immediately preceding [words] fall within the scope of this sūtra; however, [the application] to *priyaviśvāya* and so forth is not tenable. For *priyaviśvā* and the others are not names of all [beings], nor...
For the words *viśva* and others, which constitute parts of that [compound], the application of certain pronominal operations is justified;

for while the suffixes beginning with *smai* are operations dependent on the *aṅga* (the stem), the words *viśva* and others are not *aṅgas*. He thinks thus: [this is stated] so that the suffix *akac* shall not occur in forms such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*.

Therefore, this must be undertaken; for even in cases such as *priyaviśvāya*, it will serve to clarify the meaning. Indeed, by means of this Nyāsa text, the very fact that [the designation] does not depend upon the technical name *aṅga* (suffixal base) is obtained as the meaning, whereas that [point] has been utterly cast aside in his own speculative commentary.
As for what they have explained— that although this view belongs to both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Vārttika,
it is nevertheless called "the view of the author of the Nyāsa" because it was elucidated by him— that too is quite gross,
since this meaning was not touched upon by the author of the Vārttika; rather, it was [addressed] by the author of the Nyāsa after the compound had been formed.

Furthermore, by stating "it being so" (*satīti*) and so forth, the meaning you have asserted is cast far away, as there is no possibility of a double application (*dvivṛttatva*). As for what they also say— that the author of the *Nyāsa* intends the author of the *Sūtras* himself by the word "author" (*kṛt*), etc.— that too is not correct,
because it contradicts the preceding passage beginning with "in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīhau*) according to the view of the author of the *Sūtras*.

Furthermore, because that [view] has been severed by the passage beginning with "But in the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya," it follows that here the ancient grammatical treatises (*prakriyā-grantha*) and the works of their commentators are merely superficially pleasing;
let this matter rest for now.

If, however, there is an insistence that even the *prakriyā* (grammatical derivation) text must be explained in some way so as not to contradict the *Bhāṣya*, then let it be explained as follows: "But [the form] *priyaviśvāya* has its meaning already established through its secondary (*gauṇa*) sense; therefore, he states the essential point: 'In the opinion of the author of the Sūtras,' [and] 'in a Bahuvrīhi compound.'"

The word "cikīrṣite" (when it is intended to be performed) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase "gauṇatvamātre" (in the mere state of being secondary), the word "mātra" serves to restrict the meaning;
that is, [the operation applies] only when there is a secondary sense, and not prior to that. Thus, the intention is that the sūtra has been effectively rejected.
This is because the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa is extremely trivial.

This should be investigated by those who have thoroughly studied ancient treatises on that subject. Let us return to the matter at hand. Regarding the phrase "the operation of technical names" (*saṃjñākāryam*): the meaning is the application of *smāy* and so forth, which is occasioned by the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*).
Regarding the phrase "the operation within the sub-group" (*antargaṇakāryam*): [it refers to] "the suffix *adḍ* for *itarādi* and so forth."

The meaning is [the application of] rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ* and *tadoḥ sa-sau*. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the third-case compound": here, the compound prescribed by the rule *pūrvasadṛśa-* is understood because it is taught as a specific (pratipadokta) rule, and not the one by *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*. Therefore, [in the example] *tvayakā*...
In the word *kṛtam*, there is no prohibition [of the designation "sarvanāman"].

It refers to the aggregate (*samudāya*); for it is precisely there that the term *dvandva* is used in its primary sense, and not a connection such as "those which are *sarvādi* members within a *dvandva*," because grammatical factors (*kāraka*) connect only with a verb. Nor is it the case in a *dvandva*...

The connection is with the words "those which exist," because it would be cumbersome to supply the verb "exists" (vidyati), and because it is more logical that the verb "to be" (bhavati)—which is what is being negated—should be the primary element to which [the subject] is connected.
Furthermore, there is no copulative compound (*dvandva*) of pronouns such as *tyad* and so on, because such a formation is precluded by the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Therefore...

In that case, there is no distinction between other [words] such as *prācīnā* and *tvadanyā*, nor between *kākacoḥ*. Nor should it be argued: "Why not apply this [rule] even to prevent the desired *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) in cases such as *na ca dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*? For, in the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātra*, the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only/inclusively) is indeed [intended to exclude such cases].
In some cases, even when words previously observed as pronouns no longer function as such, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) still occurs.

Therefore, by the force of logic and the evidence of the result, it is more appropriate to accept the inclusion of the entire compound. Although it might be easy to state the result even under the view that the word *tvad* ends in *-t*—whereby the prohibition would apply only to its constituent part—nevertheless...
The sense is that the scope of the treatise would become too narrow and it would contradict established logic (*nyāya*).

Regarding the phrase "the contingency of *suṭ*": the sense is [its occurrence] in examples such as *varṇāśrametarāṇām*. Nor can the prohibition be justified by its own force, because it serves to exclude non-aṅga forms such as *tratasil* and others.
Because its purpose has been fulfilled.
