Regarding the phrase "the substratum of *jas*": although *jas* is removed by the substitution of *śī*, nevertheless, one should understand that the status of being a substratum is used figuratively (*aupacārika*). Alternatively, *i* [substituted] for *jas* is *jasi*; [the word refers to] that [substitution].
He explains by implication that there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*): namely, "that which has *jas* as its locus.
Regarding the rule *Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.101*: *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām*, [the word] "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is understood from the preceding rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*.

Thus, [the word] "from this" (ityataḥ) is understood to carry over. The intention is that, by virtue of this, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) in cases such as *jarāyā idaṃ* = *jāram*. Regarding the phrase "by those who follow that": their view is that since the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) applies to both *in* and *āt* because they are mentioned in a single sūtra, it is appropriate to include the substitution of *syādeśa* as well.
For this very reason—
considering the usage by Bhāravi in the verse "vītajanmajarasaḥ paraṃ śuci brahmaṇaḥ padamupaitumicchhatām" to be inconsistent,
it should be read as "vītajanmajarasām" (of those who have abandoned birth and old age).

They said: "And this [is so]. For the author of the Bhāṣya, having rejected the suffixes *in* and *āt* in the rule "ṭāṅasi," prescribed the substitutes *nā* and *ad*. Then, when *nā* follows, he established the substitution of *e* by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*), as in: "In the plural, before a *jhal*-ending, *e* [is substituted]" and "also before *osi*. From that...

When *āṅ* or *āiṅ* follow [the word *ena*], there shall be the substitution of *e*. Thus, *rāmeṇa*. Then, by the rule "*āpaḥ sambuddhau ca*," there shall be the substitution of *e* when *āṅ* or *osi* follow in the vocative case. Nor should it be argued that, in this manner, there would be elision (*lopa*) of the *na* in *anena* when a consonant (*hal*) follows; for there is a specific rule prescribing [the elision] only when *na* follows a substitute (*ādeśa*) that does not begin with *na*. Likewise...

Indeed, the meaning is that *an* occurs when the letter *n* as well as the letter *ā* follow; in the sūtra, the term *a* is a neuter designation for that which ends in *n*. Nor should it be argued that once the substitution of *at* for *ṅsi* has been made, the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule would apply; for by the power of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*, the occurrence of the long vowel is possible. And thus:

It is stated in the sūtra *jarāyā jarasanyatarasyām*: "But Gonardīya says that it should be *atijaraiḥ*, according to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*. Thus, the meaning is that everything [the author has argued], such as the "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), is contrary to the Bhāṣya.

*Prau.ma.*—*paddannomāshṛnnaṣasanyūṣandoṣanyakañcchakannudannāsañcchasprabhṛtiṣu*. [Pāṇini 6.1.63] "paddanno": Here, the forms beginning with *śas* are mentioned as the conditioning causes (*nimitta*). And these...
He says—“pādadanteti”—that [the suffixes] imply specific bases corresponding to the substitutes for *pada* and so on.

Although the term “in Vedic” (*chandasi*) continues here from the rule “*śīrṣan* in Vedic,” nevertheless, it occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) in some cases, as indicated by the Vārttika: “*māsa* in Vedic.”

It will be stated that this is due to the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the word *cchanda* (desire). Regarding the term *prāmādika* (accidental/erroneous): for instance, in the mantra “*āsno vṛkas vatikāmabhīke*,” the meaning is “from the mouth” (*mukhāt*), because it is appropriate (*aucityāt*). [And as in: “*vṛkasya cidvatikāmamantarā syāt*.”

This is also because of the corroboration by other mantras; likewise in such passages as "offering oblations in the mouth" (*havyā juhvāna āsani*) and "they spoke to the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ*), and the explanation is exactly the same in the Vedabhāṣyas. Therefore, it should be noted that even Haradatta has revealed the erroneous nature of the *Kāśikā* on this point.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

"allopo'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). Regarding this, the ancients [interpret it as]: "There shall be elision of the *a* belonging to a *bha*-affix that ends in *an*. If that were the case, there would be elision of the vowel *a* even in *takṣṇā* and similar forms [where the *a* belongs to the suffix, not the stem].

It might be argued: "If the rule is explained as 'of the *an* [suffix] belonging to a *bha*-stem, the *a*-vowel [is elided],' then it would apply in cases such as *ṭhanasā* and *manasā*. Even if one explains it through methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition) as 'of the *a*-vowel of an *an* ending in a *bha*-stem,' there is still over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *ṭhanastakṣṇā*. Therefore...

He explains with the words "aṅgāvayava" (a part of the base), etc. The two—namely, the specific suffix implied by the word "bhasya" (of the bha-stem) and the base (aṅga)—are both qualifiers of "an". However, this applies to the letter *a*, and therefore the aforementioned fault does not arise; such is the intended meaning. And this [is discussed] under the rule "ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam".

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. *Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade*—"after *r* and *ṣ*, *n* becomes *ṇ* in the same word"—although the status of being within a single word (*ekapadatva*) is already obtained by the force of the term "in a word" (*pade*) alone, [the addition of *samāna-*]...

The inclusion of the term *samāna* (equal) means that which is strictly identical, that is to say, indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). In that case, so that it may apply there, it does not occur in a compound (*samāsa*). For example: *rāmanāma* (the name Rāma). [Another example: *yūṣṇaḥ*. *Yūṣa* is a broth (*maṇḍa*). As it is said: "Broth made of mung beans and *āmalaka* is digestive, appetizing, and a promoter of digestion."

Because of this observation. Regarding the phrase "in this alternative view": by this, he suggests that the use of the fifth case (pañcamī) in a compound is optional. For instance, in the Bhāṣya, three purposes are stated—namely, *bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*—yet these are established otherwise. This is so in the rule *ekāca upadeśe*.

Precisely because of the specified qualification (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no prohibition of *iṇ* in the case of *bebhiditā*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *mathitam paṇyam asya*, when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied and the single-substitute *ik* (the *ṭh*) is replaced by *i*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *i* occurs by the rule "yasyeti ca";
however, the substitution of *ka* by the rule "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" will not take place, because the *ṭha* is absent. Nor...

By virtue of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), the substitution of *ṭha* occurs because it is not a rule dependent on a phoneme (*alvidhi*). For in the rule "ṭhasyekaḥ," the vowel *a* in both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of pronunciation. Furthermore, in the form *apīpacan*, the result is established even without the status of being a substitute for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the *caṅ*-augment, and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the two vowels.

Because of its association with the *vidhi* (prescriptive) suffixes, even though it follows an abhyasta (reduplicated) root, only the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense is intended for the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*; nor should it be argued that, due to its association with *sic*, only the *luṅ* (aorist) could be meant,
because association with what precedes is weaker than association with what follows— this is the general direction of the argument.

"Not [applicable] when what precedes is unestablished. We have already stated that this is established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). Since the final three chapters (*tripādī*) are unestablished, the rule of extension (*atideśa*), "when a subsequent [element] intervenes, the operation is as if it were not," does not apply to an operation to be performed therein. Regarding the word "tasya": it refers to that [rule], namely "pūrvatrāsiddhe. And thus:

The meaning is that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) should be stated in three instances. [This applies] to the elision of the first letter of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster), as in *cakryatra*; to the substitution of *l* for *r*, as in *nigālyate*; and to the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, as in *māṣavapanī*. In this last case, by virtue of the elision of the *a* [of the suffix *an*] according to the rule *yasyeti ca*, the status of being a *sthānin* prevents the *n* from being at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur.
No;

for they say that even if there is no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) in some way, [the rule] "raṣābhyām" (P. 8.4.1) has no utility in cases such as *yūṣṇaḥ*, since the desired form is established by [the rule] "ṣṭuan" (P. 8.4.40). And thus:
It is established in the *Ākara* (the commentary) that the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* is for the sake of subsequent rules;

therefore, this has been presented here as a statement made in haste (*rabhasavāda*). Indeed, this very same absence of haste is evident, for the inclusion of *ṣ* remains here even for the sake of subsequent rules. Consequently, in examples such as *yūṣṇaḥ* and *puṣṇāti*, [the rule applies].

Who can prevent the application of the rule *raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) for the substitution of *ṇ*? If you say it is prevented by the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), that is not so, because that [rule] is considered *asiddha*. Nor can its status as *siddha* be established on the grounds of the authority of a specific statement, since it has already served its purpose in forms such as *puṣṭiḥ*. However, the portion of that [rule], *ṣayoge*, has not yet served its purpose.

If this is argued, we say no; for that [case] has not been mentioned separately. Furthermore, the statement here that [the rule] following *ṣ* is "unfulfilled" (acaritārtha) applies equally to this case as well. For in the authoritative source (ākara), the intended meaning is simply that there is no failure to establish the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*) here without the mention of *ṣ*;
it is not, however, the case that [the rule] "after *r* and *ṣ*" (*raṣābhyām*) applies in forms such as *puṣṇāti*.
Thus, there is no application [of that rule]; this is the general direction.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "The *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is elided" (Pāṇini 8.2.7). This is a case where the genitive case ending is dropped; it is so because it is a *sūtra*-formulation, and not otherwise.

The sense is that in the case of a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound, the first member [cannot take the suffix], because a compound is impossible when there is mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), and because a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves as a qualifier of a word (*pada*). Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in it" (*tadantasya*):
this is a genitive-tatpuruṣa; the meaning is "of that *n* which is at the end of it. And it has been said:

Haradata [states]: "In the rule *viśeṣyasyāntasya*, the word *na* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), and likewise, the word *prātipadika* is a qualifier of the word *pada*. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it refers to the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or at the end of a word (*pada*)—and as for...
The explanation—that the word *antasya* connects with both—is undermined by its own weightiness;
for it would entail the necessity of repeating *antasya* and result in two genitive constructions in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
However, if the word *na* is connected [to the preceding] through the relation of identity (*abheda*), just as it is with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself—[then there is no fault].

When [the base] is qualified by that [suffix], then, under the rule of *tadantavidhi* (specification of what ends with that), the mention of the word "anta" (end) in the sūtra could have been omitted.
(Prau.ma.: *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ*)

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā ṅśyoḥ*: the term *śī* refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakācca*, and not to the *śi* of *jaś-śas*, because the status of being a *bha*-stem is impossible in that case. By the word *bhasya*, only [the substitution] for non-*sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes] is intended.

Because this is implied by the root *yaj* and others, he says: "not in the place of a sarvanāman-sthāna. For this very reason—namely, because of the usage *doṣaṇī*—even though the Bhāṣya could be interpreted by applying the rule of *ekaśeṣa* to a collective dvandva compound, nevertheless it is more logical that *kakud* be treated as a separate word; otherwise, [the form] *kakuda-*...
The sense is that neither oneness nor duality of the two arms would be perceived.
In the verse from the *Raghuvamśa*: "Lifting up his right arm, the night-stalker rushed at him," the phrase "his right arm" is connected as the object of the action expressed by "lifting up."
Regarding the phrase "doṣaṃ tasya":

"Taking the fault (*doṣa*) of such a bow as it bears its string (*guṇa*)," is the usage by Śrī Harṣa. In that context, *doṣaṃ* refers to the hand (or the arm) and the defect; and *guṇaṃ* refers to the string of the bow.
The connection is: "and perceiving the excellence of the maurvī.
However, the commentators on Amara, having accepted the word *doṣā* as feminine as well, state that it is *doṣā* by means of the suffix *ṭāp* according to the opinion of Bhāguri.
They cited the *Dhanañjaya-nighaṇṭu*: "The arm is called *dordoṣā*, *bhuja*, *bāhu*, as well as *pāṇi*, *hasta*, and *kara*.

[Regarding the term *dvayahna*: "That which occurs in two days"—this is a compound formed by the rule *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), with the suffix *ṭhañ* applied according to the rule *kālāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.11).
There is elision (*luk*) by the rule *dvigor lug-anapatye*. Then, by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is added.

By the rule *ahno 'hn etebhyaḥ*, the substitute *ahn-* is applied [to the word *ahan*]. Regarding the expression *ahnaḥ sāyaḥ*: the word *sāya* denotes the end of the day and is derived from the root *si* with the suffix *ghañ*. [The compound is formed] by the rule *saṃkhyā-visāya-*.
The *ekadeśisamāsa* is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Thus end [the words] ending in /a/.

"Hāhā" is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific class of *gandharvas*. However, the followers of Kumāra (the Kaumārāḥ), asserting that it is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*) derived from "he abandons" (*jahāti*), thus "hāhā," maintain that its form is like that of the word *viśvapsā*. According to their view, the counter-example is the letter *ṭha*, which is Vāsudeva.
It should be understood that *sāḥ* means "those which exist together with it," and *tān sān* means "those [which exist] together. Thus end those ending in long vowels (*ādantāḥ*).

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *āṅe nāstriyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.120), the term *striyām* ("in the feminine") is not stated [as *puṃsi*]; rather, it says *nāstriyām*. This is so that the form may be obtained in cases such as *amunā kulena*, where the addition of *num* would not suffice for the formation of the word because the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha* with respect to the application of the rule *iko 'ci* (Pāṇini 7.1.73).

[The substitution of *ṣatvam*] does not apply because [the condition] has not been reached (*aprāpteḥ*). However, in the case of [the form] *nādeśa*, there is no status of being non-established (*asiddhatvam*), due to the prohibition by the rule "namune. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition "namune" should apply only to *num*, since the vowel *a* in "ne" is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārthatvāt*); [for otherwise, it would lead to the undesired result in] *amuṣmai*.
Because [otherwise] there would result the non-establishment of forms such as *kulāya*;
[this is shown by the following rules]: *acca gheḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.119), *idudbhyām* (7.3.120), *ReĀ* (7.3.121), and *āṬt* (7.3.122).
With the intention that [the word] follows the three preceding words, he explains [the rule] by saying "of what follows after *i* and *u*" (*idudbhyām uttarasya*),
and so forth. It is not stated as "of what follows after *ghi*" (*gher uttarasya*), because in the sūtra the term "of *ghi*" (*gheḥ*) is in the genitive case,
and because there is no authority for [applying] *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so on, as was the case in the previous sūtra "āṬt."

Furthermore, because it is improper to abandon the established relationship [of the rule] *idudbhyām* with the subsequent *ReĀr*, [the form] *āṬtsyāt* would result. Regarding this, they have explained: the presence of the *t* in *āṬt* is for the sake of making it a circumflex (*svarita*) accent. As for the prohibition of *it* by the rule *na vibhaktau*, it does not apply here, because that rule is non-universal (*anitya*).

And regarding impermanence (*anityatva*), it has been stated in that very [work] that it is obtained from the fact that the letter *m* in the suffix *tham* (in the rule *idamasthamuḥ*) is marked with the *it*-designation for the purpose of protecting it [from elision]; however, that is to be reconsidered. In the rule *vibhaktau*, the letter *t* in *ReĀraut* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Because it has been stated by [the author] himself that [the term] is a "name for the net," there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Furthermore, it is logical that its purpose is for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārthatva*), and not for the sake of the *svarita* accent; for in such passages as "on the strewn sacrificial grass, when the fire is kindled," the *svarita* accent is not observed. As for the *tapara* (the *t* following the *ṭha*), however—

Regarding the statement that [the rule] "budhau" and so forth was formulated so that the suffix *ṭāp* would not apply when *atva* (the substitution of *a* for *i*) has been made in the feminine, that too is to be reconsidered. For by virtue of the mention of *ta-paras* (the marker *t*), let there be no long vowel with *ṭāp*; however, *ṭāp* should indeed still occur, as there is no evidence for the subversion of two grammatical rules simultaneously. Therefore...

Thus, in the commentary on the sūtra *kṛnmejantaḥ* and in the Vārttika, it is stated that by the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*, the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply; for if there were an intervention by *ṭāp*, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be destroyed. Therefore, [the suffix] applies here just as it does after [a stem ending in] *au*.
It should be noted that the inclusion of the long *ā* (tapara) is solely for the purpose of pronunciation.

Regarding the rule *anaṅ sau* (Pāṇini 7.1.93): since the result would have been established by the rule *sor ḍā* alone, the prescription of *anaṅ* indicates that [the substitution] should also apply in other instances.

[The suffix] is for the purpose of making this known. Therefore, the ancients maintain that *anaṅ* is established in the vocative case of *uśanas*. That is to be considered; for if [the rule] were stated as *soḥ ḍā*, then by the subsequent sūtra *ṛduśanas-puru-daṃśo-nehas-tṛjvaktavyaḥ*, *ḍā* would also apply.
Consequently, in the form *uśanā*, there would be lengthening according to the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*.
It might be argued that in the word *purudaṃsa*, there would be a long vowel by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*. Alternatively,

the resolution should be understood either through the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably applicable" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ*), or by the *paribhāṣā* concerning what occurs within the constituent element (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

Regarding the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktam hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), he states that the term *dīrghāt* ("from a long vowel") is a qualifier specifically for *ṅī* and *āp*, and not for *hal* ("consonant"), because a consonant cannot be long. He says: "from long [vowels]"; however, this is not [the case].

The sense is that [the definition] is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *yaḥ* and *saḥ*, and under-extensive (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *kā* and *yā*, because the former are not prescribed after a consonant-ending base, while the latter are. Nor can the requirement be satisfied there by taking them as being prescribed after a consonant-ending base; for the same reason, there would be over-extension in *yaḥ* and *saḥ*, and under-extension in *kartā* and the like. As for the word *hal*: and of that...
The nature of being *sutisī* should be understood by means of the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). Regarding the word "is elided" (*lupyate*):

although the term "elision" (*lopa*) is carried over from the rule "elision of *v* and *y*" (*lopo vyoḥ*), and while that [term] there functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), here it functions as an accusative noun (*karmasādhana*) in connection with the nominative *hal*.

The intended meaning is "because of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Why is the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) made? [Consider] *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. Now, one might object: "In these cases, the entire compound does not end in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*). Nor should it be said: "There is no rule of initial reference (*tadādiniyama*) regarding feminine suffixes. For [that rule applies only] when the suffix is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*).
Likewise: "But here, because [the word] is a subordinate member (upasarjana), the restriction that it must begin with that [specific element] certainly applies. True;

nevertheless, since the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅy-āp*), its status as following that [suffix] remains unchanged. For we have already stated that this [restriction] is not a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). Precisely for this reason, there is elision of the case-ending (*su*) in the form *bahuśreyasī*.

It might be argued: [from the root] *gaṅgīyati* with the suffix *kvip*, we get *gaṅgīḥ*. Here, because the vowel *i* possesses the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would have the nature of both *āp* and a long vowel; thus, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). True. However, by compounding (*praśliṣya*) *ṅī* and *ī*, as well as *ā* and *āp*, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is rejected, and thus there is no fault whatsoever.

What is the purpose of the condition "after a suffix ending in *s* or *t*"? [Consider] *bhetā*. [The rule would otherwise require] the elision of the *t* in the root *tras*. Nor does this [condition] lead to the undesirable consequence of the elision of *sic* in forms such as *abhaitsīt*, because by virtue of its association with *su* and *ti*, only a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is understood [by the term *apṛktam*]. Why is the condition "single-consonant" (*apṛkta*) stated? [Consider] *bhinatti* and *chinatti*.
They offer a counter-example; however, that must be considered, because the [term] *ah* is qualified [by the condition of being a consonant].
For it is improper to introduce an over-extension by laboriously explaining [the rule] *suti-sīnāṃ hal* as "after *su*, *ti*, and *si*, when a consonant follows.
Furthermore, they say: "One who presses *surā* is a *surāsut*; one causes him to speak is *surāsayati*."

From that, with the *kvip* suffix, we have *surāḥ*, *surāsau*, *surāsaḥ*. Here, the mention of *apṛkta* (non-composite) is intended to exclude the elision of the *s* which is a part of the root *su* (to press). But even that is not correct, because by virtue of mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*), only the case-endings (*vibhakti*) *su*, *ti*, and *si* are understood; otherwise, [the rule would apply] to the *sic* [affix].

Because it has been stated by the Lord of Lopāmudrā (Patañjali), and because between a suffix and a non-suffix, only the suffix is to be understood [as the referent]. Why "hal" (consonant)? [Consider] *bibheda*.
Now, is not the mention of "the first consonant" (*prathamahal*) redundant? [For] of those [suffixes] following a word ending in a consonant...

Because of the possibility of the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). On this point, they say: "For if there were elision of a final conjunct, the elision of *n* and so forth would not be established; rather, the elision would occur by that [rule] alone. Therefore, the rule for the elision of a consonant (*hal*) is prescribed."

For instance, in the word *sakhe*, the elision of *n* would not occur, because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This might be argued: the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct is not non-existent, as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *sambuddhi* (vocative singular) in the rule *na ṅsimbudhyoḥ*.

And thus, there is no risk of the elision of *n* occurring in cases such as *gomān* (possessing cows), because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies specifically to a particular scope. For, according to the traditional explanation, the rule is established only where there is immediate sequence between the letter *n* and a case-ending (*vibhakti*). As for what they say—that in the vocative *he brahman*, [the elision does not occur] because it serves the purpose of the neuter gender—[this is incorrect].

"This is not an indicator (jñāpaka). That is not so; for since there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule when a suffix has been elided by *luk*, the rule "optionally [the nasal] in the vocative of neuter nouns" would otherwise be necessary. Consequently, the inclusion of the term "vocative" (*sambuddhi*) could not possibly refer to neuter nouns, which establishes the validity of the aforementioned indicator. Therefore, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)...
And what is the purpose [of this]? Well then, in the case of *abhino 'tra*, the substitution of *u* for *ru* would not occur.
This is why it was stated: "the elision of *n* and so forth. Likewise, in *abibhar bhavān*, the elision of *t* would not occur due to the restriction [*niyama*] "after *r*, there is elision of *s*."
In this regard, the following should be noted: the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is a qualification only for *su*, and not for *tis* and *tīs*, according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
The *Bhāṣya* on this very sūtra—"In this [sūtra], the mention of *dvihala-apṛkta* and the mention of *tis* and *tīs* need not be made"—is the authority here. For if the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*...

In that case, how could one say that the mention of *ti* and *si* need not be made, since they too require qualification? As for the claim that *ti* and *si* are impossible after words ending in *ṅī* and *āp*:
it is true that they are impossible after a word ending in *ṅī*, but they are possible after an *āp*-ending word derived from a root formed with *kvip* in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*).

The suffixes *tip* and *sip* indeed exist [in forms such as *bhavati* and *bhavasi*], just as in *agaṅgāt* and *agaṅgāḥ*. Nor is there an intervention by the *śap* augment, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*).
Nor does the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) apply, because this is not a rule concerning a previously non-existent operation (*apūrvavidhi*).

In this regard, the following is the essential point: the rule *ṅyāpaḥ soḥ* alone is appropriate. Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the *s* of a verbal root in forms such as *surāḥ* or *surāsau*; for, due to the association with *ṅī* and *āp*, and by the maxim *pratyayāpratyayayoḥ*, [the elision applies] only to the *s* of an affix.

Because of the inclusion of the word *saḥ* [in the rule]. As for the elision of the *n* in *rājā* and so forth, it is indeed established by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na ṅsimbudhyoḥ*. Furthermore, the substitution of *u* in *abhino'tra* is also easily justified, because of the reading in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*: *saṃyogāntalopo rorutve*. [In the case of] *harivo*...

Just as in the case of *medinam tu*, there is no fault even here in the example *abibhar bhavān*. This is because, in the rule *rāt sasya*, the letter *t* is also included by *praśleṣa* (elision), resulting in the analysis *tsasya*. Now, one might object:

"In cases such as *ukhāsrat*, would there not be the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*)? No; for once the substitution of *d* (*datva*) has been applied, [the condition for that elision no longer holds].

Because that [substitution] has not been obtained. If it is argued that the substitution of *d* for *t* is unestablished, we say no; for in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*, there is the reading: "the substitution of *d* occurs in *vasu* and so forth. If it is further argued that the substitution of *d* would not occur because it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), we say no;
for one may rely on the position that even [in the nominative singular] it is a word (*pada*). The basis for this is the rule: "not in a non-sarvanāmasthāna [case ending]."
Having analyzed [the sūtra] as "yaci," the explanation is that the designation *pada* does not apply before a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with *ya* or *ja*.
Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *rājā*, once the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has occurred, the rules for *ru*tva and *visarga* would still apply;
for [the rule] "pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne" is established by the presence of the word "itaḥ" [in the sūtra].

Because, by prescribing this specific form, the elision of the *su* suffix is first made known. Now, one might object: "This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), for its purpose is already fulfilled in the vocative singular; for example, *he panthāḥ*, *manthāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣāḥ*. In those cases, the long vowel is excluded by the rule 'except in the vocative' (*asaṃbuddhau*), and the elision of *n* is prohibited. If you say this:

If that is the case, then let the rule *na ṅsiṃbudhyoḥ* itself serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the meaning that the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) occurs prior to the elision of the *n*. For instance,
in the phrase *ṅsiṃbudhyoḥ*, the genitive case is used rather than the locative, because [the suffixes] *ṅsi* and *ām* have been elided by the rule *reĀr-luk*.

Because of the absence of a condition (*pratyaya*) [to trigger the elision], there is a coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word ending in *ṅī* and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, a nominal stem ending in the vocative suffix *sambuddhi* cannot be obtained without first applying the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Therefore, the rule should be formulated as "the *su* [of the nominative-accusative singular] after a feminine stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*" (*ṅyāpaḥ sor iti*).

There is no contradiction whatsoever. However, if the Vārttika "the substitution of *d* occurs in the case of *uṣṭra* and so forth" is rejected—since the absence of the long vowel in forms such as *ukhāsrad* and *aśvasrad* is already established by the very mention of *adhātu* [in Pāṇini 6.4.130]—then let the rule be *halṅyābbhyaḥ suḥ*. As for the rule as it is heard in its traditional form, the ancients [have explained it thus]:

It has been explained [by some] that [the suffix] follows from a word ending in *ṅī*, a word ending in *āP*, and a long vowel (*dīrgha*). That is not correct; for while *ṅī* and *āP* are themselves long, it is not their end (*tadanta*) that is necessarily so. Nor can the meaning "from a long [vowel] which is a *ṅī*-ending" and so forth be obtained from the rule "from a long [vowel]" (*dīrghāt*), because there is no grammatical connection (*ananvaya*) with the ablative case (*pañcamī*).
In a compound, because the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are subordinate (*upasarjana*) and thus connected with qualifiers, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"There is no compound formation (*vṛtti*) for those accompanied by qualifiers, nor is there a connection with qualifiers for that which has already undergone compound formation.
By this, the ancient commentary (*vṛtti*) which defines the term *anadī* as "a short vowel ending in *i* or *u*" is also refuted.
[The sūtra] is answered:
*sakhyurasaṃbuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.1.92). Here, [the word] *sakhyuḥ* is understood from the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 7.1.86).

The term "sarvanāmasthāne" (in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna suffix) is understood from the previous context. That [term] is qualified by "asambuddhau" (except for the vocative). From the rule "goto ṇit," the word "ṇit" is carried over; since this stands in grammatical apposition, the locative case is transformed into the nominative. Thus he says: "excluding the vocative."

Regarding the term *sarvanāmasthāna*: it would be more appropriate for the sūtra to read simply *sakhyur asaṃbuddhiḥ*. [In the rule] *khyatyāt parasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.91), the word *khya* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the words *khi* and *khī*, which have undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*.

Thus, regarding the two words *titau* and *tya*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) in both cases; it is not an imitation of a portion of primary words such as *apatya*. [This is illustrated by the following rules: "The suffix *yaḥ* after *sakhi*," "The suffix *naḥ* after *pati*," "After a numeral and a word denoting a year," and "And after an *apatya* [suffix] when followed by a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *at*."
Because of such indications as these; with this intention, he says: "by the two words *khi* and *ti*, etc.

The inclusion of the word *parasya* ("of the subsequent") is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "one [substitute] takes the place of both the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*). [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *āṬt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.93)]

The term *āṬt* is superseded by the preceding rule, *idudbhyām*, among those items designated as *nadī*, and by the subsequent rule, *acca gheḥ*, among those designated as *ghis*. Therefore, its scope consists of those items devoid of both designations (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, there exists no such *u*-vowel [that falls within this scope]. Thus...

He says: "The vowel *u*. As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the rule applies] to *i* and *u* following [a word] that is not designated as a *ghin* or a *nadī*—that is incorrect, because such an *u* is unestablished. Regarding the phrase "of the whole":
even in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), [the objection does not apply] to the word *sakhi*, which provides the object of the exclusion.

The possibility of its being a qualifier (*anta-gārāhakatva*) is to be suspected, because of the non-proximity of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). As for what was presented here by Haradatta in the passage beginning with "by that which possesses [the suffix] *grahaṇa*," and what was stated by Kaiyaṭa under the rule *khyatyāt*, that is not correct, because that [rule] pertains to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*).

Regarding the phrase "even though it is secondary" (*gauṇatve’pi*): the intention is that it is like the *anaṅ* substitution in words such as *asthi*. Thus, Kaiyaṭa, under the rule *yena vidhiḥ*, states: "In *paramasakhāyau*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* would have to occur. Similarly, under the rule *dvitīyā śrita-*, he cites *somasakha*.
Kaiyaṭa states that because it is a bahuvrīhi compound formed by taking only the *pratīka* (representative part), there is no application of the *samāsānta* suffix.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtras "midaco 'ntyāt" and "tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ striyāṃ ca," as well as in Mādhava’s commentary on the root *khyā*. [The form] is *ṭhanapadyaukṣaḥ*.

Furthermore, such usages as "Varuṇa is Indra’s friend," "The Maruts are indeed Agni’s friends," and "He drinks the sharp Soma which has the cow as its companion" are consistent only in this way; for in those cases,
we observe the original accent of the first member of the compound (pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara) characteristic of a *bahuvrīhi*, since [the meaning] is secondary (*gauṇatvāt*).
By this [rule], Haradatta, Nāgeśa, and others who follow them—citing "one whose friend is excellent" (*susakhi*) as an example under the rule *ghisaṃjñāsūtra* [Pāṇini 1.4.7]—are to be disregarded.
(Prakriyākaumudī: *patiḥ samāsa eva* [Pāṇini 1.4.8]).

"The word *pati* [retains its original form] only in a compound. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of restriction according to our desired interpretation; otherwise, one might suspect that the rule applies only when *pati* is in a compound. Furthermore, if one were to follow the indication (*jñāpaka*) from rules such as "of the root-initial," etc., there would be an excessive burden on the learner (*pratipattigauravam*). Now, how is it that [the form] *-sītāyāḥ pataye namaḥ* ("salutation to the husband of Sītā") is formed?
And Parāśara says:

"When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, is impotent, or has become an outcast. To this it is replied: the word *pati* is so called because it is derived from the root *pā* with the suffix *ṇi*; after the elision of the *ṭi*, the Uṇādi suffix *i* is applied according to the rule "after a vowel [ending root], *i* [is added]."
This word *pati* is not included in the rule *patiḥ samāsa eva*, because it is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*).
By this, the Mahābhārata passage "Arjuna is the friend (*sakhi*) of Kṛṣṇa" and the Rāmāyaṇa passage "with the lord of monkeys as his friend (*sakhinā vānarendreṇa*)" are explained.

Prau.ma.: *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.23). The two words *bahu* and *gaṇa* are understood here as technical terms (*prātipadika*) denoting number (*saṃkhyā*), and not as words denoting a collection (*saṃgha*) or abundance (*vaipulya*). This is because the designation is prescribed according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*): that by which something is counted is called "number."

For this very reason, the suffix *ḍati* is understood here as being exclusively a *taddhita* suffix, both because of its association with *vatu* and because it is not the *ḍati* derived from the root *pā*.
(Prau.ma.: *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.22).
"ṣaḍbhyo luk" (P. 7.1.22): [the word] "from the six" (*ṣaḍbhyaḥ*) means "after [stems ending in] the six. The use of the plural number is intended to indicate that the meaning is primary.
The resulting sense is: "[after stems] expressing a number residing in the meaning of the six."
*Pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.62):

"When there is the elision of an affix (*pratyayalope*). Since this is already established by the rule *sthānivat*, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). When the specific form of the affix is the operative cause (*prayojaka*), only that grammatical operation (*kārya*) [pertaining to that specific form] takes place when the affix is elided.

When [the suffix] exists, [the rule applies], but not when it is common to both a suffix and a non-suffix. Therefore, in the example *sudṛṣat prāsādaḥ* ("a palace with beautiful stones"), the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *atvasantasya ca yatri* does not occur. Alternatively, this [rule] is for the purpose of providing a prescription even in cases where there is no *al*-vidhi (a rule concerning phonemes), provided that the suffix is relied upon as the primary factor.

Therefore, in the case of *atṛṇeḍ*, even though the *im* augment—prescribed before a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*)—has been elided, it still takes effect. However, the rule "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treatment as if a suffix were present) when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*)" concerns cases where the phoneme is predominant. Consequently, in the example *gave hitam* → *go-hitam*, the suffix *av* does not apply.

Regarding "asmad": here, the reading *prācām avyayāt* is also found; however, that has been raised [as an objection] because indeclinables generally lack gender, and thus even though an *avyayībhāva* compound is neuter, there is no other gender [to distinguish it from]. In reality, however... [this refers to] that which indicates the predominance of the meaning.

The intention is that because the plural number is absent, even though the term is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*), the substitution of *traya* is appropriate, just as in the case of *anaṅ* for *asthi* and other such words. Thus, it should be stated that [the word] ends in *a*; and so, in the absence of plurality, the word *ĀṬḍulomi* ends in the vowel *i*.
However, one should not be confused by the fact that while the word *uḍulomi* ending in *a* is used in the plural, the word ending in *i* takes the form ending in *a* in the plural.
Thus end the words ending in *i*.
The sense is that by that [rule], there is the elision of the long *ā* according to "āto lopa iṭi ca.

Regarding the forms *yayī*, *papyā*, and so on: as for what was previously stated—that likewise *devayajyā*, *atilakṣmī*, and so forth [are formed]—that is not correct; for in the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "one who sacrifices to the gods" (*devān yajate*), the suffix *in* is applied by the Uṇādi sūtra.

This is because the word *devayaji* with a short vowel at its end has been established by Ujjvaladatta and others; furthermore, the usage of Bhāravi in the verse, "Let us slay the twice-born who sacrifice to the gods" (*admo dvijān devayajīn nihanma*), has been explained as referring specifically to the short vowel. Moreover, the suffix *ī* after the root *yaj* does not result in a long vowel.

It is explicitly stated [in the rule]. If it is argued that it is inferred due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases), this might indeed be so, provided that an inferential ground (*kalpaka*) not otherwise established were found. Even in the Veda, the short vowel alone is employed—as in "āyajim tvā manave jātavedase. However, as for the word *atilakṣmī*:

Because of the feminine suffix *nadī*, when the short vowel *ā* is added (*āḍāgama*), the augment *nuṭ* is applied, and the case-ending *ām* is formed, there is a great difference [in the resulting forms], and thus there is no similarity with *vātapramī*. This will become clear in the root text itself. Regarding the term "ending in *kvip*," this is found in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *māṅ* (meaning "to measure" and "to sound").

This is clear. Regarding the term *bahuśreyasī*: the suffix *kap* is not applied by the rule *īyasaśca*, nor does the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*) apply, because of the prohibition: "the [vowel] of *īyas* is not shortened when it occurs in a *bahuvrīhi*. Prakriyā-kaumudī: Feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū* are called *nadī*. (Pāṇini 1.4.3)

Regarding the rule *yū stryākhyau*: the phrase "ending in *ī* or *ū*" (*īdū-dantau*) refers here to the two phonemes themselves; for there is also a view that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applies to the phonemes alone, as evidenced by the natural phrasing of the sūtra *ācchīnadyor num*.

Their status as being called "feminine" (*stry-ākhyau*), however, occurs either inherently in the case of *ṅī* and so forth, or in some cases by virtue of being constituent parts of a collection of phonemes that denote a feminine entity.
Because of the inclusion [of the word *antāt*]; for the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the completion of the capacity (*śaktiparyāpti*) is not intended to be expressed.

Therefore, the conventional usage such as "ending in a nadī" is not contradicted. Likewise, regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *ghis*, one should understand that there are two alternative views: either the vowels *i* and *u* are designated as *ghi*, or that which ends in them is designated as *ghi*. If it were a designation of the phoneme itself (*varṇasaṃjñā*), [the rule] would be *ṭhasakhi*.

The meaning of this [sūtra] is "a part of that which is distinct from *sakhi*," and not "excluding the word-element *sakhi*. Therefore, it should be noted that forms such as *atisakhinā* are free from objection.
Regarding the word *pūrvam*: it means "prior to the formation of the compound" (*vṛti*). Regarding the word *vaktavyam*: [it refers to] in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

This [application] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*) when the rule proceeds according to its enunciation (*yathoddeśa*); however, it is based on explicit statement (*vācanika*) under the view that the rule applies at the time the operation is to take place (*kāryakāla*).

In the *Paribhāṣā-pradīpa*: "In the presence of an *ac*, for the *śnu* affix, verbal roots, and *bhrū*, *iy* and *uVaṅ* are substituted for *y* and *v*" (Pāṇini 6.4.77). Here, the term "*yvoh*" is a qualifier of the verbal root alone, and not...

He says "because of the non-deviation between *śnu* and the eyebrows" (*śnubhruvor avyabhicārāt*), meaning "of a root ending in the vowels *i* or *u*" (*ivarṇovarṇāntadhātoḥ*). However, if one were to explain it as "of *śnu* and so forth, [ending] in the vowels *i* or *u*," then the prescription of *ṅtva* for *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, and *ṅit* would be redundant, and there would be the fault of grammatical discordance (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Examples are: *kṣipati*, *adyautat*, *didivatuḥ*, and *ūyatuḥ*.

In such cases as these, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti). To avoid this, if one were to qualify the vowels *i* and *u* by their being followed by a vowel (*ac*), the result would be cumbersome; this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase "due to proximity" (*āntaratamyāt*), the meaning is "due to the point of articulation" (*sthānataḥ*).

Prau.ma.: *eranekāco’saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.82). Regarding the rule *aci śnudhātu...* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.77), although it contains a copulative compound (*dvandva*), only the term *dhātu* (root) is connected here, and not *śnu* or *bhru*, because the vowel *i* cannot occur in those two.

He explains that the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) qualifies both [the preceding term] by repetition—namely, the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) and the *aṅga* (stem)—in the phrase "conjunction consisting of a portion of a root," and so forth. Therein, because the conjunction is qualified by the root, *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs here in *unnyau* and *unnayaḥ*. However, as for the qualification of the stem (*aṅga*)...

For the sake of establishing forms such as *ṭhharinam*, *harī*, and *harīn*, the base (*aṅgam*) must indeed be qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*). For if the base were not so qualified, then even here— in cases such as *pradhyaṃ* and *pradhdyaḥ*—
the *yaṇ* substitution would occur, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*.
The *it* sound [of the suffix] does not result from the conjunction of the constituent parts of the base (*dhātu*), because the *aṅga* (the base) ends in that [vowel].
This refers to the word *vṛścika*. For the author of the Bhāṣya, relying on a removal (*āpāya*) imagined by the intellect, has rejected the rule "bhītrārthānām"; and consequently...
The intention is that when there is a desire to express mere relationship (*sambandhamātra*), the genitive case alone is used.
Even according to the view of the Sūtra, he says: "related to the scorpion" (*vṛścikasambandhinī*).

[Regarding the form *vṛścika*: "the elision of *at* and the elision of *ya*" (*allopayalopau*). Nor can it be argued that [the rule] "verapṛktasya" would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī].

It must be stated [as an exception] that "the elision of the *ṭh* [augment] and the elision of the single-consonant (*apṛkta*) suffix take precedence by way of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) when *val* follows," according to the statement of the Vārttikakāra. Regarding the phrase "elided in *kvip*": the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
Thus, the meaning is "elision in *kvip*. All of this should also be understood to apply to the form *kumārī*, as in the case of one who desires a maiden (*kumārīm icchan*).

Regarding the term *ananyatayā*: it should be understood that even though [the rule] is secondary (*gauṇa*), the application of the suffixes *anaṅ* and *ṇit* has already been stated. Regarding the phrase *dīrghasyāpi*: the intention is that the mention of the substitution of *yaṇ* was made for this very purpose.
Now, one might object: is the mention of *yaṇ* intended to exclude cases like *atisakheḥ* and *bhūpateḥ*, which fall under the domain of *guṇa*?

If this is argued, let it be so; nevertheless, the application [of the rule] to long vowels remains unavoidable. For there is no authority for the claim that the operation should apply to short vowels and not to long ones. This is because the modified reference in the Sūtra serves to exclude both under-extension (avyāpti) and over-extension (ativyāpti).

This is because [the latter interpretation] possesses that essential core, is likewise appropriate, and is established in the Bhāṣya. As for what the ancients said—stating "some say... and then citing *sakhyuḥ* and so forth—and as for what their commentators stated, that both of these views are established in the Bhāṣya.
And regarding that which was stated here for the sake of support by one acting out of favor—

"Pāṇini says that [the suffix] *khyat* is used for the sake of establishing the friend (*sakhi*) and the husband (*pati*)," those who consider that to be common [to both] would [erroneously] derive forms such as *sukhyuḥ*, *sutyuḥ*, *sakhīḥ*, and *sutīḥ*.
It is known that for the two roots *sukhīyati* and *sutīyati*, which end in the suffix *kvip*,

forms such as *lūni* and *ūrṇuḥ* arise because the substitution [of the penultimate vowel] prescribed by the rule for the *niṣṭhā* suffix is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it.

The verse from the *Vicāracintāmaṇi* beginning with "sukhya" and ending with "bhāṣyagauravāt"— which states that both [the views] are correct— is cited here; let those of refined intellect understand that this entire passage is based on a failure to thoroughly examine the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary.

Regarding the term *śuṣkiya*: as for the examples they cited, such as *śuṣkyuḥ*, *pakvyuḥ*, *śuṣkyaḥ*, and *pakvyaḥ*, and their concluding remark that "this is established in the Bhāṣya," that was due to excessive haste.
Thus end those [stems] ending in -ī.

Prau.ma.: *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.95). The root *kruś* means "to cry out. From this root, the word *kroṣṭṛ* is derived with the suffix *tun* according to the rule *ṣitanī* etc.; however, with the suffix *tṛc*, the word *kroṣṭṛ* is formed. Both words denote a jackal.

In this context, since the application of both [suffixes] would otherwise apply without distinction, the three sūtras are commenced for the purpose of restriction: namely, that before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix and in the feminine, only the form ending in *-tṛc* is used; in the case of the third case and those following, both forms are used; but elsewhere, only the form ending in *-tuN* is used. Thus, *kroṣṭuḥ* is the nominative singular derived from the stem ending in *-tuN*.

The nominative case [is used] after a word ending in *tṛc*. The suffix *vati* is applied after the third-case form *tṛjvat*. Although an extended application (*atideśa*) is sixfold—based on cause (*nimitta*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), identity (*tādātmya*), scripture (*śāstra*), operation (*kārya*), and form (*rūpa*)—here, because of its primacy, only the form is extended. And that [form] is not...

Although it could apply to any root beginning with *pac*, it applies to *kruś* alone because of its proximity, its semantic relevance, and its internal phonetic similarity; intending this, he states the result: "in place of the word *kroṣṭu*.
He says "for the sake of restriction," meaning for the purpose that it should not apply to other technical (*saṃjñā*) words.

Regarding *kroṣṭu*: [the substitution of] *anaṅ* [occurs]. Because it is subsequent to the elision [of the final vowel] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* etc., the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghaḥ*) takes place.

Although that [lengthening] could be obtained by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, nevertheless, because it is subsequent, the rule *aptṛn* is more appropriate. Even when *anaṅ* has been applied, since a modification of a single part does not alter the identity [of the word], [the condition for the application of *aptṛn* remains satisfied].

Because it is a *tric* (a suffix consisting of three letters). The sense is that otherwise, even if the *guṇa* substitution were applied, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would not occur. [From] the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*: "After *ra*, the *s* [is elided]" (*rātsasya*). In this context, there is another view that the letter *ta* is also included by *praśleṣa* (elision/insertion); by that...

If, in place of the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), one were to formulate the refined rule *ṅyāpaḥ soḥ*, then forms such as *abibhar bhavān* would be established. However, in the case of *ajarghāḥ*, because the substitution of *c* for *j* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha* (not yet applied), the elision of the suffix *t* does not take place. If it is objected that [the form] *kīrt* should occur here from the root *kīrtayati* by means of the *kvip* suffix, we say: no.

It should have been stated as *yathālakṣaṇam aprayukte*; for once the substitution of *tṛjvat* has taken place, the suffix *naṭ* would be difficult to obtain due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. As for the rule *num-acira-*, one might object:
"Surely everything that applies within its own scope by the suffix *reṇ* must be superseded, because the general consideration of what is to be superseded (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*) is being adopted."

And so it will be stated: "It is an exception to [the application of] *guṇa*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and *utva*. In this way, since there is no distinction, the augment *nuṭ* would also be barred by this [rule]. If it is asked, "How then can there be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)?
For that is impossible between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*)," [the answer is: True; for that very reason, in that respect—

Having refuted the objection regarding the contradiction, one should be satisfied by the fact that the author of the Bhāṣya stated that the augment *nuṭ* occurs on the basis of the indicatory evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "na tisṛcatasṛ.
Thus end [the words] ending in *-u*.

"Hūhū" is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) technical name (*saṃjñā*). Regarding the word "aticamū," however, this is because of the statement: "And there is the inclusion of the original gender. Thus, the sense is that the older texts stating "in this way, *aticamū* and so forth" are in contradiction with the Bhāṣya.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *varṣābhvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.84): since the word *varṣābhū* is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), it would have been more appropriate to state this sūtra specifically within the section on feminine gender. However, it is stated here with the intention of referring to the word as a masculine action-noun (*kriyāśabda*).
They explained that it should be construed somehow or other, but that is due to haste; for *dardura* is masculine—[as in:
"The words *bheka*, *maṇḍūka*, *varṣābhū*, *śālūra*, *plava*, and *dardura* [denote] a frog."
Thus it is stated by Amara; for he has prescribed the rule that there is no *dvandva* compound of words with different genders:
"The word *bhekyā* [referring to] the frog-lady is feminine, while *varṣābhū* [referring to] the male frog is masculine."
This is also from the *Yādava-kośa*. Regarding "dardure ṣaṇī," there is an alternative reading, "ṣaṇī.
The term "ṣaṇī" is a masculine designation according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*). Regarding "dūbhati": the root *dṛbh* (meaning "to weave") belongs to the *tudādi* class.
As for the statement "it is derived": although Ujjvaladatta [lists] *dṛmph* with the second letter of the labial class (*pavargīya*), [the form here is derived differently].

Although it has been explained that, after reading [the root], the absence of the elision of *n* is prescribed as a *nipātana*, nevertheless, in other commentaries (*vṛtti*) it is stated that from the root *dṛbhī* (to weave) with the suffix *ḍūap*, the augment *nam* is prescribed as a *nipātana*. And this...

This is clear in the *Mādhava-grantha*. However, in the commentary on the *Daśapādī*, it is stated: "In *darbhaṇa* and *dṛmbhūḥ*, the addition of the augment *num* and the substitution of *anusvāra* are irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*). Since this vowel *ū* is not part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution *uvaṅ* does not apply; therefore, by the rule "iko yaṇ aci," there is the *yaṇ* substitution. And that [occurs] in *ami*...

With the intention that [the present rule] is superseded by the two preceding rules—"pūrvaḥ" and "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ"—he provides the examples beginning with *dṛnbhūm*. Nor should one suspect the application of *yaṇ* (vowel coalescence) here as in the case of *dṛnkara*; for in that instance, only a meaningful (*arthavat*) element is taken, whereas this consists of the word *dṛn* and the word *bhū*.

The sense is that [the suffix] is meaningless; thus, the result is that this [word] is like *hūhū*. According to the opinion of Śrīpati, he says "dṛn"; however, Mādhava states that by the rule *andūdṛnbhū*, when the word *dṛḍha* is the upapada, the suffix *kū* is applied, and the substitution of *dṛn* for the upapada is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
Regarding *dṛnbhūḥ*: some say it is a tree, a specific species of serpent; others say it is a monkey. Regarding *dūnkara*:

here, the reading ending in *n* (*dṛn*) is primary, though for some there is also a reading ending in *m* (*dṛm*). It should be stated [as an exception]: "and [the substitution of *u* for *o* occurs] in *varṣābhvaḥ*."
The letter *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; the intention is that what remains unmentioned must be determined by the force of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.
Thus, having explained the Vārttika *varṣābhū-punarbhv-au*, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This which is stated is too little; [the rule should be] *varṣāt ṛn-kāra-punaḥ-pūrvasya bhuvaḥ*."
It must be said that Vāmana, however, did not read the word *dṛś* at all. This being the case, as for what was read by the ancients as *dṛkkāra*, and as for what was stated by his grandson—
that he was repeating the words of the author of the Mahābhāṣya in substance— and as for what others [have said] regarding the *vārttika*:

To claim that [the word] *avatārita* means "he cites a meaning already established" is entirely a product of haste. Nor should one be deluded into thinking that even in the Bhāṣya the reading is simply *dṛk*; for such a view would contradict Mādhava’s statement that [the root] is derived as *andūdṛnbhū*, as well as the works of Kaiyaṭa and others.

This is of little consequence. Regarding the reading "dīrghapāṭhe" (in the long recension): this is the reading agreed upon by many texts such as the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti; however, in the *Anusmṛti*, the short vowel is read. As for what was stated in its commentary—that because a modified form is not distinct from the original, [the rule applies] even to that which is preceded by the letter 'kā'— [The text continues: ...[it is said that] in the case of the word *kāra* being preceded by the letter 'k', since the modified form is not different from the original, the elision of the final syllable occurs according to the rule "allopo 'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). But this is not correct. For if it were so, then in the case of the word *kārya*, where the letter 'k' is present, the elision of the final syllable would follow from the same rule, and thus the form *kārya* would result in *kārya* with the final syllable dropped, which is not desired. Therefore, the author of the *Vṛtti* has stated: "In the case of the word *kāra* being preceded by the letter 'k', there is no elision of the final syllable, because the rule 'allopo 'naḥ' is superseded by the subsequent rule 'anekācaḥ' (Pāṇini 6.4.82). Thus, the reading "dīrghapāṭhe" is indeed the one accepted by the majority of authorities. Furthermore, in the *Kāśikā-vṛtti* on Pāṇini 6.4.140, it is stated: "In the case of the word *kāra* being preceded by the letter 'k', there is no elision of the final syllable. This is also the view of the *Śabdakaustubha*. Moreover, in the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, it is explained: "In the case of the word *kāra* being preceded by the letter 'k', the elision of the final syllable does not occur, because the rule 'anekācaḥ' is stronger than 'allopo 'naḥ'. Hence, the reading "dīrghapāṭhe" is the most authoritative. As for the reading "hrasvapāṭhe" (in the short recension), it is found in the *Anusmṛti* and other minor works, but it is not supported by the great commentaries. Therefore, the reading "dīrghapāṭhe" is the one to be followed. [End of excerpt]

As for the claim that it is established (*siddham*), that is not so; for even then, [the form] qualified by the *aṇ* suffix is different. Indeed, the *aṇ* suffix itself is not a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, the distinction is this: in the short-vowel reading, there is *uvaṅ* for that preceded by *kāra*, and likewise in the long-vowel reading, there is *uvaṅ* for that preceded by *kara*. As for "like *svayambhū*," however, according to the Easterners (*prācām*)...
The words *dṛnbhū* and *kārābhū* are cited like the word *varṣābhū*;
the sense is that they should be disregarded because they lack a valid source. Thus end those [words] ending in *-ū*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

*nṛ ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.6). Here, from the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the term *ubhayathā* ("in both ways") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), while *chandasi* ("in Vedic [usage]") has ceased to apply (*nivṛtam*). Consequently, [the form] *nṛṇām* occurs in the phrase *cintājarjaracetasāṃ bata nṛṇām*.

Some maintain that the phrase "What talk can there be of peace? You alone are the one to be approached by men" [is the meaning]. That is incorrect, because the rule *nṛ ca* would become redundant since its purpose is already accomplished by the preceding rule. Furthermore, some maintain that the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are carried over (*anuvartayanti*) from the preceding rule.
That too is incorrect, because the distinction is not observed in all cases; for instance, in the mantra "dhātā dhātṝṇām," the Taittirīyas read a short vowel, whereas the Bahvṛcas read a long one—
this is the general direction.
Thus end those [stems] ending in ṛ.
"It should be stated as *ota*": the meaning is that, instead of saying *gota*, one should say *ota*.

Thus, having raised the objection that in the case of *gām*, since the rule for *vṛddhi* (P. 7.2.115) applies first due to its higher status, the substitution of *āt* (P. 7.1.94) would not occur, [the author] replies in the sūtra *āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ* (P. 6.1.93) that the *vṛddhi* is superseded by the *āt* substitution because the former has no other scope (*niravakāśatayā*).
The author of the Bhāṣya has stated this. Kaiyaṭa also says thereon: "The reading in the sūtra is *otaḥ*.

Regarding the word *smṛtau*: as for what some say—that by the word *go*, due to similarity, the word *dyo* itself is indicated (by *lakṣaṇā*) and not merely that which ends in *o*, [it follows that] *smṛtau*, *smṛtavau*, *smṛtavaḥ*.

To say "it is exactly thus" contradicts that Bhāṣya; for if one were to accept that the suffix following *go* and *dyo* is indeed *ṇit*, then the rule "āṬto'mśasoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.24), which prescribes the substitution of *āT*, would find its scope in cases such as *anityādiḥ*. And so, in the case of *gām*:

Since the substitution of *vṛddhi* is more powerful due to its higher status, it would be unavoidable; thus, the fact that the substitution of *āt* mentioned in the cited Bhāṣya serves as a sublater and possesses no other scope becomes logically consistent—this is the general direction of the argument.
Thus ends the section on vowels.

Prakriyāmañjarī: Regarding the rule *rāyo hali* (Pāṇini 7.2.85), the word *rāyaḥ* is masculine because of the Amarakośa’s statement, *arthare vibhāṣā api*, and because of usages such as *saṃ rāyā bhūyasā sṛja*. The Bhāṣya states: *rāyiḥ chāndasaḥ* ("The form *rāyiḥ* is Vedic").

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra "vānto yi," states that the form [of the root] with the suffix *kyac*— namely *rai*— is intended to illustrate its Vedic character, but not that of the simple root alone. He further mentions another view, namely that the simple root itself is also Vedic.
Thus end those [stems] ending in -ai and -au.
According to Amarasimha, *ṭhglormṛṅkaḥ kalānidhiḥ* (the moon is the storehouse of digits). Similarly, one who protects people is called *janauḥ*.
By the rule *jvaratvara*, the substitution *ūṭh* occurs; then by *etyedhati*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). Thus, the forms *janāvau*, *janāvaḥ*, and so forth, are derived.
Thus end the masculine nouns ending in vowels. Now begins the section on feminine nouns ending in vowels.
It causes delight. By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding gender-distinctive forms), since it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are applied.

As for the argument that it is because of the suffix *-ā*, and as for what others have explained—that although it is not a nominal stem because it ends in a suffix, the meaning is that the separate mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [in the rule] applies here—that is incorrect.
Since it has already been stated that the inclusion of the term *ṅī* serves another purpose, [one might object]: by the rule *eṅhrasvāt*,
because it is subsequent and because the word is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), once the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) has occurred by the rule *saṃbuddhau ca*,
the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel (*halṅyādi-lopa*) would not apply.

The point is that even if [the substitute] were treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva) regarding the status of being a *āp* suffix, it would lack the form of the vowel *ā*; for the long-vowel (*dīrgha*) rule has been rejected by including the vowel *ā* within the term *āp*. Furthermore, even according to the literal reading [of the sūtra], the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "eṅhrasvāt" is more logically applicable due to its superior status.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: *yāḍāpaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.113). Although it would have been more appropriate to state simply *yāṭ*, there is no occurrence of the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe*, because that is precluded by the very force of the vocalization of the letter *a*.
Nevertheless, one might suspect that the letter *a* [in the rule] is for the purpose of pronunciation; therefore, *yāṭ* has been added for clarity.

As for the example "vṛddhireci" cited by the ancients as "āṭaśca," that is incorrect, because since the *ṭ* of *yāṭ* and *syāṭ* is a marker for the entire group (*samudāyānubandha*), there is no occurrence of *āṭ* here.
Prau.ma.: *sarvanāmnaḥ syāḍḍhrasvaśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.104). The long vowel [in *syāṭ*] is for the sake of the previous [rule], as before. Here they say:
let the sūtra simply be *sarvanāmno'suṅ ca*. And thus, when *yāṭ* follows...

Because [the substitute] *ṅt* is final, the substitution of *asuṅ* for the whole [of *adas*] and so forth is established. However, the purpose of the addition of the marker *ṭ* and the prescription of the short vowel must be considered. Herein lies the consideration: if it were stated simply "and *asuṅ*," forms such as *amuṣmai* would not be established. In reality, however, [the rule] applies to the genitive plural marker *ām* following a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

It would be more appropriate to formulate the rule as *suṭ* and *yāṭo hrasvaśca*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of shortening only for *yāṭ*, because of the force of its long-vowel pronunciation.
Even if a short vowel were pronounced, the force of the letter *a* itself would suffice to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of *ataḥ*.
It should be noted that this is because it is possible [to apply the rule].

Prau.ma.: *vibhāṣā jasi* (Pāṇini 1.1.32). This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) because [the application] would otherwise not have occurred due to the secondary nature (*gauṇatva*) [of the word]. As for what they say—"not in a *bahuvrīhi*"—[that is incorrect].

Regarding the phrase "iti niṣedhe prāpte" (when the prohibition would have thus applied): that is merely superficial, because the former [rule] pertains to all nouns beginning with *sarva* when included within an *alaukika-prakriyā* (preliminary analytical stage), whereas this [present rule] pertains specifically to the context of a compound (*samāsa*). As for the expression "yat-itarā": as they say—she who is the first (*pūrvā*) is the "other" (*itarā*) of her.

Regarding the term *uttarapūrvā*: because of that [preceding rule], there would be the undesirable consequence of reversing the required position of the prior member (*pūrvanipāta*). Regarding the phrase *tīyasya*:
this is indeed necessary for both masculine and neuter genders. The sense is that since the desired result is established by this very [rule], the sūtra "vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyā" need not be composed.
*Prauḍhamanoramā*:

*ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). Regarding this, there is a *vārttika*: *māturmātajputrārthamarhate*. Upon the utterance of the word *mātṛ*, the substitute *mātaj* occurs [before the suffix *ap*] when it is intended for the sake of the son of the mother.

When excellence (*ślāghyatva*) is to be expressed: *gārgīmātṛkaḥ* means "one whose mother is Gārgī. Its vocative is *he gārgīmāta*. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix prescribed by the rule *nady-utaś-ca*. However, where excellence is not to be expressed, but there is merely a statement of the actual form (*svarūpa-kathana-mātra*), [the suffix does not apply].

*Kabavana*—that which ends in *ā* is a feminine stem (*aṅga*). As for what was stated by those explaining the rule *yāḍāpaḥ*: "In the case of *atikhaṭvāyai*, because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical derivation), the augment *yāṭ* does not apply;
however, in the case of *atisarvāyai*, it would not [apply] either"—this is due to haste. For in the domain of extended application (*atideśa*), [the rule applies].

The paribhāṣā "the rule applies to that which is taught by its specific technical name" (lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā) operates here; otherwise, the extension [of the rule] would be rendered useless. Consequently, *yāṭ* is unavoidable. However, there is no possibility of *syāṭ* at all, because it is excluded by the fact that it is listed among both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). As for the phrase "some, however," this refers to the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* and others.

Prau.ma.: *ṅiti hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.6). This is an option where there was no prior application (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*). For while the short vowels [the feminine stems *stri* and *bhrū*] were not subject to this rule, and for the other two [the masculine *pati* and *nadī*], the prohibition *neyaRuvaṅsthānau* (Pāṇini 1.4.4) had already applied, this sūtra is introduced [to provide an option].

The three terms *īdūtau*, *strīśabdabhinna*, and *nityastrīliṅgau* are qualifiers of [the vowels] *ī* and *ū*; however, for the short vowels (*hrasva*), only *striyām* applies, and not the further qualification of being "always feminine" (*nityastrītva*). Otherwise, [the rule would apply] to words such as *iṣu* and *aśani*, which possess both genders.

Furthermore, even though all *liṅga* (grammatical genders) are feminine, they would not necessarily be treated as "rivers" (*nadī*), because according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, they lack "eternal femininity" (*nityastrītva*); and even in Haradatta’s opinion, there is no instance to be excluded by the inclusion of the word "eternal" (*nitya*) regarding the short vowel portion. For this very reason, one should abandon the mention of the term "designation" (*ākhyā*) and use the word "feminine" (*strī*) alone.
It is extracted and connected [to the previous rule]; this is what he says: "The vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*, as well as *i* and *u*, [are short] in the feminine.

Regarding the phrase "when *āṬtva* would have been applicable," the intention is that it is due to its being a subsequent rule (*paratvāt*). As for the explanation given by the ancients (*prācā*) under the rule "āt"—namely, that [the rule applies] "excepting those designated as *ghit* and *nadī*"—that is not the literal meaning of the syllables; rather, [it is a secondary interpretation].

This is obtainable from the two preceding sūtras. Thus, the omission of the citation of the sūtra *idudbhyām* by the ancient commentators is merely due to oversight (*prāmādika*). [Prau.ma.: *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.100)]

Regarding the phrase *aci ra ṛtaḥ*: this refers to the substitution of *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva*. For example, in *tisra tiṣṭhanti*, there is the *guṇa* substitution [of *ṛ*] by the rule *ṛto ṅi* (Pāṇini 7.3.110); in *tisraḥ paśya*, there is the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* substitution by the rule *prathamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102);
and in *priyatisra āgataḥ* and *priyatisraḥ svam*, there is the *utva* substitution by the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111).

The meaning is that "ratvam" (the substitution of *ra*) is an exception (*apavāda*); the sense is that in a consideration of the general category of what is to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything that has obtained its scope is sublated. However, in a consideration of specific cases (*viśeṣacintā*), by the maxim "exceptions [sublate] those in their midst," there would be a sublation only of the long vowel and the *utva*, but not of the *guṇa*.

It is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others that the positions regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are established in accordance with the requirements of the specific grammatical targets (*lakṣya*), just like the positions regarding the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).
As for what they [the commentators] have explained— that the word "exception" (*apavāda*) indicates sublation (*bādhakatva*)— it is by means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

The intention [of the opponent] is that [the *guṇa* substitution] also subverts [the application of] the *guṇa*. That [argument] is baseless and flawed. As for what Prasādakṛt has stated—"the meaning is that the *guṇa* is the subverter by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), while the other two are subverters by means of a subsequent prohibition (*paravipratiṣedha*)"—that is not correct, because the injunction [of the *guṇa*] would otherwise have no scope for its operation.
Nor do the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṅasi-ṅas* have their purpose fulfilled [by the substitution of *yaṇ*], because that purpose has already been served by the *yaṇ* replacement.

This is because of the qualification "of three or four. For, since the word "three or four" (*tricatur*) is directly heard in the rule, it is this very term that is qualified by "in the feminine" (*striyām*), and not the *aṅga* (the base). Thus, in the example *priyatri*, [the following applies]: In this case...
They explain [the objection] as follows: since "woman" (*strī*) is the referent of the compound, the *bahuvrīhi* form of the body (*aṅga*) resides therein;
however, because the word "three" (*tri*) applies only to the masculine and neuter genders, the substitution *tisṛ* does not occur, and so forth. Here, this must be said:
in the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) view, the word "three" has multiple meanings; but in the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) view, however—
[The word *tri*] indeed occurs in the feminine; how then can its occurrence in the masculine and neuter be consistent?
Herein lies the truth: here, a "meaning-abandoning" (*jahatsvārthā*) function is intended, in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*).
Therefore, [the statement] "the limb (*aṅga*) in the feminine" is perfectly correct. As for the word *tri* denoting both masculine and neuter—

This is because the established doctrinal tenets—such as "a *tatpuruṣa* compound is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant"—must be explained in this very way by recourse to the state of having previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). Likewise, in the case of "the man who has a beloved wife" (*priyātasā pumān*), even the application [of the feminine suffix] to the woman is based solely on the state of having previously existed. This is according to the view that [the compound] does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthāpakṣe*).
However, the intended meaning here is "of the words *tri* and *catur*, which convey a number residing in a feminine.

The textual passage from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "pratyayottarapadayośca" serves as the authority for this point. As for the phrase "because of its non-eternality," the inclusion of the term *ac* in the rule "iko'ci" is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this matter.

For that [prohibition] was indeed made to prevent *num* in the vocative; because even when *num* occurs in the case of *bhyām* and so on, its elision is possible. Furthermore, since the vocative is elided by *luk*, the application of *num* would have to be stated by means of the rule for "the presence of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). And the rule for "the presence of a suffix" depends on the non-universality of the prohibition "not when [an element] marked by *lu* or *mu* follows" (*na lumatā*).

That [the suffix -tva] is difficult to obtain without [a preceding vowel] is clear from the grammatical source (ākara). Nor should one insist that this impermanence (*anityatva*) applies exclusively to the domain of the *saṃbuddhi* (vocative singular) case-ending;
for there is no obstacle to accepting it in other instances as well, provided it conforms to the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). And so:
The two forms *priyatisṛ* and *priyatri* are both supported by Kaiyaṭa in the manner already described.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*), there is no lack of evidence here; for the very examples cited in the Bhāṣya, such as *priyatisṛṇi*, serve as proof in this regard. [The rule applies] when *dvir̥* has become *atva* (the substitution of *a*) and the suffix *āP* is present.
