The meaning is that even the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (i.e., *tad*), which is occasioned by the occurrence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), serves as the cause for the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; this is because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory, as evidenced by the rule "na yāsayoḥ."

Regarding the term "iyādeśa": the substitution of *iy* prescribed for [the word] when followed by a vowel-initial suffix applies only to the four cases beginning with the nominative (*au*, etc. when the feminine word *strī* is used as a secondary member (*upasarjana*) in the masculine gender, and not elsewhere; the meaning is that it is precluded in other instances by the previously mentioned rules concerning *guṇa*, *nābhāva*, and so forth.

*Prau.ma.*: *neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.4). Those two in which [something] stands are called *sthānau*; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). The compound *iyaRuvaṅsthānau* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, meaning "those that have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes."

He states the purpose of the meaning [of the word *sthiti*]: "the presence (*sthiti*) of *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ* for which two. This prohibition applies only where *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ* are produced; however, where they would be sublated by an exception (*apavāda*), there is no prohibition.
It is for this reason that the term *sthiti* (presence) is employed.

Prau.ma.: *vāmi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.38). Although the ancients held that this rule provides an option for the previously established prohibition, nevertheless, when there is an option regarding a prohibition, it results in an option regarding a positive injunction. And thus, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that [positive injunction] alone is adopted.
With the intention that this meaning of the sūtra is appropriate, he says: "Or, they are both termed *nadī*. This is exactly the same in the sūtra "ṅiti hrasvaśca" as well.
[The opponent asks: "How then? [The answer is: Because there is an absence of *nadī*-status due to having *uvaṅ* as its substitute, the short vowel is untenable.

This is the objection. Regarding the word "many": some resolve this by carrying over the mention of the option (*vā*) from the rule "vāmi" and relying on a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). That is weak; for if that were the case, the mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) here and the subsequent rule "vāmi" would both become redundant. Others, however...
They somehow justify [the neuter gender] by the rule *sāmānye napuṃsakam* ("the neuter is used for general reference").
Regarding the sūtra *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.7), because it is explained as "that which was prescribed for the feminine does not apply," the immediately preceding [rule]...
With the intention that the suffix *ṭāp* is also prohibited just as the suffix *ṅīp* is, he says: "The suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṭāp* do not [apply].
The meaning is that this is because the word *rai* is traditionally remembered (*smaraṇāt*) as being feminine.
Thus, Kṣīrasvāmī states: "Some say that *rāḥ* is a feminine noun, derived from the sense 'she gives' (*rāti enam*). [This applies] in the feminine.
"Naustaraṇi and tari are synonyms for a boat," according to Amara.
Thus end the feminine nouns ending in vowels.
Now begins the section on indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Prau.ma.: *svarādinipātamavyayam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.37). The compound *svarādinipāta* is a collective dvandva meaning "the group beginning with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*). *Svar* refers to heaven and the world beyond; *antar* means in the middle.

*Prātaḥ* means at dawn; *punar* means again or in a special sense; *sunutar* means in concealment. [The following] five particles begin with *svar* and end with *repha*. *Uccais* means great; *nīcais* means small; *śanais* means slowness of action; *ṛdhak* means truth.

Others [list] *viyoga* (separation), *śīghra* (speed), *sāmīpya* (proximity), and *lāghava* (lightness); *ṛte* is used in the sense of exclusion; *yugapat* means at the same time; *ārāt* means at a distance or in proximity; *pṛthak* means separately or differently; *hyas* means on the past day; *divā* means during the day; *rātrau* means at night; and *sāyam* means at the onset of night.
*Ciram* means for a long time; *manāk* and *īṣat* mean slightly; *imau* (these two) mean small; *joṣam* means in happiness or silence;
*tūṣṇīm* means in silence; *bahiḥ* and *avas* mean outside; *samayā* means near or in the middle; *nikaṣā* means in the vicinity; *svayam* means by oneself; *vṛthā* means in vain.

*naktam* means "at night. *nañ* is used in the sense of negation. *hetau* means "on account of" or "by reason of. *iddha* signifies "manifestness. *addhā* denotes both "clarity" and "certainty," though some say it refers to "reality" and "excellence. *sāmīpya* signifies "proximity" and "disgust. *vat* is the suffix *vati* prescribed by rules such as "that which is equal to that" (*tena tulyam*).
The suffix *pratyaya*—specifically that which is prescribed by the rule "upasargāddhātvarthe"—is not included here, as in the example:

*yad udvato nivato yāsi*. The forms *sanā* and *sanat* are eternal (*nitya*). The form *upadhā* denotes distinction. *Tiras* is used in the sense of disappearance, lateral direction, and contempt. *Antara* is used in the sense of the middle.

*Vinā* is used in the sense of "without. *Antareṇa* is used in the sense of exclusion. *Jyok* is used in the senses of time, abundance, inquiry, swiftness, and the present moment. *Kam* is used in the senses of water, head, censure, and happiness. *Śam* means happiness. *Sahasā* is used in the senses of suddenness and lack of deliberation. *Vinā* is used in the sense of exclusion.

*nānā* is used in the senses of "many" and "separately"; *svasti* in the sense of "auspiciousness"; *svadhā* in the offering to ancestors; *alam* in the senses of "ornament," "sufficiency," "capability," "prohibition," and "negation"; *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *śrauṣaṭ* are used in the offering of oblations;
*anyat* in the sense of "other"; and *asti* in the sense of "existence."

*Upāṃśu* denotes that which is uttered inaudibly or in secret; *kṣamā* denotes forbearance; *vihāyas* denotes the sky; *doṣā* denotes night; *mṛṣā* and *mithyā* denote falsehood; *mudhā* denotes in vain; *purā* denotes the unrestrained, the distant past, and the near future; *mathas* and *mithas* [denote together].

These two [words] are used in the senses of "secret" and "purpose. *Prāyas* is used in the sense of "mostly" (*bāhulye*). *Mahus* is used in the sense of "again" (*punararthe*). *Pravāhukam* is used in the sense of "simultaneously" (*samakāle*) and "accomplished purpose" (*siddhārthe*). *Pravāhikā* is an alternative reading. *Āryahalam* is used in the sense of "force" (*balātkāre*). Śākaṭāyana, however, [states that] *ārya* is used in the sense of "obstruction" (*pratibandhe*), and *hala*...

He says [the following apply] in the sense of negation and dispute: *ābhīkṣṇya* means repetition; *sākam* and *sārdham* have the meaning of "together" (*saha*); *namas* is used in the sense of bowing; *hiruk* in the sense of exclusion;
*dhik* in the sense of censure, contempt, and reproach; *am* in the sense of slowness and smallness; and *ām* in the sense of acceptance.

Some maintain that the suffix prescribed by the rules "kimettiṅavyaya-gomahat... and "kās-pratyayād ām am... is also included here; for example: *papācatarām* and *kārayāmāsa*. [The roots] *pratām* in the sense of fatigue (*glāni*), *praśān* in the sense of tranquility (*samāna*), and *pratān* in the sense of expansion (*vistāra*) are included. [The particles] *mā* and *māṅ* are these two.

Regarding "doubt" (śaṅkā) and "prohibition" (niṣedha): it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Therefore, others should also be understood [as belonging to this category]. For instance: *kāmaṃ* is used in the sense of "according to one's will" (*svācchandyena*);
*prakāmam* in the sense of "excessively" (*atiśaye*); *bhūyaḥ* in the sense of "again" (*punararthe*); and *sāmpratam* in the sense of "properly" (*nyāyye*).

*param* means "but" (*kiṃtu*); *sākṣāt* means "directly" (*pratyakṣe*); *sāci* means "obliquely" (*tiryagarthe*); *satyam* means "half-acceptance" (*ardhāṅgīkāre*); *maṅkṣu* and *āśu*—these two mean "speedily" (*śaighrye*); *samvat* means "in the year" (*varṣe*); *avaśyam* means "certainly" (*niścaye*); *sapadi* means "speedily" (*śaighrye*); *balavat* means "excessively" (*atiśaye*); *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* [mean "manifestly"].
Thus in the *Prakāśa*: *aniśam*, *nityam*, *nityadā*, *ajasram*, and *santatam*—these denote continuity.

*Uṣā* means at night. *Rodasī* signifies heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). *Ai* denotes acceptance and also Brahman. *Bhūḥ* refers to the earth. *Bhuvaḥ* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). *Jhagiti*, *jhaṭiti*, and *tarasā* [denote speed].

*Śairghye* means slowness; *suṣṭhu* in the sense of excellent praise; *duṣṭhu* in the sense of difficulty or distress; *su* in the sense of worship or honor; *aha* in the sense of wonder; *ku* in the sense of reproach or deficiency; *añjasā* in the sense of reality or swiftness; *mithu* in the sense of "two"; *bhājak* in the sense of slowness; *cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*.

*ciraṃ*, *cirāt*, and *cireṇa*—these have the sense of "long. *astaṃ* signifies destruction. *ānuṣak* signifies succession (*ānupūrvya*). *anuṣak* signifies lack of support (*anudāna*). *amnaḥ* signifies both coldness and the present time. *stāne* is used in the sense of "fitting" or "proper. *varam* is used when something is said to be "slightly" so. *sudi* refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). *vadi* refers to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
And so forth.

*Vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so on; "vā syādvikalpopamayorevārthe'pi samuccaye" (vā may be used in the sense of option, comparison, the meaning of *eva*, and also in conjunction).
*Ha* is used in the sense of renown (*prasiddhi*). *Aha* is used in the sense of reverence (*pūjā*).

*eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and for impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). *evam* is used for referring back to what has been said (*uktaparāmarśa*). *nūnam* is used for certainty (*niścaya*) and for reasoning (*tarka*). *śaśvat* is used for repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), for the eternal (*nitya*), and for the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). *yugapat* is used for simultaneity (*aikakālya*). *bhūyas* is used for the sense of "again" (*punarartha*) and for excess (*ādhikya*). *kūpat* is used for questioning (*praśna*).

And [the particle] *praśaṃsāyām* (in the sense of praise). *Kuvid* is used in the sense of prosperity (*bhūti*) and in praise. *Ned* is used in the senses of apprehension (*śaṅkā*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), deliberation (*vicāra*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). *Cet* is used in the sense of "if" (*yadī*). *Caṇ*—this has the indicatory letter *ṇ* when it means "if"; however, when used in the sense of conjunction and so forth, it is without an indicatory letter (*ananubandha*). *Kaccit* is used in an inquiry regarding something desired (*iṣṭapraśna*).

The particle *yatra* is used in the senses of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), impatience (*amarṣa*), censure (*garhā*), and wonder (*āścarya*). For example: "I do not believe it, I cannot endure it, I censure it, or I am amazed that you, sir, should officiate at a sacrifice for a low-caste man (*vṛṣala*). The particle *na hi* is used in the sense of a counter-undertaking (*pratyārambha*). The particle *hanta* is used in joy (*harṣa*), dejection (*viṣāda*), compassion (*anukampā*), and the commencement of a sentence (*vākyārambha*). [The particles] *mākiḥ* and *mākiṃ*...
The three words *nakiḥ*, *mā*, and *nañ* are used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

*Mā* and *nañ* have already been mentioned among the *svarādi* (the list beginning with *svara*) particles. Their inclusion here, however, is for the sake of their being treated as *nipātas* (indeclinables).
According to the ancients, this ensures that they possess the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*); but that view is questionable.

Since the desired result is achieved even by means of the *phiṭ-svara* accent, that which they say—that the inclusion [of these words] in the list beginning with *svar-ādi* is for the purpose of assigning the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) even to those expressing existence (*satva-vacana*)—is also to be considered. For otherwise, the word *mā*, which denotes the goddess Lakṣmī, would undesirably incur the status of an indeclinable. Therefore, the purpose of including them in both lists must be investigated.

In all these cases, *yāvat* and *tāvat* function as particles of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Regarding totality: "As much work as there was, so much has been done" (*yāvat kāryaṃ tāvat kṛtam*). Regarding limit: "Stay as long as you have to go" (*yāvad gantavyaṃ tāvattiṣṭha*).

Regarding measure: "As much as was given, so much was eaten" (*yāvad dattaṃ tāvad bhuktam*). Regarding restriction: "Invite as many Brahmins as there are vessels" (*yāvadamatraṃ brāhmaṇān āmantrayasva*).

*tvai* is used for emphasis (*viśeṣa*) and deliberation (*vitarka*). *Dvai* is used for deliberation (*vitarka*). *Nvai* is another reading. *Rai* is used in the sense of giving (*dāna*) and disregard (*anādara*). In *rai karoti*, the meaning is "he gives. "What will you do? *Śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are used in the offering of oblations (*havirdāna*). *Svāhā* is used in the offering to the deities. *Svadha*—[is used in the offering to the ancestors].
To the ancestors. The reading of polysyllabic words such as *śrauṣaṭ* and others in both places is for the sake of distinguishing their accents.

*Tum* refers to the sound *tuṅ*. Having uttered *tuṅ* toward the teacher—that is, having uttered *huṅ*. For instance, it is shown in the illustration. *Khalu* is used in the sense of prohibition, sentence ornamentation, or certainty. *Kila*...

[The particle] *vā* is used in the sense of news (*vārtā*) and falsehood (*alīka*). Now, *atha* is used in the senses of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), immediately following (*anantara*), commencement (*ārambha*), inquiry (*praśna*), entirety (*kārtsnya*), authority (*adhikāra*), promise (*pratijñā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

This [particle] also begins with a vowel (*svarādi*). Therefore, although it denotes auspiciousness, it possesses the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because its meaning is existent (*satvārtha*).
And so it is said by Śrī Harṣa: "Then,
having lifted the golden jars onto the interior of the altar-platform, which was beautiful with its fourfold splendor,
the group of women bathed the king’s daughter according to the family custom."
For here, the phrase "snapayāmbabhūva" means "he performed an auspicious bathing";

however, the particle [the initial *s- sound] is auspicious by its very nature, like the sound of a drum. The reading with the prefix *su-* is for the purpose of distinguishing the accent. The word *smā* is used in the sense of the past tense and as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*).
The word *ādaha* is used in the senses of beginning, injury, and reproach.
Regarding *avadatam*: here, because it is not a preposition (*upasarga*), the rule "after a vowel preceded by a preposition" does not apply.
*Aham* is an indeclinable that resembles a case-inflected form (*subanta*). By this [analysis], [the objection] "by whom were you two trained in what is to be sung? is addressed.
This has been explained. For *vām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) used in the sense of "you two. *Asti* is a form resembling a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Similarly, *asmi* is used in the sense of "I";
thus, *tvāmasmi vacmi* means "I speak to you. *Āha* means "he said" (*uvāca*). *Āsa* means "he was" (*babhūva*), and so forth.
*a* is used for addressing, censuring, and prohibition; *ā* for sentences and recollection; *i* for addressing, disgust, and wonder; *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *āṬ* for addressing;
*paśu* for the sense of "correctly"; as in *paśu manyamānāḥ* ("regarding [it] correctly"); and *śukam* for speed.

*yathākathāca* is used in the sense of disregard. *pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *he*, *hai*, and *bho*—these are used for addressing (*sambodhana*). *dyā* is used in the senses of "so be it," prohibition, opposition, and as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*). *viṣu* is used in the sense of "various" (*nānārtha*). *ekapade* is used in the sense of "suddenly" (*akasmāt*). *yut* is used in the senses of censure (*kutsā*) and cause (*hetu*). *ātaḥ* is used in the sense of "even from this" (*ito 'pi*).

It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of particles). For example: *yat* and *tat* are used in the sense of cause; *āhosvit* in the sense of an alternative; *sima* in the sense of totality; *kaṃ* for filling a verse-line (*pādapūraṇa*); *sukam* in the sense of excellence; *anukaṃ* in the sense of deliberation; *śamvaṭ* in the sense of the internal organ and also in the sense of facing toward; *va* for filling a verse-line and in the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*); *diṣṭyā*.

Thus: *ānande* (in joy); *cuṭua* and *cāṭua* (in endearing speech); *hum* (in reproach); *iva* (in similarity); *adyatve* (in the sense of "now" or "at present"), and so forth. Here, this should be noted: although there is no difference in the fact that both the *svara*-group and the *ca*-group are *ākṛtigaṇas*, [only those...]

The accent of particles (*nipāta*) is seen among those beginning with *ca*; others [the indeclinables] are among those beginning with *svar*. However, it should be understood that those possessing both accents belong in both groups. For example, the word *uta* is among those beginning with *svar*, as seen in the usage *ṭhīḍaḷe nūtanairuta*, where it has the final acute accent (*antodātta*). As for the word *uta*:

Having stated that [the word] begins with a vowel (*svarādi*), they attempted to resolve the objection regarding its accent by resorting to the rule for *nipāta*s ending in the acute (*antodātta*), but this was done impulsively; for it does not begin with a vowel, and because it is an *antodātta* *nipāta*, such a designation would result in redundancy. Furthermore, as it has been stated in the *Kāśikā*:

The statements that *svar*, *śanais*, *ṛdhak*, *divā*, *vṛthā*, *naktam*, and so forth are oxytone (antodātta), and that *sanat*, *sanāt*, and so forth are proparoxytone (ādyudātta)— all of this is merely due to negligence (*prāmādika*), because it contradicts the observed usage (*lakṣya*) and lacks any authoritative basis (*nirmūlatva*). Thus it is stated in the *Śabdakaustubha*.
This has been explained. *Prakriyā-pradīpa*: "And a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that does not take all case-endings" (Pāṇini 1.1.38).

Regarding the word "all": the meaning is that it consists of the three numbers (singular, dual, and plural). Regarding "not": the sense is that only the singular number is produced. What is an example of a *taddhita*? *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *trayaḥ*.
What is the meaning of "asarva" and so forth? [The answer is: *aupagavaḥ*. [From] Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.39:

*kṛnmejantaḥ* ("A word ending in a suffix beginning with *m* that follows a *kṛt*-suffix is indeclinable"). [An example is] *jīvase*; here, the suffix *ase* is applied by [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.9]: *tumarthe sesen* ("The suffixes *se*, *sen*, and *ase* are used in the sense of the infinitive marker *tum*").
Regarding the form *pibaddhyai*: the suffix *śadhyai* is added for the sake of the sense of obligation (*śadhyai*), and by the rule *pāghrā*, there is the substitution of *piba*.

As for what they say—that [the suffix] *śap* occurs when there is an agent—that is due to haste. For the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "kṛt suffixes added to indeclinables denote the action (*bhāva*). The inclusion of the term "end" (*antagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of understanding that [the substitute] must be taught as such (*aupadeśikatva*). Therefore, it does not apply here.

[The word] *ādhaye* [is used as an example]. [The word] *cikīrṣave* [is used as an example]. This [sūtra] is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of these two [rules], so that they may be established by both the rule for forms explicitly stated (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) and the maxim regarding the combination of operations (*sannipātaparibhāṣā*). (Prau.ma.: Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.40: *ktvā-tosun-kasunaḥ*).

Regarding the rule *ktvātosunkasunaḥ*: *udetoḥ* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut*, with the suffix *tosun* added according to the rule *bhāvalakṣaṇe stheṇkṛñvadicarihutamijanibhyastosun*. *Visṛpaḥ* is derived according to the rule *sṛpitṛdoḥ kasun*.

Regarding the inclusion of the term *āp*: likewise, the Vārttika states—"The prescription of elision (*luk*) of *āp* after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is purposeless, because [indeclinables] lack gender. However, the possibility of stating this rule should be understood by adopting the alternative view in the sūtra "striyām" that [the word *strī*] is in apposition with the feminine noun. This is because [indeclinables] are devoid of gender (*aliṅgatva*).
Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the scriptural statements found in the *Atharva-vidyā*, he says: "similarly" (*sadṛśam*).

Regarding the phrase "liṅga-kāraka": the intention is that the words *vibhakti* (case) and *vacana* (number) refer to *kāraka* (grammatical relation) and *saṃkhyā* (number). As for the example "by speech" (*vācā*): some say this is an exhaustive enumeration, while others say it is merely an illustration.
Regarding the term *vagāha*: only the initial vowel *a* is elided, not the final one, due to its association with the word *api*. Thus end the indeclinables.
Now, the avyayībhāva compound.

Regarding the phrase "based on capability" (*samarthāśrita*): the sense is that in the Sūtra, the word *samartha* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). Regarding the phrase "only a few": although the author of the Vārttika has stated in the section on obligatory compounds (*nityādhikāra*) that there is a compound of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) with [a word] possessing the meaning of "like" (*udātavat*) or "possessing motion" (*gatimat*), nevertheless, that is not mandatory, as in the example "he brought it" (*ty ānayat*).

Because [the formation] in examples such as *abhiprabharadhṛṣata* is not seen to result from a compound; for this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya established this by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) using the word *saha*. The intention is that the authority of the sages increases in successive order.
And as for the phrase *sa ca*: this too is solely for the sake of establishing the desired result through *yogavibhāga*.
This is clearly stated in the *Padamañjarī* on the sūtra defining the technical term *sampradāna*.

For if this were the case even in common usage (*loka*), then in examples such as *abhipraiti*, the case endings beginning with *su* (i.e., nominative and so forth) would arise from the compound, just as they do in *pacatikalpam* and similar forms ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*). And this is not [the case].

The resolution [of the objection] by accepting that the universal gender (sarvanāman) *liṅga* is neuter is untenable, because in forms such as *prakurute*, there would be the occurrence of a short vowel, and in *prakurvīran*, there would be the occurrence of the elision of the *n*.

[Regarding the phrase] "because of the specific mention" (*nirdeśāt*): for otherwise, even though there is no distinction in being mentioned in the nominative case, [the rule would apply indiscriminately].
The intention is that, because the designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) is based on its literal meaning (*anvartha*), the word *pūrva* alone would be placed first [in the compound].
Regarding the rule "with *iva*" (*ivena*): this compound also occurs only in certain instances, as previously mentioned; for example, *jīmūtasyeva*.
In such instances as these, the Taittirīyas read the words separately; thus, even the separate usage in "udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ" and similar examples is consistent.
[Prau.ma.: Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.48—*go-striyor upasarjanasya*]

Regarding the rule *gostriyoḥ*: [the phrase] "that which is an *upasarjana*" refers to the word *go*. As for what the Easterners (Prācāḥ) stated—that it refers to an *upasarjana* ending in *go* or a feminine suffix—that is incorrect; because in examples such as *citragu*, although the word *go* is an *upasarjana*, the entire compound ending in it (*citragu*) is not so.

Furthermore, because there would be an over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *gaurīpatiḥ* and others. If it is asked, "How then [do you explain] *sugokulam* and *rājakumārīputraḥ*?"—listen: since a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is by nature relational, with respect to the meaning of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for which the shortening is prescribed, [the rule applies].

The shortening of the vowel occurs only when the two members [of the compound] have become subordinate (guṇībhāva) as the final members. Regarding "diśayoḥ": even if the analysis is made with the form ending in a consonant, *diśoḥ*, the resulting form remains the same; for the word *diś* takes the suffix *ṭac* because it belongs to the *śarad-ādi* group.

"By virtue of the force of the statement": for by the word *vibhakti* (in the rule), only that case-ending which forms part of the *subanta* (inflected word) with which the compound is formed is understood, due to proximity (*sannidhāna*).
And the sense is that the particle *adhi* indicates the meaning of that [case-ending]. However, in the *Parishishta*, this [is stated] with a nominative ending.

There are two established positions: that the compound is formed with a word ending in the genitive case, or otherwise. As for what was stated by the ancients—that in the analysis (*vigraha*) "having Hari as the subject" (*harim adhikṛtya*), the form "harāv adhi" results—that is incorrect, because an analysis is impossible due to its being an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). As they say: "An obligatory compound is one that lacks an analysis."

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that even a non-synonymous analysis (asvapadavigraha) is accepted, as in 'he makes a jar' (*kumbhaṃ karoti*)? Let this [term *adhikṛtya*] also be like that, since the form ending in the suffix *-lyap* does not enter into the compound"?
[Response]: No, because in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), that which does not convey even a trace of the meaning of the compound cannot [be so treated].
Because entry itself is impossible.

As for what they have explained—that "vigraha" (analysis) is like "vigraha" (body), being merely an explanation of the meaning—therefore, because it lacks a formal analysis (*avigrahatva*), its status as a *nityasamāsa* (invariably compound) is not contradictory. For this very reason...

He shows another non-worldly sentence which serves as the basis for the compound: "it stands as 'harau adhīti'. Here, this must be said: [the claim] that it is "like the analytical statement" (vigraha) is inconsistent, because the very sentence used to explain the meaning is itself the analytical statement; therefore...

This is because there is no difference [between the two cases]. Nor is it merely a statement of the meaning, for the suffix -lyap does not touch upon the meaning of the compound. Furthermore, as for what was said—that *hari adhīti* is ungrammatical (*alaukika*)—that too is incorrect, because in that case only *hari ṅ* enters [into the formation], according to the rule: "Even those operations which are internal... (*antaraṅgān api*).
This follows from logical necessity (*nyāya*); otherwise, it would follow that the vowel *i* in the word *hari* would be difficult to obtain within the compound.

As for what they [the commentators] have explained—that because it is extra-ordinary (*alaukika*), the locative case occurs even though the sense is already expressed by the prefix *adhi*, for otherwise it would not occur due to the governing rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1)—that too is merely superficial.

For "extraordinary character" (*alaukikatva*) indeed means "not being fully established" by virtue of being the object of another permanent rule (*nityavidhi*); however, it is not easily established that the locative case (*saptamī*), which is itself untaught [by a specific rule], enters into that [definition] merely on this basis.

Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As for what was explained by his grandson— that because of the enumeration (*parigaṇana*) "by means of verbal suffixes, *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes,

and compounds," the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs even when [the sense] is already expressed by *adhi*— that is not correct, because such an enumeration does not exist in the original treatise (*ākara*).

Because [the use of the accusative] has been rejected, because it was stated by the author himself in the very same manner in the rule "The second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), and because it would contradict such usages as "He recognized him as Nārada in due order" (*kramādamuṃ nārada ityabodhi saḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "of the second and the fifth [cases]": this is clear in the *Rakṣi* commentary. As for what they say—that in examples such as *caitrasya vanād ārāt*, because the word is dependent on another (*sāpekṣatva*), it has already fulfilled its purpose in not forming a compound, and thus there is no capacity for the rule to apply—this is to be questioned, because [the rule applies to] obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*).
For if [the compound] were logically valid, the employment of qualifiers such as "of Caitra" and so forth would be impossible.

Indeed, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "There is no connection with a qualifier for that which has already undergone composition (*vṛta*). If it is objected: "But is it not also stated in the Bhāṣya that 'there is no composition for those possessing qualifiers'?"—True; however, that refers to the domain of non-obligatory compounds (*anityasamāsa*).

Consequently, if the *nitya-samāsa* (invariable compound) were not to apply even when qualifiers are present, such forms as *mahataḥ kumbhasyopa* would result. As for what the ancients stated— that [the rule applies] "after *kṛṣṇa*"— and what their commentators explained—
that this occurs "when such an analytical sentence (*prakriyā-vākya*) stands"— both of these are merely due to oversight, according to the reasoning previously stated.

"Now, *samprati*. The indeclinable *samprati* means "now" (*idānīm*). As Amarasimha states: "In this sense [are used] *etarhi*, *samprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, and *sāmpratam*. Furthermore, because it primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it is fit to be construed only with a verbal form. The negation (*niṣedha*) as well—
It belongs to the action itself.

Thus he says: "it is joined" (*yujyate*). Regarding "not being current" (*asamprati*): in a compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*), however, the action of joining (*yujikriyā*) is included, just as the action of sprinkling is in the case of "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*). As for that which...

It was stated previously: "Non-present" (*asamprati*) means the absence of the present. By this, it is intended that only the present time of the object to be enjoyed is negated. That is not correct, because the logical connection of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the negation is contrary to all established systems (*sarvatantra-viruddha*). For indeed...
Some maintain that by the statement "there is no jar on the ground," the ground itself is negated;

however, this is not tenable, so let us set that aside for now. Regarding the phrase *iti harau*: there is a compound of the word *iti*, meaning "thus" or "in this manner," with the word *hari*, which ends in the genitive case and refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Regarding the word *pratiśabdasya*: as for what they say—that in the case of *grāmasya vṛkṣaṃ prati*, the prescription of the second case (*dvitīyā*) has its scope when there is no compound due to the state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*)—that has already been refuted previously.
Haradatta, however, says that because of the usage by the author of the Bhāṣya in *arthamarthaṃ prati*, the sentence form is also correct.

Alternatively, the indeclinable here does not function as a distributive (*vīpsā*) particle; rather, because it is a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits a relationship. Distributive repetition, however, is indicated by reduplication.

[The example] "together with the forenoon" (*saha-pūrvāhṇam*) is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of totality (*sākalya*). [The phrase] "even though it is subordinate" (*guṇabhūte 'pi*) means that if...

The point is that if "sādṛśya" (similarity) were not mentioned [in the rule], then the compound would occur only where similarity is the predominant factor, because it is a general principle (*autsargikatva*) that in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is predominant. Regarding the word "anta" (end):
it refers to the delimitation of a specific extent of text, such as "this much portion is to be studied now."

In this context, "end" (anta) is intended to mean completion in relation to that [study]. And since that [completion] occurs even when the study is incomplete, it is mentioned separately from "entirety" (sākalya). The word *agni* refers to the treatise concerning its subject matter;
that word, ending in the third case, is compounded. Although the expression *agninā saha* (together with Agni) would indeed be appropriate for usage, [it is not used here].

Nevertheless, it is so in the case of mere proximity (*sāhityamātra*). However, when there is an intention to express "finality" (*antatva*), the compound is obligatory. For this very reason, the analysis (*vigraha*) *agnigrantham* is shown as one where the members do not stand in apposition (*asvapadavigraha*).

As for the claim that the analysis is either with the nominative ending—*agniranto 'syeti* ("fire is its end")—or with the genitive ending—*agnerantatvam* ("the state of fire being the end")—it refers to the nominative ending.

"Or [it may be] a compound with a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is not correct, because the word *saha* does not denote an end (*anta*), and an "end-ness" is even more impossible to obtain. Furthermore, it would lack syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the act of study (*adhyayana*). Moreover, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) when joined with *saha* is the logical rule, as in the example "he passes over [eating] even with grass" (*satṛṇam atītya*), where it expresses totality (*sākalya*).

In the case of *sāgni*, since even the state of being "ending with" (*antatva*) is expressed by the co-occurrence (*sāhitya*), one accepts a compound there with the word ending in the third case; therefore, its abandonment here would be without foundation. Regarding the phrase *yāvacchlokam*: the indeclinable *yāvat* is compounded. However, the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is as follows:

By the term *taddhita*, it should be understood that there is no co-occurrence within the same word (*asvapadatvam*). [From] the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.11). Regarding this: this is an indication of a principle established by logic.

Since the designation *samāsa* (compound), like the designations *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so forth, is always applicable, there can be no optionality for these designations either—just as there is none for other rules—unless there is an explicit statement [to that effect]. It might be argued: "In that case, the rule *supsupā* would also be compulsory. But this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Because it would contradict your own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*). For instance, in the *Cāraṭ-sūtra*, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) stated: "That which was previously a *bhūta* is called *bhūtapūrva*;

this is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. Likewise, regarding the *Śākala-sūtra*, in the statement "there is a prohibition of the *śākala* [substitution] in the case of a *sin* [ending] and in obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*)," there is no need for the inclusion of the word "obligatory" (*nitya*), because this [case of *bhūtapūrva*] is also...
Regarding the *bhāṣya* statement, "The compound *vāpyaśvaḥ* (‘a horse for a pond’) is established," Kaiyaṭa explained:

"In the form *vāpyaśvaḥ*, it is a compound formed by the rule *sup-supā*. Because the compound is obligatory by the rule *saṃjñāyām*, the prohibition [of the accent] is established. Likewise, [he says] "anudātam..."
This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on such rules as "padamekavarjam" and "asiddhavadatrā.

Therefore, he says: "By the rule *sup supā*, [the compound] is a *samāsa*. Since the formation of the compound is already established by the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the fact that it is prescribed again by subsequent rules indicates that the former [rule] applies only in certain instances (*kvācitkatā*). And thus...

Since a compound with *iva* is also occasional, forms such as *udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ* ("a dwarf like one with arms raised") are established. Although the Vārttika *ivena* is recited under the rule *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), Kaiyaṭa maintains that it is merely a reminder of the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) within the context of the section on obligatory compounds (*nitya-adhikāra*). This being the case:
Thus, those who assume that the compound [in *jīmūtena*] is Vedic have been refuted; for although the Bahvṛcas accept the compound in the phrase *jīmūtasyeva*,
the Taittirīyas read it as an uncompounded form— this is the general direction of the argument.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "The words *apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, and *añcu* [govern] the fifth case (*pañcamī*). [Pāṇini 2.3.10]. Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the fifth case is employed in connection with *bahiḥ*. That which is established by an indicator does not apply everywhere. Consequently, the expression "the young elephant (*karabha*) is outside (*bahiḥ*) the trunk (*kara*)" is established.

Regarding the phrase "down to children" (*ābālam*): as for the expression "from the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) up to the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*)" used in the *Kiraṇāvalī*, that is an error, because the use of the particle *ca* ("and") within a compound is impossible.
The correct reading, however, is "up to the terrestrial globe" (*ābhūgolakāt*).

Regarding the phrase *yaṃ padārtham*: in the sūtra, the word *yat* is neuter because it expresses a general sense. Although the form is already established by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti*, this sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). Consequently, as an alternative, one may cite *vanasyānu*.

Regarding the term *anugaṅgam*: here, the prefix *anu* expresses both extension (*āyāma*) and the state of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*). The thing defined (*lakṣya*), however, is the meaning of the compound as a whole. For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "the length of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgādairghya*) and "Vārāṇasī. [As for the etymology: *varānaḥ* is that which is both excellent (*vara*) and not decaying (*ana*).
*Śreṣṭhodaka* means "located not far from that [excellent water]. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *adūrabhavaśca*. There is vṛddhi of the first vowel.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. Because it ends in *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. [This is governed by] Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.7: *nadībhiśca*.

"And by rivers" (*nadībhiśca*). Here, there is no inclusion of the individual form (*svarūpa*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*), or the word "river" (*nadī*) itself, because of the use of the plural number; rather, it refers to the meaning (*artha*). Furthermore, that [meaning] does not itself constitute a compound name (*saṃjñā*); therefore, this compound applies to those words which denote that meaning. And these are not merely specific terms (*viśeṣa-śabda*), but also...

Even the word "sāmānya" [is used here]. It is a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*), as is clear from the commentary (*vṛtti*). Kaiyaṭa’s intent in his commentary on the *Śākala-sūtra* is also thus. But if this is so, then by parity of reasoning, the same would apply to the *bahuvrīhi* as well.
If it is argued that this would result in the word being a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*), it is not so;

for through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words such as *yasya* ("of whom"), there is the cognition of another referent (*anyapadārtha*). For this very reason, it is stated [in the Vārttika] that "the name is not understood," and not that "the referent of another word is not understood. Regarding the name:
What? The region of Śīghragaṅga.
Now, he states the unique compound-endings (samāsānta) for avyayībhāva compounds: "avyayī. Regarding the term "compound-ending":
it means the final member of the compound, or the final member of the word that constitutes the latter part of the compound's meaning.

By this [rule], in the case of *upaśaradam*, the suffix *am* is established by the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*; and in cases such as *dvipurī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is established by the rule *dvigoḥ*. Regarding *jarāyāḥ*: this is a *gaṇasūtra*.
Regarding *pratipara*: the meaning is "beyond the range of the eyes" (*akṣṇaḥ param*), that is, outside the scope of vision. In the context of the word *vṛta*, the word *akṣi* [is used].
"Intent on the sense-faculties alone. Regarding "in the presence of": it means suitable for the eyes (*akṣi*).

"River" (*nadī*): here, there is the apprehension of the actual form itself, not of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), because *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* are mentioned separately [in the rule]. In the case of *upanadī*, it is when the suffix *ṭac* is absent.

The neuter short [vowel]. However, this should be noted: it was stated under the rule *nadībhiśca* that there is no evidence for the inclusion of the actual forms (*svarūpa*) [of the words] as there is for their specific meanings (*viśeṣa*), in the sense that only the specific meanings are intended. By that, the form *pañcanadam* is established. And here—
It is eternal (nitya). As it has been said:
"If [the word] follows after the number 'nadī' and 'godāvarī'...
This is established by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) into "ac" and "praty-anv-ava" within the rule *ac-praty-anv-ava*.
"‘For the sake of worship’ (pūjārtham): the meaning is that the mention of ‘either one’ (anyatarasyām) is understood from the context. Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds.
[Repeated vertical lines]

Regarding the term *anvādeśa*, the commentators explain that this refers specifically to the pronoun *am*. They state that although this [suffix] is elided by *luk*, the designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) still applies due to the force of the explicit statement. In reality, however, this should have been stated directly in the sūtra itself; forms such as *enam* and *enau* are established through the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class pronouns. [This rule applies] in the neuter before the case-ending *am*.

Even though the *luk* elision has occurred, the substitution of *enad* takes place by virtue of the power of the explicit mention of the suffix *takāra*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of that substitution occurring in the case of *etac-chritaḥ*, because [the rule for *enad*] is already satisfied by its application to the internal *su* and *am* case-endings (which depend on a single word), whereas the compound-based *luk* elision is external.
Because that [substitution] does not apply. [Pradīpa]:

Regarding *ro'supi* (Pāṇini 8.2.69), the example given as *ahar bhāti* is cited by the Easterners (*prācā*); however, its introduction here is inappropriate. How could it serve the purpose of forms such as *ahobhyām*?
The word *cid* is to be joined.

Regarding the phrase "but the word *asṛk*," this is clear in the work of Kṣīrasvāmin. Regarding *bahūrji* and *antayāt*, these are based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). And thus says the Vārttika: "In *bahūrji*..."

There is a prohibition [of this view] in the statement: "Some say that the *num* augment precedes the final letter. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the first *vārttika* is rejected by adopting the meaning: "The *num* augment belongs to that which ends in a *jhal* consonant following a vowel (*ac*). In this way, however, there would be no *num* for *kvip*-derived forms such as *urda* (in the sense of measuring) and *garha* (in the sense of censuring).
It must indeed be cultivated—this is because of the authority of the sages in successive order; such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "allopasya" (of the elision of *a*):

the rule "that which is elided before *kvi* is not *sthānivadbhūta*" is not adopted here, because that rule is only occasional (*kvācitkatva*). It applies only to the specific rule "before *kvi*, with respect to a grammatical operation, [the elided element] is not *sthānivadbhūta*."
"Because it is universal" is stated clearly in the source text (*ākara*).
Regarding "becoming horses and eyes": the meaning is five hundred and twenty-seven. To explain:
there are eighteen from the doubling of the final [letter] of the nine *sū* sounds; and among the four *āṅ* sounds, those used in the sense of worship...

In the case of the three [cases], there are seven when the nasalized (*ñat*) and non-nasalized forms are doubled; however, the nasalized form does not exist [in the nominative] because it is a *pragṛhya*. In the *jas* [ending], there are twelve due to the optionality of both the doubled nasalized and non-nasalized forms. By summation, there are thirty-seven. It is the same for the second case as well. In the *ṭā* [ending], there are fourteen. In the *bhyām*...
Forty-eight [forms], because *bha*, *pra*, *avarṇa*, *ya*, and *mān* occur twice. In the *bhisi* case, there are twenty-four. In the *ṅi* case, there are seven.

However, there is no nasalized form, because this single [suffix] is not *anaṇ*. In the *bhyas* case, it is like the *bhyām* case. In the *ṅsi* case—and in the five beginning with *ṅsi*—there are fourteen. In the *sup* case, there are three for the meaning of "going."
By doubling the *k* and *ṣ*, and by nasalizing the *u*, there are twenty-four forms.
Thus, in the case of the *ku*-suffix, when the six [consonants] *ṅ* and *ṣ* are doubled and the vowel is nasalized, there are forty-eight.
In the absence of *ku*, when the three *ṅ*s are doubled and the vowel is nasalized, there are twelve. *Su*: 18; *āṬ*: 7.
jas 12, am 18, āṬ 7, śas 12, ṭā 14, bhyām 48, bhis 24, Re 7, bhyām 48, bhyas 48, ṅsi 14, bhyām 48, bhyas 48, ṅs, os, ām, ṅi, os—each [ending] 14;
sup 48. Here, this is to be noted: when the augment *num* is applied to *jas* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), of that...

In the case of the two optional forms, there are six forms including the three *ñ* sounds; likewise for *śa* as well, thus making twelve in total by summation. And so it is said: "The form is called 'the planets, the fires, and the elements' (539)," which refers to a view other than that of the Bhāṣya; this is the general direction. As for what they say:
"In this manner, through the options of [repeated] doubling and the omission of subsequent doubling,
by increasing the fifty-eight [forms], one arrives at one hundred and seventy-three.
This [calculation] is to be considered, for the repeated doubling lacks scriptural authority and leads to the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of forms.
And because there is no possibility of [the elision of] *vṛddhi* in the case of the forty-eight [vowels], such is the direction [of the argument].
Regarding the word *tiraścī*: because it is a *bha*-stem, there is elision of *ac* by the rule *acaḥ*; and because of the statement "there is no elision of *al*," there is the substitution of *tiri*.

*Suvāpī*: This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a lake (*saras*) in which the waters (*āpaḥ*) are beautiful (*śobhanāḥ*). Although the suffix *a* (as in *ṛkpūḥ*) would have been expected by the rule "ṛkpūḥ," there is a prohibition by the rule "na pūjanāt. As for what the ancients said—that it occurs because [the rule] is not universal—that is merely an error. Furthermore, the suffix "dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ" does not apply here.

In this regard, it will be stated that *apaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in a compound-affix (*samāsānta*). As for *supumāṃsi*: according to the view of the ancient [grammarians] who explain the word *suṭ* in the rule *puṃso 'suṅ*, this would not be established in the case of the *śas* [ending], and there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the [dative/ablative] ending *auṅ*. However, in our system...
The intention is that for those who state "in the case of a sarvanāmasthāna" exactly as prescribed by the sūtra, all desired results are achieved.
Thus end the neuter gender nouns ending in consonants. Now begins the section on indeclinables (*avyaya*).
Now, the masculine stems ending in consonants.

Regarding *liṭ*: [the root] *lih* (to taste) with the suffix *kvip*. In *liṭ-su*, *liṭ-su*: by the rule "ḍaḥ si dhuṭ" (*ḍaḥ si*), *dhuṭ* is added after *ḍ* before *s*; by the rule "khari ca," the *ḍ* is changed to *ṭ* by *cartva*; because that [change] is not considered established (*asiddha*), *dhuṭ* is applied by "ḍaḥ si"; then *cartva* changes it to *t*. [This is prohibited] by the rule "na padāntāṭṭoḥ."

There is a prohibition against the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*. However, the rule "the second letter of a *cay* [group] is substituted" does not apply here, because the *car*-substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). By this, the statement made by those explaining the older texts—that there are forty-one *pratyāhāras*, such as *liṭsu* and *liṭhasu*—is refuted; for in the case of *ṭaṭhabhyām*, [the rule would otherwise apply].

Regarding the phrase "two forms," that has already been explained. Likewise, in the *Prātiśākhya* as well, in the verse: "Some say that a first [stop-sound] followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) becomes a second [stop-sound] when it does not stand at the end of a word," the qualification "not at the end of a word" and so forth is consistent [only with this view].

Prau.ma.: *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.32). The word *dhātoḥ* is repeated; among these, the one that remains over indicates the time of instruction (*upadeśakāla*). With this intention, he says: "at the time of instruction."

He asks about the result of the restriction: "What [is the purpose] in the instruction? He states that the result is the avoidance of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), beginning with the words "adhog" and so forth. *Prakriyākaumudī*: *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37).

"An *ekāc* [root] whose *baś* sounds become *bhaṣ*. The term *jhal* has ceased to apply here. As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the rule applies] to that which is designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when followed by a *jhal* sound and at the end of a word (*padānte*)—that is merely an error, because it would result in the non-attainment of forms such as *adhok*, *adhoṅ*, and *ajarghā*.

Furthermore, since the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not under discussion there, and since a *jhal* [consonant] cannot serve as a cause (*nimitta*) in that context, [the rule would apply unnecessarily].

For in forms such as *dhugbhyām* and *dhukṣu*, the result is already established by the rule "at the end of a word" (*padānte*) alone. As for the explanation given by Tatpaura—that [the elision applies] only to that which is designated a nominal stem when a *jhal* follows—that too is groundless.

And it should be disregarded as being fruitless. Regarding "the substitution of *bh*": the sense is that because the substitutions of *jaś* and *car* are not established (*asiddha*), [the rule for *bh*] applies prior to those two. Regarding "the substitution of *ṣ* and *car*":
the sense is that because the substitution of *car* is not established, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs first, and after that, the substitution of *car*.
Prau.ma.-vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.60):

"vā druha". Since *druh* belongs to the *ad-ādi* class, it would normally take the substitution [of *na* for *śn*] obligatorily; however, since this does not apply to the others, this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. Now, one might object: *druh* and the others are recited in the *div-ādi* class in this very same order.

In that case, let it simply be "druhādīnām" (of *druh* and so on); let *radhādi* be a sub-group within the *puṣādi* sub-group, which itself is within the *divādi* group. Do not say so. For if that were the case, [the rule] would not apply in the *yaṅluk* formation, because of the prohibition: "that which is specified by its class (*gaṇa*)... and so forth.
*dodhrak*, *dodhruṭ*.
[From] Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.45: *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* ("The *i*-vowels and *y* are termed *saṃprasāraṇa*").
This means "in place of a *yaṇ*. [This applies] in the various rules where the term is prescribed.
The intention is that the future designation [of the term] is adopted, as in the case of the word *sūtraśāṭaka*.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *vāha ūṭh* (Pāṇini 6.4.132)]. The term *samprasāraṇa* is carried over from the rule *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.4.131).

The term *samprasāraṇa* is a qualifier for *mūṭ*. Consequently, the rule "allopo 'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134) does not apply. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it applies to the word *vāśabda*—that is not the meaning of the sūtra; rather, it should be understood as an explanation of the resulting sense derived through some interpretive maneuver. [The phrase] "only in the Veda" (*cchandasyeva*) refers to the Vedic usage.

The intention is that [the forms] *sahaḥ* and *vahaḥ* are derived according to the rule "sahovahaśca," because the term *chandasi* (in the Vedic language) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
As for what the Easterners (*prāc*) have stated—that after applying *ūṭh*, a long vowel by class (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*) is formed, resulting in *bhūhaḥ*, *bhūh*, and so on—that contradicts the Bhāṣya.
For it is as follows: let the mention of *ūṭh* be omitted; let only *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) be prescribed. Of that...

When the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) has been applied, and then the *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule "vṛddhireci" has occurred, forms such as *viśvauhaḥ* are established. This being the case, the fact that [the rule] is formulated indicates the existence of the *paribhāṣā* concerning what is external (*bahiraṅga*).
For if that *paribhāṣā* were operative, the internal (*antaraṅga*) *guṇa* would not apply because the external (*bahiraṅga*) *samprasāraṇa* would be considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*).

"It would not occur"—this is established in the Bhāṣya. If it is argued that there would be a difference in form when the upapada ends in *a* (other than *an*) and the prefix [also] ends in *a*, we say: not so;
for in such a case, [the desired form is secured] precisely by the force of the *jñāpaka* stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.

Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that this is because the absence of the *ṇvi* suffix is inferred. By this, usages such as *vāryūhaḥ* and *prauhaḥ* are also refuted. Alternatively, it should be understood that the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ūh*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*: "For *vasu*, *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *anaḍuh*, [the final consonant] becomes *d*.

(Pāṇini 8.2.72). The term *vasu* refers to the suffix *vasu*; by this, words ending in that suffix are to be understood. From the rule "for *sa* and *sajus*, *ru*" (8.2.66), the word "*sa*" is carried over (*anuvartate*). And that (*sa*) is a qualifier specifically for *vasu*, and not for the others.

Regarding the roots *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*, [the suffix *kvasu* does not apply] because they do not deviate [from their specific conditions]. Nor does it apply to *anaḍuh*, because that is impossible.

With this intention, he says: "of that which ends in *sa* or *vat*. Regarding the phrase "at the end of a word": the claim of the ancients that it applies "before a *jhal* consonant" is an error, because it would lead to over-extension in cases such as *srastam*.
Prau.ma.: *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.56).

Regarding the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*: what is the purpose of [specifying] *sah-*? [Consider] *saḍaḥ*, meaning "one who exists with *ḍa*" (*ḍena saha vartate*). This refers to that which contains the word *ḍa* in its name, such as *mṛḍa*. [The derivative] *sāḍiḥ* is the offspring (*apatyam*) of *saḍa*.
Thus end those [consonants] ending in *ha*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

"diva āṬt" (Pāṇini 7.1.84). Regarding the term *prātipadikasya* ("of the nominal stem"): it refers either to the underived stem [as in *dyauḥ*] or to the derived stem [as in *divam*] formed by the rule *diverḍiviḥ* as supplied in the *Nyāsa* commentary; however, it does not refer to the root *divu* in the sense of "playing" (*krīḍādi*).
[This is so] by the paribhāṣā: "When a root is mentioned without an *anubandha*, it does not include [the same root] with an *anubandha*.
Therefore, [the substitution] does not occur in cases such as *akṣadyauḥ*. The letter *t* in *āṬt* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
In the case of *sudyaubhyām*, since the *u* is a *samprasāraṇa*, the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule "halaḥ" would have applied.

By virtue of the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), which prescribes lengthening when *ṭh* follows, [the substitution of *ā*] does not occur. As for what was stated by the ancients—"there is optionally an *ā*-substitution for *div* before *am*"—that is disregarded, because it is not taught by the three sages [of the Pāṇinian tradition] and because it would be fruitless.
It should be understood that the form *dyām* belongs to the word *dyo* itself.
Vomited.
Prau.ma.-ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.55):

"ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca. Because of the use of the plural number in the indication [of the word *ṣaṭcatubhyaḥ*], the predominance of the meaning (*artha*) is intended. And the status of being subsequent to *ām* is established through the medium of the word (*śabda-dvāraka*). Therefore, by the rule of extension to what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*), [the suffix *ṅīp* applies] after words ending in *ṣaṣ* and *catur*.
Even though [the condition] exists, [the augment *nuṭ*] occurs only in cases such as *parama-caturṇām* and the like, but not in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

This he will state with the words, "But when [the word is used] in a secondary sense (*gauṇatve*), *nuṭ* is not desired," and so forth. Regarding "doubling" (*dvitvam*), it is by means of the rule *aco rahābhyām*.
Those ending in *r*.
Kamalā and Lakṣmī [end in -l]. Those ending in -l.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: *mo no dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.64). Regarding the phrase "at the end of a word" (*padānte*), although the condition "before a *jhal* consonant" (*jhalīti*) was carried over by the ancients, it should nevertheless be disregarded because it is absent in the *Kāśikā* and other such works, and because it would be fruitless [in this context].

Prakriyā-mañjarī: *kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.103). [Objection: Why not simply formulate the rule as *imaḥ*? It could be explained thus: "For the words beginning with *tyad*, *ima-* is substituted for *asya*.
Furthermore, the word *kim* will be recited before *dvi-* [in the list of pronouns]. And [the rule] *nānarthake* [will apply].

One might object: "Since there is a prohibition [of the *at* substitute] and because of the force of the initial undertaking [of the rule], the rule for the final letter (*alo 'ntyavidhiḥ*) will not apply; so what is the need for the substitution of *ka*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when accompanied by *akac*. [The point is: if the substitution of *at* were applied to the final letter, the form would become *kaka*;
therefore, one must necessarily state "kimaḥ" in rules such as "ku tahoḥ. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: But in that case, since it would not be the result of a collective operation (*gaṇakārya*), would [the substitution] not occur even when [the pronoun] is subordinate (*upasarjana*)? [Reply: Not so;

for, carrying forward the word "of *tyad* etc. (*tyadādīnām*) and modifying the number [to the singular], one explains it as "of *kim* which begins with *tyad*" (*tyadādeḥ kimaḥ*). Furthermore, by the force of this carry-forward (*anuvṛtti*), in this rule [it is understood] "of those ending in *dvi*."

Because of the abandonment of the restriction (*niyama*). Regarding the term "general rule" (*utsarga*): by this, the Bhāṣya statement "In the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*, what is the purpose of [specifying] *anantyayoḥ* (not being final)?"—namely, "O *sa*! as well as "O Acyuta! O venerable Acyuta!"—is not contradicted.
This is the state of affairs. As for the root reason why [the pronoun] does not exist here, it is simply the non-observation of its extensive usage. As they say:
"One should know that *idam* is used for what is proximate, *etad* for what is very near; *adaḥ* for what is remote, and *tad* for what is out of sight. (1)
The claim that "by this very statement, such a thing is unfit to be brought before one's mind" is merely superficial;

for there is no contradiction in words such as *idam* (this) serving to present the person being addressed, just as words like *sannikṛṣṭa* (near) do. Even that which is distant can be [presented] by means of the intellect.
Because it is frequently observed that [the word] is brought near [to the verb] and is addressed; and likewise Bhaṭṭi says:
"O fair-browed one, where have you gone? Alas!"—thus did he lament excessively.
[Prakriyākaumudī: By the rule *anāpyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).

"Anāpyakaḥ" refers to a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation), and not to the suffix *ṭāp*; this is because of the qualification "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*). "Not a modification of a reduplicated syllable" (*anabhyāsavikāra*); by this, [the rule applies to] "bhṛñām it" [Pāṇini 7.4.76].
By the rule "artipipartyośca," the substitution of *ī* certainly applies to the final letter [of the root]. Thus we have *bibharti* and *piparti*.

Now, one might raise the objection that because it is further [in the order of the rules], the substitution of *an* should take precedence over the substitution of *smai*; anticipating this, he says: "Because it is obligatory, *ḍeḥ smai* [applies]. This means: "In order to prescribe the grammatical operation. That is to say, in order to make known something not previously established.

In the verse "ṭhīṣadarthe kriyāyoge," however, the meanings such as "slight" (īṣadartha) and so forth are not being prescribed (*vidhīyante*), but rather restated (*anūdyante*). Therefore, there is no substitution with *enad*. By this [logic]—[in the example:
"O Rādhā, this one is timid at night; you yourself must lead him home."
This has also been explained, because cowardice is intended to be expressed as that which is being restated (the *anuvādya*).
Those ending in *m*.

Regarding *sugaṇ*: there is lengthening by the rule "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ. Nor should one suspect that, when that [lengthening] is to be applied, the status of being a *sthānivat* (as if the original element were present) applies to the elision of *al* and the elision of *ṇi*; for the reason is that this is prohibited in the prescription of lengthening, and it is also prohibited with respect to a prescription concerning *kvip*. By this, [the form] *sugaṇṇīśa* [is explained].

Thus, he suggests that those who explain the ancient text of Gaṇapati as "kvip" [being the suffix] should be disregarded. However, if there is a persistent insistence that his own work must also be justified, let it be defended in this way: *kvip* is so called because it behaves like *kvip* by virtue of having all its phonemes elided (*sarvalopitva*).

From the word *kvap*, which has the suffix *kvip* added in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), another *kvip* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); thus, it has the meaning "one who conquers. Thus end [the words] ending in *ṇ*.

Regarding the term *upadhādīrgha*: this is by means of the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*. The phrase *ṅai sambuddhau ca* has been explained in this way in accordance with the tradition of the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*). However, it would be more appropriate to explain it as a genitive construction, namely, "of a word ending in a *ṅī*-suffix or ending in the vocative (*sambuddhi*). For in this way, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of suffix-based rules) is maintained.
Since [the result] is easily obtained, one should not undergo the trouble of following the implications of that prohibition.
Anticipating the objection that there might be *sthānivadbhāva* even with respect to the preceding rule, he says: "na ca" (and not). Regarding "ṣāṣṭhīm" (belonging to the sixth [chapter]):
the sense is that because it is taught in the rule "vāha ūṭh," it resides in that same location.

The phrase "because it is not established" (*asiddhatvāt*) refers to the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "dyudbhyo luṅi" (Pāṇini 1.3.91), which suggests the view that restrictive rules (*niyama-sūtra*) function both by way of positive injunction (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*) and by way of restricting the intended scope of general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*). [The other view is] that they function by way of negation (*niṣedha-rūpeṇa*).

However, in the view that [the rule] is *pravṛtti* (active), it should be understood that this occurs by means of the rule "pūrvatrāsiddham. He illustrates a rule concerning *sub*-suffixes with the words beginning with "ātvam," etc.; but in the case of a rule concerning accent (*svara*), [the example is] *pañcārmam*.
When the compound is formed by the rule "diksaṅkhye saṃjñāyām," and the *n* has been elided, it ends in the vowel *a*.

Regarding the word *pūrvapada* [in the analysis of *pūrvapadajāta*], the rule "arme cāvarṇaṃ dvyactryac" (Pāṇini 6.2.117) would have required the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the first member (*pūrva-pada*). However, this does not occur because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*) for the purposes of accentuation. He will explain this further under the section on feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), starting with the commentary on the rule "pañca" (Pāṇini 4.1.10), where he states: "even when the elision of *n* has been performed," and so forth. [This applies] in the case of a *kṛt* suffix.
But in the case of the *tug* augment—[as in] *vṛtrahabhyām*—the *tug* [augment] does not apply because of the rule "after a short vowel, before a *pit* suffix. Why say "before a *kṛt* suffix"?

Consider *vṛtrahaccchatram*; here the *tug* would indeed occur by the rule "also before *cha*. [The word] *pratidivā* is formed with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule "the suffix *kanin* is applied after the roots *kan*, *yu*, *vṛṣi*, *takṣi*, *rāj*, *dhanvi*, *dyu*, and *pratidiv*."
Prau.ma.:
*Hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). As for the fact that the ancient grammarians introduced [the rule] as *upadhāyāṃ ca*, that is incorrect, because the letter *v* in the root *div* is not an *upadhā*.
Prau.ma.: *Inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau* (Pāṇini 6.4.12). Regarding the rule *upadhāyāḥ*: this restriction applies specifically to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
Consequently, in the form *vṛtrahāyate*, the lengthening prescribed by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25) indeed occurs.

Likewise, in the case of *vṛtrahaṇī*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* is also excluded by this restriction; the point is that the restriction is understood to apply specifically with regard to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
He explains the sūtra *hanteratpūrvasya* by means of a yogavibhāga (splitting the rule): "*hanteḥ*". In connection with this, he provides an example: *prahaṇyāt*.
He states the portion relevant to the present context: "*atpūrvasya*" [and] "*ekājuttareti*"; and not when there is elision (*alopa*) of the *a*.

It must be stated that once [the substitution] has been performed, the status of being a single syllable (*ekāctva*) no longer exists, because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as the original) even with respect to an operation prescribed for what precedes. Nor should it be argued that "there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when an operation is prescribed for what precedes an *asiddha*" (P.

1.1.58), because it is stated: "The fault [of that rule applies] only in the case of the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*, the substitution of *latva*, and the substitution of *ṇatva*. As for the point—

Taking the commentary on the sūtra *aṭkupvāṅ* which states "vṛtraghnaḥ, srughnaḥ," Kaiyaṭa explained: "There is the contingency of the application of the rule for *ṇatva* [nasalization] by the term 'prātipadikānta'.
This was intended to mean that there should be no compound with the fifth case (pañcamī-samāsa); thus, in the phrase "tasya doṣaḥ," the mention of *ṇatva* is included.

Or it should be understood that [the rule] is intended with the intention that [the *ṇatva*] should not occur. However, the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the inclusion of the term *ṇatva* is indicated in the *Bhāṣya* and explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*. In reality, however, the application of *ṇatva* here by the rule "kumati ca" is invariably (*nitya*) more logical. In any case, whether optional (*vaikalpika*) or obligatory (*nitya*), the *ṇatva* is what is obtained.

It is established that [the substitution] is invariably set aside. However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated: "A prohibition must be formulated regarding the substitutes for *han* when there is an intervening *k*. What is the purpose? [Examples: *vṛtraghnaḥ*, *srughnaḥ*, *prāghāni*.
Thus, the mention of 'not preceded by *a*' (*atpūrva*) in the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* need not be made."
And this is merely a description of the intention of the Vārttika, but not the actual state of affairs;

for it is more logical to subsume the meaning of the Vārttika by resorting to a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) than to rely on the rejection of a portion of the Sūtra— this is the general direction.
It was stated by Mādhava as follows: "For in this way, his own text [states]: 'In the case of elision of *a* when a *bha*-designation applies, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would lack a vowel;

and since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply because it is not a rule concerning a phoneme (*alvidhi*), there is an absence of the condition of having a single-vowel subsequent member (*ekāj-uttarapadatva*). Consequently, [the rule] "prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca" [would not apply]. "

An option arises—[the forms] *vṛtraghnaḥ* and *vṛtraghnah*. [The opponent says: "That is its explanation. Furthermore, [the statement] "it is not so because it is not an *al*-rule" is incoherent; for the rule *acaḥ parasmin* was indeed commenced for the sake of an *al*-rule, and since that [present rule] would otherwise not apply, another justification must be stated. [Thus, the option remains.]
This too is inconsistent; it should be noted that the application of the rule *kumati ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.46) is unavoidable here.
[From] *prau.ma.*—*maghavā bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.4.128): following from the rule *arvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.127), the element *tṛ* is understood to carry over.
And with respect to that, in the word *maghavā*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. Thus he says: "of the word *maghavan*.

[The rule applies] "even when it was not previously a verbal root (*adhātu-bhūta-pūrva*). For the mention of *añcati* is for the purpose of restriction: "if it occurs after a verbal root, then only after *añcati*. And thus...

In examples such as *gomān ivācarati gomān*, although [the word] is currently a verbal root (*dhātu*), the mention of "non-root" (*adhātu*) is for the sake of the prescriptive rule (*vidhi*). This will become clear in the root text itself. Now, one might object that, as in the case of *kurvan* and so forth, because the elision of a final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is non-existent (*asiddha*), [the form would not be established].
Anticipating the objection that "length [of the vowel] would not occur because there is no finality [of the suffix]," he says: "here" (iha).
Regarding "because of the inclusion of the term *bahula*": this means it has the sense of "in some cases something else indeed [occurs]. Regarding "due to irregular derivation" (*nipātana*):
this refers to the triad consisting of the substitution of the letter *gh* for the letter *h* in the root *mah*, the augment *avuk*, and the suffix *kan*.

The meaning is: "by virtue of an irregular derivation (nipātana). Regarding the phrase "it has been rejected": thus Kaiyaṭa stated in his commentary on the rule *cchandasīvanipau*: "The rule *maghavā bahulam* need not be formulated; for by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *śvan* and *ukṣan*, and by the suffix *matup*, both words [i.e., *maghavan* and *maghavat*] are established even in the common language (*bhāṣā*)."
"Because it is established.
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika has stated: "The forms *arvan* and *maghavan* need not be taught [as exceptions], for they are Vedic (*chāndasa*)."
"Because of the prescription of both the *matup* and *vani* suffixes, both [forms] are seen in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.4.157).

Furthermore, what Kaiyaṭa stated during the occasion of that commentary—that [the form] is ungrammatical in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*)—refers specifically to the word *maghavan*, which is derived from the suffix *vani* and has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*). This applies only within the Vedic context.

Because of the prescription [of the suffix] *vanip*. Thus, indicating that there is no contradiction between Kaiyaṭa’s earlier and later statements, he says: "In Vedic [usage]," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "but [it is] oxytone": although, by virtue of the authority of works such as Ujjvaladatta’s, these words (*śvan*, *ukṣan*, etc. are derived from the suffix *kanin* and thus would be obtained as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), [the present case is different].

Nevertheless, in cases such as "ukṣā samudro aruṇaḥ suparṇaḥ," "pūṣā tveto nayatu," "agnimūrdhā," "nirmajvānaṃ na parvaṇo jabhāra," and "tvamaryamā bhavati yat," there is no dispute regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of words like *ukṣan* and others that are included in those sūtras.

The intention is that the suffix *kan* alone is appropriate. Regarding the rule *maghavā bahulam*, having taken *maghonaḥ* as the illustrative example (*pratīka*), one might suspect the elision of the vowel *a* of the word *magha-* by the rule *yasya*. [The author] objects:
"This is not so; for this is another base (*prātipadika*) which is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*). To explain:"

The author of the Nyāsa, stating that "its usage is also seen in the spoken language (bhāṣā)," is likewise favorable to the view that the word *maghavan* has an udātta accent on the final syllable and is correct even in the spoken language. This being the case, the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika reject the substitution of *trā* by relying upon the suffix *matup*.

Even in the view that *trā* is the substitute for *maghavat* in the word *maghavān*, one must indeed accept the lengthening of the vowel; for since there would be a difference in the result (*phalabheda*), it is impossible to reject the rule. Therefore, what was stated—that due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely), there is no status of being "as if not established" (*asiddhatva*)—is indeed in agreement with the Bhāṣya and other authoritative works.

As for what they say—that even in the *matup* alternative, the long vowel does not occur because it is Vedic (chāndasa), and that this is the intention of the Bhāṣya—that is incorrect. For there is no evidence that a word ending in *matup* is Vedic, and because it contradicts the examples cited by Bhaṭṭi and Kaiyaṭa. This is the general direction [of the argument]. By this, [the rule] *śvan-nukṣan-*... [is explained].

Because there is no lengthening of the vowel when *maghavan* is substituted for *nipatita* (as in *maghavan*), Kṣīrasvāmin’s statement that the form is *maghavan* has been refuted. Accordingly, the Kātantra Sūtra states: "In the nominative singular (*sau*), [the forms] *maghavān* and *maghavā*.
Furthermore, in the *Vicāracintāmaṇi*, it is stated: "*Maghavān* alone is *maghavā*."
Even in the *Kāśikā*, only the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is observed; therefore, enough of this prolixity.
[From] *Prau.ma.*—*arvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.127):
*arvaṇastṛ*. From the root *ṛ* with the suffix *vic*, and after applying *guṇa*, the form *ar* is obtained; from that, the suffix *matup* is applied.
The form *arvantau* and so forth will be established. By the rule *chandasi vanip*, the suffix *vanip* is applied in the Veda to yield *arveti*.

In common usage (*loka*), however, it will be established from the root *ṛ* itself with the suffix *vanip*. Furthermore, this is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*), as evidenced by the Amarakośa: "Vājin, vāha, arvā, gandharva, haya, saindhava, and sapti [are synonyms for horse]."

Therefore, the meaning also does not differ. Nevertheless, since the use of both *arvan* and *maghavan* would otherwise apply everywhere, this sūtra is intended to establish a restriction, similar to the three sūtras beginning with "tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ. As for what Haradatta stated—that both the words *arvan* and *maghavan* are indeed ungrammatical in the common language (*bhāṣā*)—[that is incorrect].

The statement "from the Bhāṣya on *ṛtvyavāstvyavāstva...* and so forth" is merely superficial, because it has already been stated that the Bhāṣya concerns a specific case. Thus, Śrī Harṣa employed [the form] in the verse:
"The pride of the thousand-eyed Indra was shattered by horses."

Regarding the position that "the qualities [of the vowels] are non-differentiators," one might suspect that even when an *anunāsika* (nasalized) vowel is not explicitly uttered in the sūtra, an *anunāsika* would still occur due to *āntaratamya* (phonetic proximity); anticipating this, he says: *ā ād iti*. As for what some have said—"Here there is no *anunāsika*, because since it is not an *aṇ*, there is no inclusion of homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds"—and so forth... [the text continues].

It must be stated that the rule *taparaḥ tatkālasya* serves as an injunction (*vidhi*) for vowels other than *aṇ*, because of the prohibition: "A vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).
