Even though phonetic qualities (*guṇa*) do not differentiate [vowels], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because in the Sūtra only a single pure individual (*ekavyakti*) is indicated. In this regard, the following...

It must be said: if there were a doubt that the mention of *anaṇ* is for the purpose of prescribing [the substitution], then the subsequent statement beginning with "bhāvyamāna" would be inconsistent. Otherwise, a prohibition would undesirably apply even in rules such as "coḥ kuḥ. If it is argued that the prohibition does not apply there because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the inclusion of the marker *it*, then what is the point of this [present rule]?

[This is] due to the effort involved in the "binding of the jar" (*bakabandhana-prayāsa*), and because the author of the *Bhāṣya* did not carry forward the mention of "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*) in the rule *taparas tatkālasya*. Furthermore, [the claim] that "only a single pure individual is [meant]" is inconsistent;
for if there were no distinction [between individuals], the fault would be difficult to avoid. For it has been stated that "only one individual is grasped."

The resulting meaning is that no other individual instance (vyakti) has been specified. And that [specification] is only possible if qualities function as differentiators, not otherwise; let this matter rest for now. By this, it follows that the vowel *ā* is not nasalized (*anunāsika*), due to the prohibition: "An *aṇ* being taught does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."

The *prasāda* commentary has also been employed [here], because the root is undermined by the fact that a long vowel is not atomic (*anaṇ*). [In the rule] *tho nthaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.87), both the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are devoid of vowels (*anackau*). Since the form would be established simply by saying "tho nthaḥ,"...

Regarding the statement "from here [the substitute] 'tha' [is used] for 'ṛbhukṣin'": some say there is a substitution of 'antha'. In that case, the elision of the vowel 'a' (ākārapraśleṣa) would be purposeless. As for what was stated by the author of the Nyāsa and by the ancients—that even though [the substitute] consists of multiple letters, this is a substitution of the letter 'tha' alone—[that is incorrect].
[The opponent argues: "This is because of the maxim: 'Substitutes apply to that which is being specified [as the object of substitution]'; but that is not correct.
For since there is no occurrence of that [base] as qualified by those [suffixes], the aforementioned paribhāṣā has no scope here.
Incidentally, he says: "In the feminine. [The example is] *supathī*; however, the suffix *kap* applies according to the rule "inaḥ striyām."

It was not applied; for the rule regarding the addition of suffixes at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*), as evidenced by the *bhāṣya* on the rule *yuvoranākau* which gives the example *supathī*. Furthermore, this is not the scope of the prohibition "not after a word denoting praise" (*na pūjanāt*), because it will be stated later that this [prohibition] applies only to those [words] prior to *ṣac*. [In the case of *pathin*,] the substitution of *ā* occurs for *tho* by the rule *pathimathyṛbhukṣām āt*.

Furthermore, although [the substitution] would have applied by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, it does not occur because a word-form qualified by gender is not grasped when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows. Regarding the form *śau*: as for the fact that the ancient grammarians explained the two rules "ito 't sarvanāmasthāne" and "tho 'thaḥ" as applying to the suffix *suṭ*, [that is incorrect].

That is incorrect, because it would result in the fault of [the suffix] having no seed (*nirbīja-lakṣaṇāpatti*). Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *klībe āṬṅḥ śyām* and *supathī*, and there would be the undesirable consequence of the form *sapanthāni* being unestablished in the *śas* case; this is the intended meaning. Here, this should be noted: [in the case of] *panthānam ātmanaḥ*...
It is so desired; thus it is recited. From that [root], the suffix *kvip* is applied. There is elision of the vowel (*alopa*). There is elision of *y* (*yalopa*).

Because that which is modified in one part is not different from the original, the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule "pathi-mathi-". *th* is replaced by *nth*. Thus, *panthāḥ*. The substitution of *ā* by the rule "ito't sarvanāmasthāne" does not take place here, because of the word "itaḥ" [in that rule].

Because of the inclusion of *ra* [in the rule], the *yaṇ* substitution [prescribed by] "eranekācaḥ" is superseded; due to its higher status and its obligatory nature, "tho nthaḥ" applies. Because it is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no *yaṇ*. [The forms are: *panthiyau*, *panthiyaḥ*, *panthiyam*, *panthiyau*.
[In the case of the stem *pathi*:]* "the elision of the final syllable of a *bha*" [applies]. [The forms are: *pathaḥ*, *pathībhyām*, *pathībhiḥ*.

And so forth. By this, Haradatta’s statement in his *Padamañjarī*—that in the rule *itaḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, the inclusion of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) in both the original form (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation—is refuted. As for the claim by the author of the *Nyāsa* and others following him that [forms like] *sukhīḥ* and *sutīrīḥ* are like *pathīḥ*...

The examples cited, such as *pathyau* and *pathya*, are to be considered; for the occurrence of the suffix *sāV* is unavoidable. As for the claim that *pathimathīṛbhukṣām* is an imitation of a base ending in *n*; that too is useless, because the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) is unavoidable. [Thus,] *panthāḥ*.

In this case as well, since the substitution of *āt* (by Pāṇini 7.1.84) is both permanent (*nitya*) and specifically prescribed (*viśeṣavihita*), it would apply first; and once that has been done, because the word would no longer end in *an*, the substitution of *nth* (by Pāṇini 7.1.90) would not even be applicable. As for what they say—that because the elision of *a* (*allopasya*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no occasion for the substitution of *āt* and so forth—and that the rule "what is elided before *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*" is not relied upon here—that too is questionable.

If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *yaṇ* substitution; for in the rule *khyatyāt*, Kaiyaṭa and others have relied on the principle "that which is elided by *ṭi* or *ku* is not *sthānivadbhūta*" in order to justify forms such as *sukhīḥ* and *sutīḥ*. This is because the author of the grammar [Pāṇini], when employing the *tapara* marker in the rule *ito't*, [intends to exclude such cases].

And because the author of the Sūtras also conforms to this here, it is established that the substitution of *āt* and the replacement by *nth* are indeed correct. By this, forms such as *mathīḥ*, *mathyau*, and *mathyaḥ* are also refuted, since *manthāḥ*, *manthiyau*, and *manthiyaḥ* alone are correct. As for *ṛbhukṣīḥ*...

*ṛbhukṣyau*, *ṛbhukṣyaḥ*, and so forth; in these cases, it has already been stated that the presence of the long vowel *ā* (sātvatva) is unavoidable. However, the substitution of *yaṇ* in the case of *auṭ* and other endings is difficult to obtain because of the preceding conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
Therefore, one should understand the forms to be *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣiyau*, *ṛbhukṣiyaḥ*, and so on.
Prau.ma.-ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ (Pāṇini 1.1.24): "Those ending in ṣ or n are called ṣaṭ. The mention of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) is intended to qualify the number (*saṃkhyā*).

By virtue of that [feminine designation], the term *saṃkhyā* (number), which in the preceding rule was a technical name (*saṃjñāpara*), is here understood as referring to the thing named (*saṃjñipara*).

With the intention of explaining how [the number] is accomplished, he says: "The number" (*saṃkhyā*). As for what the predecessors have stated—that at the time of instruction (upadeśa) it ends in *ṣ* or ends in *n*—that contradicts their own text, such as the passage beginning with "even when the *n*-elision has been applied in the case of 'five' (*pañca*)"; for even though it does not end in *n* at present, it did so at the time of instruction.

If it is asked, "Is the statement 'there was no end' unestablished?"—or if it is argued that this contradiction between earlier and later statements is equally present in the *Kāśikā* as well—what of it? For according to the maxim: "When a sublation is firm, why should another thing, merely by virtue of similarity to something else, also be sublated? (even if there is similarity, it does not follow that everything must be rejected).

As for what they have explained— that the meaning is "ending with those [phonemes] which were the *ṣ* and *n* at the time of instruction," and that because of the connection with the whole (the compound), it is not an *asamartha-samāsa*, as in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher's family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*)— that is merely superficial. For after explaining the connection with the individual parts, [they then claim] the connection with the whole...

Because it has been stated that [the compound] arises from a relation, there is a mutual contradiction. Furthermore, in cases where the meaning of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) possesses a relation, there are two possibilities: one is that even when it is dependent (*sāpekṣa*), it may be compounded;
the other is that the primary member (*pradhāna*) alone—such as "family" (*kula*)—has a relation with both the secondary factor (e.g., "teacher") and the external factor (e.g., "Devadatta").

And that [relation] is "containing an originator" (utpattigarbha) together with the teacher; however, the second type is "teacher-constituted" (gurughaṭita), consisting in Devadatta's being produced by that very teacher. And it has been stated by Hari:
"Every relative term is always compounded when it is dependent [on another];
for that very dependence which exists in a sentence is not lost even in a compound. Thus [it is said].

"And: 'Those things which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher's family and so forth, when their parts are touched, they are joined with that [whole] which possesses those parts. Thus it is said.
In this context, the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is not something that possesses a correlative relation, such that two distinct modes of application could find scope.

If it is argued that even here the word "end" (*anta*) has a meaning involving a correlative relation, we reply: no, because when [the sūtra] says "those which are the *ṣ* and *n* at the time of instruction," the connection with that [correlative] has been abandoned. Otherwise, indeed...
At the time of instruction, one ought to say "that which has its end [in something else]"; however, in reality, even that is not the case.

For the word *anta* (end) is dependent upon a whole (*avayavin*), and not upon just anything; otherwise, one would have to say "the king's man of wealth" (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*). This is because even for a ruler (*īśitṛ*), there must be something over which he rules (*īśatavya*).
Because it requires a complement;
for the lexicon states: "The word *rājā* [is used] in the senses of a sovereign, a king, the moon, a yakṣa, a kṣatriya, and Indra.
If you argue that it does not require a complement when meaning "prosperous," then the same applies to the present case as well.
He brings them together. Thus, the explanation that "it is likewise at the time of instruction" is pointless; this is the sense.

As for what they say—that there would be elision (*luk*) because a *paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory—that is mere recklessness. For if it were not to apply even in the desired instances, the *paribhāṣā* itself would result in being useless.
Furthermore, the claim that "it is taught" (aupadeśika) is baseless.
As for what they say— that its status as being taught is obtained by the force of the mention of "extremes" (antagrahaṇa)— that too is not correct,
because [the word] "number" (saṃkhyā) is drawn back [to the previous context] and [the term] is thereby made to refer to the named objects (saṃjñin).
Because of the exhaustion of its capacity.

[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "nopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7)] "nopadhāyāḥ. The word "na" is a genitive in apposition (*lipta-ṣaṣṭhī*), qualifying the member (*aṅga*). In the case of secondary application (*gauṇatva*)...
The sense is that the use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is for the purpose of emphasizing the meaning [of the whole].
In "priyapañca," there is a *cakāra* between the two *ñakāras*.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.21)].
Regarding "aṣṭana ā": the word "hali" (before a consonant) is drawn over from the subsequent sūtra "rāyo hali"; the intention is that this [term] qualifies the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Consequently, in the form *aṣṭānām*, the *nuṭ* augment occurs precisely after [the substitution of *ā*], because of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

The substitution of *āt* occurs because of its being non-eternal (*anityatva*), but not before [the application of other rules]. Otherwise, when the form *aṣṭan-ām* is established, since the substitution of *āt* would apply due to its higher status and its being eternal, the stem would no longer end in *n*; consequently, the designation *ṣaṭ* (six) would be absent, and the augment *nuṭ* would not occur.
Nor can it be argued that, under the *yathoddeśa* view, the designation *ṣaṭ* is applied earlier because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

One might argue that [the form] is easily obtained even when *kṛt* has been substituted [for *kṛd*], by virtue of the maxim regarding partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). However, the point is that this maxim is inapplicable in a rule concerning an *al*-substitute (*alvidhi*). — *Prakriyākaumudī*: *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21).
Regarding the rule *aṣṭābhya āṬś*: [the question is raised] "from what that has the form *aṣṭan*"? Now, it was stated that the word *hal* is drawn back [from the previous sūtra];

how then can it be said "from that which has the form *aṣṭan*"? To this he says: *aṣṭabhyaḥ*. This is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of [the form] after the substitution of *ātva* has occurred; it is not an *ātva* produced by the force of a grammatical rule. For if that were the case, then by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) to be mentioned later, its...

The intention is that, for the sake of brevity, one might simply say "from eight" (*aṣṭabhyas*) by way of optionality. Regarding the word "this" (*idam*): it means both what is heard (*śruta*) and what is inferred (*anumita*). Regarding the rule "after *aṣṭan* ending in a long vowel": a case-ending (*vibhakti*) other than the nominative and the accusative plural (*asvanāmasthāna*) following *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel shall be acute (*udātta*). For example: *aṣṭābhiḥ*. Why "ending in a long vowel"? [To exclude cases like *aṣṭabhiḥ*].

By eight [rules]. This [sūtra] has the middle syllable as its udātta (accent). Its meaning is: "In a word ending in a case-ending that begins with a *jhal* consonant following six, three, or four [consonants], the penultimate syllable shall be udātta. This being the case, the meaning is that if the substitution of *ā* were mandatory (*nitya*), then the effort made to exclude short vowels would be rendered useless.

Regarding the phrase "even from the preceding [rule]": the intention is that, in this way, the *ṣṭutva* substitution does not occur in the example cited by Haradatta, namely *priyāṣṭṇa*. Nor is there a prohibition based on the rule "that which was previously non-existent [as a result of a grammatical operation] is not treated as a substitute (*na sthānivat*)," because that rule has exceptions, such as the one stating "this is a fault. Now, one might object regarding the rule "from *ra* and *ṣa*... [the following applies].

If it is argued that we shall accept the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) as specifically prescribed there [in the rule], and not as obtainable through the rule for the substitution of *ṣṭu*, this is not so. For according to the view of the Bhāṣya, that is untenable. To explain: in the rule *raṣābhyām*, the term *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*), and thus the mention of *ṇ* [in the rule *raṣābhyām*] applies to what is not at the end of a word; whereas [the rule *raṣābhyām*] itself pertains to what is at the end of a word (*padāntasya*).

Furthermore, the prohibitive sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. Nor can a discrepancy be easily asserted regarding the letter *ṇ* when it is being produced by the term "mūrdhanya" or the term "ṣṭutva";
for, according to the principle that "the authority of the sages increases in successive order," the application of the rule of "substitution of the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) alone is appropriate.

In the *Śabdakaustubha*, a conclusion was reached stating that the mention of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) in the rule "tasya doṣaḥ" need not be made; following that same reasoning, he says: "in the view of *kāryakālapakṣa*. Nor should it be argued that one may instead adopt the *yathoddeśapakṣa* and allow for *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣṭu*), because when there is a difference in results (*phalabheda*), a refutation [of the objection] is impossible.

The intention is that, in this context, the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that grammatical operations take effect at the time they are required) alone is logical. For this very reason, one should not harbor any hope for the status of *ṣṭutva* even by supporting the rejection of the *pañcamī-samāsa* (the compound with the fifth case ending); because, since the *kāryakālapakṣa* alone is logical for the sake of uniformity of result (*phalaikya*), the state of being *asiddha* (unestablished) is unavoidable. [In the rule] "niṣṭhāyām... [etc.]...

Regarding the mention of *seṭ* in the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.18], it is argued that because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional identity) after a preceding [element] is non-eternal (*anitya*), and thus it does not apply here. However, to prioritize such non-eternality is indeed improper; let us leave it at that for now. [The rule] *jaśśasoḥ*...

For the substitution of *auṣ* does not occur when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇatva*), just as the elision (*luk*) and the augment *nuṭ* do not; this is because of the use of the plural in the rule "aṣṭābhyaḥ. Otherwise, even if it were an imitation of the form where *ātva* has already been applied, he would have indicated it with the singular alone—as "aṣṭā auṣ" or simply "aṣṭa. And this is understood from the rule "ṣṇāntāḥ ṣaṭ."

This is clear from the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya, and the Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa commentary. Likewise, since the substitution of *ātva* (the replacement of *aṣṭan-* by *aṣṭā-*) is inferred by the force of the mention of the form with *ātva* (*aṣṭābhyaḥ*) in the rule for *auś*, it is appropriate that this *ātva* should occur only when [the word] is predominant.
Thus, having raised the objection that in the case of the suffix *jas*, the form would be *priyāṣṭānaḥ* and not *priyāṣṭāḥ*, it was stated:

In the Bhāṣya, it says: *yathālakṣaṇam aprayukte* ("as prescribed by the rules, provided it is not [actually] employed"). Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning is that the substitution of *ātva* (the replacement of *aṣṭan* with *aṣṭā*) does not occur at all in such cases. Vāmana also, regarding the rule *aṣṭābhya auś*, states that because the inclusion of the word ending in [the stem] is intended, one says *paramāṣṭau*, and then [gives the example] *priyāṣṭānaḥ*.

Thus, he states that because the substitution of *āt* is absent here, the substitution of *auś* does not occur. Haradatta, however, having cited the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that very point— "in the case of *priyāṣṭānaḥ*"— proposes that he will explain how the substitution of *āt* does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*), even within that same rule.

By stating that because of the singular-number indication (*ekavacana-nirdeśa*) in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the substitution of *ā* occurs even when [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and that in the domain of the nominative-accusative dual (*bhaviṣaya*), there is elision of the *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*) as in *priyāṣṭau paśya*,
one contradicts the meaning previously promised and opposes the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other such works.

He alone should be asked how he stated it. Regarding the phrase "only when *hal* [consonant] follows": although an interpretation appears in the Bhāṣya even without extracting the word *halī*, the sense is that its being overcome by dissatisfaction has been explained elsewhere. [The example is] *priyāṣṭā*.
The nominative singular. He summarizes what has been stated with the words "priyāṣṭnaḥ. [Those ending in] -n.
*bhud* [is derived] from the root *budh* with the suffix *kvip*. [These are] those ending in *dh*.
Prau.ma.: *ṛtvigdadhṛksragdiguṣṇigañcuyujikruñcāñca* (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
Regarding *ṛtvigdadhṛk*: "something [is added]" means that when *ṛtu* is the upapada, *yaj* takes the suffix *kvip*;
from *dhṛṣ*, there is reduplication and the accent on the final syllable; and from *sṛj*, when it is the object, there is *kvip* and the substitution of *am*.

The meaning is: [the suffix] *kvin* is applied after the root *diś* in the sense of the object; after *snih* preceded by the prefix *ud*, there is elision of the final vowel of the prefix and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*;

and after *añc* when a *sup*-ending word is not the accompanying word (*apapada*), *kvin* is applied. Regarding "of *yuj*"—the same applies to *kuñc* as well, with the additional feature being the absence of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Regarding "with *kan*"—the intention is that the letter *i* is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "sannihite" (when [the suffix] *san* is present): as for the claim of earlier commentators that this occurs within the third governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), that is incorrect. For in the prescription of *san*, there is no subsequent recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "verbal root," and thus there is no threefold governing rule. [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *yujerasamāse* (Pāṇini 7.1.71)]

Regarding the rule *yujerasamāse*: as for what was stated by the Easterners—that [the condition applies] when *suṭ* follows—that is incorrect. This is because the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is the very subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and there is no basis for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the dual form *yujī* when used in the neuter. As for what they say regarding the neuter gender...

Regarding the statement that the *num* augment should not occur here in the form *śasi yuñji*, that is incorrect; for the *num* augment is possible by the rule "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ. As for the phrase "elision of *su*": since the substitution of *ku* (for *k*) is considered asiddha, the *num* occurs first because it is subsequent [in the order of rules];
thereafter, the elision of the case-ending occurs according to the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal. This is the intended meaning.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62) applies at the end of a word (*padānte*). As for what was stated by the ancients—that it applies when a *jhal* sound follows—that is incorrect, because the condition *jhalī* is not present here and would be useless [in this context]. As for the explanation given by the grandson [of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita]: "from the rule *jhalo jhali*..."
[The opponent argues: "Even if *jhalī* from [Pāṇini 8.2.26] *maṇḍūkapluti*-style [anuvṛtti] were to carry over, there would be no fault.
This is not so, because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *spṛṣṭa*.

Regarding *khan*: it is called *khan* because it causes one to limp (*khañjati*). [The root] *khaji* means "to have a defect in gait" (*gativaikalye*). [Regarding *parivrājaka*, the rule is] "after *pari*, [the suffix *kan* is added] to *vraj*."

And [the word] "dīrghaḥ" (long). As for the explanation given by the earlier [commentators], namely that "viṇ" [is the suffix], and that due to its being marked with Ṇ (ṇit), there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel—that is not correct, because in both the *Pañcapādī* and the *Daśapādī*, only the suffix *kvap* and the long vowel are prescribed by this rule.
[Prakriyā-kaumudī]: *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29).
He explains that in the rule *skoḥ*, the term *saṃyoga* has its genitive case ending elided and qualifies *jhal* and *ankau*;
this is shown by the words "at the end of a word" (*padānte*) and so forth. [The form] *bhṛṭ* is derived from *bhṛjjati* with the suffix *kvip*. Regarding the phrase "of *s*" (*sasya*):
the meaning is that because the substitution of *ś* for *j* (*jaśtva*) is considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *c* for *ś* (*ścutva*) occurs first. By this, [the view of] the ancients...

The objection regarding the incorrect expression has been answered. Regarding the word *ūrj*: from the root *ūrj* in the sense of "strength" (*bala*) and "vitality" (*prāṇana*), with the addition of the causative suffix *ṇic* (belonging to the *curādigaṇa*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "bhrājabhāsa... etc. There is the elision of the *ṇic*. And that [elision] does not behave as if it were present (*na sthānivat*) when the change of *c* to *k* (*kutva*) occurs, because it is a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*) and because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it. In this case...

The form *avayāḥ* is not cited as an example for word-final positions because, although the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed by the rule *ave yajaḥ* following the base *śvetavāh-uktha-* in a mantra, its exception (*apavāda*)—namely the suffix *ḍas*—is applied at the end of a word, and this is due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*). As for the statement: *śvetavāḍ-ukthaśāspuroḍāśāvayajāṃ ḍas*.
The predecessor stated this; that is not correct, because there is no long vowel in the *prakṛti* (base forms) *vahis* and *yajis* of which *ḍas* is the suffix.

Furthermore, regarding the citation of *avayāḥ*, the predecessor explained it as being due to the suffix *ṇvu*; that too is not correct, because the general rule (*utsarga*) *ṇvu* does not apply in the domain of the exception (*apavāda*) *ḍas*.

Prau.ma.: *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106). Why [specify] "not being final"? [Consider: *he sa*. Due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratvāt*), the substitution of *sa-* would apply, overriding the substitution of *yatva* for *tyad* etc.; thereafter, the elision of the consonant and following vowel (*halṅyādilopa*) would occur.

The *ru*-substitution and the *visarga* would [otherwise] occur; furthermore, the form *sā* in the feminine would not be possible. In reality, however, the mention of "not being final" (*anantyagrahaṇam*) can be omitted. Nor is there the aforementioned fault, because when the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*) is recognized, the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so on becomes possible. Even under the view that "once a rule has applied, it does not apply again" (*sakṛdgatau*), the rule "for *ta* and *do*, *sa* occurs before *su*" (*tadoḥ saḥ sau*) applies.

Furthermore, immediately after this [sūtra], one can explain by dividing the *yoga* as "of *adas*" (*adasaḥ*), such that the substitution of *sat* applies only to *adas* and not to any other *da*. Now, if it is argued: "In the original formulation, from the root *dvi-īyati* with the suffix *kvip*, the form *sva* would result; but under the restricted rule, it would be *dva*," do not say so. This is because [the restriction applies] to the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense.
Because of the impossibility of [the existence of] vowels and consonants [in that context], the reading *dvīḥ* alone is more logical.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *ReĀ prathamayoram* (Pāṇini 7.1.28)]. *ReĀ* is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided; the word *prathamā* [refers to the nominative case].

He explains that [the term] "secondary" (gauṇa) refers to the combination of the first and second [cases] by means of the words beginning with "of *reĀ*," etc. It would be easier to say "after *reĀ* and *suṭ*. [The phrase] "with the intention of expressing the locus" (*adhikaraṇatva*) is used because, if "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) were a qualifier of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), [the rule would apply otherwise].

In that case, it would indeed be useless; for since the rules prescribing *āt* and *yat* are specifically ordained, they can sublate the elision (*lopa*) within their own scope. Nor does this result in the position that there is elision of the final letter (*antyalopa*) becoming baseless; for by the mention of the form with the augment *suṭ* in the rule "sāma ākam," that [elision of the final letter] is also [indicated].
The meaning is that this has already been explained.

Regarding the example *yuvaṃ vastrāṇi*: there is elision (*lopa*) of the remainder. As for what is stated in the *Kāśikā*—"Of the fifth and the fourth cases, and also of the sixth and the first"—it refers to the following:
In this case, elision is prescribed for all dual endings except for those remaining [in the specific cases mentioned].

Thus, this is with respect to that [ordinary] speech. However, it should be understood that even the nominative dual is indeed within the scope of the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopa*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The question "Why [is it said] 'ending in *map*'"? asks for the purpose of this governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*).

Regarding the phrase "in the operation of a subordinate element" (*aṅgakārye*): by this, the *paribhāṣā* "when that which applies to a subordinate element has already operated, there is no further application [of another rule]" is established by implication. That is to say: when a rule (*śāstra*) that applies to a subordinate element—that is, whose scope of operation (*vṛtti*) lies within the domain of the subordinate element (*aṅga*)—has already taken effect (*pravṛte*), then another [rule] does not apply again.

For its meaning is that when an operation has already taken place, there is no further application of a rule; this technical principle (paribhāṣā) is established in the Bhāṣya as being indicated by both the two rules "jyādādīyasaḥ" and "jñājanorjā". Otherwise, indeed, [the author] would not have mentioned the vowel 'a' in "jyādādi". [The same applies to] "bahorlopa".

Therefore, one should simply maintain the elision (*lopam*). Since the lengthening is established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, the form *jyāyān* is achieved. One should also prescribe *jaṃ* for the roots *jñā* and *jan*. [Objection: The lengthening will occur by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*. [Response: It is not so; for in the case of *dvābhyām*, once the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class has been applied, [the lengthening would apply] when followed by a *sup* suffix.
Should it not be said that [the rule] "ca" would not result in a long vowel?
No, because by the mention of "of two, one," etc., it is indicated that the aforementioned *paribhāṣā* is non-eternal (*anitya*).
As for what some read as "of the fully established" (*pariniṣṭhitasya*), [they hold that] the long vowel occurs in "dvābhyām."

Furthermore, they claim that [a form] is not fully established (*pariniṣṭhita*) without [the application of a rule]; however, this contradicts the Bhāṣya. For if [the forms] *jyāyān*, *jānāti*, and *jñāyate* were also considered unestablished without the long vowel [substitution], then even the indication provided by the Bhāṣya would be undermined at its very root. This is because, if [the rule] "bhyaso 'bhyam" [were applied...].

If the reading "pariniṣṭhitasya" (of that which is already established) indeed occurs thus in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, then it should be interpreted as referring to an alternative view by relying solely on its status as a specific textual injunction (*vācanikatā*). Alternatively, let it be understood that this is merely a statement of the result obtained through the force of the rule's non-eternality (*anityatva*), and not something included within the scope of what is being taught (*jñāpyāṃśa*).

In this way, even the *Kāśikā* and other texts can somehow be interpreted; such is the direction [of the argument]. The phrase "another method" (*makārāntaram*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). In the rule *jasaḥ śī*, by blending the *s* of *jasaḥ* (i.e., reading it as *jasaḥ s*), one explains it as "of *jas* ending in *s*"; thus, by the rule *ato'm*, [the desired form is obtained].
It should be understood that this is either by carrying over the non-inclusion from the previous sūtra, or by explaining it as "only *am*.

Regarding the term "without a case-ending": thus, the doubt raised in the Bhāṣya is that this is a prohibition of the *am* that would have been obtained by the preceding rule, "ReĀ prathamayoḥ. And why not [accept] it exactly in that way?

Should it not be said that [the substitution] would not occur? For the substitution of *na* is not applicable to feminine and neuter genders— as in "yuṣmān brāhmaṇīḥ" or "kulāni"— and because if there were no gender distinction, forms such as "yuṣmān brāhmaṇān" and so forth would result in being unestablished.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:
*yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89). Why "before a vowel" (*aci*)? [Consider: *yuvābhyām*. However, if [the rule] "yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe" [is applied], [it would follow] from "rāyo hali" [in the preceding sūtra].

The word *hal* continues [from the previous rule]. In that case, let the term *aci* not be applied here, since the desired result is established by the process of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*). [This refers to] Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.89: *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* ("of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when there is no substitute [for the case endings]"). [The commentary states: "when followed by a consonant."

This [form] is established either by the inclusion of *ac* (vowels) in the term *aci* or by the complete drying up [of the vowel]; or it is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "rāyo halī" (Pāṇini 7.2.85). [Objection: If this is so, what is the purpose of including the mention of "non-substitute" (*anādeśa*), for there is no substitute [for *rāy-*] that begins with a consonant?
[Reply: Not so; because [the form] *bhyas* undergoes the substitution of *sat* (i.e., *su*). However, in the view that accepts *abhyas*, [the mention of non-substitute is necessary].
It should be understood that the mention of *anādeśa* (non-substitute) here is for the purpose of ensuring the application [of the rule] in the case of *acīti*.

Regarding the phrase "in both alternatives": one should not argue that, in the alternative where there is elision of the final letter (*antyalopa*), the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel-lengthening of homogeneous vowels) would apply by overriding the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form), on the grounds of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*.
This is because the purpose of pronouncing the letter 'a' [in the rule] is fulfilled by its non-occurrence [as a substitute].
Prau.ma.: *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso'ś* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.27). The presence of the indicatory letter *ś* is for the sake of making it a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa); otherwise, indeed—

The rule *ādeḥ parasya* would apply. Nor is it redundant, because its purpose is to ensure that the substitution (*yatva*) occurs by means of the designation of the substitute (*ādeśa*). Nor should it be argued that even when there is a substitution for a part, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) remains unsubstituted; for [it is established that] "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words."
From the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): this very fact that [the substitute] is *śit* indicates that "all substitutes are substitutes for entire words.

The meaning is that the application of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) rests only upon that which possesses meaning. However, by the force of specific rules, it should be understood that forms such as *sic*, *caṅ*, and others may also apply even to that which is meaningless.
However, this must be noted: in the view that there is elision of the final *y*, the [substitution of] *ś* for *s* would apply to *eṣaḥ*;

this must be prevented by the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*. This is provided that the said maxim applies specifically to operations concerning the *aṅga* itself, and not merely to those falling under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *aṅga*.

If it is argued that *aś* here [in Pāṇini 7.1.28] is a persistent misconception, then it should be explained as follows: by means of the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) according to [Pāṇini 6.1.97] *ato guṇe*, another vowel *ā* is superimposed [upon the *as*], so that *aś* remains in the very form of the vowel *ā* and does not undergo modification.

As for the claim that *aś* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *syāt*, that is not correct; because at the time when the substitution of *aś* is about to take effect, [the condition *śeṣe* applies].
Because there is no elision [of the final *i*], the substitution of *sy* does not apply.

Regarding the word *bhāvinaḥ*: the intention is that when the *śeṣe lopaḥ* elision has been applied, the augment *suṭ* would have applied because the stem ends in the vowel *a*; however, it is precluded by the force of the designation [of the whole] as the substitute for that which possesses *suṭ*. But on the view that *śeṣe lopaḥ* means the elision of the *ṭi* (the final phoneme), the mention of *suṭ* would indeed be redundant. [This applies] to *ākam*.

The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of homogeneous vowels); otherwise, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) would apply. Nor can it be argued that the explicit pronunciation of the long vowel *ā* serves as a functional indicator (*jñāpaka*), because its purpose is already fulfilled by the prevention of *etva* (the substitution of *e* and *o*) in the case of *abhyam*, just as in other instances. Here, in the two rules "yuvāvau dvivacane" and "tvamāvekavacane"...

It has been explained that the words *dvivacana* (dual) and *ekavacana* (singular) do not refer to the suffixes themselves, but rather to their meanings. He demonstrates the result of this [explanation] with the passage beginning "when being compounded," etc.
Regarding the term *dvyekatva* (duality and singularity): even in the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, number is also included.

The sense is that [the pronoun] denotes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). "The meaning of the compound" refers to the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). "If it has another number" means: if it possesses a number other than the number residing in the meanings of *yusmad* and *asmad*.
"They exist"—this is established precisely by the force of resorting to the primacy of the meaning, even in the case of a past state (*bhūtapūrvagati*).

The meaning is that because of their acceptance [as primary meanings], if they were dependent on a suffix (*pratyaya*), those two [forms] would not occur, and thus there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Similarly, in the fourth verse as well, by stating "the forms *yuvau* and *tvamau* do not [occur]," the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when dependent on a suffix is indicated. Thus, it follows that the dependence on the meaning (*arthaparatva*) has been adopted in order to avoid both under-extension and over-extension. Nor is there a contradiction with the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), because that [maxim] is set aside precisely by the force of the inclusion of the word "vacana" (number). For otherwise, one would simply have said "in duality" (*dvitve*) and "in singularity" (*ekatve*); for it would have been possible to explain it as: "of that case-ending which occurs in duality and singularity, [there is] *ām*. This is the intended sense.

Regarding the expression *atitvākam* and *atimākam*: although in the rule *sāma ākam*, the mention of *suṭ* is not a qualifier of the substitute (*sthānin*) because it would be redundant due to sublation, it nevertheless serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, only that *ām* which is to be preceded by *suṭ* must undergo the substitution of *ākam*. And this [substitution] does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*).

The suffix *ākam* does not apply [to the word *sambhavati*]. Furthermore, when there is a designation of a collective (*samudāya*), no third alternative exists apart from being either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nor is a separate status as a substituendum (*sthānitva*) here assigned to both the augment *suṭ* and the suffix *ām*, nor to the word *ca* and the dual number.

Because of its non-existence. However, if the compound *sa-ām* were explained as a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*), and by the force of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) the word *s-* were understood to refer specifically to *suḍ*, even so, if the inclusion of *suḍ* were merely an incidental prescription (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*), then the compound would not be valid. But in other cases...
It is argued that because there is a desire to express [the form] *sāhatya*, the suffix *ām* alone is not applicable here.
To this, the following must be said: first of all, the statement "for which *ām* is to be followed by *suṭ*" and so forth is sublated;
for there can be no connection with *suṭ* for an *ām* that has been superseded by *ākam*. If it is argued that *suṭ* applies to *ākam*?

In that case, one should indicate that very [element]. If it is argued that the substituendum (*sthānin*) is indicated through a mediated relationship by means of the substitute (*ādeśa*), then alas! in forms such as *yuṣmākam*, the augment *suṭ* would be heard. If it is argued that it is not heard because of the force of the technical designation *sāma*, we say no; for the designation...

Because its purpose is fulfilled by the exclusion of the secondary meaning, it lacks the capacity [to convey the primary sense]. Furthermore, the objection raised regarding the status of being a subsequent prescription (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*) concerning the collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) is likewise untenable; for since there is no possibility of the individual [members] occurring alone when the intention is to express their conjunction (*sāhitya*), such a contingency does not arise.
Only the *ām* remains; yet even that does not [constitute a basis for the application of the rule], because the coexistence (*sāhitya*) of the *ām*—

which exists at the stage of grammatical derivation— and the *suṭ*— which is merely postulated as occurring at a later time— is accepted solely on the basis of a single cognition, just as one says, "this is the seer of both the past and the future."

If it is argued that in those [other systems] the relationship exists between two things within a single view, here too it is the same: the relationship exists within a single substitute (*ādeśa*). And thus, in the rule *irayoḥ*, in forms such as *dadhre*—where the *jha* of the root *dhā* is replaced by *ir*, the *ā* is elided, and *ra* is substituted—the substitution of *ra* has its purpose fulfilled in roots such as *kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *bhṛ*.

When this has been done, it is established in the original treatise (*ākara*) that because of the dual-number indication in the rule *irayoḥ*, the substitution of *re* is applied again even to that which is derived through grammatical derivation (*lākṣaṇika*). In the expression *irayoḥ*, there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a pair of similar items);
however, in the expression *sāma*, it is a *dvandva* (copulative compound). The intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*) is indeed equal in both cases.

In reality, however, in the sūtra *sāma ākam*, the suffix *ām* alone is also indicated by means of *tantra*. Because of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it possesses the quality of being final (*antva*) and is accompanied by the augment *suṭ*; thus, the rule *sāma* applies. But in the case of secondary (gauna) usage, the operation concludes with the very first application. For this very reason, [the rule] *śeṣe*...

Under the view that "the elision of *ṭi* is [treated as] an elision" (*lopaṣṭilopa*), the identity of result with the alternative position is also established. In any case, one should not be dogmatic in attempting to justify the forms *atitvayām* and *atimayām*, which have been conjectured by some; for [the correct forms are] *atitvākām*, *atimākām*, and so forth.
This is merely a direction [for further inquiry], since it has already been illustrated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself.

Regarding the phrase "of the two [words] characterized by the sixth case (genitive) and so forth": this is obtained through the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the word "of every *pada*. However, he will explain that the inclusion of the term "standing" (*sthagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the operation] occurs only when the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is actually present, and not when it has been elided. [The example is] "by all the Vedas."

"May Govinda protect you; may Kṛṣṇa always protect us"—this reading of the ancients has been rejected, because [the word] "us" (asmān) cannot be applied since it does not belong to the same sentence. This is due to the mention of the word "standing" (sthagrahaṇāt).

The verb *tiṣṭhati* here functions in the sense of "not abandoning" (*ahāni*). As in the example, "tiṣṭha sugrīva," it is understood as "abide by your agreement; do not abandon the agreement. Therefore, the meaning is that the substitutes [of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] occur only when [the word] does not abandon the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth.
Thus, in the case of *yuṣmat-putraḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "the son of you two" (*yuvayoḥ putraḥ*) or "the son of you all" (*yuṣmākam putraḥ*). [This occurs] after a word-end (*padāt*).

The word "para" is used in order to establish the state of being subsequent (*paratva*). However, it was not employed by the ancient [grammarians]. In that case, since the substitute would simply not occur due to the absence of being subsequent to a word (*pada*), what is the purpose of including the term *stha*?

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "Nor [is there elision] when joined with *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *āha*, or *eva*" (Pāṇini 8.1.24). Regarding the phrase "the group beginning with *ca*": the meaning is conjunction with any one among these five.
Regarding the word *yukta*: the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when applied to a neuter noun.
Prau.ma.: Regarding the rule *paśyārthaiścānālocane* (Pāṇini 3.1.137):

the term *paśyārthaiḥ* [is used]. Precisely because of this, by the addition of the suffix *śa*, it denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, *darśanam* becomes *paśyaḥ*. And here, that refers to mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), just as in the rule *adarśanaṃ lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.60), where it does not mean only visual perception. It is not merely ocular knowledge.
Because of the prohibition [stated] as "not in the case of non-contemplation," he says this: "by means of objects of non-visual knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "I am a devotee," etc., they have explained here: "The construction is that by the very same cause through which you are a devotee of Hari, I too am a devotee. However, if by the word "by that" (tena) devotion...

The reason for protection is being pointed out; therefore, if there were a prescription dependent on that [previous mention], then the subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*)—expressed as "you yourself [are] this"—would not occur. To this, it must be said:
first of all, the claim that there is no status of subsequent reference (*anvādeśatva*) in a prescription dependent on something else is untenable.

For an *ādeśa* (substitute) is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*). An *anvādeśa* (re-injunction) is an injunction of something else after [the injunction of] a certain thing for the sake of its prohibition; it does not, however, contain the sense of independence, because that is not the literal meaning of the word, and because it has not been so defined in the technical treatise (*śāstra*).
Nor should it be argued that such a meaning is merely inferred from observing usage.

For instance, in such examples as "vanyadvipenonmathitā tvagasya" (the bark of this tree was stripped by a wild elephant) and "athainamadrestanayā śuśoca" (then the daughter of the mountain grieved for him),
the form *ena* is observed even though there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*). If it is argued that in those cases the causality is not expressed by a word, we say no.

"Therefore, having violated the injunctions of the Creator, he has become a guest in the abode of the Destroyer (Yama). Because of such usage by Māgha, this is not a mandatory rule [that a hero must always be described as brave]; however, the statement "this one is timid at night" is not a mandatory rule either.

However, this is a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, the expression "tad imam" is not contradictory. This being the case, the labor of supplying the word "yat" in the sense of "by whom you are protected" is useless;

rather, the connection is simply "by that [he] is saved. Furthermore, because the subject matter has already been introduced, there is no requirement for the word "yat"—this is the general direction [of the argument]. Here, the word "tena" [is used].

The word *vidyamānam* exists; from that follows *hariḥ* ending in the nominative case, which is the substitute for what follows it. Likewise, after the word *trāyate*, there is *saḥ* ending in the nominative case. One should not be deluded into thinking that *trāyate* belongs to a separate sentence; rather, [the construction is] "May that Hari protect you."

Because of the connection with multiple factors through the *tantra* principle; and because even if *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) is accepted, there is no loss of the status of being a single sentence as defined by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which has a single finite verb is a sentence" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*). [Prauḍhamanoramā—Samantritam (Pāṇini 2.3.48)]

Regarding the term *āmantritama*: even in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the inclusion of that which ends in [the word] is understood by virtue of the capacity of employing a major designation (*mahā-saṃjñā*). *Āmantraṇam* means "addressing.

By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the term refers to the instrument used for that purpose. Furthermore, one is addressed by means of a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), and not by the bare stem alone.
With the intention that [the word] ends in a case-ending, he says: "tadantam" (ending in that). Prakriyākaumudī: "The preceding vocative is as if non-existent" (Pāṇini 8.1.72):
"āmantritam pūrvam". As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the preceding word] is preceded by the qualified object—[that is not the case].

Some say that these substitutions do not occur after [the words] following another vocative, provided that the preceding word is itself a vocative; however, the phrase "some say" (*kecit*) there is inappropriate, because the stated meaning is already established by the present sūtra. Furthermore, as for what they have explained as the meaning of the three sūtras:
This is not so, because that [objection] does not touch upon the meaning of the third sūtra. [The sūtra is:

*pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130). [The word] *tadavayavasya* ("of that which is its constituent part") is used [in the commentary], based on the principle that "substitutes apply to that which is being specified."
This is obtained by means of this technical definition (paribhāṣā).
Thus [are] the tamed.

Regarding the form *agnimanth-* as in "he churns the fire" (*agniṃ manthati*): this very form arises from the roots *mathnāti* and *manthate* with the suffix *kvip*. However, because these roots are marked with the *idit* designation, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Thus, the forms are *agniman*, *agnimanthau*, and *agnimanthaḥ*. Here ends the section on words ending in *th*.
"Regarding the syllable *ṅ*": the sense is that it is due to "proximity" (*āntaratamya*).

"Between a short vowel and a consonant": the sense is that for a consonant, a short vowel is slightly similar, whereas a long vowel is dissimilar. "And it has been stated": the remainder is that this was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*. Some, however...

Because the preceding [sūtra] itself possesses the *mutva* quality, they cite examples where it does not possess *mutva*. That was not mentioned at the beginning of the Bhāṣya and was therefore overlooked.
[Prakriyākaumudī]: *uda īt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.127).
"uda īt": this is an exception to [the rule regarding] the vowel *a*. [The roots] ending in *c* [are as follows]: *cāntāḥ*.
Prau.ma.: *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14).

Regarding the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*, the phrase *adhātoḥ* is here separated as a distinct *yoga*. By virtue of that [separation], the prohibition applies only to what ends in *as* immediately following [the preceding rule], and not to what ends in *at*.
Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others [have discussed this]. He demonstrates that [distinction] by stating: "that which is different from a verbal root and ends in *as*.
In the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "Both are called *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.5).
Since the word "both" (*ubhe*) is already established by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "two" (*dve*), the explicit mention of "both" (*ubhe-grahaṇam*) [is for a specific purpose].

He explains that [the term] is for the purpose of indicating a collective application: "both combined. For otherwise, in the case of *nenijati*, the acute accent on the initial syllable—by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated [roots]" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*)—would apply alternately to each [syllable] individually.

Prau.ma.: *Jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.6). The word *jakṣiti* is a separate term; by the word *iti*, only *jakṣiti* itself is referred to. In the phrase *iti ādir yeṣām*, it is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi] compound.
This is what the *bahuvrīhi* compound expresses: "the other six elements. These end in the suffix *-t*.
The root *gup* means "to protect. When the suffix *kvip* is intended, there is an absence of the *āya* augment according to the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā. [These are] those ending in *p*.
Prau.ma.: *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane'kañ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.60).
Regarding *tyadādiṣu*: what is meant by *anālocane* (not perceiving)? [Example: *tat paśyati iti taddarśaḥ*. [This is formed] by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*.
However, words such as *tādṛśa* and others are derived etymologically even with an unreal meaning of their components because they are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words. For this very reason...

The [explanation] "from the root *dṛś* in the sense of 'not knowing'" is consistent. However, in the Bhāṣya, a derivation as a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*) is shown: "People see him as it were" (*tam iva imam paśyanti janāḥ*), or "he sees as it were" (*sa iva ayam paśyati*).

The meaning is that he becomes an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣaya*). In that case, even though the function consists merely in attaining the status of being an object (*viṣayatvāpatti*), [the term applies].
It is consistent [with reason] because it has as its object the meaning of ignorance, since it is not an obscuration that takes an object.
*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding the rule *naśervā* (Pāṇini 8.2.63): here, the phrase *jhali api* is un-Pāṇinian; furthermore, it would lead to over-extension in cases such as *naṣṭam*.
[The forms] *nāga* and so on follow the same six *aṅga*-markers as before. [The section on] the *śānta* [consonants] is concluded.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.3.58), [the term] "by way of becoming a *ṣṭu*" means that after the substitution of *ru* and *visarga* for the *s* of the suffix *san*,
there is optionally a *sakāra* in one alternative by virtue of the rule *vā śari*.

The meaning is that because of that [rule], when there is an intervention by a *śar* sound, the *s* of a *sup* suffix undergoes *ṣatva*, while the preceding [consonant] undergoes *ṣṭutva*; however, it does not become *ṣ* by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ," because of the prohibition "apadāntasya.
This being the case, since the desired result is established by the mention of *sakāra*, the purpose of mentioning *śar* must be considered.

Regarding the phrase "from the commentary": Haradatta’s statement that [the rule] is impossible should be disregarded, because [the application] is possible in the case of *suhinsu*; this is the intended meaning. As for the term "saṃyogānta" (end of a conjunct): one should not suspect that the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga* when this [operation] is to be performed.

Because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is indeed extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on the designation of a word-base (*pada-saṃjñā*), one might ask: "How then was it previously stated that there is no elision of the final conjunct when denoting *kāvya*, *kalatra*, or *śālva*? If this is asked, the answer is: "In those cases, there is a prohibition of [the rule] 'after a vowel' (*yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*), according to the principle 'or not, because of the elision of the *jhal* [consonant]' (*na vā jhalo lopāt*)."

Since it has been determined that there is no deletion (*lopa*) in either of the two views (*pakṣa*), it is appropriate to adopt the principle that "the preceding is more internal" (*antaraṅga*) for the sake of uniformity; for it is clear that the status of being a word (*padatva*) obtainable through extension (*atideśa*), as well as the deletion conditioned by it, find their application in the portion of the *lakṣya* (the form to be analyzed) that precedes [the suffix]. But here, however—

In the first two positions, since the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is evident, it is more logical that the rule "that which depends on an external cause is *bahiraṅga*" should apply in order to maintain uniformity with that; such is the direction of the argument.
[Examples include] *takṣirakṣibhyām* and so forth. As for what they say regarding those who speak of a white wheel (*śuklaṃ cakram*) or a bright one (*śukraṃ*):
*Kalopaḥ*, *śul*, *śuklau*, *śulbhyām*, *caḥ*, *cakrau*, *carbhyām*, *śūḥ*, *śukrau*, *śūrbhyām*, and so forth—all of this has been refuted by this [rule]. However, there is this distinction:
in the case of *tagÂraḥ*, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is beyond dispute; yet even that is difficult to establish in the other case.

Thus: *didhak* (as in *didhag*). Regarding this, Naimiṣīya has stated that because the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* (via Pāṇini 8.2.40, *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*) is considered asiddha, the final consonant is dropped due to the rule on the elision of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), and then the *ḍh* undergoes the *jaś*-substitution to become *ḍ*, resulting in *didhaḍ*.
However, that is an error, because the substitution of *gh* for the root-initial *dh* (via Pāṇini 7.3.35, *dāder dhātor ghaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ḍh*.
Because of being wakeful. Those ending in *ṣ*.
Regarding *vidāna*: from the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* is replaced by *vasu*; because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap*. Regarding *sedivān*:
the suffix *kvasu* is applied according to the rule "In the common language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* are applied] after the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*.
Regarding *seduṣaḥ*: [one might object] that "when a term containing a specific *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one that lacks that *anubandha*."

By way of explanation: according to the rule *videḥ śaturvasuḥ*, it is appropriate that the *samprasāraṇa* applies only to the suffix *vasu*, and not to *kvasu*; this is true. However, the inclusion of the indicatory letter *ū* (in *ūdit*) for the suffix *vasu* is intended to include *kvasu* as well, since the status of being marked by an *uk* (*ugit*) would otherwise be established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. In this case...

The suffix *kvasu* has not been cited after roots such as *gam*, because its usage is restricted to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*). Nevertheless, poets employ it, as seen in examples such as "of him who had attained all excellences" (*śreyāṃsi sarvāṇy adhijagmuṣe*) and "him standing near the city" (*taṃ tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe*). Thus, even forms belonging to the Vedic language occasionally occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
This may somehow be resolved by relying on the general indicative (*jñāpaka*) rule *māsaśchandasī* [Pāṇini 6.1.63].
Regarding the rule *puṃso'suṅ* [Pāṇini 7.1.89]: it is intended that [the form] be specified; therefore, in the case of *paramapumān*, [the substitution does not apply].
Because it is subsequent, once *asuṅ* has been applied, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātatvam*) occurs specifically for the vowel of *asuṅ*.

However, if [the rule were governed by] a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*), this would not be established; for if the acute accent were already applied to the vowel of the masculine word before the production of the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, then [the accentuation] would apply to the place of a consonant (*hal*) characterized by elision (*sraṃsanadharmī*).

For it would follow that only an unaccented substitute for that base would occur. Nor can it be argued that even if an accent were applied to the vowel *u*, it would be precluded because it is not final; nor can it be argued that the suffix *asuṅ* will be applied because it is final—because the internal accent must first be applied.
The sense is that [the substitution] *asuṅ* is not established because it is *bahiraṅga*. And this has been stated in accordance with Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others.
In reality, however, the view that the locative case [in the rule] refers to what follows (*parasaptamī*) is also easily justifiable, by virtue of the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*.

It should be noted that this is because [the substitution] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the final member of a compound. Now, one might object: even in the case of a non-compound, once *asuṅ* has been applied, the accent of the suffix would be superseded by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), which is subsequently prescribed;
thus, *asuṅ* would become acute, whereas it is desired that the vowel *ū* be acute—as in *pumān*, *pumāṃsam*.

If it is argued that this is because the word *paripāṭu* and others are read in the same way [with the udātta on the final syllable], that is true; however, Haradatta and others maintain that by the force of making the suffix *ḍumsun* marked with *ṅ* (i.e., *nit*), the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) does not apply here.
But is this not improper? For the rule "phiṣaḥ" applies only to those words where the division between base and suffix is absent.
If it is argued that this refers to the "application" (pravṛtti) [of rules], that is true; however, in some cases where even parts are involved, this is an indicator (liṅga) for such application.

Although this is already established by the rule "that which is external (bahiraṅga) is as if unestablished" (asiddha), nevertheless, the use of the marker *n* is intended to indicate that the paribhāṣā regarding external elements is not universally obligatory (anitya).

The conclusion is that [the vowel *u*] is for the purpose of pronunciation. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it is "marked with *u*" (*uṅidita*)—and what was explained by his grandson—that the vowel *u* is for the sake of the grammatical operations of an *uṅit* suffix—the sense is that those views are inconsistent.
In the example "he pumann," there is no long vowel because of the rule stating "except in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*). [In the example] "puṃsu,"...

When the final consonant of a conjunct is elided, the rule *mo 'nusvāraḥ* applies; however, because this refers specifically to an *anusvāra* that replaces *num*, the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vaḥ* does not cause the change to *ṣ*. Regarding the phrase "in the vocative singular" (*asya sambuddhau*), this is based on an explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). As for what Haradatta and others [have said]...

They say: since it has been made known that in certain instances only *anaṅ* is heard—by the rule stating that when *suṭ* is to be applied, *anaṅ* [is substituted] for *s-*—this [result] is established. But that has already been refuted;
or rather, it should be resolved by means of the maxim regarding operations within a stem (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).

*Prakriyākaumudī*: *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.107). Now, one might object: let only the vowel *au* be prescribed for *su*, since the form *asau* is already established by the substitution of *ya* for *tad* and the other pronouns (*tyadādyatva*). Why, then, prescribe the elision of *su*? Do not say so; [for otherwise] it would result in *asakau*.

In the case of *strī*, if the suffix *ṭāp* were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ī* by the rule *pratyayasthāt*. Regarding *asuka*: in the absence of the substitution of *āṬ*, the *yatva* (change to *ya*) of the *tyadādi* group occurs, followed by the substitution of *s* for *t*. The form *amuka*, however, is incorrect, because the substitution of *m* (mutva) is superseded by the substitution of *s*. Similarly, forms such as *amukī* and *amukaśarmā* are likewise incorrect.
Because [the forms] *asukaḥ*, *ādakaḥ*, and *śarma* are alone logically consistent.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *eta īd bahuvacane* (Pāṇini 7.3.103). If the technical term (*paribhāṣika*) "bahuvacana" (plural) were taken [in this rule], [it would lead to an inconsistency].

Even if [the forms] beginning with *amībhiḥ* were established by this rule, the form *amī* would not be established in the nominative plural (*jas*), because here the vowel *e* does not have a plural suffix following it; therefore, he explains: "when denoting a plurality. Prakriyākaumudī: *na mu ne* (Pāṇini 8.2.3).

"na mu ne" || He says that *ne* is a locative case denoting the object (*viṣayasaptamī*)—meaning "when *nā* is to be applied. The implication is that otherwise, because the condition of being followed by a *ghi* stem would be absent, the substitution of *nā* would not occur. [Objection: Even so, once *nā* has been substituted, wouldn't the lengthening rule "supi ca" apply? Regarding the lengthening...

Because the substitution of *m* for *n* (*mutva*) is not established [at that stage], he says: "And when [the substitution] has been made. Alternatively, the matter may be resolved by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Here, this should be noted: while one could have said *amuna* just as one says *adhuna*, the statement "na mu ne" is intended to effect a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). By means of that, forms such as *rāmaḥ* and *rāmebhyaḥ* are established.
[The substitution] is established. Otherwise, how could the *it*-designation and the elision of the vowel *u* occur due to the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of *ru*?
Nor should it be argued that the *it*-designation and elision are not subject to non-establishment by virtue of the force of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) notation [of *ru*];
for in examples such as *tarumūlam*, the rule "ato roḥ" is stated to exclude the application of the rule "haśi ca."

In this context, since the rule has its purpose fulfilled by the mention of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) itself, one might argue: "Let there be no nasalization in the rule *ato roḥ*, as it can be managed simply by taking the word as it is explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*). But even so, in the case of *deva ruhī*, the [nasalization] from the root *rudh* would be unavoidable. Rāma.

Furthermore, in such instances as these, it is easy to maintain that the rule finds its purpose through the resulting audibility of the nasalized *r* (*anunāsika*). Thus, when the rule *sthānivat* (P. 1.1.56) also applies, the visarga is obtained because the status of being a word (*padatva*) is present. Moreover, the mention of *aś* in the rule for the substitution of *y*—in the indications such as *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca*—is intended here [to prevent the application of the *sthānivat* principle].
The term "liṅga" serves as an illustration; such is the direction [of the argument].
Thus end the masculine stems ending in consonants.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34). It was not stated simply as *naḥ*, for if that were the case, in the word *naddham*, the substitution of *na* [for *da*] would occur by the rule *radābhyām* (8.2.42), and the rule *jhaṣastathoḥ* (8.2.40) would not apply.

In this regard, the following should be noted: regarding the *bahuvrīhi* compound *suṣṭhu anaḍvāho yasyām iti* ("that in which there are excellent oxen"), the citation of *svanaḍvāhī* is to be considered doubtful, because it contradicts the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from what is not a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*). As for *gīḥ*: the root *gṛ* (in the sense of swallowing and sound) takes the suffix *kvip*; [the form is derived as] *añ-anta-*...

In *it*, there is the substitution of *it* [for the penultimate vowel]. In *pūri*, there is lengthening by the rule "rvor upadhāyāḥ. The root *pṛ* means "to protect" and "to fill. In *pūri*, there is the substitution of *ut* by the rule "ud oṣṭhyapūrvasya. In *āśiṣau*, there is the substitution of *it* for the penultimate vowel by the rule "āśāsaḥ kvāv upasaṃkhyānam."
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "śāsivasi. Thus end the feminine nouns ending in consonants.
Now begins the section on the euphonic combination of consonants (*hal-sandhi*).
*Prakriyākaumudī*: *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40).

The term *stoḥ* is a collective dvandva compound; its masculine gender is due to Vedic usage (*sautra*). Regarding *ścunā*: according to the rule *saha yukte'lpīyasya*, the third case is used even in the absence of actual conjunction.

It will be stated [later]. The word *yoga* is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Here, the correspondence between the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*) follows their respective order; however, this does not apply to the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), as evidenced by the rule *śāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.44). But in rules such as *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34), etc., [the correspondence holds].

Because it is based on the Sūtra, the substitution of *ś* does not occur [in cases where it would otherwise be expected]; however, it certainly does occur in examples such as *tajjñānam*. It is more appropriate to state the rule as "for *st*, there is *ś* before *ś*" (*stoḥ ścau ścuḥ*).
Nor does the presence of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when something is specified by the word *tasmin*" (Pāṇini 1.1.66) prevent the derivation of forms such as *yajñaḥ* and *yācñā*.
Because of the indicator (liṅga) in the rule *śāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.44), that [suffix] is not present here.
Prakriyāmañjarī:
Regarding *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), here too there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*).
This is because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *toṣṣi* (Pāṇini 8.4.43). It would be more appropriate to state it as *ṣṭau ṣṭuaḥ*.
In forms such as *īṭṭe* and *īṣṭe*, there is no fault because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) "na padāntāt—
" (Pāṇini 8.4.42). In *sarpiṣṭamam*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "hrasvātādau— " (Pāṇini 8.3.101).
Regarding the statement "in the case of a grammatical rule (pratyaya) [the form] is used in speech": as for what was read by the ancients as "nityam" (always) in the case of the suffix *mayaṭ*;

and as for the examples "ṣaṇṇām" and "ṣaḍṇām" cited in the section on stems ending in consonants; and as for the rule "yaro 'nunāsika—" (Pāṇini 8.4.45), which states that the nasalization is optional—[all these apply] there.

That which has been explained should all be disregarded due to its contradiction with the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "the *yavādi* group": in the reading of the *saṃhitā*, "yaci bhaṃ tasau matvarthe," one can resolve this by eliding a *da* before *tasau*—that is, reading it as *tadau*—and thus establishing its status as a *bha*.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *udaḥ sthāsthambhvoḥ pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.61), [the word] *udaḥ sthā* [is mentioned]. In this context, even the entire term *savarṇagrahaṇa* from the rule *anusvārasya yayi—* (Pāṇini 8.4.58) is extracted and connected here; that is, it applies to one part [of the rule].
With the intention of asserting that [the vowel] possesses the *svarita* accent, he says: "It shall be the same as the preceding.
Regarding the phrase "of the unvoiced," etc., by this the works of the ancients stating that "s becomes t" are refuted.
Furthermore, the citation here of the rule "the second letters of the *caya* group [are substituted] before *śar*" is due to excessive haste.

Regarding that [form] *tacchiva*: as for what was stated by the elder [grammarian] concerning *tacchiva*—namely, that once *jaśtva* (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop *d*) has been applied, the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55) applies—that is not correct, because since *tad-* ends in a dental (*d*), the proposal of applying *jaśtva* would be redundant. As for what was stated by his grandson (*tatpautra*) regarding *tad-*...
The claim that, after applying the *car*-substitution by Pāṇini 8.4.56 (*vāvasāne*), there is a connection with the word *śiva*,

followed by the *jaś*-substitution by 8.2.39 (*jhalāṃ jaśonte*), and then the *car*-substitution again by 8.4.54 (*khari ca*)— that is highly implausible; for [the rule for] *jaś*-substitution applies specifically with respect to the pause (*avasāna*).

Because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *cartva*; because the substitution of *jaś* does not depend on the word *śiva*; and because, when the future destruction of the pause (*avasāna*) is imminent, the rule *vāvasāne* (Pāṇini 8.4.56) has not yet applied; or because there is the possibility of the cessation of that which had already applied. And it has been said:
It is said, "The followers of Pāṇini are those who do not arrange [their rules] in a systematic order," and "they set aside even a rule that has already been established.

Otherwise, in the case of *harir ayam* as well, by what could the visarga—which would apply according to your own stated method—be prevented? Furthermore, if you say that *tat* is a form ending in *kvip* derived from the root *tan* (as in "it extends"), even so, by the rule of *jaś*-substitution...

Let there be the substitution of *da*. However, it is not logical to say that the substitution of *ścu* occurs after the substitution of *car* has been applied; for, with respect to the substitution of *ścu*, the substitution of *car* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). As for the claim that, in the rule *na mu ne* (Pāṇini 8.3.3), one should split the word *na* into a separate *yoga* to prevent the application of non-existence (*asiddhatva*) here—that too is incorrect, even if [the rule] were non-existent.

For when the derivation of the form is unimpeded, there is no evidence for resorting here to a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), which constitutes a recourse to a path only when no other is possible.

Regarding the form *ākraṃsyate*: the suffix *taṅ* (i.e., the middle voice ending) is applied by Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.3.40, "āṅ udgamane," and the augment *iṭ* is not inserted by sūtra 7.2.36, "snukramoḥ."

This is a rule concerning equal correlative relations (*samasambandhividhi*). However, it is not stated as a rule for equal objects (*samakarmaka*), because a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is also desired between two things that are merely being restated (*anuvādya*), as in the case of the rule: *samūlākṛtajīveṣu hankṛñgrahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.36).

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *ṅṇoḥ kukṭuk śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.28)—because the *kuk* and *ṭuk* augments are considered as belonging to the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), in the case of *prāṅ sāye*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* does not apply. However, in the case of *sugaṇ sāye*, [the rule *na*... applies.
Because it follows a word-final [consonant], the substitution of *ṣṭu* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.4.42) does not apply.

One who sits (*sīdati*) at Puṣkara, a particular sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), is called *puṣkarasat*. The descendant (*apatyam*) of that person is the teacher Pauṣkarasādi. The suffix *iñ* is applied because he belongs to the *bāhū-* group [of nominal stems].
The vowel lengthening occurs in both members of the compound because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group.
Prau.ma.:

Regarding the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* (Pāṇini 8.3.29), [the author] says "of *s*" (*sasya*), intending that "in the case of a mention of both [cases], the mention in the ablative case is stronger" because it is subsequent. However, the mention of the locative case as *si* is for the sake of brevity.

Regarding the form *ṣaṭ santaḥ*: the letter *t* becomes *c* by the rule of *cartva*. As for what some say—that according to the view "the second consonant of a *caya*-group [is substituted]," it would become *th*—that is not correct, because *cartva* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). For this very reason, in the absence of *dhuṭ*, in the form *ṣaṭ santaḥ*, there is no substitution of *ṭh* for *ṭ*. [This applies] to the letters *ṭ*, *n*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*).

From the doubling of the *dvitva* [of the consonants], there are sixteen. According to the rule "the *śara*s [are doubled] after the *khaya*s," when the *sakāra* is doubled, there are thirty-two. Nor should one suspect that the substitution of *cartva* (the change to *c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*) is *asiddha* in that context, because it is stated: "that which is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes does not apply to *dvitva*. Nor should one suspect a prohibition of doubling by the rule "a *śara* is not doubled before a vowel" (*Pāṇini* 8.4.49).

Because that [rule] has as its sole object the doubling of a consonant prescribed by the Sūtra itself; for this very reason, the examples *vatsaḥ* and *apsarāḥ* are established in the Bhāṣya for the Vārttika *śaraḥ khayaḥ*.
