The fact that the *dhuṭ* augment follows [the preceding sound] is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ṣṭu* by the rule *na padāntāt—* (Pāṇini 8.4.42). For this very reason...

The [suffix] *tu* that is about to be mentioned is not applied here; for they say: "Even so, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), it would be more appropriate to apply *tu* alone. That is not correct, because under the alternative view that "the second consonant of a cluster [is doubled]," the letter *th* would result [in *aṭth*]. [In response to this, it is said: "The substitution of *ś* [for *ṣ*] before a *dhuṭ* [consonant] must be stated as established," as in the case of *aṭ* (from *aṭati*) followed by *ścotati*.
In this context, *dhuṭ* does not occur.

[From] Pāṇini 8.3.31: *prau.ma.-śi tuk* (*śi tuk*). The locative case in *śi* is used to denote the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) "naḥ" which was established in the preceding rule.

He says "kalpayati" (he fashions) and explains "nasya" (of that). Now, one might object: let the *dhuṭ* augment itself be applied as prescribed; what is the need for the *tuk*? Do not say so. For the established meaning in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) of the rule "śaś chāe 'ṭi" (Pāṇini 8.4.63) is that *cha* replaces *śa* when it follows a consonant (*jhay*) at the end of a word (*padānta*). And thus, because the *dhuṭ* augment is added at the beginning [of the following element], [the condition of being at the end of a word is not met].

In the word *sañcchambhuḥ*, there would not be the doubling of the *ch* (i.e., *cch*). This is because when the suffix *śa* is added to the root *rap* preceded by *vi* according to the *uṇādi* rules—as in examples such as *madhvaścotanty abhito virapśan*—the augment *tuk* is applied as a final element of the preceding part (*pūrvānta*). [Objection: But if that were the case, then in the example *kurvañc śete*, [there would be no doubling].
If it is argued that the prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) by the rule *padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.37) would not apply [to the *t* of *tuṅ*], we say no;

for under the *kāryakāla* view, the *tuk* augment is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being *bahiraṅga*. Under the *yathoddeśa* view, the rule *stoḥ ścunā* is divided: the word *na* is understood to carry over, as is the word *ṇaḥ*.

When there is a conjunction with *ś* or *c*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *s* of *stoḥ* shall not occur. This [rule] is for the sake of the letter *n*. The mention of *sakāra* and the mention of the entire class (*varga*) are for the sake of subsequent rules. From that, [the rule] "ṣṭuan" (Pāṇini 8.4.41) follows; "pūrva" is carried over [from the previous rule]. Thus, in the sūtra "naśca" (Pāṇini 8.3.30), in the example *kurvantsīdati*, [the rule applies].

The statement in the works of the ancients— that the purpose of treating [the augment] as *parādīya* (occurring after the whole word) in the prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.37) is to be understood according to the *yathoddeśa* (eternally present) view;
for they say that this purpose is already covered by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*.

As for the statement "it has been replied": that is only partially correct; furthermore, the claim that this *paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding external and internal elements) does not apply when an internal element resides within the three-quarter portion [of the rule] contradicts one's own statement regarding the example *sudhyupāsya*. Let this matter rest for now. Regarding *sañc chambhuḥ*: here...

One should not suspect the occurrence of *ru* (the substitution of *r*) by the rule *naścchavi* (Pāṇini 8.3.7), on the grounds that the rules concerning *ścutva* and *tuk* are considered asiddha; for *chatva* is [likewise] asiddha. [This is stated in the] Pradīpa: *ṅmo hrasvādaci ṅmuṇnityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32).

*ṅmo hrasvāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.32). *ṅm* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term). Although the status of being *ṭit* is assigned to it for the sake of its technical designation (*saṃjñā*), by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is connected with the things designated (*saṃjñin*). Consequently, *Ruṭ*, *Ṇuṭ*, and *Nuṭ* are applied respectively. The mention of *naty* is for the sake of clarity. [This refers to the rule] *he mapare* (Pāṇini 8.3.26).

Thus, because it is read between the two optional rules "maya uño vo vā" (Pāṇini 8.3.33), its obligatory nature is obtained by that very fact. In the case of *sugaṇṇīśa*, the substitution of *ṇ* and the elision (*al-lopa*) are not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if they were the original element), because that [treatment] is prohibited when a preceding operation is *asiddha*. Regarding the fact that *ṅmuṭ* is placed at the beginning [of the word], as in the example *kurvann āste*:

This is for the purpose of prohibiting *ṇatva*. For this very reason, the rule "ṅmo hrasvād aci dve" was not formulated as a sūtra. The ancient commentators (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that since the preceding element is established (*siddhatva*) with respect to the subsequent *ṇatva*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *ṇatva* occurring [again]. As for what they say—that both [objections] are irrelevant because the matter is already covered by the *paribhāṣā* concerning external elements (*bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*)—that too is incorrect.

That too is merely one-sided. For, as in the case of the rule *rājñaḥ*, since it has been stated that the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* is absent in the *yathoddeśa* interpretation of the three chapters (*traipādika*), the treatises of the ancients are excellent.
Otherwise, how could he have himself stated "dviyam" and "triyam"? This is the direction [of the argument].

If it is objected that in examples such as *paramadaṇḍinau*, the augment *nuṭ* should occur because the status of being a *pada* is established by the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), we say no. This is because of the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule: "When the following member is a *pada*, the rules concerning what is not the beginning of a *pada* do not apply. For this very reason, [the augment does not occur] in cases such as *paramavācau*, *paramagoduhau*, and *paramalihau*.

The [substitutions] *kutva*, *ghatva*, *ḍhatva*, and so forth do not apply. As for the statement by the earlier commentators that *ṅmuṭ* does not occur—on the grounds that they carry forward the word "pada" from Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.3.21 (*uñi ca pade*) and explain it as referring to a pada beginning with a vowel (*ajādeḥ padasya*)—that is refuted by this very [work]. For it is precisely by the method already stated that the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is prevented in this very instance.
Because it must also be followed by that [other].

Prau.ma.: *samaḥ suṭi* (Pāṇini 8.3.5). Although the form could have been established by the substitution of *m* with *anusvāra*, this rule is nevertheless stated for the sake of ensuring the presence of the nasal quality (*anunāsikatva*) and the occurrence of three *s*-sounds.
Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.2), there is a dual view as to whether this is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading) or a *vidhi* (an actual injunction).
In the first case, the mention of *atra* (here) is redundant, because the context of the *ru-prakaraṇa* (the section concerning the substitution of *r*) is obtained from the *adhikāra* itself.

The word *tu*, however, serves to indicate a distinction from the subsequent subject in the case of the *adhikāra* (governing) interpretation—namely, that for the subsequent [sound] there is always *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), whereas for the preceding [sound] there is optionally the nasalization (*anunāsika*); in the case of the *vidhi* (injunction) interpretation, it would be redundant. The inclusion of the word *vā* (optionally) is for the sake of clarity, as in the rule *anunāsikātpara-* (Pāṇini 8.3.4).

Because it is established by the very indicator (jñāpaka) itself; for it is not possible to have a "non-nasalized" alternative without an option (vikalpa). To indicate this very point, the words "but" (tu) and "or" (vā) were not mentioned in the Vṛtti.
Prau.ma.: *Anunāsikātparo 'nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.4).

Regarding the term *anunāsikāt*, he states that it is the ablative case used in the sense of "leaving behind" (*lyablope*), meaning "having left aside the nasalized [sound]. And thus, just as with conjunction, so too with separation.

Intending to show that, because it is the cause for understanding a specific distinction— as in the case of "let the cow without its calf be brought"— the letter *r* alone, possessing the quality of potential nasality (*anunāsikya*), is connected as the limit (*avadhi*) due to its proximity and its being required, he says: "of *r*" (*roḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "from the preceding" (*pūrvasmāt*) and "the addition of an *anusvāra*": the status of being an augment (*āgamatva*) is understood precisely through the word "following" (*para*), as in the rule "the diphthongs *ai* and *au* precede those two" (Pāṇini 7.3.3), where the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) refers to the diphthongs *ai* and *au*.
This is the intended meaning.

*Prakriyāmañjarī*: Regarding *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.34), the word *visarjanīyasya* [is understood]. And the word *khari* follows by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) from the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15).
Now, since the anusvāra is not a vowel (anac), doubling of the following consonant would certainly not occur; therefore, he says:
"anusvāravisarga... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "after the letter *a*":
if, however, it were recited after the letter *i*, then in forms such as *payaḥsu* and *yaśaḥsu*, there would be the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule *iṇaḥ parasya*.

The intended meaning is "it might be so. Regarding the phrase "because it is not an *act*": even if this were the case, there would be no undesirable application of *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth in examples such as *hariḥ kartā* or *hariṃ smaret*, because the visarga and other such elements are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to their being situated in the final three chapters (*tripādī*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there is also doubling of the *anusvāra*": [this refers to the doubling of the *anusvāra* when followed by a consonant].

The word "api" (also/even) implies the letter *ka*. By another rule, the meaning is that even when [the doubling] has been performed by the rule "aco rahābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.46), the substitution [of *ya* for *ra*] still occurs by the rule "yaṇo mayaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.67).
This is the intended sense.

Prau.ma.: *pumaḥ khayyampare* (Pāṇini 8.3.6). Regarding *puṃsaḥ khayi*: this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the remaining portion [of the word] after the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) has been applied to the word *puṃs*. This is because it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
The intention is that this refers to the rule prescribing *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), namely Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.3.41: *idudupadhasya ca*.

This is stated according to the opinion of the ancient grammarians (*prācām*) who explain [the sūtra] through a construction of different case-relations (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), namely: "the *visarga* which belongs to what is not a suffix (*apratyaya*). However, if the connection were made through a construction of the same case-relation (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the manner that will be explained hereafter...
It should be understood that this applies when the attainment of the state of being a *ṣaṭ* occurs.

Regarding the term *khyāñ-ādeśa*: for the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indeed *khśāñ* in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). In the section on what is "not established" (*asiddha*), the substitution of *y* for the *ś* of *khśāñ* is considered after the rule for *ṇatva*. By means of that, [in the case of] *sauprakhya*, derived from *suprakhyena nirvṛtam*, and *sauprakhyīya*, meaning "born there," because the substitution of *y* is not yet established, [the rule applies].

The purposes for [the rule] "from a word ending in *dhanvan* with a penultimate *y*, [the suffix] *vuñ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.121), such as the application of *na*, are established in the original treatise (*ākara*). And thus, because the substitution of *yatva* is not established (*asiddha*), there is an absence of a following *am*; consequently, [the rule] "after *pum*, [there is *ru*] before a *khari*" (Pāṇini 8.3.6) [does not apply].

The meaning is that *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) does not occur. Regarding the form *puṃkhāyanam*: [it is derived] from the root *cakṣiṅ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, resulting in the substitute *khyāñ*. If it is objected: "But this substitute is difficult to obtain here, because of the Vārttika rules 'there is a prohibition in the case of exclusion (*varjana*)' and 'and in the case of *as* and *ani*'?"—True. [It is justified] by the rule "in many cases (*bahulam*)."

This is to be resolved by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases) in the *Vārttika*: "for the sake of [the forms] *taṇi*, *annavadhaka*, *gātravadaka*, *gātravaca*, *kṣaṇāja*, *rī*, and so forth. Accordingly, there is a *Vārttika* enumerating the purposes for the inclusion of the root *khyā* [in the list of roots]:
the prescription of *ru*—as in *puṃkhyānam*; and the substitution of *ṇa*—as in *paryākhyānam*.

And it is stated that [the word] *niṣṭhāna* has the quality of being nasalized (*ṇatva*). Due to the intervention of the letter *ś*, the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.29) does not apply [to produce *ṇatva*]; likewise, in the word *ākhyāta*, the rule *saṃyogāderāta-* (Pāṇini 8.2.43) does not apply [to produce *ṇatva*], because the substitution of *y* for *k* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of that rule].
Because of the absence of *yaṇ* [substitution].

And thus, the point is that in the rule *na dhyākhyā-* (Pāṇini 8.2.57), the mention of *khyā* need not be made. Nor should it be argued that this was done for the sake of the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking," because that [root] falls exclusively within the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes; and here...

The subsequent Vārttika, "saṃsthānatvaṃ namaḥ khyātre," is the authority [for this]. "Saṃsthāna" is the designation for the *jihvāmūlīya* according to the Easterners; that [designation] does not apply here, because the rule "śarpare visarjanīyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.35) applies—this is the intended meaning. If...

If the root *khyā* were also intended to be treated as independent (*svatantra*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, then this Vārttika would be inconsistent, because the substitution of the *jihvāmūlīya* (the guttural *visarga*) would be unavoidable.
As for what Haradatta, Mādhava, and others have stated— that the root *khyā* is also [included]— ...

The claim that the rule for *khśādi* [substitution] is also common to both [the present and the non-present stems] is questionable. This is because the *Bhāṣya* introduces only *cakṣiṅ*, and because it would follow that the *khśādi* forms would occur even in the *sārvadhātuka* [suffixes]. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), since Mādhava has stated that this *khśādi* substitution applies only to the *ārdhadhātuka* [suffixes].

Since one would have to resort to the very argument that [the formation] is not expressed (*anabhidhāna*) when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, it would be burdened with excessive complexity (*gaurava*); so let this matter rest for now.
It might be argued as follows: in the case of the expression *bahupumkhyāti* (meaning "there are many men in this family"), [the rule applies].
The substitution of *ru* would occur. Since the word *pum̐s* is listed in the *uraḥ-prabhṛti* group only in its singular form, the suffix *kap* does not apply here.

And since the usage of the root *khyā* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix is entirely unimpeded—if this is argued, it is accepted as desired (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, it is quite clear that when the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not intended to be expressed, the substitution of *ru* does not take place. As for that which...

The predecessor [Prācīna] stated, "Some say that [the substitution] does not occur in the root *khyā*. In this regard, if the meaning were "in the case of the substitute *khyāñ*," then the phrase "some say" would be inappropriate. If, on the other hand, it refers to the independent root (*svatantra-dhātu*), then the prohibition would apply even in the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes; yet such an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) is not desired.

Because it lacks a root. [From the *Prakriyāmañjarī*]: "O wielder of the discus, protect me! As for what was stated by the ancients as "trāhi" (save), the use of the *parasmaipada* there is incorrect.

[The word] *trāḥ* [is derived] from the root *trai* (to protect) with the suffix *ḍit*. It should be understood as being formed by the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) for the word *trāyate* ("he protects"), or by the suffix *ācārakvip* (denoting one who behaves like that). Regarding *praśān*: it is formed by adding *kvip* to the root *śam* preceded by the prefix *pra*. The lengthening of the vowel is according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.15: *anunāsikasya kvi...* ("there is lengthening of a nasalized vowel before *kvip*"). [Then] *mo naḥ*... [etc. (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the grammatical analysis of the preceding terms.)
By the rule "dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.64), the *n* [is substituted]; because that [substitution] is not established [as having taken effect], the elision of the *n* does not occur.
*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *nṛn pe* (Pāṇini 8.3.10):
the vowel *a* after the letter *p* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By this, forms such as *nṛḥ punāti* are established.
Because of the recurrence of the word "optionally" (*ubhayathā*) from the rule "optionally in the case of *ṛkṣu*" (*ubhayatharkṣu*), an option is the resulting outcome.
With this intention, he says: "Or it may be 'ru'."

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *kupvoḥ kaḥpau ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.37), [the word] *kupvoḥ* [is written with a visarga] because it follows a *khara* sound; [the visarga in] *jihvāmūlīya* [is used] because it is a *khara*.
By the rule *kharpare śari*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the visarga because the *jihvāmūlīya* is a *śar* sound. [The word *kaḥpau* is written with a visarga] optionally...

Or rather, by the rule *śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), there is simply the visarga. The two substitutes, *k* and *p*, are for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). And because of the word *ca* ("and"), the visarga [is also retained]. As for what the ancients said—that there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to the word *ca*—that is not correct; for if the *k* and *p* were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the visarga becoming a *satva* (the letter *s*).

Prau.ma.- *kānāmreḍite* (Pāṇini 8.3.12). Regarding the rule *kānāmreḍite*: although one could have simply said *kān*, the inclusion of the term *āmreḍite* is so that [the substitution] occurs only where there is a reduplication (*dvirukti*), and not here: *kān kān paśyasi*. In this case, there is only one word *kiṃ*.

In the case of an inquiry, it is the second [meaning]; in the case of censure, it means "whom do you look upon as contemptible? Regarding the rule *kaskādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.48), the Easterners have stated that there is no substitution of *ka* or *pa* for the *visarjanīya* here; that is not correct.

This is the meaning of the sūtra; for neither *ka* nor *payas* is marked with the svarita accent, and the negative particle *nañ* has not been introduced as the subject. Rather, he says "of *ka* and *payas*" while suggesting that this is a statement of the implied meaning (*ārthika-artha*). Regarding the word *kautaskuta*:
in the sense of "come from where? from where? (*kutaḥ kutaḥ āgataḥ*), although the suffix *ap* would have been applicable after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [it is not used here].

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by virtue of its inclusion in the *gaṇapāṭha* [of Uṇādi 4.124], as in *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā*. Although this would already be established by the rule "nityaṃ samāse" (Pāṇini 8.3.45), the purpose for its recitation here will be explained in that very place. Regarding the rule "senāsurā—" [Uṇādi 4.126]: for if there were *tuk* after the *cch*, then [the *cch* would not remain].

If *cartva* were to apply, there would be two *c*s. However, since *cartva* does not operate due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the intended meaning is that the letter *c* would be heard after the letter *ch*.
Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of consonants (*hal-saṃdhi*).
Now, the meanings of the case-endings (vibhakti).
The Section on Kārakas (Case-relations)

Regarding the word *mātra*: its meaning is restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Amara states, "The word *mātra* [is used] in the sense of entirety (*kārtsnya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The analysis of the compound is provided by the particle *eva* (only) as "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) and so forth alone is *tan-mātram*"; this is a compound belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group, where the members are not in their own case-forms (*asvapada-vigraha*).

Regarding the word *kṛṣṇa*: although this term primarily denotes that which possesses a blue color and thus has an indefinite gender, the intended meaning here is that it has a fixed gender when referring to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. Regarding the word *jñāna*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
As for the word *droṇa*, one should not argue that the nominative case should apply here merely to the nominal stem itself.

That being the case, since it is impossible for the relation between the delimited object (*paricchedya*) and the delimiter (*paricchedaka*) to appear as a relation of conjunction (*saṃsarga*), the relation between the meaning of a noun and [its] denotation must indeed be one of non-difference (*abheda*), according to the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*). Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a sense other than the genitive (*aṣaṣṭhyartha-bahuvrīhi*), because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted therein. Nor also...

This is because particles (*nipāta*) are admitted to be merely illuminators (*dyotaka*) of those meanings. Nor should it be argued that even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the syntactic relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is difficult to establish due to its not being observed elsewhere;
for the point is that such a relation is observed in cases such as *taddhita* suffixes denoting a deity (*devatā*). This is the statement.

Regarding the term *saṃkhyā* (number): this is likewise due to the usage of the ancients. In this sūtra, it would be sufficient to say simply "the first [case-ending] occurs when there is a meaning (*artha*) and a gender (*liṅga*). Everything else could be omitted. For instance, if it were stated that "the first [case-ending] occurs when there is a meaning," then upon the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "of what meaning?"—

Because it is indeed obtained that "the rule for *svādi* suffixes applies to that [prātipadika]," and since *svādi* suffixes are prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as well as after one qualified by gender-suffixes (*liṅga-pratyaya*), their being "for the sake of that" (*tadarthatva*) consists precisely in their having a necessary occurrence (*niyatopasthitikatva*) following it. And thus, in cases such as *mṛḍānī*, etc., [the rule applies].

Furthermore, it is favorable [to our position] that the nominative case is established even for words ending in *ṅī* (feminine suffixes) when there is the necessary manifestation of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) or greatness (*mahattva*), and so forth; however, under the other system of interpretation, that would not be possible. If, however, the word "artha" refers to the scope of the *vṛtti* (linguistic function), and *vṛtti* consists of both *śakti* (primary denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication)—while *gauṇī* (metaphorical indication)...

Whether [gender] be included within the definition [of the nominal stem] or be distinct from it—if the triplet [number, gender, and case] constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem—then even the term "gender" (*liṅga*) need not exist. Even though the objects to be designated (*lakṣya*) are diverse, there is no harm, because the restrictive portion [of the definition] is abandoned. Thus, the essence is simply that "the first [case ending] occurs when the meaning [is expressed]. As in *droṇaḥ*.

The usage of the word *vrīhi* (rice) for that which is measured by a *droṇa* is also established through metaphorical application (*upacāra*), just as one says "the Vāhīka is an ox. Furthermore, expressions such as "one," "two," and so forth, are established precisely by the prohibition that "a base form (*prakṛti*) should not be used alone," rather than on account of employing a term whose meaning is unconnected [to its grammatical function].

Because it is logical that only the application of the mere reiterative suffix (*anuvādaka*) is appropriate. Likewise, the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is also redundant; for by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "and in the vocative" (*sambodhane ca*), the nominative case does not apply when there is an excess of the object (*karman*) and other factors. As for what was stated by the ancients—that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is "existence" (*sattā*)—and as for the explanation of which meaning [is intended]:

It is intended that [the word] shines forth as merely "existent" (san), not as having the form of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, nor as being connected with gender, number, or case-role (*kāraka*). It is like the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*);
for just as the meaning of an indeclinable can be said to be merely "it exists," it cannot be described as being "of such a kind" or "of that kind."

If you say this, we reply: no, because it is contrary to all established systems (*sarvatantra*) that words such as "high" (*uccaiḥ*) or "low" (*nīcaiḥ*) generate a cognition having the form of existence (*san-ityākāraka*);
furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with verbs such as "is" (*asti*) is difficult to find in the case of words whose meaning is non-existence. It is not [the case].
Furthermore, because it contradicts your own statement that [the word] "is joined with gender, number, and case" (*liṅgasaṃkhyākārakayogi*),

if you argue that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "is" (*asti*) as presented by another word, we say no; for that [verb] does not serve to differentiate [the meaning], and furthermore, it contradicts the remainder of the sentence beginning with "not again" (*na punar*), as in the case of the word "Kṛṣṇa."

Furthermore, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "Śrī" and so forth. Nor can its establishment be achieved through the mention of the "mark" (*liṅga*), because the word "only" (*mātra*) excludes anything additional. As for what was explained by the ancients—that wherever the application of a word occurs without dependence on another object, all that [is a *yogarūḍha*]— [The author continues: This too is not correct. For even in the case of words like "Indra," "Yama," and "Varuṇa," there is indeed application without dependence on another object, since they are applied to the specific individual who possesses those particular powers and so forth. Moreover, it is observed that even in the case of words like "cow" (*go*), which are established by convention (*saṃketa*), there is application without dependence on another object, because they are applied to the individual possessing dewlaps and so forth. Therefore, this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*). Furthermore, the word "only" (*mātra*) is meaningless here, because the dependence on another object is already excluded by the very fact that the word is applied to that [object]. Thus, this [definition] is also unsound. Consequently, the definition of a *yogarūḍha* is: that which is applied to a composite object based on its constituent parts, while being established by convention. For example, words such as "lotus" (*paṅkaja*). Here, although the word "lotus" is applied to the composite object—the lotus plant—based on its parts, namely the root "jan" (to be born) with the prefix "paṅka" (mud), it is nonetheless established by convention, because it is applied to the lotus plant even when it is not currently being produced from mud. This is the intended meaning. As for the word "only" (*mātra*) in the verse, it is used to exclude the possibility of the word being applied to something other than the composite object. For instance, in the case of the word "lotus," the word "lotus" is not applied to the mud itself; rather, it is applied to the lotus plant based on the part "born from mud. This is the sense. Alternatively, the word "only" (*mātra*) may be understood as excluding the application of the word to a mere collection of parts, as in the case of the word "army" (*senā*) applied to a collection of elephants, horses, and so forth. This is the intention. Thus, the definition of a *yogarūḍha* has been stated. The meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) is, in other words, the ground for the application of a word (śabdapravṛttinimitta). For example, in the case of "high" (uccaiḥ) and "low" (nīcaiḥ), these two, being devoid of gender and number, express their own meaning independently of genus and so forth. Even that is not [the case], because here the ground for the application of the word functions as a qualifier (prakārībhūya).

It shines forth; and thus, the cognition of that alone is impossible. If even that were desired, then it would also occur from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), and consequently there would be no syntactic connection with number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth.
As for the claim that the word "droṇa" [denotes] rice and the like measured by a *droṇa* measure...

"It functions because of the relation 'this is that' (so'yam). In that case, since the principle of the primary and the secondary (gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya) would not apply, the mention of 'measure' (parimāṇa) [is made]. This is not correct, because the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this principle applies to operations concerning words (*pada*), not to operations concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*); otherwise, [the term] "lion" would [apply to] a boy.
Furthermore, because this would lead to the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).

As they also say: "Words such as *droṇa* and the like never deviate from [denoting] a measure—whether made of metal or wood—but they certainly do deviate from the object measured (*parimeya*); therefore, of that..."

The claim that the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is necessary because [the definition] would otherwise fail to apply due to the absence of being the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)— that too is not correct,

because it would result in over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases of figurative (*gauṇa*) or metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) usage, such as "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) or "The platforms are shouting" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*). In those instances, even though there is a difference from the substantive (*viśeṣya*), namely the boy and so forth...

If it is argued that in the case of *gauṇī* (metaphorical) usage, the meaning "one who resembles a lion" is necessarily present [in the mind], then it is the same in the case of rice and other grains: even though they differ [from the word *vrīhi*], the quantity measured by a *droṇa* is necessarily present [in the mind]. [Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.47:
*saṃbodhane ca*. (Prakriyākaumudī)
"And in the case of address. This rule is commenced because, due to the mention of the word *mātra* ("only"), it would not apply when address (*saṃbodhana*) is added [to the other factors].

Here, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that address is a qualifier (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), and a modifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action (*kriyā*). And it has been said:
"And that which is a vocative case is an adverbial modifier (viśeṣaṇa) of the verb;
thus, in 'vrajāni devadatta' (O Devadatta, let me go), there is the *nighāta* accent when this is the case.
And so, in the sentence "rāma māṃ pāhi" (O Rāma, protect me), the object of the vocative is related to Rāma.
Its purpose is for the sake of protecting my work.
Thus ends the first [section].

Prau.ma.: "The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.49). Regarding the word *kartuḥ*: it is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule "And [the sixth case ending is used] after a word ending in *kta* when it denotes the present time. Regarding the word *īpsitatamam*: it is derived from the root *āp* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), followed by the superlative suffix *tama*, according to the rule "Also after roots meaning 'to think,' 'to know,' or 'to honor'..."

The suffix *kta* denotes the present time. "Desire" (*mati*) here means wish (*icchā*), and not cognition (*buddhi*), because the word "cognition" is mentioned again later. Thus, the meaning is: that which is desired to be reached by the agent. And the agent is the substratum of the activity expressed by the verbal root.
When there arises the expectation of "by what [means] does he desire to reach it?", [the answer is supplied] by the qualifier.
The meaning "by means of an operation" (vyāpāreṇa) is obtained by implication. This is what he states with the word "by action" (kriyayā).

The presentness (vartamānatva) conveyed by the suffix -kta is not intended here; therefore, forms such as "he has made a mat" (kaṭaṃ kṛtavān) and "he will make a mat" (kaṭaṃ kari�ṣyati) are established. Regarding the term "kāraka": and this...

This is understood from the governing heading *kārake* (in the context of a grammatical operation concerning a case-role). For there, the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). In each individual rule, a sentence is split so that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a case-role is prescribed. For example: "In the context of departure (*apāya*), that which is fixed (*dhruva*) shall have the designation 'case-role' (*kāraka*). Then, having been thus described as a case-role, it is stated: "The *apādāna*"; that is, the case-role [previously defined] receives the designation *apādāna*.

Furthermore, by the force of the recurrence of the term *kāraka*, there is a co-occurrence with specific technical designations (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*). This designation is also etymological: "that which acts" (*karoti*) is a *kāraka*. Consequently, it does not fail to apply to that which is connected to an action—as in the example: "He asks the Brāhmaṇa's son the way. In this case...
For the term *brāhmaṇa* is a qualifier of the son and not connected with the action;

or rather, it is a word for a *kāraka* (participant in an action) which refers to the action itself, based on the etymology "that which effects the designations of agent, object, and so forth. And thus, in the rules prescribing technical terms such as *apādāna*, the phrase "in an action" (*kriyāyām*) is understood by implication.

The respective designations are prescribed only for those [factors] that participate in the action (*kriyānvayin*). However, in rules such as "kārakāddattaśrutayoḥ," the word *kāraka* is pronounced with a svarita accent. Consequently, only the sixfold set beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*) mentioned in this governing heading (*adhikāra*) is understood. On this view, even in the *vṛtti*, the term *kāraka* [refers to these].

The meaning is that it follows the action (*kriyānvayin*). However, in the first alternative (*pakṣa*), the designation *kāraka* would apply; and it must indeed be explained that such a *kāraka* would bear the designation *karman*.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.1: *anabhihite*.

Regarding the rule *anabhihite*: Now, one might object that just as in examples such as *bahupaṭuḥ*, the suffixes *kalpa* and so on do not occur because their meaning has already been expressed by the prefix *bahu-*, likewise in cases such as *kriyate kaṭaḥ*, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) would not occur because its meaning has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth. Furthermore, [what about] *kaṭam*?

In cases such as *karoti* ("he does"), the accusative case has its scope; however, in instances such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), it will be superseded by the nominative, because [the nominative] is without scope [for the accusative]. Nor is *vṛkṣaḥ* ("the tree") an instance of its scope, for even there, since the tree is understood as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the implied action of "being" (*asti*), the application of the instrumental case would follow. Now, if...

If you argue that in cases such as "this is blue, not red," where the intention is the exclusion of other qualifiers, the nominative case finds its scope because the verb "is" (asti) is not necessary; then, by the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), let the nominative prevail. And if you then claim that the governing rule concerning the "unexpressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is therefore rendered useless?
Not so; for the sūtra is commenced under the view that number is the meaning of the case-ending. Thus, the meaning is:

when the object (karman) is not already expressed [by another word], the singular number associated with it takes the second-case singular ending. And if the sūtra were not commenced, then regarding the singular number associated with the object...

The meaning of the sentence is indeed "the second case singular ending *am*. If that were the case, then in examples such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), even though the suffix *kta* expresses only the object (*karman*), the singular number of that object remains unexpressed;

consequently, the *am* ending would be unavoidable. Nor can one argue that the nominative (*prathamā*) applies by virtue of its higher status [in the order of rules], because in cases such as *kartavyaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is to be made"), [the nominative] would prevail over that [accusative].

Because [if it were an object], there would be the undesirable consequence of the genitive case characterized by its connection with a verb (*kṛd-yoga*), as in the sense of "otherness" (*paratva*). Under the view that the *kāraka* is the meaning of the case-ending, the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.1] is rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*).
As in the example "he worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*): because joy is produced in Hari by the act of worshiping, [Hari is the recipient] by virtue of being qualified by that joy.

Hari is the object (*karman*) by virtue of being the object of the action (*kriyā*). The meaning of the sentence is "worship qualified by that [object]. The same applies in the case of *hariḥ sevyate* ("Hari is served"), because of the established doctrine that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has the action as its primary meaning.

The action presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the suffix (*tiṅ*), but not with respect to the meaning of a *kṛt*-suffix, as is the case here.

For its meaning is indeed "qualification. For this very reason, *pacati vrajati* ("he cooks while walking") does not constitute a single sentence, unlike *pācako vrajati* ("the cooker walks"). For the meaning of *pācaka* and similar forms is "walking performed by one who is the agent of cooking," whereas the meanings of *pacati* and *vrajati* are "the act of cooking" and "the act of walking" [respectively] having a single agent.

The meaning is indeed distinct. Thus, the proclamation of the Naiyāyikas—that cognition has a nominative-ending term as its primary qualificand—should not be respected by those who follow the Bhāṣya and other authoritative texts.
Yāska also said: "A verb has action (bhāva) as its primary focus; nouns have substance (satva) as their primary focus. Observe.

In expressions such as "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), however, the act of running whose agent is the deer is the object of the action of seeing; indeed, the primary element is the action of seeing itself. And it has been said:
"Just as many inflected nouns (*subanta*) serve as qualifiers for a finite verb (*tiṅnta*)."
"Likewise, they say that even a finite verb (tiṅanta) can be a qualifier of another finite verb.
Thus, the meaning of "pacati bhavati" (he cooks [and] exists) is "the act of cooking exists.
However, this is the distinction: with respect to an action presented by a finite verb, [another] action...

Even if [the object] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), according to the theory of verbal ellipsis (*śabdādhyāhāravāda*), its status as an object (*karmatva*) is merely a relation (*saṃsarga*), not a qualifier (*prakāra*), because it is not the meaning of a word (*apadārthatvāt*). However, according to the theory of semantic ellipsis (*arthādhyāhāravāda*), even if it is a qualifier, this is accepted as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). In cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), the status of the fruit (*phala*) conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is likewise determined according to these differing views. For this very reason:
In cases such as "he cooks well" (*śobhanaṃ pacati*), where [the word *śobhanam*] is in grammatical apposition with that [verb], the production of the second case singular occurs;
and in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma" (*agniṣṭomena yajeta*), the production of the third case follows accordingly.

Nor is there any discrepancy between the example and the point of application, whether regarding that which conveys the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in the example or that which conveys the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the point of application.

Should it be argued that there ought to be the employment of a *sub*-case ending (such as the accusative) for a word expressing "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth? No, because both verbal roots (*dhātu*) and words ending in *tiṅ* suffixes are not nominal stems (*aprātipadika*). However, this fault would apply to the Naiyāyikas; for according to them, just as one says "he sees the running deer," one could likewise say "he runs the deer."

It might be argued: "Since the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are obligatory when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a non-nominative case, such a construction cannot occur. But even so, it remains difficult to justify the non-occurrence of the accusative case. Is it not the case that there is indeed a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), because in the word *paśya*, the object *tam* must be supplied as an ellipsis? [This applies] to the verb *pacati*.

If it is argued that [the expression] "it becomes" (*bhavati*) and so forth is indeed undesirable in the sense of "cooking occurs" (*pāko bhavati*) and so forth, do not say so; for there would be the burden of supplying ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and that [supplying ellipsis] lacks authoritative status due to its contradiction with the words of the Sage.

This is because your mere desire is ineffective. Furthermore, in cases such as "Know that Devadatta has gone" (*upakṣīd devadato'vehi*), there is no possibility at all for the application of the suffix *śatṛ* (the present participle marker).

Moreover, the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is accepted by all authorities, including the Bhāṣya and Vārttika. Nor is this the case in instances involving finite verbal endings (*tiṅanta*).

It must be said that such a cognition of another action qualified by a [prior] action certainly arises; for it is impossible to prevent such a cognition in those who are proficient in the language in that very way. Nor can it be argued that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is not intended in such a sense, because those very persons who have engaged in the instruction regarding grammatical correctness have themselves accepted it.

Furthermore, because that [distinction] is necessary in cases such as "he attacked the city" (*purīm avaskanda*), which are established under the section concerning the connection of verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha-adhikaraṇa*). If it is objected: "But if, according to the Siddhānta, even the action denoted by a verb is admitted to possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) and object (*karmatva*), would its nature as something non-substantial (*asatvarūpatva*) not be compromised? We reply: No.

This is because such a status [of the object] is established merely by the absence of gender, number, and any *kāraka* other than the agent or the object; furthermore, it is because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not accepted as a qualifier (*prakāra*). For a detailed discussion, see elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "but when [the object] is expressed" (*abhihite tu*): [an objection is raised] that if this were so, then even in the case of the sentence "he eats cooked rice" (*pakvam odanam bhuṅkte*), [the same would apply].

If it is argued that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should not occur [in such instances], it is not so; for here, two capacities for objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*) are determined by the roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhuj* (to eat).
Of these, the second case ending arises by taking the unexpressed capacity as determined by the primary action. And it has been stated by Hari:
Where there is a separate capacity for a substance belonging to both the primary and the secondary action, that capacity rests upon its qualities; in such a case, the primary action is followed.
"The power whose primary object [is the action] is designated by the suffix;
when it pertains to a subordinate factor (guṇa), then it is understood even though not expressed.
For this very reason, in the case of "Having cooked, the rice is eaten" (*pakva odano bhujyate*), since [the object] is already expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*...
It is indeed the first [case], because the act of cooking (*paci*) is not primary.

In reality, however, in expressions such as *paktvā bhujyate* ("having cooked, it is eaten"), there is a simultaneous verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) of the object with both *pac* and *bhuj*; yet, while the former [connection] is verbal, the latter is through implication (*ārtha*). And in that case—

The first and second [cases] are established as such. For example: "Having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvā bhujyate odanaḥ*). Having cooked what? By implication, rice. But when the expression "having cooked rice, it is eaten" (*odanaṃ paktvā bhujyate*) is used, then in the word "is eaten," it is understood by implication that "rice" is the object. And thus...
Depending on the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), both "Hari can be worshipped" and "one can worship Hari" are correct.

Regarding the phrase *prāptānanda* ("attained bliss"): the meaning is that he has become the object of an attainment whose agent is bliss (*ānanda*). He states the result of what was said previously regarding "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*). Regarding the phrase "poisonous tree" (*viṣavṛkṣa*): as for that which... [text ends].

It should be understood that when the connection with either *vardhi* (to increase) or *chidi* (to cut) as the object (*karman*) is intended, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) must indeed occur; for example,
in the expression "he touches grass" (*tṛṇaṃ spṛśati*), just as in the case of the Ganges or other desired objects being touched by an action.

The meaning is that *yoga* (connection) is [the object] because it is the locus of the result, such as conjunction, produced by that [action]; this applies equally to undesired things like grass. It might be argued:
let the object simply be "that which possesses the result presented by the verbal root"; what is the use of distinguishing between the desired (*īpsita*) and the undesired (*anīpsita*)?

If it is argued that [the definition] is stated separately [from the general definition], this is not so; for in the example "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the status of the boy as an *apādāna* (ablative) would be obtained by the rule "of those [verbs] having the sense of warding off" (*vāraṇārthānām*).
To set aside that [application], it must indeed be stated: "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*). And thus, in this way...
The phrase "likewise [is] so ordained" (*tathā yuktam*) is also necessary for the purpose of including those who are objects of aversion and those who are indifferent;

however, the inclusion of the term "unwanted" (*anīpsita*) is merely for the sake of clarity and is not strictly necessary. This, however, should be noted: the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding both the desired and the unwanted is of one and the same form.

Although [the desire for] acquisition (*īpsā*) and non-acquisition (*anīpsā*), etc., are utilized in the application of technical designations (*saṃjñā*) just like [the roots] *adhi-śī* and so forth, they are not included within the scope of what is to be expressed by the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). This is because only that which cannot be obtained otherwise constitutes the meaning of a word.
For in the rule "the accusative is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the designation "object" (*karman*) applies to as many things as are designated as such by various specific rules.
All those [factors] have been prescribed; they appear in that form [as the object], and among them,

the second case (accusative) is prescribed as expressing the substratum (*ādhāra*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*), since the action is obtained through the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the agent through words such as "Devadatta," while there is no manifestation of "being most desired" (*iṣṭatamatva*) and so forth.

And here, there is a relation between the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) by way of non-difference. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is the activity conducive to that pleasure which has Hari as its substratum. Although it is the same that the second case endings and others, prescribed for the object, the agent, and the locus, all have "substratum" as their meaning;

Nevertheless, the distinction in the resulting verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)— which has become the fruit— is logically accounted for by [the inclusion of] that which determines it (the object), the operation (*vyāpāra*), and both of these through their respective substrates. Nor should it be thought that the locus alone is the denoted meaning,
because [it is the property residing therein that is intended].

Because this would result in excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) due to the necessity of [the denotatum] being the delimitor of the denotability (*vācyatāvacchedakatā*), and because it would lead to a violation of the natural intent of sūtras such as "the second case-ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"The meanings of the *sup* suffixes include the object and so forth, as well as number; and likewise those of the *tiṅ* suffixes."

Nor is the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) merely the action (*dharma*); for otherwise, there would arise an inconsistency among the grammatical rules: "The *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent," "The *la* suffixes [denote] the object and [the agent]," and "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal* suffixes [denote] only those two [the object and the agent]. This is because, in cases such as "Devadatta is a cook" (*pācako devadattaḥ*) and "the rice is cooked" (*pakva odanaḥ*), one must account for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

And because it is accepted that [the word] denotes the substratum (dharmin). Therefore, in this case, just as with words such as "jar" (ghaṭa), the denotation must be specifically qualified. However, if one accepts the position of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (the section on form), then even in all cases there would be only the property (dharma) alone.
In any event, the "half-old-woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*) adopted by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others is certainly to be rejected. Not...
Indeed, the distinction between verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and kṛt suffixes is easily established.

We have elaborated upon this in the *Śabdakaustubha*, so let us suffice with this much. Regarding the phrase "an enumeration": by this, there is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor").
The state [of being an object]. In the expression "he milks the cow," the meaning is the act of milking which has as its object the milk related to the cow.

It might be argued that this is already covered by the two rules: "The object is that which is most desired by the agent" and "as well as that which is connected [to the action] though not desired. For indeed, the act of causing to abandon (*tyājana*) is subordinate to the act of abandoning (*tyajana*).

The meaning of *duh* is "causing to milk" (*dāpana*) and "accepting" (*aṅgīkaraṇa*), while that of *yāc* is "begging"; the meaning of *pac* is "softening" (*vikledana*) and "bringing to completion" (*nivartana*), and so forth. Thus, it is clear that cows and other such subjects possess the state of being the locus (*āśrayatva*) of those actions—such as abandoning, giving, or accepting—which have become the objects of the operation (*vyāpāra*) inherent in the verbal roots. For this very reason:

For the established conclusion of the ancients is that, since the status of the object (*karmatva*) for the agent (*kartṛ*) when [the action] is expressed by a causative suffix (*ṇic*) is established by logic, the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 1.4.52) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It is for this very reason that in the *Cākaḍāra-sūtra* it is stated:
"In the example 'he milks the cow for milk' (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the technical designation of 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*) applies because it is subsequent [to the designation of 'ablative']."

The commentary is consistent. However, under the view that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of five factors, this [usage] occurs when there is a simultaneous intention to express both the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) and the state of being the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*);
[the compound] refers to that activity conducive to the flowing of milk which resides in the cow that serves as the limit.
If it is argued that, since the sense is already established by the meaning "impelling that which is most closely connected," the rule *akathitaṃ ca* is therefore redundant,
we reply: when there is a desire to express the object (*karman*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), as in "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇāmaśnīyāt*).

Thus, a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been expected; this rule is intended to set that aside. Consequently, it is established here that the meaning of the accusative is merely "relation," just like the genitive.

However, when there is a desire to express only the status of being an ablative (*apādānatva*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) alone is used. But when the cow is a qualifier of the milk (*kṣīra*), [the following applies].
The genitive case [is used here]. Therefore, the usage *goḥ payo dogdhi* ("he milks the cow's milk") is indeed correct.
The same should be inferred for what follows as well. As for that which was stated by the ancients:

"The object of the roots *duh* (to milk), *aci* (to ask), *rudh* (to obstruct), *pracch* (to ask), *ci* (to gather), *brū* (to speak), *śās* (to command), *ji* (to win), and *muc* (to release) is connected [with the sixth case]."

"nī-hṛ-kṛṣ-manth-vah-daṇḍ-grah-muṣ-pac share the property of having two objects. Regarding this, the following must be said: the inclusion of *grah* (to seize) is without authority; thus, the example "jagrāha dyautaruṃ śakram" (he seized Indra by the sun-stone) is also incorrect. As for the others, although they possess the property of being transitive with two objects—

Nevertheless, the textual integrity remains authoritative; for instance, after listing the roots beginning with *duh* (to milk) and those ending in *ad* (to eat) in two separate groups here, and then, in the remainder of the section on the formation of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*), there arises the inquiry:

"In the case of roots with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), do the affixes *la*, the *kṛtya* suffixes, the *kta* suffix, and those having the sense of *khal* apply to the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) or to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*)?"

He himself has stated: "Verbal roots such as *nī* (to lead), when followed by a causative suffix (*ṇic*) and having the sense of motion with no [other] object, take the suffix [denoting the agent] in relation to their primary object;
roots such as *duh* (to milk) do so in relation to their secondary object; others, however, according to their preference."

And in this way, [the application] would also occur with respect to the primary [referent] in the case of *daṇḍin* and *manthin*. Consequently, the Bhāṣya statement, "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," would be contradicted; for here, the hundred is the primary element, not the Gargas, as indicated by the supplementary passage:
"Kings become desirous of gold. And here, *daṇḍin*...
The purpose is for inclusion, not for exclusion. For this very reason, it would apply to *manthi* even when it is primary;
however, it is desired [to apply] when it is secondary. And so says Bhāravi:
"By whom the abodes of the serpents were made manifest by the waters being cast away..."
"The gods and asuras churned the ocean for nectar (*amṛta*).
In this [verse], "nectar" is primary because it is the intended object (*uddeśya*), whereas "the ocean" is secondary.
Furthermore, as for what the commentators say—that among verbs governing two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the reading of *pac* (to cook) is unauthoritative—

This is because of that [statement] being impetuous. For instance: in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, in the *vārttika* "of *duh* and *pac*, when transitive, [the object takes the agentive suffix] diversely," and in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), the fact that *pac* has two objects is obtained.
This was made clear by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta in that very place. Mādhava also says regarding *jayati*:
[The examples] beginning with *karṣati*, *manthi*, *muṣi*, *gaṇḍayati*, and *pacati* were cited; and he [Haradatta] also cited: "He cooks rice into porridge" (*taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati*).
As for what was stated by Haradatta regarding the rule *akathitaṃ ca*: the word *akathita*...

If the non-primary sense were to be accepted, then in the case of "he milks milk into a bronze vessel with his hand," the [karaṇa-saṃjñā] would apply to both the hand and the bronze vessel; however, *pacati* and similar verbs provide the scope for the [karaṇa and adhikaraṇa] designations, for there is no possibility of their application there due to the specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*) of roots such as *duh*.
This is according to the intention of that particular school of thought; otherwise, there would be contradictions with the cited texts of our own and other traditions—let that matter rest for now.

Regarding the expression "he conquers a hundred" (*śataṃ jayati*): the root *ji* means "to overcome. As for the explanation that *ji* means "to win," that is incorrect, because that [specific sense] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Although roots such as *jayati* are not listed in the Bhāṣya, nevertheless...
Kaiyaṭa states that [the suffixes] are included by means of the letter *ca*.

Regarding the phrase "based on meaning": it does not depend on the formal nature [of the word], as seen in the commentary on the *Tad-rāja* sūtra where even the root *cud*, which is a synonym for *pracch*, is mentioned in the statement: "I too shall raise this objection which should not have been raised."
The intention is that [the root *vad*] is observed to take two objects (*dvikarmaka*). And so says Bhaṭṭi:
"With a smiling face, he spoke these words of great significance loudly to Mārīca, who stood firm in battle.
Kālidāsa also [says]:
Even the mountain, as if out of great affection, spoke that very same matter loudly to the protector of the earth;
and Bhāravi [says]:
"The noble-minded king was addressed by Dvaipāyana with these noble words: 'O Mountain...'"
In this way, many verbs such as *nāth* (to seek protection) and others should be understood as taking two objects (*dvikarmaka*).

Regarding the word *deśa* (place): only [specific regions] such as Kuru and Pañcāla are intended; therefore, rules such as *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām* (Pāṇini 1.4.46) are not rendered redundant. Regarding *godoha* (the milking of cows): its establishment here is not due to its being a measure of time (*kāla*), for in common usage...

Because only those [units] such as months that are well-known as time (*kāla*) are understood [by the term *kāla*], therefore forms such as *ghaṭam āste* (“he sits for a jar”) do not occur. As for what was stated by the ancients—namely, that some say "when used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the second case is employed after words denoting place, time, distance, and action"—such as *nadīm āste* ("he sits by the river") and so forth; [that is rejected].

In this regard, the following must be said: since the designation of "object" (*karman*) has not been explicitly stated here, the *l*-affixes and others would not apply to the object, as in the example *āsya-te māsaḥ* ("the month is sat through"). Furthermore, the claim by some that "a country (*deśa*) consists only of a collection of villages, a field (*kurv-ādara*), and so forth, and not merely a portion (*pradeśa-mātra*) thereof; therefore, [one goes] to a village... is also inconsistent.

In the original source (*ākara*), it is stated that [the suffix] does not occur in the case of *svapiti* ("he sleeps"). Furthermore, the term *adhvan* ("way") is insufficient, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [applying the suffix] in the sense of "he sleeps on the way. For this very reason, in the original source, *adhvan* is qualified as "that which is to be traversed" (*gantavyatvena*).
It is explained as being something well-known as "to be traversed," such as a *krośa* or similar distance, which has a fixed duration of change (*niyatapariṇāma*).
Prau.ma.: *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.52).
"Gati-buddhi": [roots meaning] motion and cognition. *Pratyavasāna* means eating. Regarding *śabdakarmakāṇām*: [roots] having sound as their object. "Śabdaḥ" [is the word].

The meaning is "of those for whom there is an object-agent. However, in this context, the word *karman* (object) does not refer to an action—as it does in the rule "kartari karmavyatihāre"—because grammatical operations apply to technical (*kṛtrima*) terms, and because of the force of the explicit mention of "object" (*karman*). Otherwise, [the rule would be redundant].

He would have simply said: "gati-buddhi-pratyavasāna-śabdārtha-karmakāṇām. The ancient masters maintain that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): if the [Aṇ] agent of roots meaning motion, cognition, eating, sound, and those having an object, becomes the object of the causative (*ṇij*) sense, then it applies only to the agents of roots meaning motion and so forth. Therefore, in the case of *pācayati devadattaḥ*...

In the case of *yajñadattena*, since the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) remains unexceptionable in the subordinate action (*prayojya*), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is established. And it has been said:
"Because of independence (*svātantrya*) in the subordinate action, [the agent] attains the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the act of instigation (*preraṇā*)."
"By rule, because of the designation 'object' (karman), it is expressed by its own case-ending (svadharma).

This means that the agent is expressed by its own case-ending, namely the third case (instrumental). Now, one might object: since the status of being an agent with respect to the meaning of the root (prakṛti) is established by its very priority over the status of being an object with respect to the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇic), [there is no need for this rule].

And because it is internal (*antaraṅga*): for an action qualified by its own *kāraka*s is connected with the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), since the causative suffix is prescribed in the sense of "one who possesses a cause" (*hetumat*), and one who prompts an agent is the cause (*hetu*). For this very reason, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) is also dependent upon [the causative]. And thus—

If it is argued: "Let the status of agent (kartṛtva) belong to the one being employed (prayojya), because of its externality, its being internal (antaraṅga), and also because it is that upon which [the other] depends; thus, the application of the rule for 'motion' (gati) and so forth is appropriate"—then let it be so, since the object of the grammatical description (lakṣya) remains uncontradicted. What then of the statements that this is a restrictive rule (niyamasūtra)?

If you say it is the *gati* [particle], listen: since the designation of *karman* (object), which conforms to the injunction (*prāya*), prevails by prioritizing the verbal primacy of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*), there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) at all;
for even though it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and dependent, it does not confer superiority over that which is primary (*pradhāna*).

With this intention, the possibility of such expressions in the texts arises. However, it should be understood that when the primacy of the meaning is prioritized, the status of being an injunction (vidhāyakatva) alone is appropriate.
Regarding the word "śatrūn" (enemies): it is conducive to that movement which has heaven as its object and resides in the enemies.
The meaning is that whatever activity culminates in [him], He—the illustrious Hari—is my goal (*gati*). Now, one might object: "How can heaven (*svarga*) be the object (*karman*) here?

For an object is that which is most desired by the agent (*kartṛ*), and the enemies are not the agents; rather, they are the objects according to the rule *gaty-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.52). This is not so, for regarding the designation of the object (*karma-saṃjñā*)...

The mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of independence (*svātantrya*). And independence consists precisely in being the locus of the activity denoted by the verbal root. This [independence] belongs to the one being impelled even when the instigator (*prayojaka*) is present. Nor is there a lack of evidence for its being an indicator.
For the author of the Bhāṣya himself is the authority in this matter, having stated: "In the case of roots with two objects, they say that the *l*-affixes and so forth denote the principal object;

in the case of roots such as *duh* (milk), they denote the non-principal [object]. This is because [the rule] "in the case of causative forms (*ṇyanta*), the agent and the object [of the original root take the same affixes]" would not otherwise be possible without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The status of having two objects (dvikarmakatā) is thus obtained, whereby the rule "the agent of the causative [is called the object]" would have scope.
If it is asked: "How can there be a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) for that which is conventionally designated as independent (svatantra) in that very context? [The answer is:

It applies to that which is conventionally designated as being unqualified by another technical term (sañjñā), within the mere independence that is common to both [states] when qualified by that [other term].
Pay attention to this:
regarding the roots *nī* and *vah*, although their meaning is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and not "giving" (*dā*), nevertheless,
since even "going" (*gati*) enters into the category of "causing to reach" by way of being a qualification, it is on this basis alone that the [application of the rule] is considered to apply.

A prohibition has been stated. Regarding "niyantṛ" (the driver): it means one who impels animals, and not merely a charioteer; by this, the expression "he makes the oxen carry the barley" (*vāhayati balīvardān yavān*) is established. Regarding "aniṣedha" (non-prohibition):
the resulting meaning is that it should be stated that the person being employed is the *karman* (object). Regarding "sūta" (charioteer): [this refers to a specific type of driver].

*niyantā*, *prājitā*, *yantā*, *sūtaḥ*, *kṣattā*, and *sārathiḥ*. [In the case of the root *ā-dā* (to take),] because the result does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāye phale*), the *parasmaipada* ending is used according to the rule "after all [roots], when the result does not benefit the agent. However, when the result benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāye*), the *ātmanepada* ending alone is used by the rule "and after roots with the marker *ṇic*," which is an exception to that [previous rule].

Because [the rule] "nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca" is prohibited by the statement "there is a prohibition for roots beginning with 'ad'," [the suffix *ṇic* does not apply]. Regarding "sasyam": the injury (*hiṃsā*) should be understood as occurring when barley standing in the field is being eaten, because at that stage they possess sentience (*cetana*). Regarding "smārayati": as for the [rule] "ṇeraṇau"...

Thus, in the Sūtra, the example "the thicket of forest bushes itself causes him to remember" (ṭhsmarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayameva) is cited; in that case, the status of the object (karmatva) is to be understood from the usage in the Bhāṣya itself. Regarding the root *śabdāyati*:
in the sense of "he makes a sound," the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "śabdavaira... and so forth, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Regarding the phrase "dhātvarthe" (in the sense of the root-meaning): by this, those who employ an object [as a suffix] in the expression "śabdāyayati sainikairipūn" (he causes the enemies to sound/shout by means of his soldiers) are refuted. As for what was stated by the ancients—"there is no [suffix] after √krand, √śabdāya, and √hvā"—in that regard, the mention of √yat is entirely baseless; however, as for √krand and √hvā...
The possibility of [the object] being attained exists merely by virtue of its being an action involving sound; however, it has been stated that in reality this is not the meaning of the sūtra.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that [the object of] the roots *śru*, *grah*, and *dṛś* becomes the object (karma), therein the inclusion of *dṛś*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]
This is indeed authoritative. As for the verb *śru* (to hear), its status as having two objects is established because it takes sound (*śabda*) as its object.

Although the view that *grah* (to seize) has two objects is accepted by Sudhākara and others, it is nevertheless not accepted by many. For this very reason, [the author of the Mahābhārata] said: "Janaka seized that bow."
They explained that he "mastered the application of the word" (bhaṭṭiprayogamajigrahat) means "he caused [the mountain] to understand. Likewise:
"The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter, for He did not ask for her."
In this context, "to cause to grasp" means to make one understand by way of marriage.

And this is logical; for since the root *grah* (to grasp) takes two objects, in the expression *jāyāpratigrāhitagandhamālyām*, the cow—the prompted agent—is denoted by the past passive participle (*kta*).

This would be so because of the rule: "In the case of a causative verb ending in *ṇic*, [the suffix *kta* is applied] to express the agent and the object. Consequently, one would have to say *jāyayā gandhamālye pratigrāhitām*.

However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "by whom the perfume and garlands were caused to be accepted" (*pratigrāhite gandhamālye yayā*). This refers to that [woman] by whom the act of accepting the perfume and garlands was made the object of an instigation directed toward her husband.

The meaning is that the act of receiving (*pratigrahaṇa*) is the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated precisely through the inclusion of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) and by reversing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
Regarding the rule *abhivādidṛśoḥ*: [the suffix is applied] where it was not previously applicable for the root *abhivādayati*, and where it was already applicable for the root *dṛś*.
This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule).
[From] *Prauḍhamanoramā*: regarding the sūtra *abhiniviśaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.47), although the word *abhi* ought to be placed first because it has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*), [it is not].

He states that the reversed pronunciation is for the purpose of intending such a collective form, saying: "of that which is preceded by a compound. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *niviśate yadi śūkaśikhā pade*. [The rule] does not apply in certain instances.
The usage in the commentary, "eṣvartheṣvabhiniviṣṭānām," serves as the authority here.
He states the case ending for the accompanying word (*upapada*) with the rule beginning "ubhasarvatasoḥ," etc.

The meaning is that when there is a connection with words ending in *ubha* and *sarva* followed by the suffixes *-tas* (i.e., *ubhayatas* and *sarvatas*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) must be employed. In this regard—
The Easterners say that by the word *ubha*, the word *ubhaya* is indicated, because otherwise the suffix *tas* would be impossible;
however, in reality, even though *ayac* is applied in the context of a compound formation (*vṛtti*), the suffix *tas* which is prescribed after the word *ubha* [remains].

The view that "it indeed exists up to that point" is correct according to the literal text. The ancients maintain that *dhik* is an indeclinable (an avibhaktika) designation, just like the expression *gavityayamāha*. That is not correct; for if that were the case, then because it would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the rule *jaśtva* would apply in the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) just as the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* does in the model example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of non-occurrence (*apravṛtti*). Nor should one be deluded into thinking that this [word *dhik*] ends in the letter *ga*, for then the example *dhakit* in the rule *kasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.50) would result in being inconsistent. Therefore, *dhik* is indeed [the form] ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*). By the extended application (*atideśa*) "an imitation [of a word] is like its original form" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), [the case-suffix] *sup*...
*Luk* (elision). "On both sides of Kṛṣṇa" (*ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇam*) means on both flanks of Kṛṣṇa.

The suffix *tasi* is used here according to the rule beginning with *ādyādi*. The accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. This should be understood in all instances where a subordinate case is employed. In every sentence, the relationship of a noun is established in only two ways.
It may occur either through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) or, in some cases, even by means of the genitive case.
Thus, in the statement of the Elder (Vṛddha), the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its apodictic case-ending as well.

The expression "in two ways" (*dvidhā*) is to be understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), or alternatively, by taking the genitive and its apodictic case as belonging to a single category. [An example is: "Fie upon the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa! (*dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam*). Of that...

The meaning is "he should be censured. How so? [In the phrase] "Fie, you fool! Since it has already been stated that a vocative word must be construed with a verb, there is an absence of connection with the word *dhik*. Furthermore, whether a verbal form is explicitly heard or merely implied is another matter. Thus, [the sentence] has the fool as its object of address.
The meaning of the sentence is that the performance of prohibited acts and so forth is censured. By this, expressions such as "Alas, father! and "Alas, Queen, be firm! are explained.
As for what they say—that "the case-ending denoting a kāraka (grammatical participant) is stronger than the case-ending of an upapada (governing word)"—that is weak.

"It is argued that the nominative case alone occurs in the vocative, because the vocative word expresses the agent (*kartṛ*) kāraka; this is weak, because if the vocative word were the agent kāraka, there would be no possibility of its being expressed [by a verbal suffix]. In cases such as 'O King, be gracious' (*deva prasīda*), in terms of the actual state of affairs..."

If it is argued that "the Lord alone is the agent," this does not establish the status of [the agent] as a case of the *kāraka*-inflection (the nominative). Furthermore, in such instances as "O Lord, I worship you" (*deva tvāṃ bhaje*) or "they worship you" (*tvāṃ bhajanti*), the person being addressed does not possess actual agency; let that be for now. Regarding the expression "higher and higher" (*uparyupari*): how then [is it used]?
[The question is: "Do the cognitions of the Lord move above the successive cognitions? It is said:

the meaning is that they move above the higher cognitions or the lower cognitions. And thus, because there is no repetition (*āmreḍita*), the accusative case is not used. Or else, [it refers to] the rule for the specific mention of "upari," "adhi," and "adhas": [Pāṇini 1.4.90].

The rule "sāmīpye" (Pāṇini 8.1.7) refers here to that which has already undergone reduplication; therefore, when reduplication occurs for the sake of distributive repetition (vīpsā), this [rule] does not apply. It was stated that "[it is seen] elsewhere as well," and he demonstrates this with the examples "abhitaḥ" and "paritaḥ. Regarding the word "pratibhāti": this prefix *prati* is an upasarga because it qualifies a verbal action.
But it is not a *karmapravacanīya*, as in "antarā tvāṃ mām" ("between you and me"), which means "in the middle of you and me.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the semantic force" (*sāmarthyāt*): for this very reason, even the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is an object of verbal cognition.
The sense is that [the relation] is accepted.
