In the expression "nadīm anv" (along the river), the meaning of the second case ending is relation; and here, since that [relation] takes the form of accompaniment (*sāhitya*), it is indicated by the prefix *anu*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*: Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.90 states: *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyānabhāgavīpsāsu pratiparyanavaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *lakṣaṇettham*: in the example *vṛkṣaṃ prati*, the meaning is "the manifestation of a connection with the tree.

And since that connection consists of the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), the prefixes *prati* and others express this. [Example: *bhakto viṣṇuṃ* ("devoted to Viṣṇu").
In the case of *pratīti*, the relationship between Viṣṇu and his devotee as that of the object and the subject is indicated by the prefix *prati*.

In the case of *lakṣmīḥ*, the relationship of owned and owner between the portion in the form of Lakṣmī and Hari [is indicated]. In the expression *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam*, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated solely by the reduplication, whereas the word *pari* is indicated by the verb.

It is connected [to the verb]. The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*). Because the designation *karmapravacanīya* supersedes the designation *upasarga*, there is no change of *s* to *ṣ*. It has been explained in the original treatise (*ākara*) that "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are mentioned as the objects [of these prepositions] precisely for this reason. However, the rule "pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ" does not apply here.

Because of its association with the sense of "avoiding" (*varjana*) in the word *apeti*, [the meaning here is different]. "May it fall upon me" (*mām abhiṣyāt*) means "may it become my portion. The ancient grammarians also cite *mām abhiṣyāt* as a counter-example; in that case, it means "may it reach me," due to the influence of the prefix on the root *as*.

Because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the word *mām* takes the second case (*dvitīyā*); furthermore, since the meaning here culminates in "my portion," the designation of *abhāga* as a *karmapravacanīya* is precluded,
and thus the rule "upasargaprādurbhyām" applies, resulting in the cerebral *ṣ*.
"And in the case of *pūjā*. From the preceding rule, "the prefix *su-* [is used] in the sense of *pūjā*," the mention of *pūjā* is drawn over here.
(Prakriyākaumudī: *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*)

*kālādhvanoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). *Atyantaḥ* means that which has transcended the end (*anta*), i.e., cessation (*virāma*); and that is *saṃyoga*, meaning uninterrupted proximity. It follows that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should be used [after words denoting time or distance]. Because it is explicitly stated [in the rule], it applies only to those functioning as time (*kāla*) or distance (*adhvan*). As in the example *māsasya* ("of the month"). [This occurs] when there is usage with words having the sense of *kṛtvas*.

Some say that the genitive case here is prescribed by the rule *kāle 'dhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.64), but that is incorrect; for in that rule, due to the continued application of the term *śeṣe* (the remainder), the result would simply be the non-application of compounding with a *kṛt*-derived word—as in the example *dvirahno bhojanam*. Therefore, the truth is that the genitive here is indeed prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50).
Thus ends the second [section].

Prau.ma.: "The independent agent" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.54). Independence (*svātantrya*) consists in being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root that constitutes the primary sense.
And it has been said:
"When the action is not explicitly stated by the verbal root, the agent is always intended to be the *kāraka* [instrument]. Thus [it is said].
*Prakriyākaumudī*: "The most effective means is the *karaṇa*. Regarding "most effective": that whose operation immediately [precedes the result]...
The accomplishment of the action is its excellence. And it has been said:
"When, in a particular instance, that whose operation immediately precedes the complete accomplishment of the action is intended to be expressed, that is then remembered as the instrument (karaṇa)."
By the phrase "it is intended to be expressed," he indicates that even things such as a cooking pot possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) depending on the speaker's intention. And he says:
"In reality, that [agency] is indefinable, for an entity is not fixed [in one state], since we observe the intention [of speech] expressed as 'the pot cooks'.
This is the meaning: agency, as well as the sixfold set beginning with "kartṛtva" (the state of being an agent) which is pervaded by it, reside in a particular entity.

It does not remain fixed in the same way as the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified; for it cannot be rightly said that "a qualifier is always a qualifier," in the same manner that one cannot say "a cow is a cow for everyone, but is not a non-cow for someone.
And thus, when a meaning is presented by a particular verbal root-form, [one must ask] what its agent and so forth are.

In the context of verbal cognition (*praśna*), the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended as the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*) that is expressed by the verbal root; the object (*karman*) is the substratum of the result (*phala*) which resides in a locus different from the operation;
and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum through a relationship mediated by the agent or the object. This is the meaning of the root *pac* (*to cook*).

And the operation (*vyāpāra*) is of many kinds. Thus, when [the action] has as its purpose placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring rice, or fetching fuel, Devadatta, who is the locus of that [action], is the agent; when it has as its purpose flaming, the fuel is the agent.

When the focus is on the containment of the rice and so forth, the pot (*sthālī*) is the agent (*kartṛ*); when the focus is on the separation of parts and so forth, the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are the agents. In the expression "he cooks with a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*), although the pot is the locus of the operation expressed by the instrumental case, it is merely an instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the agent, because the agency belongs solely to the operation of Devadatta and others.

Because it is included within that verbal root (*dhātu*): likewise, when an object is expressed by roots such as *ā-di* (to eat) and *khā-di* (to eat), the agent (*kartṛ*) is the grammatical factor to be employed; in that very same sense, when expressed by the root *bhakṣ-ayati* (causative of "to eat"), the object (*karman*) is [employed]. When an object is expressed by roots such as *śī* (to lie down) preceded by *adhi*, the locus (*ādhāra*) is the object; when expressed by those [roots] alone, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is [employed], and so forth. By this, [the status] of cognition...

The objection that there is a contradiction between the agent and the object (*kartṛ-karmavirodha*) regarding self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) and so forth is refuted, because [such a contradiction] cannot be asserted in the case of perception and the like, since agency and the rest are merely adventitious (*upādhika*) based on specific words.
By this, [the following is also addressed]: if "objecthood" (*karmatva*) were defined as possessing a result produced by an action inhering in another [substance],...

Having raised the objection that the definition does not cover the ablative (*apādāna*), those who attempt to refine the definition by stating that "the object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root" are also refuted; for in cases such as *grāmaṃ gamayati devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to go to the village"),
there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the goer, even though according to their view, the act of going is the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*).

Because that [definition] lacks the property of being a non-delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*). In that case, the suffix *ṇic* would have the meaning of "activity" (*vyāpāra*), not the base (*prakṛti*).
Or, even if that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) in examples such as *pācayati*.
Therefore, by the force of the statement, the technical definition of "object" (*karmatva*) useful for the grammatical instruction is [to be accepted].
If you argue that [the designation *apādāna*] is established [by the rule *dhruvam apāye’pādānam*], then understand that it does not exist even in the case of the *apādāna*,

because within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*), a designation that has no scope (*anavakāśā*) sublates one that has scope (*sāvakāśā*). For this very reason, in examples such as "he kills himself by himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*), the designation of agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*) prevails due to its higher status.

Anticipating the objection that this would contradict the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "action" (*karman*), the Commentary provides a resolution by relying on the distinction between the self as qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.
Regarding the word "by Rāma" (*rāmeṇa*): although here, with respect to the action, the case-factors (*kāraka*) are presented by their respective case-endings...

Nevertheless, while [the action] is indeed a qualifier, that which is presented by the verbal suffix (*kṛt*) is the qualificand, according to the statement: "Nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning. Even in the case of the result and the operation presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*), when used in conjunction with a *karmavat* (an agent-like object), there is a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualificand. And thus:
The meaning of the sentence is: Vālī is the substratum of the separation from life, which is to be accomplished by the operation of the arrow that is the object of the activity desired by Rāma.

As for what was stated by the Mīmāṃsakas in the section on the Vājapeya— that even the expression "cooking with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*) would be possible— that is refuted by the admission of our own position. This is because the rules such as *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* and *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* establish the connection of the *kāraka* with the meaning of the base of the *kṛt*-suffix.

The wise should reflect that there is simply no possibility for the occurrence of *vinokti* (the figure of speech based on negation) in such cases. What is an example of [an affix] not being expressed (*anabhihite*)? *hariḥ karoti* ("Hari does"). *jīvanaḥ* ("one who lives by this")—[derived from] *jīvanti anena*. *śābdikaḥ* ("a grammarian")—[derived from] *śabdair dūraṃ karoti* ("he makes [his way] far by means of words"), with the suffix *ṭhak*. *kṛtaviśvaḥ* ("by whom the universe was made").

The meaning is "the locus of the activity of Viśvakarman"; for in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the sixth [case] (genitive), another derivation is accepted. As this will be explained later, this [category] is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Therefore, examples such as "by name Sutīkṣṇa, by conduct Dānta" and so forth are included.
The object [of the action] is as follows: the combination of two *droṇas* is *dvidroṇa*.
Due to its inclusion in the *pātrādi* group, it lacks the feminine gender. The meaning is "grain related to two *droṇas*.
Regarding the word *ca* ("and"): by the recurrence of the term *karaṇa* (instrument), [the sūtra states] "in the case of hiring, [the instrument is] the recipient (*sampradāna*)."

Thus, since the option (*anyatarasyām*) from the subsequent rule has been brought forward [to this point], the particle *ca* serves to ensure the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the two designations when they would otherwise have been obtained as alternatives. Consequently, in the example *manasādevaḥ*, both are established: the suffix *aṇ* by virtue of the rule for the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*), and the instrumental case ending by virtue of its being the instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*). Furthermore, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending in *manasaḥ* by the rule "manasaḥ saṃjñāyām."

Furthermore, regarding the example *akṣairdevayate yajñadattaḥ*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the root is transitive, the agent of the causative (*ṇic*) does not become the object;

nor does the parasmaipada suffix apply by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*. As for the explanation given by the ancients (*prāc*) that the [agent] may optionally receive the designation of "object," [that is incorrect].

This should be disregarded because it contradicts the form [of the word]. It might be argued as follows: there is scope for the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) in the case of "the dice are for gambling" (*devanā akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument; whereas there is scope for the designation *karman* (object) in the case of "the dice are being played with" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of an object. Thus, in the phrase "he plays with the dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), when there is a conflict between the two operations resulting from the two designations, [the latter prevails] due to its higher status.

If it is argued that [the accusative] must be the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and not the second (*dvitīyā*), they say here: according to the view that the application of a rule occurs at the time the word is used (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the presence of the rule "the second case-ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) has no scope [in such cases], and thus the second case-ending applies. Now, one might object: even though the object is already expressed in the example "the dice play" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*),...

Since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not expressed [by the suffix], there would have to be a third case ending; likewise, in the example "the dice are the means of playing" (*devanā akṣāḥ*), even though the instrument is expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, since the object (*karman*) is not expressed, there would have to be a second case ending?
Not so; for here there is only one power (*śakti*) which is associated with two designations (*saṃjñā*). And thus:
In both cases, there is indeed expression (*abhidhāna*), and not non-expression (*anabhihitatva*).

[Prakriyā-kaumudī: Regarding the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), in the example *putreṇa*, the connection with the action is expressed verbally (*śābda*) for the father, but for the son...

The word "atha" (now/then) indicates its lack of predominance (*aprādhānya*). The mention of "non-predominance" could have been omitted; yet, even so, there would not be the undesirable consequence of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) for the father [in an expression like *pitur āgamanam*]. This is because, in that case, the first case ending (*prathamā*) arises by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned) with respect to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). As in the example: "the arrival of the father."

And because the case-ending denoting the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) possesses greater force. [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "By that which there is a modification of a limb" (*yenāṅgavikāraḥ*, Pāṇini 2.3.20)]. The word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *aC* added after the class beginning with *arśas*; thus he says: "of the possessor of the limb" (*aṅginaḥ*).
By the pronoun "by which" (*yena*), it is precisely the member that constitutes the primary referent of the base word that is grasped, due to its proximity.
And that [member] is necessarily modified by implication, for a modification of the body is not possible through an unmodified member. This is what he states: "by whichever limb is modified."

Regarding the form *saṃjānīte*: the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix is applied by the rule *sampratibhyāmanādhyāne*. Since it is joined with a *kṛt*-suffix, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies by virtue of its higher priority, resulting in *pitussaṃjñātā* ("the father’s cognizer"). As for what Haradatta stated—that because it refers to *ādhyāna* (thinking of/longing), the genitive is applied by the rule *adha-gartha* due to its higher priority, as in *mātuḥ saṃjānāti* ("he thinks of his mother")—that is not correct, because in that case...
This is because of the governing rule concerning the remainder (*śeṣādhikāra*).
Regarding "substance and so forth" (*dravyādi*): it has been stated— "The cause (*hetu*) whose object is substance and so forth is the instrument (*karaṇa*), which performs a restricted action."
"But when no operation [of the cause] is dependent [on another], it is accepted as a *nimitta*-cause" (Patañjali).

And "the result (*phala*) also [is such a cause]. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *pratyaya*. Thus, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used alongside the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*). For example: *adhyayanāya vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study"). This...

However, the distinction is this: with respect to the fruit (*phala*), there is a relation of identity (*abheda*) with study; but with respect to the benefactor (*upakāraka*), there is a relation of characterization (*nirūpakatā*). The phrase "being understood" (*gamyamāna*) implies that there is no insistence that it must be explicitly heard (*śrūyamāṇa*).
The term "means" (*sādhana*) refers to the meaning of the stem portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) in the word *sādhya*. [The particle] *mā*...

In the phrase "cāpalāya gaṇān vyanaiṣīt," however, the word "yatadhvam" (strive) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the term "aśiṣṭa" (unrefined): this is made known by the rule "dāṇaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe" (Pāṇini 1.4.35).
Thus ends the third [chapter].

By the force of the name being according to its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), he says "of giving" (*dānasya*). The intention is that, by this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he leads the goats to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*) or "he places his hand on the tree" (*hastaṃ nidadhāti vṛkṣe*). And giving is the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership, for the purpose of non-reacquisition. Precisely for this reason...
In cases such as "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), [the designation of *kāraka*] does not occur; for there, the verb *dadāti* ("gives") is used figuratively.

This is the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti. However, according to the Bhāṣya, there is no insistence on the literal meaning [of the term], because of the usage: "The teacher Khaṇḍika gives a slap to his pupil" (*khaṇḍikopādhyāyaḥ śiṣyāya capeṭāṃ dadāti*).

However, the statement "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (ṭhrajakasya vastraṃ dadāti') should be understood as being intended to express the status of the recipient as a subordinate element (śeṣatva). Nor does this lead to an over-extension (prasaṅga) in cases such as "he leads the goat to the village" (ṭhajāṃ nayati grāmam'), because by the rule "towards whom he intends," the status of the primary object (śeṣitva) is obtained for that which is indicated by the word "whom" (yam), while the status of the subordinate element (śeṣatva) is obtained for the object of the action (karman).

The village has no status as a recipient (*śeṣitva*) with respect to the goat. [In the term] *dānīya*, the suffix *anīyar* is applied in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). [This is illustrated by] Pāṇini’s sūtra: "In the case of verbs meaning 'to please' (*ruci*), the one who is being pleased is [the recipient]. (Pāṇini 1.4.33).

*rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (A 1.4.33). The root *prīñ* means "to satisfy"; from this, the present participle (*laṭ*) is formed in the passive sense. In the example *haraye rocate*, the meaning is "he pleases Hari. Since the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would otherwise apply here, this rule is stated as an exception. Why "being pleased" (*prīyamāṇaḥ*)? Consider: *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ pathi*. Here, [the designation of the object does not apply to] the path (*pathaḥ*).
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.34: *ślāghahuṅsthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ*.
Regarding *ślāghahuṅ*: *ślāghā* means praise (*stuti*). [Examples: *kṛṣṇāya ślāghate* (he praises Kṛṣṇa); *kṛṣṇaṃ*... [he praises].

The meaning is "he praises. Others, however, say: the meaning is that he speaks of himself or another as praiseworthy for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. In that regard, in the first case, since [the object] would attain the status of a *karman*, and in the second case, since it would be a mere residual factor (*kāraka-śeṣa*) and thus the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply, this rule is stated. [The example is] "she hides herself" from her co-wives (*sapatnībhyaḥ*).

The meaning is that she makes Kṛṣṇa understand that very same matter by whispering into his ear; or, it means she whispers into anyone's ear. Regarding "tiṣṭhate": the meaning is that she makes her intention understood through her standing [in a certain posture].
The Ātmanepada ending (taṅ) is applied here according to the rule "prakāśanastheyākhyayośca."
Prau.ma.-dhārerutamarṇaḥ (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.35):

"In the case of the root *dhṛ* [meaning 'to owe'], the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) [is the agent]. This is a rule intended to provide for the application of the genitive case where it would otherwise have been expected.
Prau.ma.-spṛherīpsitaḥ (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.36): "In the case of the root *spṛh* [meaning 'to desire'], that which is desired (*īpsita*) [is the object]."

Regarding the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ*: because it is subsequent [in the order of the *Pāṇini-sūtras*], by it [the genitive is superseded] in cases such as *paraspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham* ("mutually desirable in beauty") and *spṛhaṇīyaguṇair mahātmabhiḥ* ("by great souls possessing desirable qualities"). However, when there is an intention to express the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive case applies. By that [rule]: [Example: *rājñaḥ spṛhayati*. (He longs for the king.)

"Like maidens toward their beloved, they both tremble and long [for him]"—this is established. All of this has been stated according to the method of Haradatta and others; however, in the *Vākyapadīya* and the work of Helārāja, regarding the application of the verb *spṛhayati*, there is [the rule for] the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*).
It is established that this designation of "recipient" (sampradāna) supersedes the remaining genitive case.

According to that view, in the expression *spṛhaṇīyam*, a *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the recipient, as in the word *dānīya*. However, in the expression *kumārya iva*, one should explain it by changing the case-ending as "longing for a lover" (*kāntāya spṛhayanti*).

Prau.ma.: *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.37). The sūtra begins with *krudhadruha*. *Krudh* means "to be angry," *druh* means "to injure," and *īrṣya* means "to envy. *Asūya* is a root ending in the *ya*-suffix belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. The meaning of the phrase is: those verbal roots whose meaning is similar to the meanings of these [roots]. Among them:

*Krodha* is anger; *droha* is malice or injury; *īrṣyā* is intolerance; whereas *asūyā* is the attribution of faults to those who possess virtues. Since *krudh* and *druh* are intransitive, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply when used with them; since the other two are transitive, the second case (*dvitīyā*) would apply.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.39): the term "kāraka" [in the commentary] refers to the *karmakāraka* (the object case-role); however, the claim of the ancient commentators that it refers to the *karman* alone is an error, because of the governing heading *ekasaṃjñādhikāraḥ* (the section on singular designation). Nor can it be argued that this is intended merely to indicate the first application [of the designation].

The designation as the object (*karmatva*) [of the word *kṛṣṇasya*] follows because, by accepting the meaning "he reflects upon the auspicious and inauspicious deeds related to Kṛṣṇa," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is obtained.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.40: *anupratigṛṇaśca*.

"And [the word] *anupratigṛṇaḥ*. Because *gṛṇa* is an imitation of a form ending in *śnā*, the genitive case is used. Regarding the word *hotre*: although the status of being the object (*karman*) would have applied, [this is not so]. Paribhāṣā-sūtra: "In the context of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the person for whom something is done] is optionally the recipient (*sampradāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.44)

"In *parikrayaṇe*": *Krayaḥ* (purchase) means the absolute acquisition [of ownership] through the surrender of wealth and so forth; the prefix *pari-* denotes that which is proximate (*samīpam*) to that. And because it is less than that [absolute acquisition], it is for a limited time—thus he explains with the word "limited" (*niyata*). "By service" (*bhṛtyā*) means by means of wages (*vetana*) and so forth. Regarding "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*): for that purpose.

"For this effect, for that purpose"—this is the *kāraṇa* (cause). Its state is *tādarthya* (the state of being for that purpose). By the suffix *ṣyañ*, a relationship consisting of the nature of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is expressed, according to the established principle: "From *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, and compounds, the notion of a relationship is conveyed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). This [relationship] is the state of being a benefactor.

And [this rule] applies in many ways. Therefore, it also occurs in cases such as *brāhmaṇāya dadhi* ("curd for the Brahmin"). In the case of *bhaktir jñānāya* ("devotion for the sake of knowledge"), the meaning is that it transforms into the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). When there is an intention to express a distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), the fourth case ending is used after the word denoting the modification. However, when there is an intention to express non-distinction, the nominative case alone is used because it is of higher priority.

"Devotion is transformed into knowledge. However, when one intends to express that devotion is the *apādāna* (starting point) according to the rule "janikartuḥ," then, because knowledge has its agency (*kartṛtva*) already expressed, only the nominative case is used: "knowledge is produced from devotion" (*bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpate*).
With the intention that the root *klṛp* is taken here in its general sense, he says "it becomes" (*sampadyate*), etc. Regarding the word "by a portent" (*utpātena*):

An *utpāta* is a modification of natural elements that indicates the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of living beings; the meaning is that the fourth case ending is used when [a word] denotes an object made known by such a sign. In the example *vātāya*, the meaning is "that which makes the wind known.
In the word *hita*, the sense is that it is a signifier because of the rule for forming the compound. The same applies in the case of connection with *sukha*.

The object to be attained (*bodhyam*). With the intention that, by the power of the rule *tumuṇvulau kriyāyām*, an accompanying word (*upapada*) denoting an action results in being expressed as an action itself when it has an action as its purpose, he says: "an action. That which has an action as its fruit.
The meaning is that [the word] has a verbal root as its base (*kriyāvācaprakṛtika*). The mention of *tumun* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *ṇvul*.

For there is no obstacle to explaining "he goes for fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*) as "one who brings fruits" (*phalānyāharakaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*): the intention is that this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).

As for the explanation given by the predecessor—that this sūtra is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama) so that [the karmasañjñā] may apply only to an action not being employed [as a means], but not to one being employed—that is incorrect, because a restriction cannot apply to what has not been previously established. Nor is there establishment [of the karmasañjñā] by the rule "tādarthye" (P. 5.1.12), for [an action] is not for the sake of a result.
Is the action of "going" (yāna) for the purpose of "bringing" (āharaṇa)? But bringing has "fruit" (phala) as its object; this is another matter.

Since the suffix *tumun* is prescribed only in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*), it is already established that its meaning denotes a state; nevertheless, the explicit mention of the word "state" (*bhava*) is for the purpose of including a specific rule. Thus he says: "by the rule... (*iti sūtreṇa*).

Nor should it be suspected that the meaning [of the suffix] is already conveyed by the word "tādarthye" (in the sense of being for that purpose) alone; for since the sense of being for that purpose is already indicated by the verbal noun itself—just as it is by the suffix *tumun*—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the nominative case (*prathamā*) applying to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).
As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the suffix] should apply only after a verbal noun, as in "pācako vrajati" ("the cook goes")—[that is incorrect].

"It is argued that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), so that [the suffix] *ṇvul* does not apply after a word ending in *ṇvul*; but that is not correct, because in a word ending in *ṇvul*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the predominant factor, and there is no sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) toward the agent;
furthermore, the vehicle (*yāna*) which has become a *duṇ* [suffix] cannot be construed with the meaning of the case-ending."

One might object: "Why [mention] 'also the sixth case'? Let there simply be the sixth case; let the word *alam* be understood as having the meaning of 'sufficiency' and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It prevails over that," and "not even a blade of grass for you," etc. Now, one might further object: "In the alternative view, just as with words like 'grass,' from the word *yuṣmad* (you) as well..."

The fourth case [the dative] should be used. Not so; for in the rule "ṭhanādare" (Pāṇini 1.4.95), the word *karma* (object) is a qualifier—meaning, that object which indicates disregard. Such an object is only the grass, not the referent of *yuṣmad* (you).
Thus ends the fourth [chapter].

Prau.ma.: *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.24). Regarding the word *dhruvam*: the root *dhru* is used in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and "steadiness" (*sthairya*). From this root, which belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 to form *dhruva*. Alternatively, if the reading is *dhruva* in the sense of "steadiness," then the suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* followed by a single consonant (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Thus, *dhruvam* means "steady."

[A locus] is that which, while not being entered by the action denoted by the root in question, serves as the substratum for the *vibhakti* (case-ending) produced by it; and since this [non-entry] follows logically from the very fact of being a limit (*avadhi*), he says "that which has become a limit. Regarding the word "running": here, even though the horse is qualified by the action [of running], it does not possess the status of a limit with respect to the action denoted by the root in question.

[It would be] contradictory. However, in the case of "the two rams move away from each other" (*parasparasmān meṣāv apasarataḥ*), since the root *sṛ* (to go) denotes both movements, the status of the ablation (*apādāna*) for one [ram] toward the movement residing in the other is not contradictory. And it has been said:
That which is indifferent toward a departure, whether it be moving or unmoving,
is called the *apādāna* (ablative) because it remains fixed due to its lack of involvement in that movement.
Since the horse certainly falls from the wall, and that horse falls from the wall,
the wall is also necessarily considered to fall when that horse falls.
"The status of being a limit (avadhitva) for two rams is distinct and distinct, depending respectively on the action of the other ram;
and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct and distinct, depending on their own respective actions.
However, in the case of "he falls from the horse falling from the mountain," [the situation is different].

The meaning is that the horse is the locus of the falling action delimited by the mountain, while Devadatta and others are the loci of the falling action delimited by that [horse]. In the sense of the ablative case, the referent of the base (prakṛti) is a qualifier of the delimited [object] through the relation of identity; however, the referent of the suffix is the action, and that is the substratum (dharmin), not [the delimited object itself].

It is merely the property (*dharma-mātra*), because there is no dispute regarding the fact that a *bahuvrīhi* compound, prescribed for the sense of a case-ending, has as its referent the substratum of the property (*dharmin*). For in the example "a pot from which rice has been removed" (*uddhṛtaudana sthālī*), the meaning is "that which serves as the limit (locus) for the removal whose object is the rice. Regarding the word "jugupsā," the author of the Bhāṣya, however—

They state that the proof for this is established by the Sūtra, based on the fact that [terms] such as *jugupsā* (disgust) indicate the cessation [of an action] preceded by that [disgust]. This is likewise the case in the subsequent Sūtras as well. [Prakriyākaumudī]: "The cause of fear [is the agent] in the case of roots meaning 'to fear' (*bhītrārtha*). (Pāṇini 1.4.25).

"Bhītrā. How then is one to explain the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "Whom do even the gods fear when he has become enraged in battle"? On this point, they say: [the reading is] "kasya saṃyuge" (whom in battle), and it is not as [you suggest].

The designation *apādāna* (ablative) applies specifically to *saṃyuga* (battle), because it is superseded by the subsequent designation *adhikaraṇa* (locative). However, when the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the desired result follows. Regarding the example "from study" (*adhyayanāt*), the meaning is "weariness connected with study."

Prau.ma.: *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30). The term *jani* means birth or origination (*utpatti*). The suffix *iñ* is applied to the root *jan* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the rule *ṭhiñādibhyaḥ*, or the suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* sūtra *janighasibhyāmiṇ*.

By the rule *janivadhyośca*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*. The compound [of *kartṛ*] with that [genitive] is a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, it occurs even in connection with another verbal root, as in: *aṅgādaṅgāt sambhavasi*. This is what he states with the words *jāyamānasya*. By this, [the suffixes] *ik* and *śtip* [are accounted for].

The sense is that the authors of the *Mīmāṃsāvārttika*, having relied on the view that this [reference] in the rule *dhātunirdeśe* is a reference by means of the vowel *i*, raised objections regarding the undesirable consequence of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) according to the rule *gamahana*, as well as the incoherence of the meaning and the impossibility of compounding; however, they have been answered here in this sūtra by the inclusion of the term *prakṛti*.

The author of the *Vṛtti* holds that [the sūtra] refers only to the cause (*hetumātraparam*), citing "joy arises from a son" as an example. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa hold that it refers only to the material cause (*upādānamātraparam*).
He provides an example common to both views: "of Brahmā. Here, Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha; and he...

It is indeed the cause (*hetu*), but not the material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, Brahman qualified by *māyā* is the material cause of all effects; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Vedānta school.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.31: *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ*]

"Bhuvaḥ. The word *bhū* means "becoming" (*bhavanam*). The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *sampad*. He says "of the agent of becoming" (*bhūkartuḥ*), because the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*), although specified in a compound in the previous rule, is understood here due to its being marked as *svarita*. "Source" (*prabhava*) means that from which something originates; this involves the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that because the form ending in the suffix *lyap* has its meaning already implied, it is not employed [separately]. As for "yataśca":

the meaning is "from that," referring to that which is resorted to as a limit (*avadhi*) for the purpose of establishing or delimiting a path or time. By means of that, through the sense of the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), [the connection is established] by way of the meaning.

The first and seventh case endings occur after words denoting a path when they are used in connection with the act of being traversed. Regarding the word *kalāt*: it is understood as being qualified by the phrase *tadyauktāt* (from that which is joined with it).
Regarding the phrase *prapañcārtham* (for the sake of elaboration): this is because [the rule] "the word *itara* [is used] in the senses of 'other' and 'inferior'" does not apply here.

It should not be argued that this [term] is taken here because of Amara’s statement that it has the sense of "low," for it is already established by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), just as in examples such as *asmāt tāro mandro vā*.
As for the claim that the word *itara* is used only when it refers to a correlate (*pratiyogin*) being pointed out—for instance, as in *caitraḥ*... [the opponent continues]... [it is not so].

"One is a hero, the other is a coward"—therefore, this [word *ṛte*] does not have another meaning. That is weak, because the expectancy for a correlative (*pratiyogi*) is equal in both cases, and because it contradicts the cited lexicon. As for "except for Kṛṣṇa" (*ṛte kṛṣṇāt*), how then is the expression "without the propitiation of the Person" (*puruṣārādhanam ṛte*) to be explained?

Some say this is an error; others, however, maintain that because of the inclusion of the root *dṛś* in the rule "ubhasarvatasoḥ," the accusative case is also correct when used with *ṛte*, just as in examples such as "caitraṃ yāvacchītam. This is indeed reasonable, based on the Cāndra sūtra: "ṛte dvitīyā ca" (with *ṛte*, the accusative [and other cases] are also used).

Regarding the phrase *prabhṛtyarthayoga*: the meaning is "connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti* (starting from). Accordingly, Kaiyaṭa, while explaining the Bhāṣya passage "from the full moon of Kārttika" (*kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti*), employed the gloss: "the meaning is 'beginning from that' (*tata ārabhya*)."

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of *vacana*": by implication, only the limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed. The sense is that the qualifying portion, namely "without that," is not [intended]. Alternatively, it is called *maryādāvacana* because the word *maryādā* is expressed therein—referring to the rule "āṅ is used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*)."
Regarding the sūtra: the meaning is that the prefix *āṅ* which is seen there is designated as "stated" (*ukta-saṃjñā*).

Regarding *parihareti*: by the vārttika "the statement [of the doubling] after *pari* is optional when used in the sense of exclusion," there is an absence of doubling in one alternative. Regarding *pariratreti*: here, in the rule prescribing the fifth case (*pañcamī*), [the word *pari*] is used with the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) by means of *apa*.

The meaning is "due to concomitance. [From] *Prau.ma.*: "And with regard to that from which there is a substitute or a counter-gift" (*pratinidhipratidāne ca*, Pāṇini 1.4.92). By virtue of this very indication, [the genitive case is used] in connection with these two.

They say [the word] *pañcamī* [is used here]. In the absence of the primary [substance], that which is substituted for it is called a *pratinidhi* (substitute). *Pratidāna* is the repayment of what has been given.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.11]: "The fifth case-affix (*pañcamī*) is used when the sense is that of a debt, provided it does not denote the agent."
"In the sense of other than the agent" (akartari): the fifth case (pañcamī) should occur. This is an exception to the third case (tṛtīyā). Regarding the example *śatena*:

here, a hundred is a debt (*ṛṇa*) because it is being held by the creditor. By the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca*, the technical designation of "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) is also applied.

Regarding the phrase "due to the division of the yoga": this is clear in the commentary of Haradatta on the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "and in the feminine": the mention of the Vārttika, *bāhulakaṃ prakṛtestanudṛṣṭeḥ*, is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in this context.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *pṛthagvinānānābhis tṛtīyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.32), the word "samuccayārtham" (for the purpose of inclusion) is used because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings; this is the intended sense.

As for "pañcamī" (the fifth case): there, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is understood by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkagati*), while the second case (*dvitīyā*) is already present [from the preceding rule].

[The forms are] *dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*. Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) will also be mentioned. Furthermore, because the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.35) is carried forward into the subsequent rules, these [words] take four case-endings even when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is what is to be understood. And thus it is applied: "mūtram dūrād āvasathāt" (urine [is to be discharged] far from the dwelling).

The meaning is "far from the dwelling. Regarding the term *asatve* (in the absence of a substance): its being a denotation of a substance consists in its having that [substance] as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
And in this way, by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that which has the meaning of the nominal stem as its qualificand is excluded. Thus he says:

Regarding the statement "The path is distant," this explains the commentary of the ancients on the rule *karaṇe ca stoka-* (Pāṇini 2.3.18), which asks: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *karaṇe*? Let it not apply to an accusative that qualifies an action—as in *stokaṃ pacati* ('he cooks slightly')—because an action is not a substance. As for that [commentary], having restated it... regarding the action:

They said that it must be considered because substancehood (*dravyatva*) necessarily follows from being a qualificand (*viśeṣya*); however, that very point is what must be considered, since it is well-established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that action denoted by a verbal root is of a non-substantial nature (*asatvarūpa*). Nor is there any inconsistency in its being a qualificand.

This is because such [usage] is justified merely by the lack of connection with gender, number, and so forth, as in the case of an abstract state expressed by a *kṛt* suffix. Although the *Bhāṣya* accepts the connection with number in examples such as "those who were killed lie down" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*),
and the connection with agency or objecthood in examples such as "he cooks, [and thus] exists" (*pacati bhavati*), nevertheless, [this does not apply] to gender.
Furthermore, the absence of any other grammatical factor (kāraka) is indeed a contradiction. And it has been said:
"An action is not joined with gender, nor with the factors of action that do not serve as the substratum for the action;
let this very nature of its being non-substantial (asatvarūpatā) be firmly grasped."
Thus ends the fifth [chapter].

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs after the subordinate element alone, because the meaning of the suffix is predominant with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, that meaning [of the suffix] serves as a qualifier for the "man. The genitive does not, however, occur after the predominant element, because that would contradict the aforementioned logic and because there is no status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) in that case. For the word "man," accordingly—

When [the word] functions solely in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or denotes a grammatical relation (*kāraka*), then [the sixth case ending does not apply]. However, when it is not so, the sixth case ending certainly occurs even after the word *puruṣa*. As for the claim that "the subordinate is the *śeṣa* (remainder)," that is incorrect;
for [the term *śeṣa* applies] even to a qualifier in cases such as "a white jar" (*śuklo ghaṭaḥ*), where there is merely the sense of the nominal stem.

Because there would be the contingency of the sixth case (genitive). Nor is there sublation by the first case (nominative), since that [first case] has fulfilled its purpose in expressing predominance (*prādhānya*). Regarding the phrase "of the object and so forth": just as one uses "rūpavān" when the specific [quality] is not intended to be expressed, but one uses "nīlaḥ pītaḥ" and so on when that [specificity] is intended to be expressed.
The sense is that this [point] is likewise established by logic (*nyāya*).

Regarding the phrase "of existing things" (*satām*): thus, the readings found in the works of the ancients—namely, "when there is a connection with a *kta*-suffix in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and when there is a desire to express the status of being a 'remainder' (*śeṣatva*)," and "the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is optionally used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) of roots meaning 'to satisfy'"—[are justified].

The sense is that this is not a statement of something previously unknown. Regarding the word *sarpiṣaḥ*: [these are the examples for] "the instrument of a verb meaning 'to know' when it does not mean 'to find out'" (*jño'vidarthasya karaṇe*);

"the object of verbs meaning 'to remember,' 'to love,' or 'to rule'" (*adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*); "the object of *kṛñ* when used in the sense of 'improvement'" (*kṛñaḥ pratiyatne*); "the object of verbs meaning 'to cause pain' which express a state, except for *jvar*" (*rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānāmajvareḥ*); "the object of *nāth* when used in the sense of 'blessing'" (*āśiṣi nāthaḥ*); and [the objects of] *jas*, *ni-pra-han*, *naṭ*, *krāth*, and *piṣ*.

The group of eight sūtras beginning with "hiṃsāyām," "vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ," and "kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe" is not explained here, because its purpose is to preclude compound formation (samāsa). For instance, in that context, the word "śeṣa" (remainder) is understood to carry over.

And when the *karaṇa* (instrument) and other factors are intended to be expressed as the *śeṣa* (remainder), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is already established. Thus, the meaning here is this: in these instances, only the genitive occurs and there is no elision (*luk*) of it; consequently, the very compound that would cause such elision does not even exist. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "The genitive prescribed by specific rules [is not elided]," and so forth.
And Hari said: "Furthermore, when the action is explicitly heard and the case-role (kāraka) is designated [by a word],
the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) is prescribed after every individual word to prevent compounding."

Therefore, when the sense of "remainder" (śeṣatva) is intended, forms such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee") and *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembrance of the mother") are correct only when they remain uncompounded. On the other hand, forms such as *harismaraṇam* ("remembrance of Hari") should be understood as compounds formed with the genitive case used for the "kṛt-yoga" (connection with a verbal derivative), even when the sense of "remainder" is intended. And in that case:

Because [the compound] is preceded by a *kāraka*, the accentuation is that of the base of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) when it ends in a *kṛt* suffix. However, if it were a compound with a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), there would be an oxytone (accent on the final syllable), which is undesired. Thus, the ultimate conclusion is that these eight sūtras are for the sake of regulating accent. Furthermore, in cases such as *mātuḥ smṛtam*, even the absence of compounding [is established].
The result [is not expressed by the genitive]. For in that case, the genitive of the agent (kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī) is not permitted, due to the prohibition [by Pāṇini] in the rule "na loka...".
And it is said:
"In the case of a past passive participle (niṣṭhā), the genitive referring to the object (karman) is prohibited."
"In that case, a compound with the genitive case by way of *śeṣalakṣaṇā* (the remaining senses of the genitive) is not desired.

This being the established position, whatever examples or counter-examples involving non-finite verbs (*atiṅanta*) are seen here in this section within numerous works such as the *Vṛtti* and others, all of that is intended merely as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇatayā*).
Haradatta and others maintain that this [rule] does not apply. [Pāṇini 2.3.27:
*sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* ("And the third case suffix [is optionally used] after a pronoun"). Here, *sarvanāmnaḥ* is in the genitive case; thus he says: "after a pronoun."

Regarding the word *prayoge*: the intention is that if the ablative (*pañcamī*) were used, the genitive and instrumental would not occur after a word meaning "cause" (*hetu*). Regarding the phrase *nimittaparyāya*: he illustrates the purpose of including the term *paryāya* with the words beginning "in this way" (*evam*). However, the ancient commentators have cited "for what purpose? (*kimartham*) as an example.

In that case, how is the neuter gender of *kim* difficult to justify? It may somehow be explained by resorting to the neuter gender for general categories (*sāmānya*) and to compound formation (*samāsa*). Regarding the rule "not after a pronoun" (*asarvanāmnaḥ*), although the Vārttika—"in the sense of cause, motive, or reason, all [case endings] are generally seen"—was indeed cited here by the author of the Vṛtti, [it does not apply here].

Nevertheless, the author of the Bhāṣya read [the word] "hetau" (in the sense of cause) here; therefore, it functions even when no pronoun is employed. However, because of the inclusion of the term "generally" (prāya), the meaning is that it occurs only in the third case and so forth.
Vardhamāna, however, desires it even in the nominative case.
Prakriyāmañjarī: Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30), [the word] *pañcamyāḥ* [is understood]. How then is [the form] *tataḥ paścāt* derived?
It is because of the usage in the Bhāṣya: *tataḥ paścāt sraṃsyate dhvaṃsyate ca*, which shows that [the suffix] *paścāt* is used in conjunction with *tataḥ*.

The fifth [case-ending] also [is used]. The mention of the word *pratyaya* (suffix) is of doubtful utility. [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "With words ending in *ena*, the second case is used. How then [is it explained in the verse]: "There (*tatra*) is the house"?
"Is it 'to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth is ours'?"—it should be understood that "uttareṇa" (in the instrumental case) is in grammatical apposition with "toraṇena" (the archway).
[Prakriyākaumudī]: By the rule *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.34), [the use of the instrumental is optional].

Regarding the rule "with words meaning 'far' or 'near'" (*dūrāntikārthaiḥ*): the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). By that, the ablative (*pañcamī*)—though remote—is also conjoined on the basis of the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), but not the genitive, accusative, or instrumental cases. This is what he states: "and the ablative."
*Prakriyākaumudī*: *divastadarthasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.58). By the word *tat* (that), the two roots *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ* are referred to.
These two were included in the preceding sūtra as having the same meaning in the context of gambling (*dyūta*) and the business of buying and selling (*krayavikrayavyavahāra*).

With this intention, he says: "In gambling" (*dyaūte*) and "in an action" (*karmaṇi*). The point is that here the term "remainder" (*śeṣe*) is not connected [to the rule], because of the commencement of the two subsequent sūtras. For this very reason, he provides an example of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) within this group of three sūtras: "he plays for a hundred" (*śatasya dīvyati*).

Prau.ma.: Regarding the rule *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsampradāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.34): the word *preṣya* is the second person singular imperative of the root *iṣ*, which belongs to the *adādi* class and has the sense of "going"; by virtue of its association with that, *brū* is also understood [to be used here].

It is understood as being exactly so. For this very reason, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not connected here, because the formation of a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not applicable.
[Prakriyākaumudī: *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65)].

"Of the agent and the object, when a *kṛt* suffix follows. Regarding "guṇe": it has been said—"The genitive case is fixed for the primary [object], but for the subordinate [object] it may be either way. Regarding "kṛtapūrvī": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one by whom something was done previously" (*kṛtaṃ pūrvam anena*). The meaning is "one who has done [it] before."

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because the action is not intended to have an object (*avivakṣitakarmakatayā*). The compound is formed by the rule "sup-supā. The suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by the rules "pūrvādiniḥ" and "sapūrvācca," since the word "anena" is understood from the rule "śrāddhamanena" in that specific prescription. Now, how is it [justified] in the case of "dhāyairāmodamuttamam"?
Bhaṭṭi? Regarding this, they say: this [rule] is not eternal (*anitya*), because of the mention [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] “*tadarham*” (P.

5.1.117). As for the phrase “of the two feminine suffixes” (*strīpratyayayoḥ*): how then is the Vṛtti on the sūtra “*suṭtithoḥ*” (*suṭ* does not sublate *sūyuṭ*) to be explained? It is by taking the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of expressing instrumentality (*karaṇatva*).
Take this:

*prau.ma.*—*na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.69). The analysis of the compound is as follows: *u* and *uka* are *ūk*, and *la* along with *ūkau* are *lauk*. Thus, it is *na* [the negation] applied to *lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛn*.

Because of the qualification made by the letter *u*, the rule of "extension to that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; thus he says: "desirous of seeing Hari" (*didṛkṣuḥ*) or "desirous of adorning" (*alaṃkariṣṇuḥ*). As for the phrase "but the genitive in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī tu*), by this [he means that the genitive is used] as in: "In matters difficult to achieve for the Ikṣvākus, success indeed depends on you," or "Even for the Lord of Speech, there is speech that is difficult to utter."

The passage beginning with "tadvidadhīta vismayam" has been explained. Alternatively, the syntactic connection is "the successes of the Ikṣvākus," and not "inaccessible to the Ikṣvākus"; likewise, the connection is "astonishment of the Lord of Speech," and not "difficult to speak for the Lord of Speech."

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72), [the sūtra states]: "with words having the sense of *tulya*. How then is one to explain Kālidāsa’s usage: *tulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsasā* ("when he ascends the scale with Dantavakra"), and Māgha’s: *sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā* ("clearly comparable to Śiva, white with ashes")? It is said in reply: [The word *tulya* here] refers to words expressing similarity (*sādṛśya*) other than *tulā* and *upamā*. Therefore, there is no fault. Alternatively, since the word *tulya* is used as a synonym for *sadṛśa*, it includes all words signifying likeness. Thus, the application of the third case ending is established even in these instances. Furthermore, because the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood from the preceding rule (*tṛtīyā ca hoḥ*), the second case ending is also obtained. Consequently, forms such as *dantavāsasam* and *bhūtisitena* are also valid. Moreover, because the word *tulya* is mentioned in the sūtra, the sixth case ending is also obtained; hence forms such as *dantavāsasaḥ* and *bhūtisitasya* are also correct. However, the first case ending is not obtained, because the word *tulya* is not mentioned in the sūtra *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.115). Thus, the form *tulam* is not used. Nor is the seventh case ending obtained, because the word *tulya* is not mentioned in the sūtra *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116). Therefore, the form *tule* is not used. This is the established conclusion. However, some say that the word *tulya* is mentioned in the sūtra *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* for the sake of including the suffix *vati*. But this is incorrect, because the suffix *vati* is not included in the present context. As for the mention of *tulā* and *upamā* in the sūtra, it is for the purpose of excluding those very words. Hence, the forms *tulayā* and *upamayā* are not used. This is the final view. However, others say that the mention of *tulā* and *upamā* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *vati*. But this is also incorrect, because the suffix *vati* is not included in the present context. Therefore, the mention of *tulā* and *upamā* is indeed for the purpose of excluding those very words. Thus, the forms *tulayā* and *upamayā* are not used. This is the final view. However, others say that the mention of *tulā* and *upamā* is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *vati*. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used according to the rule *sahayukte’pradhāne* ("when joined with *saha*, the subordinate [element takes the third case]"). This is as in the verse: "of one who desires equality with the young offspring of the yak, together with the weight of his own tail-hair. For it has been stated: "the third case occurs even without connection to that [the word *saha*]."

Regarding the phrase "because of the explanation": the word *artha* is also a separate cause [for the compound] in the sūtra; thus, it is indeed a *dvandva* (copulative) compound, and not a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound with the word *artha*. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the sixth case.
"The substratum (ādhāra) is threefold"—this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "saṃhitāyām".

"Four [types]"—the intention is that these refer to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha). Furthermore, because the sūtra "dūrāntika" is also understood to apply here, these [four] should be understood as including the locative (adhikaraṇa) as well. "Of the *kta* [suffix]"—[the suffix] *in*.

The meaning is: "that which has as its object a word whose end is *sīmā* and which functions as a boundary. It should be understood that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), and the fourth case (*caturthī*) is also used in the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*). Regarding the passage beginning with *sīmā*, this was stated by Kulacandra in his *Durgavākyaprabodha*. The author of the *Medinī* lexicon also says:
"In the fields situated at the boundary, in testicles, and in a woman. And:
"Furthermore, *puṣkalaka* [is used] for a musk deer and for a wooden peg.
Haradatta and others, however, state that *puṣkalaka* refers to a stake (*śaṅku*) driven into the boundary for the purpose of knowing the limits.
They say [the word] *nikhāta* [is used].
*Prau.ma.*—The sūtra *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37): "And of that [action]... An action whose time is well-known [serves as a marker] for an action whose time is not well-known.

A *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) is so called because it delimits time. This locative case (*saptamī*) expresses the agent or the object which serve as the substratum for that indicator. Among these, "having gone while the Brāhmaṇas were studying" is an example where the agent is indicated. Regarding the object, he says: "in the cows. Here, the Brāhmaṇas who are studying and the cows who are being milked [serve as the indicators].
And the state of being an indicator through implication (*pratīyamāna-lakṣakatva*) rests upon the two actions of studying and milking, which have become qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).
"Only a distinction" means that there is no superimposition of a generic form conveyed by another word; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the example *māthurāḥ*: here, as in the case of *gavāṃ kṛṣṇā* and so forth, there is no relation of general property and particular instance (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), but rather a contradiction between two properties conveyed by the words.
Regarding *nipuṇo rājñaḥ*: when a correct word (*sādhuśabda*) is employed, the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs even in the absence of honor (*arcā*).
It is indeed so, according to the Vārttika: "And [the suffix *ka* is added] when used with a word signifying either good or bad.

Regarding *prasita*: Amara states that *tatpara*, *prasita*, and *āsakta* are synonyms. Regarding *mūlena*: by the rule "time conjoined with a lunar mansion," the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule "elision when no distinction is intended," there is elision (*lup*) of that suffix.

"By way of alternative [explanations]" (paryāyeṇa): the word *īśvara* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). One explanation is that it refers to the lordship (*īśvaratva*) of a master (*svāmin*). Here, "of whom" (*yasya*) points to the master. Another explanation is that it refers to the one who is called the lord of a possession (*sva*). Thus, due to these different modes of explanation, it is said "by way of alternative."
The case ending (*vibhakti*). And that [ending] follows from the qualifier, just as in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*); such is the sense.
Thus ends the seventh [section].
Thus ends the section on *kāraka* (case-relations) in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita. *The Prauḍhamanoramā*.
Prakriyākaumudī: Maṅgalācaraṇa—
Meditating again and again upon the Supreme Brahman, and repeatedly recollecting the words of my guru,
we compose this *Prakriyākaumudī* commentary titled *Prauḍhamanoramā*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*, *Imāḥsūtrāṇi*:

*ha ya va ra ṭ*. The instruction of the letter *ha* is for the purpose of including *ha* in the rules concerning *aṭ*, *ś*, and *ṣi*. [For example,] in *arheṇa*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "*aḍ-ḷ-v-ay-e'pi*". [And in] *devā hasanti*.
The substitution of *u* [for the vowel *i*] occurs by the rule "haśi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.114). Thus, we have *lilihidhve* and *lilihidhve*;
the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* occurs by the rule "vibhāṣeṭaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.79).
*Pradīpa-mañjūṣā on Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.2:

haL.* This sūtra is for the purpose of including the letter *h* among the *val*, *jhal*, and *śal* [classes]. [Examples are: *rudihi*, *svapihi*; [and] by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76), the suffixes beginning with *val* [are characterized as having the *ṅit* marker].
*iṭ*: having become affectionate (*snehitvā*, *snehitvā*); here there is optionally the status of being *kit* by the rule "ralo vyupadhāt" (Pāṇini 1.2.26).
*adāgdhām*: here there is the elision of the *sakāra* by the rule "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26).
*alikṣat*: here there is the suffix *ksa* by the rule "śala igupadhāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.45).
*Prakriyākaumudī*, *Iṇpāda*, Sūtra 1.3.3:

*halantyam*. Regarding the term "final" (*antya*) in the sūtra: the analysis is *hali antyam* (the final [element] before a *hal*). The intention is that this is either a compound formed by the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), based on the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "in the locative" (*saptamī*), or it is a locative absolute construction.
Alternatively, this may be a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.

It might be argued that let there be one of the options—tantra, repetition (*āvṛtti*), or single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*)—for the single-remainder [compound] *hal* [in Pāṇini's rule]. And it will be explained as *ha-l*, where the genitive case signifies proximity (*sāmīpya*). Or rather, let there be no tantra and so forth; let it be a collective *dvandva* compound: *hal*.

And as for the [interpretation] "ca l ca"—if it is argued that the *l* of the *lakāra* is elided by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, do not say so; for in the first case, the compound would be strained (*kliṣṭa*). Indeed, in examples such as "brāhmaṇakambala," a blanket belonging to someone other than the one near the Brāhmaṇa is not understood, nor is it [the case here].

From the word *citragu*, a tree or similar object situated near the cows that possess the variegated color is understood. For this very reason, it is clearly stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that there is no compound formation with words such as *anantara* (immediate), because they are not conventionally expressed in that way. Furthermore, to say much more:
even the analytical usage (*vyasta-prayoga*)—such as "the blanket of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇasya kambalaḥ*) or "his cows are variegated" (*citā gāvo 'sya*)—is undesired in those cases.
In the second case as well, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is difficult to achieve, because of the initiation of the prohibition regarding *yaṇ* sounds.
Even in the view that rejects that [prohibition], [the rule] follows from "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26).

Furthermore, because the elision (*lopa*) of *jhal* is prescribed by extracting the mention of *jhal* [from this sūtra], and because the understanding of the meaning of a sentence is impossible without the understanding of the meaning of its constituent words, it follows that the meaning of this sūtra cannot be understood prior to the establishment of the *hal-pratyāhāra*. Therefore, this effort is made to resolve that difficulty. And at this stage, since the meaning of the word *hal* is not yet established...
A copulative compound (*dvandva*) is indeed impossible because there can be no intention to express [the members] together; therefore, what has been stated above alone is logical. (Prau.ma. i.1.71)

Regarding the phrase "of those situated in the middle": by means of the two constituent parts—the initial and the final—the whole collection is implied. Since it is impossible to apply that [name] to the whole simultaneously in the object to be designated (*lakṣya*), the name, descending upon its constituents, comes to rest upon those situated in the middle, and not upon the initial and final ones, because those two are included within the very form of the name itself.

The sense is: "because of the determination of being for the sake of another. Regarding the phrase "and its own," this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*).
And "its own form" is understood as belonging only to the first [word], not to any other;
for the third case ending in *antena* indicates a subordinate status. This is because pronouns, by general rule, [refer to the nearest antecedent].
Because it refers to the primary [object].
(Prau.ma.i.1.3.2) "The first utterance"— this is so even though, by the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) "that by which something is taught," it is taught [as a means].

Although it is explained in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other works that "śāstra" means "instruction" (*upadeśa*), that is nevertheless merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is because the suffix *ghañ* is difficult to obtain in this sense, as it is superseded by *lyuṭ*.
Nor can it be *gh*, because it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñātva*), according to the interpretation that [the rule for *ghañ*] generally applies only to technical names (*saṃjñā*).

Because it is afflicted (*kliṣṭatvāt*); and because of the disregard shown by the author of the Bhāṣya in such statements as "for a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) cannot itself be a limiting adjunct," and so forth. For this very reason, even the *ghañ* suffix [prescribed] by the rule *hal-śca* does not apply here. As for the term *bāhulaka*, it is a resort only when there is no other way out. For this same reason, [the word *prakṛti* is explained as] "those by which words are derived (*prakriyante*)."

The derivation based on the sense of instrument (*karaṇavyutpatti*) is also refuted; thus, the *Vārttika* states: "The suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *na* [supersede] *striyām*, while *khal* and *na* [supersede] *striyām* by way of prohibition. Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is only logical for the suffix to express the abstract state (*bhāva*).

As for what they recite beginning with "In the Dhātusūtra," and what they explain— "The status of being an *upadeśa* belongs to those [terms] mentioned in the first half [of the work] through the derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas for the *āgamas* and so forth, it is through the derivation based on the object (*karman*).
Since the *uṇādi* [sūtras], the *liṅga-anuśāsana*, and the *anuśāsana* are also established as *sūtras*, their separate mention [is made here]..."

[The objection continues: "By the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalivardanyāya*), since [the term *dhātu*] is already established as a class (*gaṇa*) by this very fact, [there is no need for a formal rule for] the verbal root (*dhātu*) as well," and so forth.
Here, this must be addressed: Is this a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for these [roots], or is it merely a grammatical connection (*yoga*)?
It cannot be the first, because the author of the treatise has not stated that this is a technical designation; and since it is not a technical designation, the suffix *gha* does not apply.

Furthermore, because of the statement in the Bhāṣya; and because if a technical designation (saṃjñā) created by ourselves were to establish the system of the treatise, it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For it is not the case that *ām*—from which the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) has been dropped—is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), such that it would lack the status of having *m* as its indicatory letter (*mitva*). Moreover, in this way, regarding the rule for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), [the use of] the ablative case...

If it were assumed that the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) functions as a determiner (*prakalpakatva*), one might suspect that the substitute *san* itself should be the designation; however, this would contradict what was stated by the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, namely that because there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) would not apply. Furthermore, [the question arises]: "What is the purpose of mentioning 'root' (*dhātu*)? [Consider] *lūñ*..."

This would contradict the *Bhāṣya* which states, "lavitā, pūñ, pavitā," as well as Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which intends to show that the designation of a verbal root (*dhātusaṃjñā*) occurs only after the elision of the suffix has been performed. Furthermore,
in the rule "ghvasoreddhau" (Pāṇini 6.4.119), the term "lopaśca" contains two *ś* sounds.

The explanation [of the rule] would contradict the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa, and other works on the *alontya* sūtra (*Pāṇini 1.1.52*), which state that the second *śakāra* is *it*. It cannot be the second [alternative], because if the *yoga* (the rule itself) alone were prioritized, the enumeration [of specific cases] would be redundant. Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency: that the *karaṇa* (instrumental) derivation applies to roots (*dhātu*) and so forth, but not to augments (*āgama*) and the like.
Furthermore, because [the definition] is difficult to establish;

and because of the contradiction with your own text, which states that the meaning is "the final consonant (*hal*) of a collection delimited by adventitious properties (*upādhi*) such as *dhātu-tva* (being a verbal root), which are the factors that motivate its status as an instruction (*upadeśatā-prayojaka*). In both views, [this applies to] the teaching on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*).

This is because it would be of no use in the present context, and because the letter *ś* is not included in the rule *lopaś ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.66); furthermore, it is universally accepted that in rules such as *ādeca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 6.1.45) and *upadeśe 'tvataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.62), the term *upadeśa* refers exclusively to the initial enunciation [of a word]. This is the general direction [of the argument].
Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|3|2:

*upadeśe 'janunāsika it*. Although, due to its being a prerequisite (*upajīvyatva*), it would have been more appropriate to state the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "nasalized" (*anunāsika*) first, nevertheless, by following the etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "that which follows the nose" (*nāsikām anugataḥ*), [the definition is established].

Since its purpose has already been explained, the sūtra defining the technical term *anunāsika* is of little utility; this is what is intended to be suggested by its not being cited here. [Question: What is the purpose of the word *upadeśe*? [Example: *ababhra āṅ apaḥ*. Although it might be argued that here, as in the case of the rule *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17), the nasalization does not occur due to the force of the specific prescription (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*), [the word *upadeśe* is necessary].

Nevertheless, the inclusion of the term *upadeśa* right here has been made for the sake of clarity, so that it must necessarily be understood as referring to the subsequent purpose. Why [is this necessary]? So that [the rule] does not apply to the *makāra* of *manin*. That which is promised (*pratijñāyate*) is a *pratijñā*.
[The suffix] *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.3.106, *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, it is a *pratijñā*.

The analysis of the compound is *ānunāsikyam yeṣām* ("those for whom there is nasality"). Thus, one need not resort to the strained interpretation that the word *pratijñā* (promise/undertaking) implies *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) with respect to what is understood through the undertaking of the rule; for this can be explained without *lakṣaṇā*, just as in expressions such as *pāṇinyupajñaṃ vyākaraṇam* ("grammar [is] known from Pāṇini").

The sense is that although the nasalized reading composed by the author of the Sūtras has now been lost, nevertheless, on the strength of the usage of the authors of the Vṛtti and others, it is inferred that it existed previously according to the requirements of the grammatical operation.
One might object: "Is it not the case that [the rule] *ralayoḥ* is deficient, since the letter *ṭa* is also situated between them?
To this he replies: "In the *pratyāhāras*. Regarding the word *vyavahriyante*: [it means] those in which the phonemes (*varṇas*) are *pratyāhriyante*—that is, they are abbreviated or condensed;
the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), according to the rule for irregular formations (*bāhulakāt*).

Although the mere application of etymological derivation (*yoga*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakta*) regarding the designations *akāra* and so forth, the intended meaning is that these are "conventional based on etymology" (*yogarūḍhi*).
The ancients maintain that there are forty-one *pratyāhāras*;
those formed by the *hal* and *it* sounds found in the fourteen aphorisms are employed throughout the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

The meaning of that [sūtra] is "forty-one. Therefore, they say that the term *su-p-t-i-ṅ-ādi* refers to the suffixes beginning with *su* and ending with *tiṅ*; that *ra-pratyāhāra* refers to the consonants from *r* to *ha*; and that the author of the Vārttika used the term *ña* in the rules "the second [consonants] are *ca*" and "among the roots *yam*, *ram*, and *man*, only one is desired as being without the augment *iṭ*.
However, this is a statement made in haste.

Because the first [rule] belongs to the *uṇādi* sūtras and the second is found in the *kārikās* of Vyāghrabhūti; let this matter rest for now. Furthermore, this restriction regarding the number [of suffixes] is not of much practical utility, and thus it has been disregarded.
Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|1|37:

*ūkālo 'c*. This is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), and "protracted" (*pluta*). The masculine gender is used according to the rules of the Sūtra. The phrase "*vāṃ kāla iva*" is a statement of the resultant meaning; however, the actual analysis (*vigraha*) is "*voḥ kālo*."
The word *yasya* is to be understood [as follows]: by the sound *ū*, its own time of utterance is indicated. Regarding *ādyai*:

according to the rule "particles have the acute accent on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.2), the vowel *ā* is acute; however, the word *yat* [is acute] by the Phiṭ-sūtras. As for *ṅ*: the vowel *a* is grave (*anudāta*).
(Prakriyākaumudī, Īpāda-sūtra 1.2.32):

*tasyāditaḥ* (of that, from the beginning). Regarding *atantram* (not intended as a restrictive rule), the meaning is that [the prefix] is not intended to be significant there, just like the prefix in the word *upeyivān*. But [one might object]: in that case, [the text reads] *īyivāṃsam atisridhaḥ*.

If you argue that non-intentionality [of the rule] may be accepted because of the observation of such usage elsewhere, then what is the proof for its non-intentionality here? To this, understand that the evidence consists in the observation of the actual linguistic forms (lakṣya) as well as the Prātiśākhya and other treatises.
For instance, in the word *yerāḥ*, the vowel *e* occurs; and in the word-pāṭha (*padapāṭha*) of *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpatim*.
It is well known among all the Bahvṛcas that [words] beginning with *ū* are *ardhodātta* (partially accented).

When the initial syllables of the two words *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati* are made *udātta* by the rule "In the case of *vanaspati* and others, both [members of the compound] are [accented] simultaneously" (*Pāṇini* 6.2.140), [the remaining syllables become] *anudātta*.
By the rule "padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), there is the suppression of the accent of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*).
Regarding the two preceding words *snū* and *śacī*, the Prātiśākhya states that the final syllable of each may optionally be circumflex (*svarita*).
"Or, as in *jātyavat*, the two [preceding sounds] remain as they were, with *tanū* and *śacī* in the case of the former two";
likewise, regarding the udātta nature of the half of a svarita, the Prātiśākhya also states:
