Nor should it be argued that the Sūtra should simply have been formulated as *bahu-c pūrvaḥ*; for [otherwise], in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, [the rule would not apply].

Because there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to [the suffix] being a *kṛt* affix. Nor can one find deliverance by claiming that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because without the formulation of the *arthavat-sūtra*, it is impossible for the mention of "compound" to function as a restriction. This is the general direction [of the argument].
Prau.ma.- *kṛtaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46):

"And [words ending in] *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* [are *prātipadika*]. The term *arthavat* ("meaningful") is understood from the previous rule; by virtue of its presence, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in those [suffixes]. For in the case of a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound, the *kṛt* suffixes [do not apply to the final member alone].

Furthermore, the meaning of *taddhita* suffixes does not exist [independently]; rather, it is obtained through the understanding of what previously occurred (*bhūtapūrvagati*), but that is not commendable.

Even in the case of the *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning) view, the meaning is not fully established by the suffix alone. With this in mind, he says: "Those ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes."

In cases such as *liṭ* and *dhuk*, since the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) [of suffixes] by the rule "that which is not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) would apply, this is a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Regarding the statement "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*): one should not suspect that, because the exclusion based on being "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayānta*) would otherwise apply, this is instead for the purpose of a positive injunction.

Because the word *vākya* does not end in an affix (*apratyayāntatvāt*), and because when an affix is mentioned, only that which begins with the element immediately preceding it is included. If it is argued: "But is it not the case that the restriction regarding 'beginning with that' (*tadādiniyama*) is prohibited in the case of feminine affixes? Therefore, let this [rule] apply for the sake of the injunction in examples such as *rājakumārīm*"?—it is not so.

Even though the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (and so forth) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it does not apply in the domain of *luk*-elision; therefore, the compound formation occurs only when the case-ending (*sup*) is actually heard. Furthermore, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies there because the item does not end in a suffix (*apratyayānta*), that designation remains easily available even after the elision of the case-ending by virtue of the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). For this very reason...

In examples such as *gomatpriya*, the augment *num* and others do not apply; however, they would indeed apply if the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) were to take effect prior to the elision (*luk*). If it is argued that even so, this rule must exist for the sake of prescribing [the application of suffixes] to meaningless compounds—such as *daśadāḍima* and the like, which are "compounds of the incapable" (*asamarthasamāsa*)—we say no, because it has already been stated that the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood as an underlying requirement (*anuvṛtti*).

If it is asked, "How then can this be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) within an incapable compound (*asamartha-samāsa*)?", understand that it is so by the very means of the evidence that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). For, by the rule "asūryalalāṭayoḥ," the suffix *khaś* is prescribed when the word *asūrya* is used as an *upapada*. And an *upapada* is a word uttered in proximity (*upa-uccārita*), and a word is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

He states the body of the restrictive rule (*niyama*)—beginning with "in which aggregate" (*yatra saṃghāte*) and so on. The phrase "the preceding portion" (*pūrvo bhāgaḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that the subsequent element is not a suffix (*pratyaya*). Otherwise, in cases such as *janmavān*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply, because the mention of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) [in the definition] is intended for forms like *aupagava*.

Because its purpose has already been fulfilled. Why is it stated that "the preceding portion is a *pada*"? So that the designation *prātipadika* may apply to that which is qualified by the suffix *bahuc*. By means of this, in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, when the first *jas* is elided, the word *bahupaṭu*—which bears the accent of a *cit* suffix—subsequently regains the *jas* ending, whereby the acute accent on the penultimate syllable (*upottama*) is established. Or else:

Let it be that the rule concerns a composite [form] that has not entered into the relationship of base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*). Nor should it be argued that, under the first alternative, in cases such as *rājapuruṣau*, the designation would apply to the portion *puruṣau* and so on;
for this is precluded precisely by the condition of being "meaning-bearing" (*arthavat*). For the meaning of the suffix connects only with the qualified [base], and not...
[Otherwise], the term *puruṣau* would have its meaningfulness [only] in the mere sense of the second member of the compound.

He states the result of the restriction with the words "by that," etc. But even so, in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, the designation of the sentence (*vākya*) would be unavoidable; for when there is the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix, it applies even to that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*.

If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the inclusion [of the term], it is not so; for the restriction established by the inclusion of the word "compound" (samāsa) prevails due to its higher status [in the order of rules].

And thus, in the sūtra *kṛttaddhita-*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of the term "kṛt" does not apply at all, as it would be fruitless—this is the truth. As for what they say—that the inclusion of the word "compound"...

It is not for the sake of restriction, but rather for the sake of an injunction. For "possessing meaning" (arthavattva) consists in having a function (vṛtti). And function is twofold: primary denotation (śakti) and indication (lakṣaṇā). Nor does that [function] exist in a compound (samāsa). To this, it must be said: according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), since the state of unified meaning (ekārthībhāva) is accepted, there is no such thing as a function [in a compound].
This is indeed refuted. Even in the Mīmāṃsā system, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) certainly exists.

As for what they say—"It is established that in every case the sentence-meaning is indeed indicated"—if this were stated according to the Naiyāyika method, that too would not hold, because [examples such as] "bahupaṭavaḥ" (many cloths) and so forth would remain unestablished.

If it is argued that the mention of *taddhita* refers to that which is qualified by it, [we reply: no, because this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pacatakī*. Furthermore, in this way, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*, over-extension in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam* would be unavoidable; let us leave that matter for now.

The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this, the statement “the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) should be prescribed for a meaningless particle” becomes redundant; this [present rule] is intended for those cases where even a suggested meaning (*dyotya*) does not exist. For example: *avadyati*. However, in the case of imitations (*anukaraṇa*), [the status of being a nominal stem is determined] by the original to be imitated (*anukārya*).

When there is no intention to express a distinction [between the base and the suffix], it does not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) precisely because it lacks meaning, just as in the case of *bhū* in the sense of "existence. However, when a distinction is intended to be expressed, it would indeed be a nominal stem, just as in the case of *bhuvaḥ* in the rule *bhuvo vuk*. [The phrase] "of that which is qualified by gender" [is used].
The meaning is: "even that which is qualified by a suffix indicating gender. The purpose of this *paribhāṣā* is as follows:

in the word *ayaskumbhī*, there is the substitution of *s* [for *t*] according to the rule "ataḥ kṛkami-". For that [substitution] is prescribed when words such as *kaṃsa* follow as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, from the root *kumāri*, one forms *kumārayati* in the sense "he describes a young girl," according to the rule "ṇāviṣṭavat".
There is elision of the *ṭi* [suffix]. Thus, in the example *yāminyantyahāni*, there is also the result of the suffix *kvap* in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*).

Regarding the rule *ṅyābhyāṃ prāk*: by this, the forms *lohinikā* and *āryakā* are established. For instance, because it is an affix denoting its own meaning (*svārthika*), the suffix *kan*—which is both internal (*antaraṅga*) and subsequent—by the rule *lohitānmaṇau*, [precedes] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
[If that were so, it] would subvert [the rule]; consequently, there would only be *lohitikā*. However, both forms are desired.
By virtue of the inclusion of the term *ṅīp*, two forms are established from the suffix *kan* added after a stem ending in *ṅī*:
because the rule "after a low-pitched vowel denoting a color... (*varṇādanudātāt...*) is optional. But from the word *ārya*, [it is not so]—“na... [etc.]
In the rule *sāmivacane*, the suffix *kan*— which will be taught as being used in an extremely literal sense (*atyantasvārthika*)—

does not apply prior [to the application of *āp*] due to the force of the inclusion of the term *āp*. Consequently, the optional substitution of *it* (shortening) by the rule *udīcāmātaḥ sthāne yata-pūrvāyāḥ* is established.

It might be argued: "If this were so, the form *bahugomatkā* would not be established, because the suffix *ṅīp*—conditioned by the presence of a vowel (*u*) or the *it*-marker *k*—would apply prior to the addition of the *kap* suffix. This is not so. For the *samāsānta* (compound-final) suffix is added as a constituent part of the final member (*uttarapada*) precisely within the non-worldly (*alaukika*) analytical statement (*prakriyāvākya*), while the compound itself has not yet been formed.

Because it will be stated [later] that "it proceeds" (*pravartate*). Regarding this, some hold that it occurs before the case-ending (*vibhakti*); however, according to the view that it occurs after, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since it ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the case-ending (*sup*) is elided (*luk*), and only then is the compound formed. Therefore, even due to the internal interruption by the *taddhita*, [the rule applies] prior to the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*.
It is established that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the sake of the application [of the rule].
As for what some say—that the mention of *āp* is for the sake of clarity—that is refuted by this very point.
In reality, however, let there be no mention of *ṅī* and *āp*; for the formation of secondary (*taddhita*) derivatives occurs from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The conclusion is as follows: it should be noted that the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* operate even before the case endings (*sup*), because it is accepted that the operations triggered by their own meanings and so forth occur in a sequential order.
Regarding the rule *suṅsyoh*: the letter *u* in *suḥ* is for the purpose of distinguishing it in the rule *arvaṇastrasau*.

For if [the rule] were stated simply as *asi*, the meaning would be "when *as* begins with the letter *a*" (*asakārādau*). And in that case, forms such as *vāja arvatsu paya usriyāsu* would not be established. The vowel *i* in *ṅsi* is for the purpose of ensuring that this [genitive ending] is not included in the rule *yuṣmadasmabhyāṃ ṅsoś*. However, if [the rule] were [stated] as *ekavacanasya ca*...

Since the term *pañcamyāḥ* (of the fifth case) is understood [from the previous rule], it is stated that by process of elimination, the genitive suffix *ṅsi* will be understood here; if so, this is for the purpose of [the rule] "*ṭāṅsiṅsām*".
As for the letters *ja* and *śa* in *jaś* and *śas*, they are for the purposes of [the rules] "*jasaḥ śī*" and "*tasmāc chaso naḥ*".

Thus, these two [suffixes] are for the purpose of distinguishing their respective domains. If it is argued that one of them may simply be without an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), we say no; for if the *jakāra* were absent from *jas*, there would be *āv* for *āṬ*. Consequently, the suffix would also be possible as ending in *v*. Similarly, if the *śakāra* were absent from *śas*, there would be the status of being a *ṅit* for *āṬṭ*.

It might be so suspected; therefore, for the sake of removing doubt, it is appropriate to include that [ṭ]. The letter ṭ in *auṭ* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra *suṭ*. The letter ṭ in *ṭā* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*ṭāṅsi*.
The letter ṅ in *ReĀ* and the following is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*gherṅiti*. As for the letter *p*, however—

The purpose is for the sake of brevity (*pratyāhāra*). And thus, even though all [the rules] are fruitful, the statement of the ancient authors that they are "for the sake of technical names" (*saṃjñārtha*) is indeed inconsistent. Even if one attempts to explain it by breaking down the compound as *saṃjñā* meaning "correct knowledge" and interpreting them as being "for the sake of that"—that is, for the sake of specification—it remains merely cumbersome; therefore, it has been disregarded.

He explains that from the sūtra *tiṅstrīṇitrīṇi* ("the *tiṅ*s [are divided] into three groups of three"), the phrase *trīṇitrīṇi* and the entire sūtra beginning with *tānyekavacana* ("those [are] the singular," etc. are carried over (*anuvartate*).
This he does by means of the passage beginning *supastrīṇitrīṇyetyādinā*. The word *ekaśaḥ* means "one by one" (*ekaikam*).

Regarding the rule *saṅkhyaikavacanācca*, the suffix *śas* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case when expressing repetition (*vīpsā*). As for what the ancients stated—that one should say *ekaikaśaḥ*—that is incorrect; because repetition is already expressed by the suffix *śas* itself, reduplication is inappropriate. According to the maxim *yenanāprāpte*, the suffix *śas* is an exception (*apavāda*) to reduplication.
This follows from the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for what they say—that both forms are correct because of the usage of the word *ekaikaśaḥ* in the commentary on the rule "sarvasya dve" (Pāṇini 8.1.1), and because of the author of the Sūtras' own designation *ekaśaḥ* in the rule "tāny eka... (Pāṇini 2.4.1)—that is not so.

That is not so, because the cited Bhāṣya has a different subject matter. For, having begun with the statement, "Where the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is not expressed by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), there is reduplication," the Bhāṣya provides the example, "He gives one by one" (*ekaikaśo dadāti*). And Kaiyaṭa’s commentary explains that there is also a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) in the sense of "a small amount."

Regarding the word *tasya*, when it is doubled for the sake of repetition (*vīpsā*), the suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule "from words meaning 'much' or 'few'... However, this meaning is not possible in the present context, so let us set that aside for now. As for *rāma*:

on the view that this is a proper name (*saṃjñā-śabda*) and is thus unanalyzable (*avyutpanna*), its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) is established by the rule "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat-sūtra*).

The distinction is this: under the governing rule "karaṇādhikaraṇayośca," the suffix *ghañ* is applied as an exception to the suffix *ap* by the rule "halaśca" to derive the form *rāmaṇa* through the analysis "they delight in this" (*ramante 'smin*); however, the suffix is applied by the rule "kṛttaddhita-samāsāśca."

Prau.ma.: *Sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). Regarding the phrase "those which [occur] in a single case-ending": the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for homogeneity (*sārūpya*), but it is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Thus...
Furthermore, because it is not occasioned by a specific cause (*anaimittika*), the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is internal and operates even prior to the generation of the case-endings (*sub*).
If this were not commenced, then a case-ending would apply to each [word] individually, and a *dvandva* compound would also occur.
However, once the *ekaśeṣa* has been commenced, since there is an absence of multiple *sub*-ending words, the *dvandva* simply does not apply.

The sense is that [the word] becomes *phalitā* (fruit-bearing). "Only those that are similar in form"—this is obtained by the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the particle *eva* from the subsequent sūtra. Therefore, there is no single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for the two words *mātṛ*, one denoting a biological mother and the other denoting a measurer.

In cases such as *mātṛbhyām*, although there is similarity (*sārūpya*), there is dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) in forms like *āṬ* and *jas*. "Only one" [is used]—this applies only when there is a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*); that is to say, within the scope of the *itaretarayoga* dvandva compound. For where multiple meanings are combined and then connected with another word, it is of that nature.
The scope [of this rule] is understood from the indicator (liṅga) in the sūtra "idito num dhātoḥ" and also from logical reasoning (nyāya). To explain:
once it is established that "that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided," [the meaning] presented by the single word being heard [is understood].

Everything ought to be construed in a uniform manner without distinction. Alternatively, one should explain it by carrying over the term "in a dvandva compound" from the preceding sūtra, such that [the rule applies] when a dvandva is about to be formed.
It might be argued: let the meaning be "when a dvandva has been formed. This is not so, as in the case of *panthānau*.

In cases such as *pathānaḥ*, there would be the unwanted application of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*); in cases such as *karau* and *karāḥ*, there would be the unwanted application of singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*); and in cases such as *sarve* and *sarveṣām*, there would be the unwanted application of both the rules "in a dvandva compound" (*dvandve ca*) and "optionally before the [plural] case-ending *jas*" (*vibhāṣā jasi*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. As for what was stated by the ancients—namely, *rāma-rāma-au*— [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

It has been stated that [the rule applies] when [two words] stand together and when followed by a single case-ending. In this regard, the possibility of such a statement is as follows: in the expression *rāma rāma*, the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) belongs not only to the individual members but also to the aggregate, because the aggregate possesses meaning through their combination. Nor does the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) [in the definition of *prātipadika*] preclude this, even though [the aggregate] possesses meaning.

It should not be argued that this is not so because [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). For it has been stated that the restriction applies to those cases where the preceding portion of a composite form is a *pada*; furthermore, in accordance with forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*, it is appropriate that the restriction concerns members of the same class (*sajātīya*). Thus, by the principle of "doubling a single vowel" (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*),...

The dual and other case endings arise from the compound stem (*samudāya-prātipadika*) itself; for even by that much, it is possible to support the application of number to the meanings of the individual members through their connection with that number. If it is objected: "In that case, would not case endings also arise from the collective whole—even without a *dvandva* compound—in instances such as 'Rāma-Kṛṣṇau'?"—it is not so.

The direction is this: because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "in the formation of a *dvandva*, [there is] more than one inflected word," the maxim regarding the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvivacana-nyāya*) is set aside. One might ask: even though such an explanation is possible, for what reason was the alternative view—that [the *dvandva* suffix] follows the case-ending of the whole aggregate—rejected? Listen: in that view...

In cases such as *mātṛmātarau*, there would also have to be a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) [of the two words]. Now, if it is argued that one should explain the rule by repeating the phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) and drawing forward the word "only" (*eva*), so that it means "those which have the same form when they are in a single case-ending," we say no; for there is no evidence for such a repetition. Furthermore, if the case-ending were a qualifier of the single-remainder...

And because there would be no purpose [for the rule]. Nor can the exclusion of cases such as "milk digests milk" be the result, since the requirement of "intended co-reference" (*sahavivakṣā*) is indispensable; otherwise, in the case of "he carries milk [to the cow]," there would be the undesirable consequence of applying *ekaśeṣa* to both the primary and secondary objects. Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "God of gods."

On the contrary, if both [words] were to function as qualifiers through recurrence (*āvṛtti*), the formation of *bhaikṣam*— meaning "a collection of alms"— would not be established. For instance, when the sequence *bhikṣā bhikṣā bhikṣā ām a* is reached,
the elision (*luk*) would apply according to the rule "an external operation supersedes even internal operations."

Because of the absence of being followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), there would be no *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder formation). This is because, when [the suffix] is elided, there is an absence of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, in forms such as *rāmāu*, since the substitution of *vṛddhi* by the rule "vṛddhireci" applies first—due to its higher status and its obligatory nature—the single-remainder formation would not occur because of the absence of being followed by a case-ending once that partial change has been made. On both counts...
The point is that in the case of taking recourse [to this view], there is an absence of the treatment as being "like the end" (antavadbhāva) or "like the beginning" (ādivadbhāva).

As for the alternative view proposed by the ancient commentator—that there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) of words accompanied by their case-endings—that is not correct; for even if the disappearing forms were to cease together with their case-endings, [the rule would still apply] to the one remaining.
Because it would follow that there is only the hearing of the singular number.

Now, if it were argued that in the case of expressing multiple substrates simultaneously (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatā*), there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for words ending in dual or plural suffixes— and that the copulative compound (*dvandva*) is also like this— then it is as follows:

In a *ajahatsvārthā* operation, each individual [word] denotes multiple meanings due to their mutual co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*). Thus, in the non-ordinary (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) for a *dvandva* or *ekaśeṣa* compound,
only the dual and plural case-endings are introduced.
The position that there is *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of words ending in case-suffixes is indeed unassailable. However, even that is not so;

for it is incompatible with the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) theory of word-formation (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, even under the alternative view (*ajahatsvārthā*), it is impossible to abandon the singular number that was applied first. Otherwise, [the following would occur]:

[Otherwise], there would be the undesirable consequence of [the compound] being a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* or the like; for even in that case, since the prior member is subsumed into the meaning of the subsequent member, it could not be joined with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. And thus says the Bhāṣya: "This simultaneous expression of the substratum (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacanatā*) is both difficult and hard to justify."

As for what they have explained— that under the view that [the word denotes] the individual (vyaktipakṣa), since the application of each respective word would apply to every individual, this sūtra is intended so that there may be the application of only one; whereas under the view that it denotes the form (ākṛtipakṣa),
it is useless because a single [word] already conveys many individuals which are inseparable from the form— this is not correct.

Even on the view that [the word] refers to an individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), in the case of the rule "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" (*na brāhmaṇaṃ hanyāt*), it is easily explained through *tantra* (simultaneous application) that the single word "Brāhmaṇa" denotes many individuals. Otherwise, even on the view that it refers to a genus (*jātipakṣa*), the sūtra would have to be formulated in accordance with various meanings, such as "in that [place], by dwelling and by being well-restrained," and so forth.

Because [the meaning] cannot be established otherwise; therefore, although the application [of the rule] can be managed through *tantra* (simultaneous repetition) in both the view that [the word denotes] the genus (*jāti*) and the view that it denotes the individual (*vyakti*), there is no restrictive factor to ensure that it must always be understood through *tantra* alone. Consequently, without the Sūtra, an optional *dvandva* (copulative compound) would be unavoidable, as in the case of "this pot" (*ghaṭo 'yam*).

Because we observe the use of various words such as "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam*), likewise, the formation of the copulative compound *ghaṭaghaṭau* is established by logical rule. Nor does it follow that *ghaṭakalaśau* would also form a copulative compound;
for there is the Vārttika: "Even for those that have different forms, provided they have the same meaning. [In this context,] *rūpyate* means "is cognized."

Thus, by relying on the fact that the word *rūpa* denotes the meaning through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), and because the meaning of the *Vārttika* is also encompassed by the *Sūtra* itself,
[the author]—
in order to prevent undesirable optional results such as *ghaṭa-ghaṭau* or *ghaṭa-kalaśau*— proceeds in both cases.
It should be understood that the Sūtra is indispensable.

This being the case, those who have explained this [Sūtra]—saying such things as "by this, the formation of a single remainder (ekaśeṣa) is not prescribed"—have kept the very futility of the Sūtra in mind. Furthermore, regarding that which [arises] from the whole...
Having rejected the position that [the rule] applies when there is a case-ending (*vibhakti*), they state again: "when *rāma rāma āṬ* is situated.

This is a non-standard (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) that is inferred, but not a standard (*laukika*) one. And in a non-standard context, operations such as the replacement of case-endings (*vibhaktyekādeśa*) do not take effect.

"Because [grammar] provides explanations only for those forms that are actually used," and so forth—all of this contradicts both the context and reason. For it is precisely in order to explain those forms that are actually used that the *alaukika* (non-actualized/intermediate) form is postulated; and all grammatical operations apply only to these *alaukika* forms, not to the fully established (*pariniṣṭhita*) form.

For, without the application of rules such as "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ," the final established form cannot be obtained; moreover, it is difficult to justify the application of those rules once the form has already been finalized. Let this matter rest for now.
*Prau.ma.*: *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107). Regarding *ami aci*: it means "in that vowel (*ac*) which is part of *am*"; that is to say, in the vowel that constitutes a portion of *am*.
Consequently, there is no single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* for [the vowel] together with the letter *m*. Thus...
In cases such as *akṣādūhinyām* and so forth, it should be understood that the rule applies as "in the case of that *ac* which is in *ūhinī*," and so on;

for there is no dispute regarding the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *ac* from the rule *iko yaṇ aci*. Furthermore, the grammatical indications (*liṅga*) found in rules such as *padāsvairibāhyā-* serve as evidence here.

Prau.ma.: *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.1.28). Regarding the phrase *tasmāc chasaḥ*: by the word *tat*, the preceding long vowel of homogeneous quality (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is referred to as the proximate element.
The term *śasaḥ* is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and that part [of the word] follows [the aforementioned vowel].

It is specified [in the rule] as "belonging to the *śas* that follows a long vowel resulting from the substitution of a homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*)": this is what he says—"the *sakāra* which is subsequent to the *śas*. However, it is not stated as "the *śas* which is subsequent," because such a thing is impossible; for once the substitution of a homogeneous vowel has taken place, a subsequent *śas* cannot exist.

Prau.ma.: *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2). Regarding *aṭkupvāṅ*: since the rule *raṣābhyām* (8.4.1) employs a fifth-case (*pañcamī*) designation, this present rule is stated because [the application of the preceding rule] would otherwise not apply when there is an intervention. Here, an intervention by all [of these] together is impossible; rather, it refers to an intervention by each one individually.
There is no [need for a separate] purpose. This is because of the force of the inclusion of the word *kṣubhna* among the *kṣubhnādi* group, and because of the mention in rules such as "sarūpāṇām.
With this in mind, he says: "by individual [words], as far as possible, and by their combination.
But if this were so, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *ādarśena*. Nor can it be said that [the rule applies] only with *aṭ* and the like.
The rule [of non-application] applies when there is an intervention. Since it has been stated that this is an injunction (*vidhi*) where [the rule] was not previously established, it is true;
however, a division of the *yoga* (sūtra-split) should be understood here: "even when there is an intervention" (*vyavāye 'pi*) is one *yoga* for the purpose of an injunction;
"after *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, or *num*" (*aṭkupvāṅnum*) is another for the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*). The elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *bhis* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The phrase "in order to invalidate the prohibition" means that, by this [rule], the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *paryāṇaddham*—according to the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*—is established; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the mention of *num*:
it is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both the *anusvāra* in place of *num* and for the natural *anusvāra*. By this, [the rule applies] even in the case of the root *bṛh* (meaning "to grow").

After [a root] ending in *id*, there is *num*. For that [root], there is *anusvāra*. In the case of *tṛṃhū* in the sense of "injury," the *anusvāra* here is inherent. [Examples are] *bṛṃhaṇam* and *tṛṃhaṇam*; in both cases, the substitution of *ṇ* is established. In *ivi* in the sense of "pleasing," [we have] *prenvanam*. Here, [the rule] "after a *kṛt* suffix ending in a vowel or *c*" and "[after a root] beginning with *i* or *ā* that has *num*" [apply].

Thus, there is no substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]. For example, in the injunction, "Having seen a star, one should release speech," the sight of a star serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a specific time; therefore, even if stars are seen during the day, speech is not released, because the specific time indicated by that sign is absent. At night, however...
Even when the asterism is not visible, [the offering] is released because it exists [as a concept]; so too should it be understood here.

But if this is so, the mention of *num* is redundant, since the *anusvāra* is already included by virtue of being an *aṭ*. For in cases such as *uraḥ keṇa*, where there is an intervention by the jihvāmūlīya or other sounds resulting from the visarga, this same principle applies.

If this is true, he says: "And that... This might be so: according to the reasoning stated, the mention of *num* in the rule "anum-visarjanīya" (Pāṇini 8.3.58) should also be abandoned, because there too the *anusvāra* is what is to be indicated, as otherwise it would be impossible; for at the time when the substitution of *ṣ* is about to take effect...

In forms such as *sapaṣi*, the augment *num* is obtained because the substitution of *ṣ* (by Pāṇini 8.3.59) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the *anusvāra* occurs prior to that substitution. Although this is indeed possible in the case of *suhinsu*, nevertheless,
in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that very instance, [the rule applies] to the *anusvāra* that replaces *num*, in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).

If it is argued that a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must indeed be resorted to based on the explanation [of the rule], because the substitution of *ṣ* is established when there is an intervention by that [num] due to its being a *śat* [suffix], we say: not so. For even if the inclusion of the visarga in that context can be rejected according to the method already stated, the mention of *num* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

For instance, if *ṣatva* were to occur when there is an intervention by an *anusvāra*, it would then be restricted only to that which stands in the place of *num*; consequently, it would not occur in forms such as *puṃsu*. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Pariśiṣṭa-prakāśa: That from which a suffix is prescribed, beginning with that, is the *aṅga* (base) with respect to that suffix (Pāṇini 1.4.13).

Regarding the rule "yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ," the ancient commentators have stated: "from whatever [stem], whether a verbal root (dhātu) or a nominal stem (prātipadika). This is not correct, because even forms ending in *tiṅ* (finite verbs) and so forth serve as bases (*aṅga*) for suffixes such as *tarap*. Furthermore, there is no basis for such a restriction; this is evident in examples such as *āmuṣyāyaṇa*.

Furthermore, it would result in the absence of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*); for this secondary suffix (*taddhita*) does not follow from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather from that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Prau.ma.: *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9). Regarding the rule *ato bhisa ais*: one might ask, "Let it simply be *is*. But is it not the case that the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule *ato guṇe* would apply? No, because that would render the pronunciation of the vowel *e* redundant; otherwise, [the author] would have prescribed *is* alone.

If it is argued that [the rule] should be formulated as *vidadhyāt*? True; however, because there is no difference between *e* and *ai* in terms of having two morae (*dvimātra*), and thus no additional weight (*gaurava*) is incurred, *ai* has been employed. In this way, there is no suspicion whatsoever of a subsequent form (*pararūpa*), which results in great parsimony (*lāghava*). As for what they say—that the formation of *ai* is for the sake of hearing the sound *ai* in the word *nirjarasaiḥ*—[that is incorrect].

That contradicts the Bhāṣya; for, according to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*, the substitution of *jaras* would result [in an undesirable form], and thus the Bhāṣya establishes as its final conclusion that the form is simply *nirjaraiḥ*. (Prau.ma., nāmi, Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.3)

Regarding the phrase "nāmi": this is because it would contradict the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) [that *nām* refers to *nāma*]. This is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rules "śnam after *rudh*-class roots" and "elision of *n* after *śna*".
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the power of its formulation": the rule "and before a *sup* suffix" lacks such power.

The intention is that [the rule] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* has scope in cases such as *rāmābhyām*. Thus, the claim made by some—that the citation of the rule *nāmi* in the word *rāma* is due to a scribal error—is to be considered doubtful.
Prakriyā-kaumudī: *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59).

Regarding the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*: with the intention that even a single genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is divided according to the difference in its scope, he explains it as "the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the constituent of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). However, if the "constituent of a substitute" were taken [as the meaning], then there would be a fault in cases such as *tisṛṇām*. And if [the rule] meant "the *s* which is an affix," then...

In cases such as *rāmeṣu*, [the rule] would not apply. Even though, due to this lack of uniformity in the explanation, a *dvandva* compound is not justified because there is no intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), it must nevertheless be understood as being formed on the authority of Pāṇini’s sūtra (*sautratvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which has been opened up and is non-voiced" (*vivṛtāghoṣasya*): as for what they say regarding the letter *s*.

"The closest internal [substitute] for a voiceless aspirated [consonant] is the palatal *ṣ* itself"—this is insufficient, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the letter *ṭh*. Thus, the Prātiśākhya states:
"In each class (*varga*), the first two are voiceless; the pair [the second and third] are aspirated (*soṣman*); the other is nasal."

If it is argued: "But surely, in examples such as *dadhi-secaḥ*, the Bhāṣya states that the compound *padādādiḥ padādiḥ*—an ablative compound meaning 'the beginning of a word after [a word ending in] a case-suffix'—is employed to prevent the application of *ṣatva* before the formation of the case-suffixes; therefore, here too, the prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would apply? Do not say so, for [the rule applies] only in the context of *svādiṣu*.

The prohibition stated [in Pāṇini 8.3.11] does not apply based on that which is designated as a "word" (*pada*), because this is made known by the inclusion of the word *ati* [in the rule]. As for what some say—that it is made known that this prohibition does not apply in the domain of suffixes—that is not correct, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of *ṣatva* in forms such as *vyatise*. Now, regarding the view that [the designation *pada* applies] to the beginning of a word...

In the case of *ṭhvyatise*, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) would be unavoidable. Nor should it be suspected that *se* also possesses the status of a word (*padatva*) because it is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). This is because, when there is a mention of an affix (*pratyaya*), only that which begins with the element from which that affix is prescribed is understood; otherwise, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *rāmeṣu*.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of prohibiting the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, we reply: True. We do not claim that the designation of "ending in that" (*tadanta*) applies to the suffix alone; rather, we extend the technical term "word" (*pada*), which applies to the entire aggregate of stem and suffix, to the suffix even when the stem has been elided, by means of the maxim regarding partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*).

For even in cases such as *rāmau* and *rāmāḥ*, the status of being a word (*padatva*) occurs precisely by the maxim of "modification of one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), because the designation of "word" applies prior to the occurrence of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). However, once the single-substitute has been applied, there is no application of the rule "that which ends in a sup or tiṅ is a word. This is according to the principle: "When both sides are relied upon, [the resulting form] is neither like the end nor like the beginning."
From the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for what they say— that in the presence of a *prakṛti*, the suffix lacks the status of being a word (*padatva*) because of indications such as "in mantras" and "of all"— that is weak, because [the status of being a word] would be absent according to the reasoning already stated.
Because it is impossible to indicate [a meaning] when [the status of being a *sarvanāman*] is already established by logic, and because it would be useless;
[as stated in] *Prauḍhamanoramā*: "The words beginning with *sarva* are *sarvanāman*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.27). The term "beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādīni*) is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi].

It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, as indicated by the rule "hali sarveṣām. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of a *dvandva*": it will be stated that this prohibition applies to the whole aggregate (*samudāya*), and not to its individual parts (*avayava*). The point is that, without the application of the rule for designating what ends in such a suffix (*tadantavidhi*), there would be no possibility of the technical name applying to the aggregate. Now, what is the purpose of this designation for what ends in [the suffix]?
The result [of the rule] is not that *smāy* and so on apply to "paramasarva" and the like;

for under the heading governing the *aṅga*, those forms are established by the very principle of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that). Therefore, he says: "by that. Nor does this case also involve the application of the term "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), because the word "sarvanāma" (pronoun) is a qualifier of that [stem].

It should be stated that the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application to what ends with that) applies here, because of the statement: "There is a prohibition regarding the formation of compounds and secondary suffixes.
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the word *akac*: by virtue of the particle *ca* ("and"), the suffix *tasil* occurs in the case of *paramasarvataḥ*.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17)].

Regarding the rule *jasaḥ śī*: the intention is that [the substitution is applied] because it consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*), and not because it is marked with the *ś* indicatory letter (*śit*).

Regarding the phrase *avarṇāntāt*: the meaning is "from a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a*. Therefore, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yeṣām*, *keṣām*, and *teṣām*. [The expression] *sarvanāmno vihitasyāmaḥ* means "of the *ām* prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). *Sarvanāmnaḥ*...
However, the word *parasya* (of the subsequent) was not stated [in the rule], because otherwise *suṭ* would undesirably apply in cases such as *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.

For the prohibition by the rule *dvandve ca* applies to the whole compound (*samudāya*) and not to its individual parts (*avayava*). Furthermore, this *ām* is not brought forth from that [part], but rather from the whole compound itself; thus, there is no *suṭ*.
The authority for resorting to the qualification of the prior member (*vihitaviśeṣaṇatva*) is indeed the usage in the Bhāṣya itself: *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.
Regarding *pañcatriṃśat*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "five and thirty"; that is, thirty with five added to it.

Or rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding the statement made by those explaining the ancient text of the Easterners—that there are forty *pratyāhāra*s including *erac*—it was said: "This is not a *tatpuruṣa* with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī*); for if that were the case, [the rule] *rājanyabahuvacanadvandvendhakavṛṣṇiṣu* and the rule prescribing *saṃkhyā* would apply."
The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would not apply. Therefore, this is indeed a collective dvandva compound.

As for the neuter gender in cases such as *ekaviṃśati*, it does not occur because gender is dependent on worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāl liṅgasya*). This, however, is questionable, since there is a difference in accent depending on the specific type of compound.

Because this is the desired conclusion. Thus, while explaining the Vārttika on the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye*—"there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the term ‘numeral’ for the sake of *tatpuruṣa* compounds such as *nistriṃśa*, because elsewhere there is the elision of the additional member"—the author of the Bhāṣya says: "one additional... (*ekādhikā*).
"Twenty-one" (*ekaviṃśati*) [is formed from] twenty (*viṃśati*), [and] "twenty-two" (*dvāviṃśati*).

"For this very reason" means that it is logical for the dual number to apply only to the two [words *viṃśati* and *ekaviṃśati*]. [Objection: If this were so, the inclusion [of these words] among the *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) would be useless, since the pronominal operations such as *smāy* and so forth [would not apply].

Because [the form] does not exist in the dual number; nor is it correct to argue that the result [of the rule] is the optional third case (tṛtīyā) in the example *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām ubhayor hetvoḥ* by means of the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*, since the Vārttika states:
"In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all [case endings] are generally observed."

Because the meaning has already been conveyed. Nor should it be argued that this *vārttika* depends upon the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*), on the grounds that the author of the *Vṛtti* read it under the rule "sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca";
for it is read in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule "hetau". Precisely for this reason, [we see examples such as]: "He dwells because of food" (*annena kāraṇena vasati*).

Anticipating the objection that Haradatta has cited "annasya kāraṇasya" as an example, [the author] says: "But its reading here is... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "due to the contingency of *ayac*": this is the intended meaning—the rule "ubhādudāto nityam" is divided into two separate rules: "ubhādudātaḥ" and "nityam. The former [applies to the word] "ubha" when it denotes a number through its function as a part-whole (*avayava-vṛtti*).
The suffix *ayac* shall occur after the word *ubha* in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). For example: *ubhayoḥ maṇiḥ* (a jewel belonging to both). Then [the rule] "always" (*nityam*):
in the scope of a compound (*vṛtti*), the suffix *ayac* shall always occur after the word *ubha* in its own sense (*svārtha*).
Therefore, just as *ayac* is necessarily applied in such cases as *ubhayapakṣavinītanidrāḥ* (those whose sleep has been dispelled on both sides), so too [it applies here].

[The opponent argues: "It would also occur when the suffix *kap* is applied. [The author replies: "If you say that even when *akac* is applied, *ayac* is unavoidable, do not say so. For this is explained as applying only where the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is not heard, since the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of achieving the desired result and because of the mention in the rule 'both [are substituted] for the root with its reduplication' (*ubhau sābhyāsasya*)."

And so says the Vārttika: "The absence of [the dual ending] is because it is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix ṭāp. For when the *akac* suffix is present, the status of the word *ubhaya* as being within the domain of the dual is not obstructed by the maxim "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing"; however, when the *kap* suffix is present, it is indeed obstructed.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said thus": the words "by the author of the Vārttika" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Although the suffix *ṭāp* was also mentioned in the preceding Vārttika, it is not intended here; for Kaiyaṭa and others have explained that even the applicability of *ṭāp* should be understood only when followed by a dual ending. With this intention, he explains [the passage].

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of being followed by a dual ending": the intention is that because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ṭā* and *āp* is also included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*), it is indeed followed by a dual ending. Although in cases such as *ubhau*, being followed by a dual ending is difficult to establish—since the status of being like the end or the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*) is absent when there is reliance on both sides—[the rule still applies].

Nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that the rule "ayaC" applies elsewhere than where the dual number produced from the word *ubha* has been elided by *luk*. Even though, according to the Bhāṣya, the suffix *kap* is also considered *svārthika* (having its own inherent meaning), [the suffix] following the word *ubha*...

The reading of the word *ubha* has been rejected on the grounds that it possesses the status of a dual number; nevertheless, that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because here it is appropriate to accept only the technical (*kṛtrima*) dual number. Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasakta*) to suffixes such as *tratasil* and others. Now, [one might object]:

If it is argued that the suffixes *tra* and *til*, prescribed after a case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*), do not denote anything more than duality even when they are used in their own sense (*svārthika*), this is not so; for the suffix *kap* also conveys the meaning of being unknown (*ajñāta*), and furthermore, in the view that there are five suffixes (*pañcaka-pakṣa*), it necessarily conveys an additional meaning. This is the general direction [of the argument].

"It does not exist. The meaning is that it is not so expressed. And thus, since the word *ubhaya* lacks a dual ending and is not a term for all case-terminations (*asarvavibhaktika*), it would follow that it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
However, regarding the rule *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, there is the principle: "The inclusion of kṛt and taddhita derivatives occurs only when they are explicitly listed [in the gaṇapāṭha]."

Thus the commentary was introduced by Kaiyaṭa. The meaning is that since the rule [Pāṇini 5.3.94] has already served its purpose by excluding forms such as *pacatikalpam* and *pacatirūpam*, there is no evidence for the non-occurrence [of the suffix] in these cases. The phrase "ending in a *tayap* suffix" refers to the word *ubhaya*.
"Always [so]" (*nityaiva*). However, the statement "the higher, the lower, and both are enemies" (*pare 'vara ubhayā amitrāḥ*) should be understood as being due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*).
"Underived" (*avyutpannau*): this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Paspaśā* section.
"Some"—namely, the authors of the *Kāśikā*. Regarding the udātta vowel in "I consider this to be the essence" (*etattvaṃ manye*), [it is explained by] "seeing this repeatedly" (*etattvaḥ paśyan*).

The meaning is that this is because an unaccented [vowel] is also observed [in such cases]. "Ekaḥ" means the first. Even if the state of ending in "-tām" is not clear in the *saṃhitā* recitation, the word ending in "-tām" must be separated; otherwise, one would recite it only once with a single tone (*ekaśruti*). Nor should one object on the grounds of the rule: "In *tvat*, *tvasma*, *sim*, and *eti*, the vowels are unaccented."
This is according to the *Phiṭ-sūtras*. Likewise, there is a Ṛgvedic mantra: "starīru tvadbhavati sūta u tvam" (She becomes barren, but you are a father).

The commentators on the Vedas have explained it thus: this word *tvat*, listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāma*), is unaccented and is a synonym for "another" (*anya*). Jayadeva also employed it [in this sense]:

Regarding the phrase "drinking the honey-sweet nectar of your lower lip": the analysis of the compound is *tvataḥ anyasyāḥ adharaḥ* (the lower lip of another woman than you), and not *tava adharaḥ* (your own lower lip). This is because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection with the preceding sentence, "He sees you in secret in every direction. Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture]: nemaḥ | śrūyate ca — [The remainder of the passage follows].

"In this breath, Soma was seen"—thus [it is said]. Regarding the word *sama*: likewise, it is heard in the Veda: "May all others perish, *same*"; "Do not [give us] over to the wolf or the she-wolf, *samasmai*"; "Protecting us from the one who intends evil, *samasmāt*"; and "And also in *samasmin*"—and so forth.

"The word *sima* occurs in the senses of 'entirety' (*kṛtsna*) and 'capability' (*śakta*), as well as in the senses of 'boundary' (*maryādā*) and 'intellect' (*buddhi*). And it is heard [in the Veda]: 'The night spreads her garment for him, all around (*simasmai*),' and 'He has risen up from all around (*simasmāt*). In both instances, the word *sima* is a synonym for 'all' (*sarva*); such is the Vedabhāṣya."

Regarding the term *gaṇasūtra*: although the commentary (*bhāṣya*) records the *vārttika* "it should be stated that [the rule applies] except for *puri*" in reference to a sūtra within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, nevertheless, that is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the *gaṇasūtra*, and not to the rule prescribing the optional [substitution] in the *jas* case-ending. This is because the substitution of *śī* for *jas* is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *ṭā-utaḥ*.

Because there is no possibility [of the application] from a form ending in *ṭā*. Regarding the term *antarāyām*: the meaning is "in that which is outside the enclosure wall" or "in that which is inside it. Alternatively, the possibility [of the application] should be understood through the inclusion of the *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*), by virtue of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender). These two are *tyad* and *tad*.

These two [words] have been explained as *parāmarśaka* (reflexive). Regarding them, the author of the *Gaṇaratna* states that the first is Vedic (*chāndasa*). That is not correct, because it would render the inclusion of the term "Vedic" (*cchandasi*) in the rule *syaś chandasi bahulam* redundant. Furthermore: "The word *eka* has the senses of 'another,' 'principal,' 'first,' and likewise 'alone.'"
The word *sādhāraṇa* is employed in the senses of common, equal, small, and number.
"By its own denotation" (svābhidheya):

the meaning is that there is a restriction of the limit (avadhi) required by the word "east" and so forth, which is itself the denotatum. Even in cases such as "be the rival of the southern direction," there is indeed a fixed determination; however, because it is well-known [in common usage], it is not explicitly stated.

A word denoting a limit (*avadhi*) is not employed [here], nor is there a prohibition based on it being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), for a *saṃjñā* is indeed a modern convention (*ādhunikasaṃketa*). And such a convention does not exist regarding the directions (*diś*), according to Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others in the section on the suffix *astāti*. In this context, [the usage] regarding the directions is ancient (*cirantana*), whereas that regarding the Kurus is modern (*ādhunika*).

In this case of *saṃketa*, the word of the commentator alone is the authority. By this, the term "of all the gods" (*viśveṣāṃ devānām*) is explained, because it is well-known in the Veda. The sense is that although there is the possibility of connecting [the term] with a specific limit such as "skilled in this or that," there is no fixed restriction [to that alone]. In the lower [case],...

One should also cite as counter-examples "tāmbūlarāgaḥ" (the redness of betel) and "pratyuttare ca śaktaḥ" (capable of replying). How then is one to explain Kālidāsa’s usage in "tathā pareṣāṃ yudhi ca" (and likewise against others in battle) and "apare pratyavatiṣṭhante" (others stand in opposition), and so forth?
On this point, they say: [these are instances] where the word *para* refers to a location and is restricted to that specific context.

The terms *parā* and *apara* are used figuratively (*upacāra*) for the enemy and the opponent, respectively; yet this does not constitute their status as subordinate members (*upasarjana*). For being derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) does not mean being subordinate;

rather, it is the transfer (*saṃkrama*) of the word’s own meaning onto another object qualified by that meaning. And such [transfer] occurs only in the case of compound formations (*samāsa*) and the like. Therefore...

Kaiyaṭa’s statement in the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"‘These also’ means these things to be established"—is thus consistent. However, in reality, the meaning of the words *para* and *apara* is simply their being situated in different locations and so forth; whereas enmity and the like—

The meaning is "pertaining to the sense" (ārthika). Why [is the condition] "not being a conventional name" (asaṃjñāyām) stated? [Consider] "the Northern Kurus" (uttarāḥ kuravaḥ). With reference to Sumeru as a limit, the word *uttara* ("northern") applies to the Kurus; thus, there is indeed a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*) here. However, they say that this is merely a modern convention (*ādhunikasaṅketa*).

Prau.ma.— Regarding the rule *svam ajñātidhanākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 1.1.35): the word *sva* denotes self (*ātman*), what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). Since kinsmen and wealth are excluded here, the intention is that the self and what belongs to the self remain as the remaining referents.

He explains: the meaning is "one's own," or alternatively, "oneself. As for what they say—that the word *sva* in the sense of "self" (*ātman*) is neuter, and therefore an example such as *sve* or *svāḥ* is not possible there—that is to be reconsidered, because the word *sva* is masculine even when referring to the self, according to the rule "vibhāṣā jasi."

In this context, since the author of the Sūtras himself is the authority for employing this elaborate designation when he could have simply said "one's own (*sva*) means *ātmīya*," we accept his word as proof. Furthermore, to support his own statement, [the lexicographer Amara] says:
"The word *svo* refers to a kinsman; *svam* in the three genders refers to one's own (*ātmīya*); and *sva-* in the non-feminine gender refers to wealth."

Thus they cite the statement of Amarasimha. That too is to be considered. For in the lexicon, "ātmani" connects with the preceding [verse], while "svam" connects with the following. And so Hemacandra says:
"Dyauḥ [is used] for heaven and the sky; svaḥ for kinsmen and the self; svaṃ for one's own and wealth."
Medinīkāra also states:
"The word *svaḥ* may be masculine when meaning 'self' or 'known'; it is used in three genders for 'one's own,' and in the feminine for 'wealth.
Therefore, it is established that the gloss *ātmānaḥ* (selves) for the term *sve svāḥ* (their own selves) is entirely correct."

Regarding the phrase *jñātidhanavāci tu*: by means of the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*), it is implied that even for words denoting "kinsmen" (*jñāti*) and "wealth" (*dhana*), the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) indeed exists when they function by prioritizing their own-ness (*ātmīyatva*).
It is precisely for this purpose that the term *ākhyā* ("designation") was included in the sūtra.

Prau.ma.- *antaraṃ bahiryogopasaṃvyānayoḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.36). The term *antara* [is used] in the sense of being connected with the exterior (*bahiryoga*) and in the sense of an undergarment (*upasaṃvyāna*). "The exterior" (*bahiḥ*) refers to an uncovered space as well as that which is external. Taking the first meaning, he says: "the meaning is 'external'. But in the second [sense],...
The meaning to be understood is "internal" (ābhyantara). For there is a connection of the internal with the external.

Furthermore, both [the external and internal] reside in the letter *a*. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* also refers to that which is external when derived through the agentive (*karaṇa*) analysis, but refers to that which is internal when derived through the objective (*karman*) analysis.

Prau.sū.—*pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.16). Here, this should be noted: this sūtra is to be explained by carrying it over (*anuvṛtti*) to the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17) through a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the phrase *vā cchandasī* (Pāṇini 7.1.39) is to be carried over to the rule *āmi* (Pāṇini 7.1.52).

As in the case of [the rule] *pūrvaḥ* here; and thus, in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the three rules beginning with *pūrvapara-* have their purpose already served, which results in great economy. Eight meanings of the word *eka* have been stated;
regarding that, he states the specific distinction: "in the sense of number. However, in the other seven senses, there is also another grammatical form (*vacanāntara*).
The sense is: "it may indeed be so," as in the case of "some [of] some.

[Prakriyākaumudī: Regarding *na bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.29), the prohibition is rendered useless once the *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, because [the word] has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

Since it will be stated later that "not [the words] beginning with *sarva*," he says: "in the intended [formation]" (*cikīrṣite*) and "even prior to the compound" (*samāsāt prāg eva*). He explains this by the term "derivation" (*prakriyā*). Nor should it be argued that the designation [of *sarvanāman*] cannot occur even prior [to the compound], because the cause—the status of not being a subordinate element (*anapasarjanatva*)—is on the verge of being destroyed.

Because the prohibition regarding *akṛtavyūha* is not absolute (*anitya*), and because this very sūtra serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for that fact. The phrase "those who have transcended existence" (*atibhavakān*)—the sense is that this is precisely the result of that indication. Regarding the expression "having accepted the desired conclusion": [it refers to] the inclusion of the augment *t* (as in *satuk*) in the rule "cchÂavoḥ śūḍ".
Alternatively, the statement regarding the non-occurrence of *prakṛti* and *pratyaya* [in certain cases] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of their non-eternality;
the sense is that the rule is established according to the requirements of the specific forms (*lakṣya*). Regarding the phrase "as follows" (*yathottaram*):
the sense is that, in the present day, the rule is established solely by the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

As for what was stated previously—that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) should not apply to words beginning with *sarva*, as in *priyasarvāya*—according to the view of the author of the *Sūtras*, there is no status of being a pronoun in a *bahuvrīhi*; according to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, this applies whenever [the word] is merely secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus, [the forms] *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ* [are established].

Regarding this, the opinion of the author of the *Nyāsa* is that this sūtra exists for the purpose of ensuring that since *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which are components of the compound—are pronominals (*sarvanāman*), the augment *akac* would apply [to them] as a non-aṅga operation; thus, instead of the suffix *kap* alone being applied, [the rule prevents this]. On this point, the following must be said:
Is it intended that the designation [of *sarvanāman*] does not apply to the *bahuvrīhi* compound as a whole, or rather to its constituent parts,

namely *sarva* and the others? It cannot be the first, because that would contradict the subsequent text which states, "In the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which are constituents of a compound," referring to the whole.

And because of the absence of application [of the rule]. Nor is there application by means of the *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule that applies to what ends with a specified element), because the members of a *bahuvrīhi* compound are *upasarjana*s (subordinate elements), and thus, being excluded from the set beginning with *sarva*, the possibility of application to what ends in such a word is far removed. For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable. Nor can it be said of subordinate elements...
It should not be said that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* based on the recitation [of the text], but is not actually grounded in the words of the *sūtra*;

for that [exclusion] is obtained from the very syllables of the *sūtra* itself by virtue of the force of the etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). By this, the view that "according to the opinion of the author of the *sūtra*, the term 'pronominal' (*sarvanāman*) does not apply to a *bahuvrīhi*" is also refuted; for [the restriction] "only in a *bahuvrīhi*" [is established].

The meaning of that is as follows: even the view beginning with "according to the commentator's (Bhāṣyakāra) opinion" is not [correct]. For by the specific mention [of the commentators], it is understood that the opinions of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Vārttika are otherwise. This is like saying, "Devadatta sees with his left eye," which implies he does not see with his right. And that is not [the case].

Even according to the view of the *Sītravārtika*, the exclusion of the secondary sense (*gauṇaparyudāsa*) is accepted. As for the example "tvatkapitṛka" and so forth, it was explained by the ancients as follows: having analyzed the compound as "one whose father is you" (*tvaṃ pitā yasya*) and "one whose father is I" (*ahaṃ pitā yasya*), and having formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the suffix is applied] to the two members of that compound...

Since *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when occurring within a compound (*samāsa*), denote all things and thus possess the designation of pronominal (*sarvanāman*), the suffix *akac* would undesirably apply in cases where there is an intention to express meanings such as "unknown," according to the rule "avyayasarvanāmnām. To prevent that—

This is because, unlike *smāi* and other such forms, these [forms] are not prescribed under the heading (*adhikāra*) of "member" (*aṅga*), and thus they do not depend upon the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of being a member. Consequently, undesirable forms such as *tvakat-pitṛkaḥ* would result. The author of the *Nyāsa*, having already refuted the application of this designation by the force of its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), raised the objection that the suffix *akac* would therefore not occur; he then stated: "For the composite [form] functions in a specific sense, whereas the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) has not at all lost its status as referring to the whole. All of this is merely an error.

For instance: in the *jahatsvārthā* theory of meaning, the individual meanings of the constituent members of a compound simply do not exist [as such]. Even in the *ajahatsvārthā* theory, since the word functions with respect to another referent qualified by its own meaning, its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is quite evident. Consequently, the passage beginning with "because *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which fall within the compound, denote all objects," as well as the passage from the *Nyāsa* commentary beginning with "for the aggregate... are contradicted in both theories.

Furthermore, in the case of *atisarvāya*, the substitution of *smāy* (the dative ending *smai*) would be unavoidable, because under the governing rule for "bases" (*aṅga*), there is the inclusion of that which ends with [the base]. According to your own reasoning, the quality of denoting "everything" (*sarvārthatā*) does not depart from the word *sarva*. Indeed, it is not logical to claim that the quality of denoting "everything" resides in the first member of the compound but not in the second. Moreover, if this were so, then when these words are used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*), they would no longer denote "everything," which would contradict your own statement; thus, this argument is trivial.

As for what others have explained—that in a derivative analysis (*vigrahavākya*) such as *tvaṃ pitā yasya* ("he whose father is you"), the technical designation [of *sarvanāman*] applies—[that too is incorrect].

"It is prohibited"—that too is not correct. For is the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) intended to be worldly (*laukika*) or non-worldly (*alaukika*)? Not the first, because that would contradict Kaiyaṭa’s statement: "This prohibition applies to the sentence used in the act of purchase (*prakraya*), but not to the worldly [sentence]."
Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the preceding and following passages within one's own text concerning the original *san* and *darbha*. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for that [form] consists of *yuṣmad-su* and *pitṛ-su*, and thus it is impossible for it to take the form *tvaṃ pitā*.

Regarding what they have explained—namely, that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to "atisarva" and the like, yet it does apply to "tvatkapitṛka" and the like—what is the determining factor there?
To this he says: "because it is not an operation dependent on a stem (*aṅga*). The word *aṅga* here refers to the entire complex (*samudāya*).
Therefore, in the rule *atisarva*, the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) is required because the suffixes *smāy* and others are prescribed after a stem that is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
Since there is no fault even if only a constituent part possesses the status of a pronoun, [the designation applies to the whole].

Furthermore, with respect to the meaning of the whole, the initial element (*sarva-* etc. is subordinate (*upasarjana*) to that whole; thus, [the designation applies] to that which ends in such an element.

It is logical that [the designation] "saṃjñā" does not occur; however, here it is intended for the mere constituent part (avayava) and not for the whole (samudāya), and since the constituent part has its own primary meaning as its principal referent, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga). This is the intended point regarding the difference [between the two cases]. That too is not correct, because of the rule of extension to what ends in that (tadantavidhi) under the governing heading (adhikāra) of "aṅga."

This is because the statement that "there is no fault even when [the word] is a pronoun, provided it is merely a constituent part by virtue of being universally accepted" is contradicted; furthermore, it would conflict with your own text which says, "by the paribhāṣā governing the term *aṅga*, [the suffix] *smai* should occur. Now, if the intention is this: "even though the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) had already occurred..."

"If it has already occurred when there is a transition to another meaning, then let *akac* also go [by the same rule]. If it is argued that "under the view that grammatical operations take place at the time of their application (*kāryakālapakṣa*), a designation (*saṃjñā*) is required again for the sake of forms such as *smāi*, and that is difficult to obtain"—let it be so; however, this is not the intended meaning of the present text.

This is because it contradicts the supplementary statement: "The stability [of the ritual] is according to the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa, due to the inconsistency with the Nyāsa texts. The Nyāsa texts will be cited immediately below. Furthermore, as for what they have explained: "That which is primary, whether a limb (aṅga) or the principal (pradhāna), is to be set aside; that which is contrary to it is not a limb (anaṅga)."

The meaning is that it is a sublater (*bādhaka*). And thus, the meaning is that *akac* would occur because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kap*. That too is both strained and useless, and moreover, it is not accepted by the author of the *Nyāsa*. For instance, having explained the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage "tvatkapitṛkaḥ" and "matkapitṛkaḥ," the author of the *Nyāsa* [states as follows].

He raised an objection: "But surely, since the very assignment of this etymologically meaningful name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) effects the exclusion of the technical designation [of 'sarvanāman'] in this case, the suffix *akac* will not occur. For here, the status of being 'all-meaning' (*sarvārthatā*) is impossible, because it refers to a specific domain.
This is not so; for while the composite whole (*samudāya*) functions with respect to a specific [meaning], the first member (*pūrvapada*)...

It remains indeed not devoid of all-purposefulness (*sarvārthatā*). Let it be, then, that the scope of this sūtra applies to these two immediately preceding [cases]. However, it is not applicable to cases such as *priyaviśvāya* and so forth; for *priyaviśva* and the like are not the names of all [things], nor...

For the words *viśva* and others, which constitute parts of that [compound], the grammatical operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāmakārya*)—beginning with the substitution of *smai* and so forth—is not applicable;

because those operations are dependent on the status of being a "stem" (*aṅga*), whereas the words *viśva* and others do not possess the status of a stem in this context. He thinks thus: [this is stated] so that the suffix *akac* shall not occur in forms such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*.
Therefore, this [work] must be undertaken; for it will also serve to clarify the meaning in passages such as "for Priyaviśvā" and so forth.

Indeed, by means of this Nyāsa text, the very fact that there is no dependence on the technical designation *aṅga* (base) is obtained as the intended meaning, whereas that [meaning] has been utterly cast aside in your own speculative commentary.
As for what they have explained— that although this view belongs to both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Vārttika,
it is nevertheless called "the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa" because it was commented upon by him— that too is quite gross,
since this meaning was not touched upon by the author of the Vārttika; rather, it was [discussed] by the author of the Nyāsa after the compound had been formed.

Furthermore, by stating "satī" and so forth, the meaning you have asserted is cast far away, as there is no absence of doubling (*dvirvacana*). As for what they also say— that by the word "the author of the *Nyāsa*," the author of the *Sūtras* himself is intended, and so on— that too is not correct,
because it contradicts the preceding passage beginning with "in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*" according to the view of the author of the *Sūtras*.

Furthermore, because that [position] has been refuted by the passage beginning with "But according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya," it follows that here the ancient grammatical treatises (*prakriyā-grantha*) and their commentaries are merely superficially pleasing;
let this matter rest for now.

If, however, there is a persistent insistence that even the *prakriyā* (grammatical derivation) treatise must be explained in some way so as not to contradict the *Bhāṣya*, then let it be explained as follows: "But [the form] *priyaviśvāya* has its meaning already established through secondary application (*gauṇatayā*);
therefore, he states the essential point—namely, 'according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras'—in the context of the *bahuvrīhi* compound."

The word "cikīrṣite" (when it is intended to be performed) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "gauṇatvamātre" (in the mere state of being secondary): the word "mātra" (mere/only) serves to restrict the meaning;
[the operation applies] only when there is a secondary sense, and not prior to that. Thus, the intention is that the Sūtra has been rejected.
This is because the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa is extremely trivial.

This should be investigated by those who have thoroughly studied ancient treatises on that subject. Let us return to the topic at hand. Regarding the phrase "the operation of technical designation" (*saṃjñākāryam*): the meaning is the application of *smāy* and so forth, which is occasioned by the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*).
Regarding the phrase "the operation within the sub-group" (*antargaṇakāryam*): [it refers to] "the substitution of *adḍ* for [the final vowel of] words beginning with *itarat*" (*adḍḍatarādibhyaḥ*).

The meaning is [the application of] rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ* and *tadoḥ sassau*. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the compound with the third case," here the compound prescribed by the rule *pūrvasadṛśa-* is understood because it is taught as a specific (pratipadokta) rule, and not the one by *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*. Therefore, [in the example] *tvayakā*...

In the word *kṛtam*, there is no negation [of the application of the rule] because it refers to the whole (*samudāya*). This is because the term *dvandva* is used in its primary sense (*mukhya*) in that very context; it does not mean "those [words] beginning with *sarva* which occur within a *dvandva*," since grammatical factors (*kāraka*s) can only be construed with a verb. Nor [does it apply] in a *dvandva*.

The connection is with the words "those which exist. This is because it would be cumbersome to supply the verb "exists" (vidyati), and because it is more logical that the verb "to be" (bhavati)—which is what is being negated—should be the primary element to which [the subject] is connected.
Furthermore, there is no *dvandva* compound of pronouns such as *tyad* and so on, because such a formation is precluded by the rule of *ekaśeṣa*. Therefore...

In that case, there is no distinction between other [directions] such as *prācī* and the crow's beak (*kāka-cu*). Nor should it be argued: "Why could this not also serve to prohibit the desired *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) in the case of *na ca dakṣiṇa-uttara-pūrvāṇām*? For the inclusion of the word *mātra* in the rule *sarvanāmno vṛtimātra* (Pāṇini 6.3.91) is indeed for that purpose.
In some cases, even when words previously observed to function as pronouns no longer possess that designation, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) still occurs.
