Therefore, both by the force of logic and by the evidence of the result, it is appropriate to accept the inclusion of the entire compound. Although the result could easily be explained—even under the view that the word *tvad* ends in *-t*—by means of a prohibition regarding its constituent parts, nevertheless...
The sense is that the scope of the treatise would be too narrow and it would contradict the established logic (*nyāya*).

Regarding the phrase "the contingency of *suṭ*": the sense is [that it would apply] in cases such as *varṇāśrametarāṇām*. Nor can the prohibition be justified by its own force, because it serves to exclude non-aṅga forms such as *tratasil* and others.
Because its purpose has been fulfilled.

Regarding the phrase "the locus of *jas*": although *jas* is removed by the substitution of *śī*, nevertheless, its status as a locus should be understood in a figurative sense (*aupacārika*). Alternatively, *i* belonging to *jas* is *jasi*; [the rule applies] in that [locus].
He explains by implication that there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*), stating "the substratum of *jas*. Regarding the rule *Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.101*:
*jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām*, [he notes] "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*). And this refers back to the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*.

Therefore, [the word *in*] continues [from the previous rule]. The intention is that, by virtue of this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *jarāyā idaṃ jāram*. Regarding the phrase "by those who follow that": their view is that since the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) applies to both *in* and *ataḥ* because they are mentioned in a single sūtra, it is appropriate to include the substitution of *syādeśa* as well.
For this very reason—
considering the usage by the poet Bhāravi, "for those desiring to attain the supreme, pure state of Brahman,
free from birth and old age," to be inconsistent, it should be read as "vītajarājanmanaḥ" (free from old age and birth).

They said: "And this [is so]. For the author of the Bhāṣya, having rejected the suffixes *in* and *āt* in the rule "ṭāṅasi," and having prescribed the substitutes *nā* and *ad*, established the substitution of *e* before the substitute *nā* by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). [The rules are: "In the plural, when followed by a *jhal* [consonant], *e* [is substituted]" and "also before *osi*. From that...

When followed by *āiṅ* or *ci*, the substitution of *e* (etvam) should occur. [Thus we have] *rāmeṇa*. Furthermore, according to the rule "āpaḥ saṃbuddhau ca," the substitution of *e* (ekāraḥ) should occur when *āṅ* or *osi* follows in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be elision (*lopaḥ*) of the *na* in *anena* when a consonant (*hal*) follows; for there is a specific injunction for the non-substitute (*anādeśasya*) when *na* follows. Likewise...

Indeed, the meaning is that *an* occurs when *na* and *api* follow. In the sūtra, *a* is a neuter designation for that which ends in *n*. Nor should it be argued that once the substitution of *at* for the case-ending *ṅsi* has been made, the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) would apply; for by the power of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*, the occurrence of the long vowel is possible. And thus:

It is stated in the sūtra *jarāyā jarasanyatarasyām*: "But Gonardīya says that it should be *atijaraiḥ* by virtue of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Thus, the meaning is that everything [the author has argued], such as the "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), is contrary to the Bhāṣya.

Prau.ma.- *paddannomāshṛnnaṣasanyūṣandoṣanyakañcchakannudannāsañcchasprabhṛtiṣu* (0-0-0) || "*paddanno*" || Here, the forms beginning with *śas* are mentioned as the conditioning cause (*nimitta*). And these...
He says— “pādadanteti”— that [the suffixes] imply specific bases corresponding to the substitutes for *pada* and so on;

although the word “in Vedic” (*chandasi*) is understood here from the rule “*śīrṣan* in Vedic,” nevertheless, it occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) in some cases, as indicated by the Vārttika “*māsa* in Vedic.”

It will be stated that this is due to the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the word *chanda*. Regarding the term "due to negligence" (*prāmādika*): for instance, in the mantra "From the mouth of the wolf, [he took] the ewe in the encounter," the meaning is "from the face" (*mukhāt*), because it is more appropriate (*aucityāt*). As in: "May there be an interval between the wolf and the ewe."

This is also because of the corroboration by other mantras; likewise in such passages as "offering oblations in the mouth" (*havyā juhvāna āsani*) and "they spoke to the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ*), the explanation in the Vedabhāṣyas is exactly the same. Therefore, it should be noted that even Haradatta has revealed the erroneous nature of the *Kāśikā* on this point.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

"allopo'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). Regarding this, the ancients [interpret it as]: "There shall be elision of the vowel *a* belonging to a *bha*-affix that ends in the suffix *an*. If that were the case, there would be elision of the vowel *a* even in the syllable *tak* in forms such as *takṣṇā*.
It might be argued that if the rule were explained as "of the *an* [suffix] belonging to a *bha*-stem," then it would apply in cases such as *ṭhanasā* and *manasā*;

and even if one were to explain it through methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition) as "of the *an* belonging to a *bha*-stem ending in *an*," there would still be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *ṭhanastakṣṇā*. Therefore...

He explains [the point] with the words "a member of the base" (*aṅgāvayava*), and so forth. The two things—the suffixal element implied by the word *bhasya* ("of a *bha*" [suffix]) and the base (*aṅga*)—are the qualifiers here. However, [the *bha* designation] belongs to the vowel *a*, and therefore the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the intended meaning. And this [is discussed] in the rule "vocalization of the *ṣyaṅ* [suffix]" (*ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam*).

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. *Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* (Pāṇini 8.4.1), although the status of being within a single word (*ekapadatva*) is already obtained by the force of the term *pade* alone, [the addition of *samāna-*]...

The inclusion of the term *samāna* (equal) means that which is strictly identical, that is to say, indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). In that case, so that [the rule] may apply there, it does not occur in a compound (*samāsa*). For example: *rāmanāma*. [And] *yūṣṇaḥ*. *Yūṣ* means broth (*maṇḍa*). As it is said: "Broth made from mung beans and *āmalaka* is digestive, appetizing, and a promoter of digestion."

Because of this observation. Regarding the phrase "in this alternative view": by this, he indicates that the *pañcamī-samāsa* (the compound with the fifth case) is optional. To explain, in the Bhāṣya three purposes are stated: *bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*; yet these are established otherwise. This is because [the prohibition] applies to roots having a single vowel in their original enunciation (*upadeśe*).

Precisely because of the specified qualification (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no prohibition of *iṇ* in the case of *bebhiditā*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *mathitaṃ paṇyam asya*, when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied and the single-substitute *ikāra* (*ekādeśa*) occurs by the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ*, the elision (*alopa*) of the final vowel by the rule *yasyeti ca* takes place;
however, the substitution of *kā* by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* will not occur, because the element *ṭha* is absent. Nor...

The substitution of *ṭha* occurs by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), because it is not a rule dependent on a phoneme (*alvidhi*). For in the rule "ṭhasyekaḥ," the vowel *a* in both the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of pronunciation. Furthermore, in the form *apīpacan*, the result is established even without the status of being a substitute for the elision of *ṇi* and for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the final *caṅ*-vowel and the following vowel.

Because of its association with the *vidhi* (prescriptive) suffixes, the *jus* is prescribed for the *jhi* of the *laṅ* even when it follows a reduplicated stem; nor should it be argued that, due to its association with the *sic*, it should belong only to the *luṅ*,
because association with what precedes is weaker than association with what follows— this is the general direction of the argument.

"Not [applicable] when what precedes is unestablished. We have already stated that this is established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). Since the final three chapters (*tripādī*) are unestablished, the rule of extension (*atideśa*), "when a subsequent [element] intervenes, the operation is as if it were after the vowel," does not apply to an operation to be performed therein. "Of that" means of that rule, "when what precedes is unestablished. And thus:

The meaning is that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) should be stated in three instances. In the case of the elision of the first letter of a *saṃyoga*, as in *cakryatra*; in the case of the substitution of *l* for *r*, as in *nigālyate*; and in the case of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, as in *māṣavapanī*. Here, because the elision of the *a* [of the suffix *an*] by the rule "yasyeti ca" is treated as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *nakāra* does not stand at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] does not occur.
No;

for they say that even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* in cases such as *yūṣṇaḥ*, the rule "raṣābhyām" (P. 8.4.1) has no utility, since the desired form is established by the application of *ṣṭun*. And thus:
It is established in the *Ākara* that the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* is for the sake of subsequent rules;

therefore, this has been presented here as a statement of impetuosity (*rabhasavāda*). Indeed, this very same absence of impetuosity is evident, for the inclusion of *ṣ* remains here even for the sake of subsequent rules. Consequently, in cases such as *yūṣṇaḥ* and *puṣṇāti*, [the rule applies].

By what could the application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) in the rule *raṣābhyām* be prevented? If you say it is by the rule for *ṣṭutva*, that is not so, because that [rule] is *asiddha* (not established). Nor can its *siddhatva* (established status) be derived from the authority of a specific statement, because that [statement] has already served its purpose in cases such as *puṣṭiḥ*. Therefore, the portion [of the rule] concerning *ṣayoge* (in conjunction with *ṣ*) remains without having served its purpose.

If this is argued, we say no; for that [case] has not been mentioned separately. Furthermore, the statement here that [the rule] "after *ṣ*" (Pāṇini 8.3.106) would otherwise be rendered purposeless applies equally to this case as well. For the intention of the authoritative source (*ākara*) is simply that there is no failure to establish the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*) here without the mention of *ṣ*;
it is not, however, intended that [the rule] "from *ra* and *ṣ*" (Pāṇini 8.4.1) [would apply] in forms such as *puṣṇāti*.
Thus, there is no application [of that rule]; this is the general direction. *Prakriyā-pradīpa*: "The *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is elided.
(Pāṇini 8.2.7). This refers to a form where the genitive case ending has been dropped; however, because it is a *sūtra*-formulation, it is not [to be taken as a compound].

The meaning is that in the case of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, the initial member [cannot be the locus of the suffix], because a compound is impossible when there is mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), and because a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) serves as a qualifier of a word-form (*pada*). Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in it" (*tadantasya*):
it is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound; the meaning is "of that *n* which is at the end of it. And it has been said:

Haradatta [states]: "In the rule *viśeṣyasyāntasya*, the word *na* is without a case ending (*avibhaktika*), and likewise, it is a qualifier for the word *prātipadika*. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it refers to the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or the end of a word (*pada*)—and as for...
The explanation— that the word *antasya* ("of the end") is connected with both— is undermined by its own weightiness,

because it would entail the necessity of repeating *antasya* and would result in two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhī*) that have different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*). However, if [the connection] were indeed through non-difference (*abheda*), then just as with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the word *na* could also [be connected].

When [the suffix] is qualified by that [condition], then, under the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with what has been specified), the mention of the word "anta" (end) in the sūtra could have been omitted.
Prau.ma.: *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.14).

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā ṅśyoḥ*: the term *śī* refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakācca*, and not to the *śi* of *jaś-śasoḥ*, because in the case of the latter, the status of being a *bha*-stem is impossible. By the rule *bhasya*, [the substitution applies] only to that which is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*.

Because this is implied by [the rule] beginning with *yaj* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), he says: "not before a sarvanāmasthāna suffix. For this very reason—namely, because of the usage *doṣaṇī*—although the Bhāṣya could be reconciled even if a collective dvandva were formed and then reduced by *ekaśeṣa*, nevertheless it is more logical that *kakud* be treated as a separate word; otherwise, [the form] *kakuda-*...

The sense is that oneness and duality of the two arms would not be obtained. In the verse from the *Raghuvamśa*: "The night-stalker, raising his right arm, rushed at him," there, the phrase "the right arm" (*dakṣiṇaṃ doḥ*) is connected as the object (*karma*) by means of the word "raising" (*udyamya*).
Regarding the phrase *doṣaṃ tasya*:

"Taking the *doṣa* (fault/hand) and the *guṇa* (string/virtue) of that bow which was thus being handled (*bhajataḥ*)," such is the usage by Śrī Harṣa. In that context, *doṣaṃ* means the hand and the defect; and *guṇaṃ* refers to the string [of the bow].
The connection is that [the author] is perceiving an excellence in the *maurvī* (bowstring).
However, the commentators on Amara, having accepted the word *doṣā* as feminine as well, state "doṣā" by applying the suffix *ṭāp* according to the opinion of Bhāguri.
They cited the *Dhanañjaya-nighaṇṭu*: "The arm is called *dordoṣā*, *bhuja*, *bāhu*, as well as *pāṇi*, *hasta*, and *kara*.

[Regarding the term] "occurring in two days": it is a compound according to the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*), with the suffix *ṭhañ* applied by the rule "from time [expressed in terms of days]" (*kālāt ṭhañ*).

There is elision (*luk*) by the rule "dvigor lug-anapatye. Then, the suffix *ṭac* is added by the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ. The substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-* occurs by the rule "ahnohna etebhyaḥ. Regarding the expression "sāyo 'hnaḥ" (the evening of the day): the word *sāya* denotes the conclusion [of the day] when derived from the root *syati* with the suffix *ghan*. [The compound is formed] by the rule "saṃkhyā-visāya-... [etc.].
The *ekadeśisamāsa* is established by way of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Thus end [the words] ending in /a/.

"Hāhā" is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific type of Gandharva. However, the followers of Kumāra (the Kaumārāḥ), asserting that it is a verbal derivative meaning "he abandons" (*jahāti*)—thus deriving it as *hā-hā*—state that its form is like that of *viśvapsan*. In their view, however, the counter-example is the letter *ṭha*, which is Vāsudeva.
It should be understood that *sāḥ* means "those which exist together with it," and *tān sān* means "those [which exist together]. Thus end those ending in long vowels (*ādantāḥ*).
Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *āṅe nāstriyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.120), it is not stated as *āṅe nā puṃsi*, so that forms such as *amunā kulena* may be obtained.

Nor can the form be established by the insertion of *num*, because the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the application of the rule *iko 'ci* (Pāṇini 7.1.73).

[The substitution] does not apply because [the condition of] non-attainment (*aprāpti*) exists. However, in the case of *nādeśa* (the substitute *na*), there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*), due to the prohibition by the rule *namune*. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition *namune* should apply only to *num*, since the vowel *a* in *ne* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). [This is because the form] *amuṣmai* [would otherwise result].
Because it would result in the non-establishment of forms such as *kulāya* [from *kulāyī*].
[This refers to] Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.119: *acca gheḥ*; and [the rules] *idudbhyām*, *ReĀ*, and *āṬt*.

With the intention that [the word] follows the three preceding words, he explains by means of the rule beginning with *idudbhyām uttarasya*. It is not stated as *gher uttarasya*, because in the sūtra the term *gheḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*),
and because there is no authority for [applying] *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so forth, as was the case in the previous sūtra *āṬt*.

Furthermore, because it is improper to abandon the established relationship [of the rule] *idudbhyām* with the suffix *ReĀ* as stated in *ityutarasya ReĀḥ*, [the form] *āṬtsyāt* would result. Regarding this, they have explained: the presence of the *t* in *āṬt* is for the sake of the *svarita* accent. As for the prohibition of *it* by the rule *na vibhaktau*, it does not apply here, because that rule is not universally valid (*anityatvāt*).

And as for impermanence (*anityatva*), it has been stated in that very same [work] that it is obtained from the addition of the marker *it* to the *m* of *thamu* in the rule "idamasthamuḥ," for the purpose of protecting [the *m*] from being subject to the technical designation *itsaṃjñā*. That, however, is to be reconsidered; for in the rule "vibhaktau," the *t* in *ReĀraut* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Because it has been stated by [Pāṇini] himself that [the term] "net-saṃjñā" (the name *net*) applies, there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Furthermore, it is logical that its purpose is for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārthatva*), and not for the sake of the *svarita* accent; for in such passages as "stīrṇe barhiṣi samidhāne agnau," the *svarita* accent is not observed. As for the *tapara* designation in "ṭhat," however—

Regarding the statement that [the rule] "budhau" and so forth was formulated so that the suffix *ṭāp* would not apply when *atva* (the substitution of *a* for *i*) has been made in the feminine, this too is to be considered. For by the inclusion of the marker *t* (*tapara*), let there be no long vowel with *ṭāp*; however, *ṭāp* itself should indeed apply, as there is no evidence for the sublation of two grammatical rules simultaneously. Therefore...

Thus, in the commentary on the sūtra *kṛnmejantaḥ* and in the Vārttika, it is stated that by the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*, the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply; for if there were an intervention by *ṭāp*, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be destroyed. Therefore, as in the case of *autaḥ*, so too from *ataḥ*.
It should be noted that the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (taparakaraṇa) is solely for the purpose of pronunciation.
Regarding the rule *anaṅ sau* (Pāṇini 7.1.93): since the form would have been established by the rule *sorḍā*, the prescription of *anaṅ* indicates that it should apply even in other instances.

[The suffix] is for the purpose of making this known. Therefore, the ancients maintain that *anaṅ* is established in the vocative of *uśanas*. That, however, is to be reconsidered; for if [the rule] were stated as *soḥ ḍā*, then by the subsequent rule *ṛduśanas-purohitādibhyaś chaḥ*, *ḍā* would also apply. Consequently, in the form *uśanā*, there would be lengthening by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*.
It might be argued that in *purudaṃsā*, there would have to be a long vowel by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*. Alternatively,

the resolution should be understood either through the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably applicable" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ*), or by the *paribhāṣā* concerning what is internal to a stem (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).
*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68):

the term *dīrghāt* (from a long vowel) is a qualifier specifically for *ṅī* and *āp*, and not for *hal* (consonant), because a consonant cannot be "long. Thus he says: "from a long [vowel]. The word *param* (subsequent) [is used]; however, this is not...

The sense is that [the definition] is over-exclusive (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yā* (feminine nominative singular) because it is not prescribed after a suffix marked with *ṅ*; nor can there be a resolution there by means of being prescribed after a consonant (*halanta*), because it would then be over-inclusive (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *yaḥ* (masculine nominative singular) and *saḥ*, and under-exclusive in cases such as *kartā*. [Regarding the word] *hal*: and of that...
The form *sutisī* should be understood according to the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). Regarding the word "is elided" (*lupyate*):

although the term "elision" (*lopa*) is carried over from the rule "elision of *v* and *y*" (*lopo vyoḥ*), and while that [term] there functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), here it functions as an object (*karmasādhana*), being construed with the nominative *hal*.

The intended meaning is "because of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Why is the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) made? [Consider] *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. Now, one might object: "In these cases, the entire compound does not end in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*). Nor should it be said: "There is no restriction regarding the initial element [of the compound] when a feminine suffix follows. For this [restriction applies] only when the suffix is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*).
Likewise, here too, because [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the rule regarding initial position (*tadādi-niyama*) certainly applies. True;

nevertheless, since the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅy-āp*), its status as being "after that" (*tataḥ para*) remains unchanged. For we have already stated that this [rule] is not a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). Precisely for this reason, there is elision of the nominative suffix (*su-lopa*) in the case of *bahuśreyasī*.

It might be argued as follows: [from the root] *gaṅgīyati* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *gaṅgīḥ*. Here, because the vowel *i* possesses the property of being *āp* (by virtue of its being a substitute, *sthānivadbhāva*) and because it is long, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is true; however, by compounding (*praśliṣya*) *ṅī* and *ī*, as well as *ā* and *āp*, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is rejected, and thus there is no fault whatsoever.

What is the purpose of the condition "after a suffix ending in *su* or *ti*"? [Consider] *bhetā*. [The rule would otherwise require] the elision of the *t* of *tās*. Nor does this [condition] lead to the undesired elision of *sic* in forms such as *abhaitsīt*, because by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*) with *su* and *ti*, only a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is understood [by the term *apṛktam*]. Why is the condition "uncombined" (*apṛktam*) stated? [Consider] *bhinatti* and *cchinatti*.

They offer a counter-example; however, that must be considered, because the [term] *ah* is qualified [by the condition of being a consonant]. To provide an over-extension by laboriously explaining [the rule] as "after *su*, *ti*, and *sī*, when a consonant follows" is improper.
Furthermore, they say: one who presses *surā* is a *surāsut*; one who causes him to speak is *surāsayati*.

From that, with the *kvip* suffix, we have *surāḥ*, *surāsau*, *surāsaḥ*. Here, the mention of *apṛkta* (non-composite) is intended to exclude the elision of the *s* belonging to the root *su* (*sunoti*). But even that is not correct, because by virtue of mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*), only the case-endings (*vibhakti*) *sut*, *si*, and *s* are understood [as being meant]. Otherwise, [the rule would apply to] the *sic* [suffix as well].

Because it has been stated [in the rule] *lopāpatiḥ*, and because between a suffix (*pratyaya*) and a non-suffix (*apratyaya*), only the suffix is to be understood [as the referent]. Why [specify] "consonant" (*hal*)? [Consider: *bibheda*.
But is not the mention of the "first consonant" (*prathama-hal*) redundant? [For] those [suffixes] following a word ending in a consonant...

Because of the possibility of the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). On this point, they say: "If there were elision of a final conjunct, then the elision of *n* and so forth would not be established;
for in that case, the elision would occur by that [rule] alone (*tasmād eva*), and therefore the rule 'elision of a consonant' (*hal-lopah*) is prescribed."

For instance, in the word *sakhe*, the elision of *n* would not occur because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This might be argued: the elision of a final conjunct is not non-existent, as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *sambuddhi* in the rule *na ṅsimbudhyoḥ*.

And thus, there is no occurrence of the elision of *n* even in cases such as *gomān*; for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) has a specific scope. For it is established that the rule applies only where there is immediate succession between the letter *n* and the case-ending, according to the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*). As for what they say—that in the vocative *he brahman*, [the elision does not occur] because it serves the purpose of the neuter gender—[this is incorrect].

"It is not an indicator (jñāpaka) of this"—that is not correct. For when a suffix is elided by *luk*, there is an absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of rules conditioned by a suffix), and since the rule "optionally for neuter nouns in the vocative" (*saṃbuddhau vā napuṃsakānām*) is necessary, the mention of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) cannot possibly refer to neuter nouns; thus, the aforementioned indicator remains firmly established. Therefore, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)...
And if it is argued that there is no purpose [for this rule], then in this case, in the example *abhino'tra*, the substitution of *u* for *ru* would not occur.

This is what was stated [by the author]: "such as the elision of *n*" (*nalopādi*). Likewise, in the example *abibharbhavān*, the elision of *t* would not occur due to the restriction [of Pāṇini's rule] "rātsasya" (P. 8.2.24).

In this regard, the following should be noted: the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is a qualifier only for *su*, and not for *tis* and *tīs*, according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). The evidence for this here is the Bhāṣya on this very sūtra, which states: "In this rule, the mention of 'having two consonants,' 'separated by a vowel,' and the mention of *tis* and *tīs* need not be made. For if the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [were intended to apply to *tis* and *tīs* as well...]

In that case, how could one say that the mention of *ti* and *si* need not be made, since they too are qualifiers? As for the claim that *ti* and *si* are impossible after words ending in *ṅī* and *āp*:
it is true that they are impossible after a word ending in *ṅī*; however, after a word ending in *ā*, they are possible following an *ācārakviP* derivative in the *laṅ* tense.

The *tipsipau* suffixes indeed exist, as in the examples *agaṅgāt* and *agaṅgāḥ*. Nor is there an intervention by the *śap* affix, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*). Nor does the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) apply, because this is not a rule concerning something previously established (*apūrvavidhitvāt*).

In this regard, the following is the essential point: the rule *ṅyāpaḥ suḥ* alone is appropriate. Nor is there the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the *s* of verbal roots in forms such as *surāḥ* or *surāsau*, because of the association with *ṅī* and *āp*, and by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "between that which is a suffix and that which is not a suffix," [the *su*] refers only to a suffix.

Because of the inclusion of the word *saḥ* [in the rule]. As for the elision of the *n* in *rājā* and so forth, it is indeed established by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na ṅsimbudhyoḥ*. Furthermore, the substitution of *u* in *abhino'tra* is also easily justifiable, because of the reading in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*: *saṃyogāntalopo rorutve*. [In the case of] *harivo*...

Just as in the case of *medinam tu*, there is no fault even here in the example *abibhar bhavān*. This is because, in the rule *rātsasya*, the letter *t* is also included by *praśleṣa* (elision), resulting in the analysis *tsasya*. [Objection:

But would there not then be the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) in cases such as *ukhāsrat*? [Reply: No, for once the substitution of *d* has been applied, [the condition for that elision no longer holds].

Because that [substitution] has not been attained. If it is argued that the substitution of *d* for *t* (*datva*) is unestablished, we say no; for in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*, there is the reading: "the substitution of *d* occurs in the case of *vasu* and so forth. If it is further argued that the substitution of *d* would not occur because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), we say no;

for one may resort to the position that even in the presence of the nominative suffix *su*, it remains a word (*pada*). The basis for this is the rule: "not in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*... [and so on].

The explanation is that by analyzing [the sūtra] as *yaci* (meaning "before *ya*, *ac*, and *sarvanāmasthāna*"), the status of being a *pada* does not apply before a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with *yaj*.
Nor should it be argued that, in this case, once the *nalopa* has been applied in forms such as *rājā*, the rules for *ru*-substitution and the visarga would still apply;
for the rule *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* is established specifically to prevent this.

This is because, by prescribing such forms, it is first made known that there is elision of the *su* suffix. But is this not a mere indicator (*jñāpaka*), since its purpose is already fulfilled in the case of the vocative singular? For instance, in *he panthāḥ*, *manthāḥ*, and *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, the long vowel is excluded by the rule "except in the vocative" (*asaṃbuddhau*), and the elision of the nasal (*na*) is prohibited. If this is argued:

In that case, let the very rule *na ṅsiṃbudhyoḥ* serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the meaning that the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) occurs prior to the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). For instance, in the expression *ṅsiṃbudhyoḥ*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended rather than the locative (*saptamī*), because [the suffix] is elided by the rule *ReĀrluk*.

Because of the absence of the characteristic of being a condition (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there is a coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the statement "of a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*. Furthermore, a nominal stem ending in the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*) cannot be obtained without first applying the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Therefore, the rule should be formulated as "of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *su*" (*ṅyāpaḥ sor iti*).

There is no contradiction whatsoever. However, if the *vārttika* "the substitution of *d* occurs in the case of *uṣṭra* and others" is rejected—since the absence of the long vowel in forms such as *ukhāsrat* is established by the very mention of *adhātu-* [in Pāṇini 6.4.13]—then let the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ suḥ* be accepted. As for the fact that the ancient [grammarians] have taken the rule according to its literal wording...
It has been explained [by some] as "from that which ends in a *ṅī* suffix, from that which ends in an *āp* suffix, and from a long vowel. That is not correct;

for it is the *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes themselves that are long, not that which ends in them. Furthermore, the meaning "from that which ends in a *ṅī* suffix which is long" and so forth cannot be obtained from the expression "from a long [vowel] after a *ṅī* suffix," etc., because there is no grammatical connection (*ananvaya*) with the ablative case ending in "dīrghāt."
In a compound, because the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are subordinate (*upasarjana*) and thus connected with qualifiers, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"There is no formation of a compound for those accompanied by qualifiers," and "Once a compound has been formed, there is no connection with a qualifier. By this [principle], the ancient commentary's statement that "the short vowels *i* and *u*, not bearing the technical name *nadī*, [are included]" is also refuted.
[The rule] is answered:
*sakhyurasaṃbuddhau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.92). Here, [the word] "sakhyuḥ" [is understood] from the sūtra *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* (7.1.86).

The term "in a sarvanāmasthāna [suffix]" (sarvanāmasthāne) is understood from the previous context. That is qualified by the term "except for the vocative singular" (asambuddhau). From the rule "goto ṇit" (Pāṇini 7.1.90), the word "ṇit" is carried over; because of its coreferentiality, the locative case is interpreted as a nominative. Thus he says: "excluding the vocative."

Regarding the term *sarvanāmasthāna*: it would be more appropriate for the rule to simply state, "of *sakhi*, except in the vocative. In the Pradīpa commentary on *Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.1.122, *khyatyāt parasya*, the word *khya* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the words *khi* and *khī* after they have undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*. Thus, *khya* represents both *khi* and *khī*.

Thus, regarding the words *titau* and *tya*, the vowel *a* in both cases is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not an imitation of a portion of primary derivative words such as *apatya*. [This is illustrated by the rules: "The suffix *yaḥ* after *sakhi*," "The suffix *naḥ* after *pati*," "After a numeral and a word denoting a year," and "And after a patronymic (*āpatya*) when followed by a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) ending in *i*."
Because of such indications as these; with this intention, he says: "by the words *khi* and *ti*, etc.

The inclusion of the word *parasya* ("of the subsequent") is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "one [substitute] takes the place of both the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*).
Prau.ma.: *ĀT* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.130).

"ĀṬ": This [substitution] is superseded by the preceding rule, "idudbhyām," among those [stems] designated as *nadī*, and by the subsequent rule, "acca gheḥ," among those designated as *ghi*. Therefore, its scope consists of those [stems] devoid of both designations. And there is no such *u* that possesses [both]. Hence...

He says: "The syllable *u*. As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the rule applies] after the vowels *i* and *u* when they are not followed by the technical designations *gh*, *in*, or *īdī*—that is incorrect, because such an *ū* (as a single phoneme) is unestablished. [Regarding the phrase] "of the whole":
even in the case of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), [the objection does not apply] because the word *sakhi* serves to provide the very thing being excluded.
The suspicion that [the term] refers to the apprehender of that [suffix] is to be set aside, because of the non-proximity of the substantive (viśeṣya).

As for what was presented here by Haradatta in the passage beginning with "by one possessing the apprehension," and what was stated by Kaiyaṭa under the sūtra *khyatyāt*, that is not correct, because that [context] pertains to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*).

Regarding the phrase "even though it is secondary" (*gauṇatve’pi*): the intention is that it is like *anaṅ* in the case of *asthi* and so on. Thus, Kaiyaṭa, under the rule *yena vidhis*, states: "In *paramasakhāyau*, it is a *bahuvrīhi*; for if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* would have to occur. Similarly, under the rule *dvitīyā śrita-*, [he gives the example] *somasakha*.
Kaiyaṭa states that because [the word] is a bahuvrīhi compound taking a portion [of the base], there is no application of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtras *midaco’ntyāt* and *tṛjvatkroṣṭuaḥ striyāṃ ca*, as well as in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *khyā*. [The suffix] *ṭhan* does not apply to *ukṣan*.

Furthermore, scriptural usages such as "Varuṇa has Indra as his friend" (varuṇa indra-sakhā), "The Maruts have Agni as their friend" (āgneyā hi marut-sakhā), and "He drinks the sharp Soma which has the cow as its companion" (tīvraṃ somaṃ pibati go-sakhāyam) are consistent only in this way; for in those cases,
the original accentuation of the first member of the compound is observed, indicating that [the sense of "friend"] is used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense.
By this [rule], Haradatta, Nāgeśa, and others who follow them— citing "one whose friend is excellent" (*susakhi*) as an example under the rule *ghisaṃjñāsūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.7)— are to be disregarded.
[This is because] *patiḥ samāsa eva* (Pāṇini 1.4.8) [restricts the application of the term *ghi* to the compound].

"The word *pati* [is substituted] only in a compound (*samāsa*). The particle *eva* (only) serves to restrict the application according to the intended meaning; otherwise, one might suspect that *pati* alone [is always substituted]. Furthermore, if one were to follow the indication (*jñāpaka*) from rules such as "of the root-initial" (*dhātvādeḥ*), there would be excessive complexity (*pratipattigaurava*) in understanding. Now, how is it that [the form] *sītāyāḥ pataye namaḥ* ("salutation to the husband of Sītā") occurs?
And Parāśara says:

"When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen [from his caste]... To this it is replied: the word *pati* is explained as derived from the root *pā* (to protect) with the suffix *ṇi*; after the elision of the *ṭi*, the suffix *i* is applied according to the Uṇādi rule "acaḥ iḥ."
This word *pati* is not included in the rule *patiḥ samāsa eva* because it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*).
By this, the Mahābhārata passage *kṛṣṇasya sakhir arjunaḥ* and the Rāmāyaṇa passage *sakhinā vānarendreṇa* are explained.

Prau.ma.: *Bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23). The two *prātipadika*s "bahu" and "gaṇa" are understood here as denoting number (*saṃkhyā*), and not as denoting a collection (*saṃgha*) or abundance (*vaipulya*). This is because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed etymologically, based on the derivation: "that by which [something] is numbered (*saṃkhyāyate*) is a number."
For this very reason, only the *taddhita* suffix *ḍati* is understood here, because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with *vatu*; it does not refer to the *ḍati* derived from the root *pāt*.
(Prakriyākaumudī: *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.22).
"ṣaḍbhyo luk" (Pāṇini 7.1.22). Regarding the phrase "of those following after the six": the use of the plural number is intended to indicate the predominance of the meaning;
the resulting sense is that [the elision occurs] when the two [suffixes] denote a number residing in the meaning of the word "six."
*Prauḍhamanoramā*: Regarding *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.62):
since this is established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśo’nalvidhau*, the present sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
That is, when a form unique to the affix is the cause [of an operation], that operation alone takes place even when the affix is elided.

[The suffix] exists when [the word] is present, but it is not common to both a suffix and a non-suffix. Therefore, in the example *sudṛṣat-prāsādaḥ* ("a palace with beautiful stones"), the rule *atvasantasya ca* does not apply [to lengthen the vowel]. Alternatively, this [rule] is for the purpose of the prescription even in cases where there is no *al*-vidhi (a rule concerning vowels), provided that the suffix is relied upon as the primary factor.

Therefore, in the case of *atṛṇeḍ*, even though the *im* augment—prescribed before a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*)—has been elided, it still takes effect. However, the rule "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treatment as if the suffix were present) when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*)" refers to cases where the phoneme is the predominant factor. Consequently, in the example *gave hitam* → *go-hitam*, the *av* augment does not occur.
Regarding "asmad": here, the reading *avyaya* (indeclinable) is also cited by the ancients;

however, that is objected to because indeclinables generally lack gender, and thus, even though an *avyayībhāva* compound is neuter, there is an absence of any other gender. As for "in reality": [this refers to] that which makes known the predominance of the meaning.

The sense is that because the plural number is absent, even though [the word] is used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense, the substitution of *traya* is proper, just as in the case of *anaṅ* for words beginning with *asthi*.
"The vowel *a* must be stated" means that in the absence of plurality, the word *ĀṬḍulomi* ends in the vowel *i*.
However, one should not be confused by the fact that while the word *uḍulomi* ending in *a* is used in the plural, the word ending in *i* takes the form of an *adanta* (ending in *a*) in the plural.
Thus end the words ending in *i*.

The sense is that there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca. Regarding the forms *yayī*, *papyā*, and so on—though it has been stated elsewhere that this applies to *devayajya*, *atilakṣmī*, and others—that is not correct; for in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who sacrifices to the gods" (*devān yajate*), the suffix *in* is applied according to the Uṇādi sūtra.

This is because the word *devayaji* with a short vowel at its end has been established by Ujjvaladatta and others; furthermore, the usage of Bhāravi in the verse, "We shall slay the twice-born who sacrifice to the gods," has been explained specifically as referring to a short vowel. Nor is there an *ī*-suffix with a long vowel after the root *yaj*.

It is explicitly stated [in the rule]. If it is argued that it is inferred due to the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in various cases), this might indeed be so, provided that an inferential ground (*kalpaka*) not otherwise established were found. Even in the Veda, the short vowel alone is employed—as in "āyajim tvā manave jātavedase. However, as for the word *atilakṣmī*:

Because it is a river (*nadī*), when the short vowel is present, the augment *āṭ* is applied, and once *nuṭ* and *ām* have been added, there is a great difference [in form]; thus, there is no similarity with *vātapramī*. This will become clear in the root text itself. Regarding the term "ending in *kvip*": this is found in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *māṅ*, meaning "to measure" and "to sound."

This is clear. Regarding the term *bahuśreyasī*: the suffix *kap* is not applied by the rule *īyasaśca*, nor is there shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*) because of the prohibition: "there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel in a *bahuvrīhi* containing [the superlative suffix] *īyas*. Prakriyā-kaumudī: Feminine stems designated as *yū* and *strī* are called *nadī*. (Pāṇini 1.4.3)

Regarding the rule *yū stryākhyau*: the phrase "ending in *ī* or *ū*" (*īdūdantau*) refers here to the two vowels themselves; for there is also a view that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the phonemes alone, as evidenced by the natural tendency of the rule *ācchīnadyornum*.

Their status as being called "feminine" (*stryākhyau*), however, occurs either inherently in the case of *ṅī* suffixes and the like, or in some cases by virtue of being constituents of a collection of phonemes that denote a feminine entity.
Because [the suffix] *praveśa* (entry) is intended, the status of being the locus for the completion of the capacity (*śaktiparyāpti*) is not what is meant to be expressed.

Therefore, the conventional usage [of terms] such as "ending in a nadī" is not contradicted. In the same way, regarding the technical designation *ghisaṃjñā*, one should understand that there are two positions: either the vowels *i* and *u* are the *ghisaṃjñin*, or that which ends in them is the *ghisaṃjñin*. If it were a designation of a phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñā*), [the rule] would be *ṭhasakhi*.

The meaning of this [sūtra] is "a part of that which is distinct from *sakhi*," and not "excluding the word *sakhi* as a whole. Therefore, one should note that forms such as *atisakhinā* are unobjectionable.
Regarding the word *pūrvam*: it means "prior to the formation of the compound" (*vṛti*). Regarding the word *vaktavyam*: it refers to a technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

This [interpretation] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*) when the rule proceeds according to its enunciation (*yathoddeśa*), but it is based on explicit statement (*vācanika*) under the view that the rule applies at the time the operation is to take place (*kāryakāla*). In the *Paribhāṣā-pradīpa*: "In the presence of an *ac*, for the *śnu* affix, for verbal roots, and for *bhrū*, there are *iy* and *uv* in place of *y* and *v*" (Pāṇini 6.4.77). Here, the phrase "of *y* and *v*" (*yvoh*) is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, and not...

He says "because of the non-deviation between *śnu* and the eyebrows" (*śnubhruvor avyabhicārāt*), [referring to] "the stem ending in the vowels *i* or *u*" (*ivarṇovarṇāntadhātoḥ*). However, if one were to explain it as "of *śnu* and so forth, [ending] in the vowels *i* or *u*," then the rule for *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, and *ṅtvam* would be redundant, and there would be the fault of grammatical discordance (*vaiyadhikaraṇyam*). [Examples are: *kṣipati*, *adyautat*, *didivatuḥ*, *ūyatuḥ*.

In such cases, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). The sense is that, although this could be avoided by qualifying the vowels *i* and *u* as being followed by a vowel (*ac*), doing so would be cumbersome. "Due to proximity" (*āntaratamyāt*) means "due to the point of articulation" (*sthānataḥ*).

Prau.ma.: *eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.82). Regarding the rule *aci śnudhātu...* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.77), although there is a mention of a *dvandva* compound (*śnu-dhātu-bhruvām*), only the *dhātu* (verbal root) is connected here, and not *śnu* or *bhru*, because the vowel *i* (the *ivarṇa*) cannot occur in those two.
He explains that the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) qualifies both [the preceding and following terms] by repetition, as well as the *saṃyoga* and the *aṅga*, stating:

"in the *saṃyoga* which is a part of the root," and so forth. Therein, because the *saṃyoga* is qualified by the root, here [the rule applies to] *yaṇ*: *unnyau*, *unnayaḥ*. But as for the qualification of the *aṅga*...
For the sake of establishing forms such as *ṭhharinam*, *harī*, and *harīn*, if the base (*aṅga*) were not qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*),

then here too— in cases such as *pradhyaṃ* and *pradhyaḥ*— the *yaṇ* substitution would occur, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute rule) and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class).
The vowel *i* is not preceded by the conjunction of two root constituents (*dhātu-avayava-saṃyoga*), because the stem (*aṅga*) ends in that [vowel].
This refers to the word *vṛścika*. For the author of the Bhāṣya, relying on a removal (*āpāya*) conceived by the intellect, has rejected the rule "bhītrārthānām. And therefore...
The sense is that when one intends to express mere relationship (*sambandhamātra*), the genitive case alone is used.
Even according to the view of the Sūtra, he says: "related to the scorpion" (*vṛścikasambandhinī*).
[Regarding the form *vṛścika*: "the elision of *at* and the elision of *ya*" (*allopayalopau*). Nor should it be argued that, because it is subsequent, the rule "verapṛktasya" would apply.

This must be stated, because of the Vārttikakāra’s statement: "The elision [of the *ṭh*] occurs by the elision of the single-consonant (*ekapṛkta*) suffix after a *ṭh*, according to the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) when *val* follows. Regarding the phrase "elided in *kvip*": the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of an abstract state; thus, the meaning is "the elision [of the suffix] in *kvip*. All of this should also be understood to apply to the form *kumārī*, as in the case of one desiring a maiden (*kumārīm icchan*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of non-difference" (*ananyatayā*): it should be understood that this is because it has already been stated that even in a secondary sense (*gauṇatve*), the operations of *anaṅ* and *ṇit* take place. Regarding the phrase "even of the long vowel" (*dīrghasyāpi*): the intention is that the mention of the substitution of *yaṇ* was made for this very purpose.
[Objection: But surely, the mention of *yaṇ* is intended to exclude [the application of the rule] to cases like *atisakheḥ* and *bhūpateḥ*, which fall under the domain of *guṇa*.

If this is argued, let it be so; nevertheless, the application [of the rule] to long vowels remains unavoidable. For there is no authoritative evidence to suggest that the operation should apply to short vowels and not to long ones. This is because the modified reference in the Sūtra serves to exclude both under-extension (avyāpti) and over-extension (ativyāpti).
This is because [the reading] possesses that essential excellence, is likewise appropriate, and is established in the Bhāṣya. As for what the ancients said— namely,
"some say *veti*," followed by the statement "*sakhyuḥ*" and so forth— and as for what the commentators on that [work] stated, that both of these [readings] are found in the Bhāṣya.
And regarding that which was stated here for the sake of support by one acting out of favor—

"Pāṇini says that [the suffix] *khyat* is used for the sake of establishing a friend (*sakhi*) or a husband (*pati*)"— those who consider that to be a general rule [apply it] to forms such as *sukhyuḥ*, *sutyuḥ*, *sakhīḥ*, and *sutīḥ*.
It is known that for the two roots *sukhīyati* and *sutīyati*, which end in the suffix *kvip*,
forms such as *lūni* and *ūrṇu* arise, because the substitution [of the semivowel] for the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it.

The verse from the *Vicāracintāmaṇi* beginning with "sukhya" and ending with "bhāṣyagauravāt"— which states that both [the views] are correct— has been cited here; let those of cultivated intellect understand that this entire [citing] is based on a failure to thoroughly consider the *Bhāṣya* and the *Kaiyaṭa*.

Regarding the term *śuṣkiya*: as for the examples they cited, such as *śuṣkyuḥ*, *pakvyuḥ*, *śuṣkyaḥ*, and *pakvyaḥ*, and their concluding remark that "this is established in the Bhāṣya," that was due to excessive haste.
Thus end those [feminine stems] ending in -ī.

Prau.ma.: *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.95). From the root *kruś* (to cry out), the word *kroṣṭṛ* is derived with the suffix *tun* according to the rule *ṣitanī*; however, with the suffix *tṛc*, the form is *kroṣṭṛ*. Both words denote a jackal.

In that regard, since the application of both [suffixes] would otherwise occur without distinction, this set of three sūtras is begun for the purpose of restriction: namely, that before a *sarvanāmasthāna* and in the feminine, only the form ending in *-tṛc* occurs; in the case of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and those following, both forms occur; but elsewhere, only the form ending in *-tuN* occurs. Thus, *kroṣṭuḥ* is the nominative singular derived from the stem ending in *-tuN*.
The nominative case [is used] after a word ending in *tṛc*. The suffix *vat* follows the word *tṛjvat*, which ends in the third case (*tṛjvat*).

Although an extended application (*atideśa*) is sixfold—based on cause (*nimitta*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), identity (*tādātmya*), scripture (*śāstra*), operation (*kārya*), and form (*rūpa*)—here, because of its predominance, it is the form alone that is extended. And that [form] is not...

He states the resulting conclusion— “in place of the word *kroṣṭu*”— with the intention that [the substitution] applies to any root beginning with *pac*, but specifically to *kruś* alone, because of its proximity, its semantic connection, and its phonetic similarity (*āntarya*). “For the sake of restriction” means for the purpose of preventing it from applying to other technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*).

Regarding *kroṣṭu*: [the substitution of] *anaṅ* [occurs]. Because it is subsequent to the elision [of the final *u*] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (P. 6.1.68), the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) takes place.

Although that lengthening could be obtained by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (P. 6.4.8), nevertheless, because it is subsequent, the rule *aptṛn* (P. 6.4.11) alone is more appropriate. Even when *anaṅ* has been applied, by the principle that "that which undergoes modification in one part is not different from the original," [the form remains valid].
Because it is a triplet (tṛctvāt). The sense is that otherwise, even if the substitution of the guṇa vowel had been made, the long vowel would not have occurred. [From] Pradīpa:
*rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24). In this context, there is another view that the letter *t* is also included by elision (*praśliṣyate*). By that [view]:

If, in place of the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), one were to establish the refined formulation *ṅyāpaḥ soḥ*, then forms such as *abibhar bhavān* would be established. However, in the case of *ajarghāḥ*, because the substitution of *c* for *j* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha*, the elision of the suffix *t* (*talopa*) does not take place. If it is objected that from the root *kīrt* (derived from *kīrtayati*) with the *kvip* suffix, the form *kīrt* should occur here [after the elision of the suffix], we reply: no.

One should state, "it does not apply when [the suffix] is not used according to its characteristic," because once the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been effected, the replacement by *naṭ* becomes difficult to obtain due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. As for the rule *num-acira-*:
[an objection is raised] that everything applicable within its own scope must be superseded by *repha*, since one adopts the perspective of a general consideration regarding what is to be superseded.

And so it will be stated: "It is an exception to [the rules for] *guṇa*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and *utva*. Thus, since there is no distinction, the augment *nuṭ* would also be barred by this [rule]. If it is asked, "How then can there be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)?
For such a conflict is impossible between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*)," [the answer is: True; for that very reason, in that particular respect—

Having refuted the objection regarding contradiction, one should be satisfied with the statement made by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The augment *nuṭ* [is applied] because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ*.
Thus end those [words] ending in *u*.

"Hūhū"—this is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) name. Regarding the word "aticamū," however, this is because of the statement: "And there is the inclusion of the original gender. Thus, the intention is that the older treatise stating "in this way, *aticamū* and so forth" is contrary to the Bhāṣya.

Prau.ma.: Regarding *varṣābhvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.84): Since the word *varṣābhū* is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), it would have been more appropriate to state this sūtra specifically within the section on feminine nouns. However, in the masculine gender, it is intended as a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*).
They explained that it should be construed somehow or other, but that is due to haste; for *dardura* is masculine—[as in:
"The words *bheka*, *maṇḍūka*, *varṣābhū*, *śālūra*, *plava*, and *dardura* [denote] a frog."
Thus says Amara; for he has prescribed the rule that there is no *dvandva* compound of words with different genders:
"The word *bhekī* refers to the plant *punarnavā* and is feminine, while *varṣābhū* refers to a frog and is masculine."
And from the *Yādavakośa*: "In the sense of a frog, there is *ṣaṇī*. There is also a variant reading, *dardure ṣaṇī*.
The term *ṣaṇī* is a masculine designation according to the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*). Regarding *dūbhati*: the root *dṛbhī* (meaning "to weave") belongs to the *tudādi* class.
As for the statement "it is derived": although Ujjvaladatta [lists] *dṛmph* with the second letter of the labial class (*pavargadvitīya*), [the form here is derived differently].
Although it has been explained that the absence of the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṛ* of the root *dṛbh* is established by way of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), nevertheless,
in other commentaries (*vṛtti*), it is stated that the suffix *ḍūap* is added to the root *dṛbhī* (meaning "to weave") and the augment *nam* is irregularly inserted. And this...

This is clear in the Mādhava-grantha. However, in the Daśapādī-vṛtti, it is stated that *darbhaṇaṃ* becomes *dṛmbhūḥ*, where the addition of the augment *num* and the substitution of an *anusvāra* are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātyate*). Since this vowel *ū* is not part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution *uvaṅ* does not apply; therefore, by the rule "iko yaṇ aci," there is the *yaṇ* substitution. And that [occurs] in the case of *ami*...

With the intention that [the present rule] is superseded by the two preceding rules—"pūrvaḥ" and "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ"—he provides the example *dṛnbhūm*, etc. Nor should one suspect the application of *yaṇ* here in the form *dṛnkara*; for in that case, only a meaningful (*arthavat*) element is taken, whereas this consists of the word *dṛn* and the word *bhū*.

The sense is that [the suffix] is meaningless. Thus, it results in the form *hūhūvat*. According to the opinion of Śrīpati, he says: *dṛn*. Mādhava, however, states that by the rule *andūdṛnbhū*, when the word *dṛḍha* is the upapada, the suffix *kū* is applied, and the substitution of *dṛn* for the upapada is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Regarding *dṛnbhū*: some say it is a tree, a specific species of serpent; others say it is a monkey. Regarding *dūnkara*:
here, the reading ending in *n* (*dṛn*) is primary, though for some there is also a reading ending in *m* (*dṛm*). It should be stated [in the rule] as "and *varṣābhv-*".

The letter *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). The intention is that what has not been mentioned must be determined by the force of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.

And so, having explained the Vārttika "varṣābhūpunarbhvaśca," the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This which is stated is too little; [it should be] 'after *varṣā*, *ṛt*, *kāra*, and *punaḥ*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] to *bhuva*.'"

"It is established"—that is not so; for even then, that which is qualified by the suffix *aṇ* is something else. Indeed, the suffix *aṇ* itself is not a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, the distinction is this: in the short-vowel reading, there is *uvaṅ* for that preceded by *kāra*, and likewise in the long-vowel reading, there is *uvaṅ* for that preceded by *kara*. "Like *svayambhū*"—but according to the Easterners (*prācām*)...

The words *dṛnbhū* and *kārābhū* are cited as being like the word *varṣābhū*; the sense is that they should be disregarded because they lack a valid etymological basis. Thus end those [words] ending in *-ū*.
Prakriyā-mañjarī:
*nṛ ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.6). Here, from the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the term *ubhayathā* ("in both ways") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
However, the term *chandasi* ("in Vedic [usage]") has ceased to apply (*nivṛtam*). Therefore, [the form] *nṛṇām* occurs in the verse: *cintājarjaracetasāṃ bata nṛṇām*.
Some maintain that the phrase "What talk can there be of peace? You alone are the one to be approached by men" [is implied here].

That is incorrect, because the rule *nṛ ca* would then be rendered redundant, as its purpose is already accomplished by the preceding rule. Furthermore, regarding the point that some maintain the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are carried over from the preceding rule; [this too is incorrect].

That too is incorrect, because we observe such variations without distinction. For instance, in the mantra "dhātā dhātṝṇām," the Taittirīyas recite a short vowel, whereas the Bahvṛcas recite a long one; this is the general direction of the argument.
Thus end those [stems] ending in short *ṛ*.
The meaning is that instead of saying *gotaḥ*, one should say *otaḥ*. Thus,
having raised the objection that in the case of *gām*, since the *vṛddhi* (guṇa) would apply first due to its higher status [in the order of rules], the substitution of *ā* would not occur,
the [author] states in the rule *āṬto'mśasoḥ* that the *vṛddhi* is superseded by the substitution of *ā* because the latter is otherwise without scope (*niravakāśatayā*).

The author of the Bhāṣya has stated this. Kaiyaṭa also says thereon: "In the rule *otaḥ*, the reading is *smṛtau*. Regarding this, some say: by means of the word *go*, which belongs to the *uṇādi* group, the word *dyo* itself is indicated through similarity, and not merely that which ends in the vowel *o*; therefore, [the forms are] *smṛtau*, *smṛtavau*, *smṛtavaḥ*.

To say "it is exactly so" contradicts that commentary; for if the status of being *ṇit* were admitted only for [the suffixes] following *go* and *dyo*, then the rule "āṬto'mśasoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.24), which prescribes the substitution of *āT* [for the final vowel], would find its scope in cases such as *anityādiḥ*. And thus, in the case of *gām*:

Since the vṛddhi [substitution] would be unavoidable due to its higher status, it follows that the ātva mentioned in the cited Bhāṣya would be both subverting and without scope; such is the direction of the argument.
Thus end the [entries on] vowels.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *rāyo hali* (Pāṇini 7.2.85), the word *rāyaḥ* is masculine according to Amara’s statement, *arthare vibhāṣā api*, and because of usages such as *saṃ rāyā bhūyasā sṛja*. The Bhāṣya states: *rāyiḥ chāndasaḥ* ("the form *rāyiḥ* is Vedic").
Regarding this,

Kaiyaṭa states in the commentary on the rule *vānto yi* that the form [of the word] with the suffix *kyac* is intended to illustrate its Vedic character, but not the simple [form] itself; he further mentions another view that even the simple form is Vedic.
Thus end those ending in -ai and -au.
According to Amarasimha, *ṭhglormṛṅkaḥ kalānidhiḥ* (the moon is called *ṭhglormṛṅka* and *kalānidhi*). Similarly, one who protects people (*janān*) is *janauḥ*.
By the rule *jvaratvara*, the substitution *ūṭh* is applied; by the rule *etyedhati*, *vṛddhi* is substituted [for the *e* of *eti*]. Thus, the forms *janāvau*, *janāvaḥ*, and so forth, are derived.
Thus end the masculine nouns ending in vowels. Now begins the section on feminine nouns ending in vowels.

It causes delight. By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender), the suffixes beginning with *su-* (case endings) are applied because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

As for the argument that it is because of the ending in *-ā*, and as for what they have explained—that although it is not a nominal stem due to having a suffix, the meaning is that the separate mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [in the rule] applies here—that is incorrect.
Since it has already been stated that the inclusion of the term *ṅī* serves another purpose, [consider the following]: regarding the rule *eṅhrasvāt*,
because it is subsequent and because the word possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), once the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) has been applied by the rule *saṃbuddhau ca*,
the elision of the final consonant and the *ṅī*-suffix as prescribed by *halṅyābbhyaḥ* would not apply.
The point is that even if [the substitute] were treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva) for the purpose of being called *āp*, it lacks the form of the vowel *ā*;

furthermore, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) has been rejected by incorporating the long vowel *ā* through *praśleṣa* (coalescence). Even according to the literal reading [of the rule], the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "eṅhrasvāt" is more logically applicable because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules].
Prakriyā-mañjarī:

*yāḍāpaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.113). Although it would have been more appropriate to state simply *yaṭ*, there is no concern regarding the occurrence of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), because that very rule is set aside by the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*.

Nevertheless, one might suspect that the vowel *a* [in the rule *āṭaśca*] is intended for the purpose of pronunciation; therefore, *yāṭ* has been added for the sake of clarity. As for the example "āṭaśca" cited by the ancients, that is incorrect, because since the *ṭ* of *yāṭ* and *syāṭ* functions as a marker for the entire group (*samudāyānubandha*), there is no occurrence of *āṭ* here.
Prau.ma.: *sarvanāmnaḥ syāḍḍhrasvaśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.104). The long vowel [in the sūtra] is for the sake of the previous [rule]. Here they say:
let the sūtra simply be *sarvanāmno'suṅ ca*. And thus, when *yāṭ* follows...

Because [the suffix] has the marker *ṅ*, the substitution of *asuṅ* for the final vowel and following consonant is established by the rule *sarvasyāḥ* and so forth. The purpose of adding the marker *ṭ* and the prescription of the short vowel must be considered. Herein lies the consideration: if only *asuṅ* were stated, forms such as *amuṣmai* would not be established. In reality, however, [the rule] is *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ*.

It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *suṭ yāṭo hrasvaśca* (the augment *suṭ* and the short vowel for *yāṭ*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of a short vowel being substituted for *yāṭ* itself, because of the force of its long-vowel pronunciation.
Even if a short vowel were pronounced, the force of the letter *a* itself would suffice to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of *ataḥ*.
It should be noted that this is possible.

*Prakriyā-pradīpa*: Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā jasi* (Pāṇini 1.1.32), this is an optional provision (*vibhāṣā*) because [the application of the previous rule] would otherwise not apply due to the word being secondary (*gauṇa*). As for what they say—namely, "not in a *bahuvrīhi*"—[that refers to a different context].

Regarding the phrase "this being the prohibition that would otherwise apply": this is only from a superficial perspective, because that [prohibition] pertains to the category of words beginning with *sarva* within the non-worldly grammatical operations (*alaukika-prakriyā*), whereas this [present rule] pertains to the domain of compound formation (*samāsa*). As for "the other" (*itarā*): they say that "the one which is prior is its 'other'."

Regarding the term *uttarapūrva*: because of its impulsive nature, there would arise the undesirable consequence of reversing the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). Regarding the phrase *tīyasya*:

this [application of the suffix] is indeed necessary for both masculine and neuter genders. The point is that since the desired form is established by this very rule, the sūtra "vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyā" need not be composed.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: *māturmātajputrārthamarhate*. In the case of the word *mātṛ*, when it denotes a mother who is worthy of her son, the substitute *mātaj* occurs in place of *mātṛ*.

When praise (*ślāghyatva*) is to be expressed: *gārgīmātṛkaḥ* means "one whose mother is Gārgī. Its vocative is *he gārgīmāta*. This [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the compound-final suffix prescribed by the rule *nady-utaś-ca*. However, where praise is not to be expressed, but there is merely a statement of the actual form (*svarūpa-kathana-mātra*), in that case—

*Kabevana*—the word *gārgīmātṛka*. Regarding the statement that "an item ending in *-ā* is a limb (*aṅga*)," some who explain the rule *yāḍāpaḥ* have said: "In *atikhaṭvāyai*, because it is derived from a technical definition (*lākṣaṇikatva*), the suffix *yāṭ* does not apply;
however, in *atisarvāyai*, it would not [apply] either. This is due to haste. For, in the domain of extended application (*atideśa*), [the condition of being a stem ending in *-ā* is not restricted].

The paribhāṣā "the rule applies to that which is taught by its specific technical name" (lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā) operates here; otherwise, the extension [of the rule] would be rendered useless. Consequently, *yāṭ* is unavoidable. However, there is no possibility of *syāṭ* at all, because it is excluded by the fact that it is listed among both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). As for the phrase "some, however": this refers to the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* and others.

Prakriyā-mañjarī: *ṅiti hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.54). This is an optional rule where there was no prior application (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*). It is formulated because, while the short vowels (*hrasva*) would not have been subject to this rule otherwise, for the other two [long vowels], the prohibition *neyaRuvaṅsthānau* (Pāṇini 1.4.4) would have applied; thus, it is introduced to cover all cases.

The three terms *īdūtau*, *strīśabdabhinnau*, and *nityastrīliṅgau* are qualifiers of *ī* and *ū*; however, for the short vowels (*hrasvayoḥ*), only *striyām* applies, and not the full extent of *nityastrītvam*. Otherwise, [the rule would apply] to words like *iṣu* and *aśani*, which possess both genders.

Furthermore, even though all *liṅga*s (grammatical genders) may possess femininity (*strītva*), they would not attain the status of a river (*nadītva*), because according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, there is an absence of "constant femininity" (*nityastrītva*); and even in Haradatta’s opinion, there is no instance to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "constant" (*nitya*) regarding the short vowel portion. For this very reason, one should abandon the mention of the word *ākhyā* (name/designation) and use only the word *strī* (female).
It is extracted and connected [to the rule]; this is what he says: "The vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*, as well as *i* and *u*, [are short] in the feminine.

Regarding the phrase "when *āṬtva* would have been obtained," the intention is that it occurs because of its higher status (*paratvāt*). As for the explanation given by the ancients (*prācā*) under the rule "āt"—namely, that it refers to [stems] excluding those designated as *ghin* or *nadī*—that is not the literal meaning of the syllables; rather, [it is an interpretive gloss].
This is obtainable from the two preceding sūtras. Thus, the omission of the sūtra *idudbhyām* by the ancients is merely due to oversight (*prāmādika*). [Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.77: *aci ra ṛtaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *aci ra ṛtaḥ*: this refers to the substitution of *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva*. For instance, in the case of *tisra tiṣṭhanti*, there is the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *ṛto ṅi* (Pāṇini 7.3.110); in *tisraḥ paśya*, there is the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* according to the rule *prathamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102);
and in *priyatisra āgataḥ* and *priyatisraḥ svam*, there is the *utva* substitution according to the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.4.132).

The meaning is that "ratva" (the substitution of *ra*) is an exception (*apavāda*); the sense is that, when considering exceptions in general, everything that would otherwise apply to its own domain is sublated. However, when considering specific cases, by the maxim "exceptions [sublate] what lies between," there would be a sublation only of the long vowel and the *utva*, but not of the *guṇa*.

It is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others that the two positions regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are established in accordance with the requirements of the specific cases (*lakṣya*), just like the positions regarding the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).

As for what they [the commentators] have explained— that the word "exception" (*apavāda*) indicates sublation (*bādhakatva*)— it is [to be understood] by means of the "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

The intention [of the opponent] is that [the *vipratiṣedha* rule] also subverts a *guṇa*. That is baseless and faulty. As for what Prasādakṛt stated—"the meaning is that *guṇa* is the subverter by means of the prior *vipratiṣedha*, while the other two are subverters by means of the subsequent *vipratiṣedha*"—that is not correct, because the injunction (*vidhi*) has not yet fulfilled its purpose.
Nor do the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṅasi* have their purpose fulfilled [by the substitution of *yaṇ*], because that purpose has already been served by *yaṇ*.

[The reason is] "because of the qualification of 'three' and 'four'. For the sense is that, due to being directly stated (*śrutatvāt*), the qualification "in the feminine" (*striyām*) applies only to "three" and "four," and not to the *aṅga* (stem). Thus, in the example *priyatri*, here—
They explain [as follows]: since "woman" (*strī*) is the referent of the compound, the *bahuvrīhi* form of the body-part (*aṅga*) resides there;
however, because the word "three" (*tri*) applies only to the masculine and neuter genders, the substitute *tisṛ* does not occur, and so forth. Here, this must be said:
in the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) view, the word "three" has multiple meanings; but in the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) view, however—
[The word *tri*] indeed occurs in the feminine; how then can its occurrence in the masculine and neuter be consistent?

The truth of the matter here is this: it is intended that the function [of the compound] here is *jahatsvārthā* (one that abandons its own meaning), according to the usage of the target forms (*lakṣya*).
Therefore, the expression "the limb (*aṅga*) of a woman" is perfectly correct. As for the word *tri* denoting both masculine and neuter—

By way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). For the established doctrinal proclamation that "the *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense" is to be explained in this very manner. Likewise, in the case of *priyātasā pumān*, the application [of the feminine suffix] to the word *strī* is also solely by way of its former state, according to the view that the word does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*).
However, the intended meaning here is *tri* and *catur*, which convey a number residing in a feminine [referent].

The textual passage from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "pratyayotarapadayośca" serves as the authority for this point. As for the phrase "because of its non-eternality," the inclusion of the term *ac* in the rule "iko'ci" is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this matter.

For that [prohibition] was indeed made to prevent *num* in the vocative; because even when *num* occurs in the case of *bhyām* and so on, its elision is possible. Furthermore, since the vocative suffix is elided by *luk*, the application of *num* would have to be stated by means of the rule for "characteristics based on a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). And the rule for "characteristics based on a suffix" is established by the fact that the prohibition "not when [a suffix] is marked by *lu*" (*na lumatā*) is non-universal (*anitya*).

That it is difficult to obtain [only] in the absence [of something else] is clear from the source-text (*ākara*). Nor should one insist that this impermanence (*anityatva*) has as its object only the qualities of a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sambuddha*), for there is no obstacle to accepting it in other cases as well, in accordance with the observed instances (*lakṣya*). And thus:
The two forms *priyatisṛ* and *priyatri* have both been justified by Kaiyaṭa in the manner already described.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*), there is no lack of evidence here, for the very examples cited in the Bhāṣya, such as *priyatisṛṇi*, serve as proof in this regard. [This applies] when *dvir̥c* has become *atva* and *āp* follows.

The meaning is that even the substitution of *ya* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* (i.e., *tad-*, etc.), which is caused by the occurrence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), serves as the cause for the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; this is because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is not universally applicable, and because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "na yāsayoḥ."

Regarding the term "iyādeśa": the substitution of *iy* prescribed for [the word] beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) occurs only in the four cases beginning with the nominative (*ausādiṣu*) when the feminine word *strī* is used as a secondary member (*upasarjanatve*) in the masculine; it does not occur elsewhere, because it is superseded by the previously mentioned rules such as *guṇa*, *nābhāva*, and so forth. This is the meaning.
*Prau.ma.*:
"neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī" (Pāṇini 1.4.4). Those two in which something stands are called *sthānau*; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
The compound "neyaRuvaṅsthānau" is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound meaning "the substitutes for *iy*, *u*, and *aṅ*."

He states the meaning of the result: "the status of *iy* and *uvaṅ* for which [two vowels]. This prohibition applies only where *iy* and *uvaṅ* are produced; however, where [the substitution] would be set aside by an exception (*apavāda*), there is no prohibition. It is for this purpose that the term *sthāna* (status/position) is included.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

"vāmi" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.33). Although the ancient commentators maintain that this rule provides an option (*vikalpa*) for the previously established prohibition (*niṣedha*), nevertheless, when a prohibition is made optional, it results effectively in an option for the positive injunction (*vidhi*). Thus, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that [injunction] alone is adopted.
