[The word] *aci* [in the sūtra]—what is the purpose? [Consider] *yuvābhyām*. However, if [the word *aci* were not present], then from the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86), [the substitution would apply] by virtue of the rule *rāyo hali* (Pāṇini 7.2.85).

The word *hal* is understood [from the previous rule]. In that case, let *aci* not be mentioned here, since the desired result is established by elimination alone. [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.89)]—[the sūtra] *yuṣmadasmadoḥ*. [The commentary says: "When followed by a consonant (*hal-ādau*)."
This [form] is established either by the inclusion of *ac* (vowels) in the term *aci* or by the complete drying up [of the vowel].

Or it is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "rāyo halī" (Pāṇini 7.2.85). [Objection: But if this is so, what is the purpose of including the mention of "non-substitute" (*anādeśa*), for there is no substitute beginning with a consonant (*hal*)?
[Reply: Not so; because [the suffix] *bhyas* undergoes the substitution of *sat* (i.e., *bhyām*). However, in the alternative view (*pakṣa*) where [the substitution does not apply],...

It should be understood that the mention of *anādeśa* (non-substitution) here is for the purpose of ensuring the application [of the rule] even in the case of *aci*. Regarding the phrase "in both views": one should not argue that, in the view where there is elision of the final letter (*antyalopa*), the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneity) would apply—overriding the *pararūpa* (single substitution with the subsequent vowel)—on account of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*.

This is because the purpose of pronouncing the letter *a* is fulfilled by its non-removal (*anivṛtti*). [From the *Prakriyāmañjarī*: "After *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *ṅsi* becomes *aś*"] || *Yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso'ś* || The presence of the indicatory letter *ś* is for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Otherwise, indeed—

The rule *ādeḥ parasya* would apply. Nor is it redundant, because by means of the designation as a substitute (*ādeśa*), the purpose is to prevent the application of *yatva*. Nor should it be argued that even when there is a substitution of a constituent part, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) remains unsubstituted; for [the principle] holds that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words."
This is established by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). This very fact [of the rule] makes it known that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words.

The meaning is that the application of the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) rests only upon those elements that possess meaning. However, forms such as *sic*, *caṅ*, and others should be understood—even though they are meaningless—to function as substitutes by virtue of the force of specific grammatical rules.
However, this must be noted: in the view that the final *y* and *l* are elided, the form *aśaḥ* would result from *eṣaśaḥ*;

this must be prevented by the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*. This is provided that the said maxim applies only to operations concerning the *aṅga* itself, and not merely to those falling under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *aṅga*.

If it is argued that there is a persistent misconception here, it should be explained as follows: by the rule *ato guṇe*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied, and thus the substitute *aś* becomes identical in form to the original *akāra*; it does not undergo any modification.

As for the claim that *aś* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *syādeśa*, that is not correct; for at the time when the substitution of *aś* is set to operate, [the condition] remains...
Because there is no elision, the substitution of *sy* does not apply.

Regarding the word *bhāvinaḥ*: the intention is that once the *śeṣe lopaḥ* elision has taken place, the augment *suṭ* would apply because the stem ends in the vowel *a*; however, it is precluded by the force of the designation of the entire form including *suṭ* as the *sthānin*. But according to the view that *śeṣe lopaḥ* refers to the elision of the *ṭi* (the final phoneme), the mention of *suṭ* would indeed be redundant. [This applies] to *ākam*.

The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of homogeneous vowels); otherwise, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) would apply. Nor can it be argued that the explicit pronunciation of the long vowel *ā* is purposeless; for it serves its purpose by preventing the substitution of *et* (the single substitute for *e* + *a*), just as in the case of *abhyam*. Here, in the two rules "yuvāvau dvivacane" and "tvamāvekavacane"...

It has been explained that the words *dvivacana* (dual) and *ekavacana* (singular) do not refer to the suffixes themselves, but rather to their meanings. He demonstrates the result of this [explanation] with the passage beginning "when being compounded," etc.
Regarding the phrase "duality and singularity": even in the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, number is also included.

The sense is that [the pronoun] denotes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). "The meaning of the compound" means the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). "If it has another number" means if it has a number other than the number residing in the meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
Regarding the word "are" (*staḥ*), even the understanding based on what was previously the case arises solely by virtue of resorting to the fact that the rule depends on the actual meaning.

The meaning is that because [the word *vacana*] is accepted [in its primary sense], if [the rule were applied] with reference to a suffix (*pratyaya*), those two [forms] would not occur, and thus there would be an instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Similarly, in the fourth verse as well, by stating "but *yuvau* and *tvamau* are not," an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when a suffix follows is indicated. Thus, the conclusion is that the status of being "referential" (*arthaparatva*) is resorted to in order to avoid both under-extension and over-extension. Nor is there a contradiction with the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), because that maxim is set aside precisely by the force of the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*). For otherwise, one would simply have said "in duality" (*dvitve*) and "in singularity" (*ekatve"); for it would have been possible to explain it as: "of that case-ending which occurs in duality and singularity, [there is] *ām*. This is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase *atitvākam atimākam*: although in the rule *sāma ākam*, the mention of *suṭ* is not a qualifier of the substituendum because it is sublated, nevertheless, it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, only that *ām* which is to be preceded by *suṭ* must undergo the substitution of *ākam*. And this [substitution] does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*).

The suffix *ākam* does not apply [to the word *sambhavati*]. Furthermore, when a collective designation (*samudāyanirdeśa*) is employed, no third alternative exists apart from being either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nor is the status of the original bases (*sthānitva*) here indicated as distinct for the augment *suṭ* and the suffix *ām*, nor for the particle *ca* and the dual number.

Because of its absence. However, if the compound *sa-ām* were explained as a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*), and by the force of suitability (*yogyatā*) the word *s-* were understood to refer specifically to *suḍ*, even so, if the inclusion of *suḍ* were merely taught as an incidental addition (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*), then the compound would not be formed. But in other cases...
[The opponent argues: "Because of the intention to express them together (*sāhatya-vivakṣayā*), there is no possibility of the suffix *ām* occurring in its isolated form.
To this, the following must be said: first of all, the statement that "for that *ām* which is to have *suṭ* subsequently" and so forth is refuted;
for there can be no connection with *suṭ* for an *ām* that has already been superseded by *ākam*. If it is argued that "*suṭ* occurs for *ākam*," [we reply:]...

In that case, one should indicate that very [element]. If it is argued that the substituend (*sthānin*) is indicated through a mediated relationship by means of the substitute (*ādeśa*), then alas! in forms such as *yuṣmākam*, the augment *suṭ* would be heard. If it is argued that it is not heard because of the force of the technical designation *sāman*, we say no; for the designation...

Because its purpose is fulfilled by the exclusion of the secondary meaning (*gauṇavyāvṛtti*), it lacks the necessary capacity (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, the objection raised regarding the status of being a subsequent injunction (*anvācayaśiṣṭatva*) concerning the collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) is also untenable; for since there is no possibility of the word being used alone when the intention is to express their conjunction (*sāhitya*), such a contingency does not arise.
Only that [the *ām*] remains; yet even that is not [the case],

because the coexistence (*sāhitya*) of the *ām* existing in the state of grammatical derivation and the *suṭ* imagined as occurring at a later time is accepted solely through a single cognition, just as in the expression "this is the seer of the past and the future."

If it is argued that in those [other systems] the relationship exists between two things within a single view, here too it is the same, as it exists within a single substitute (*ādeśa*). And thus, in the rule *irayoḥ*, in forms such as *dadhre*— where the *jha* of the root *dhā* is replaced by *ir*,
the *ā* is elided, and *ra* is substituted— the substitution of *ra* finds its purposeful application in roots such as *kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *bhṛ*.

When this has been done, it is established in the authoritative treatise (*ākara*) that because of the dual-number designation in the rule *irayoḥ*, the substitution of *re* is applied once again even to that which is derived through grammatical derivation (*lākṣaṇika*). In the term *irayoḥ*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a pair of similar items);
however, in the term *sāma*, it is a *dvandva* (copulative compound). The intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*) is indeed the same in both cases.
In reality, however, in the rule *sāma ākam*, the suffix *ām* alone is also indicated by means of *tantra*.

Because that [suffix] possesses the property of having a final vowel (*amtva*) through its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), and because it is accompanied by the augment *suṭ*, the rule *sāma* applies. But in the case of secondary (gauna) usage, the operation terminates at the very first application. For this very reason, in the section on the remainder (*śeṣe*).

Even the identity of the result is established by means of the alternative view that there is elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*). In any case, one should not persist in attempting to justify the forms *atitvayām* and *atimayām*, which have been conjectured by some; for [the correct forms are] *atitvākām*, *atimākām*, and so forth.
This is the direction [of the argument], since it has been illustrated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself.
Regarding the phrase "of the two [words] characterized by the sixth case (genitive) and so forth":

this is obtained from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the word "of every *pada*. However, he will explain that the mention of the term "standing" (*sthagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the operation] occurs only when the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is actually present and not when it has been elided. [The example is] "by all the Vedas."

"May Govinda protect you; may Kṛṣṇa always protect us"—this reading of the ancients has been rejected, because [the word] "us" (asmān) does not apply here due to its not being situated within the same sentence. This is because of the mention of the term "standing" (sthagrahaṇāt).

The verb *tiṣṭhati* here functions in the sense of "not abandoning" (*ahāni*). As in the example, "Stay [at] the appointed time, O Sugrīva," it is understood as "do not abandon the appointed time. Therefore, the meaning is that the substitutes occur only when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth are not abandoned.
Thus, in the case of *yuṣmatputraḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "the son of you two" (*yuvayoḥ putraḥ*) or "the son of you all" (*yuṣmākam putraḥ*). [This occurs] after a word (*padāt*).

The word "para" (subsequent) is used in order to bring about the status of being subsequent; however, it was not employed by the ancient [grammarians]. In that case, since the substitution would simply not occur due to the absence of being subsequent to a word (*pada*), what is the purpose of including the term *sthā*?
Prau.ma.:
*na cavāhāhaivayukte* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.24). Regarding the phrase *cādipañcaka*: the meaning is that there is a connection with any one among these five, beginning with *ca*.
Regarding the word *yukta*: the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when the gender is neuter.

Prau.ma.: *paśyārthaiścānālocane* (Pāṇini 3.1.137). Regarding the term *paśyārthaiḥ*: precisely because of this [rule], the suffix *śa* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) due to the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*). Thus, *darśanam* becomes *paśyaḥ*. And here, that refers merely to cognition (*jñānamātra*), just as in the rule *adarśanaṃ lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.60), where it does not mean only visual perception (*cākṣuṣajñāna*).
Because of the prohibition [found in the rule] "not when there is no visual observation," he says this: "by means of objects of non-visual knowledge.

Regarding the word "devoted" (*bhakta*), etc., they have explained here as follows: one should connect the meaning thus—"for the very same reason that you are devoted to Hari, I too am devoted. However, if by the word "thereby" (*tena*) devotion...

The reason for protection is being pointed out; therefore, if it were established as dependent [on another], there would be no subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) when saying "you yourself" or "this very one. To this, the following must be said:
first of all, the claim that there is no status of subsequent reference in the case of a dependent establishment is inconsistent.

For an *ādeśa* (original injunction) is indeed a primary rule (*vidhi*). A subsequent injunction for something else, intended for the sake of a particular [operation], is an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), but it does not inherently contain the sense of independence, because that is not the literal meaning of the word and because it is not so defined in the technical treatise (*śāstra*).
Nor should it be argued that such a meaning is merely inferred from observing its usage in practice.

For instance, in such examples as "vanyadvipenonmathitā tvagasya" (the bark of this tree was stripped by a wild elephant) and "athainamadrestanayā śuśoca" (then the daughter of the mountain grieved for him),

the form *ena* is seen even though there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*). If it is argued that in those cases the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is not expressed by the word itself, we say no.
"Therefore, having violated the injunctions of the Creator,
he has become a guest of the abode of Death"—
because of such usage by Māgha, this [rule] is contradicted; however, "this timid one is at night" is not an injunction.

Rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, the expression "this [which] him" is not contradictory. This being the case, the labor of supplying the word *yat* (in the sense of "by which you are devoted") is useless; instead, the connection is simply "by that he protects. Furthermore, because the subject matter has already been introduced, there is no requirement for the word *yat*; such is the direction of the argument. Here, [the word] "by that" (*tena*)...

The word *vidyamānam* exists; therefore, *hariḥ* ending in the nominative case follows it, and [the following word] undergoes substitution. Likewise, after the word *trāyate*, there is *saḥ* ending in the nominative case. One should not be deluded into thinking that *trāyate* belongs to a different sentence; rather, [the construction is]: "May that Hari protect you."

Because of the connection with multiple factors through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application). Furthermore, even if *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) is accepted, there is no loss of the status of being a single sentence as defined by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which has a single finite verb is a sentence" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*). [Pradīpa on Pāṇini 8.1.72].

Regarding the term *āmantritama*: even in the formulation of technical definitions (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the inclusion of that which ends in [the specified element] is understood by virtue of the capacity inherent in the creation of a major technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*). *Āmantrita* means "that which is addressed.

By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the term applies to the instrument used for that purpose. And it is that which ends in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*) which is addressed, not the bare stem alone.
With the intention that [the word] ends in a case-ending, he says: "tadantam" (ending in that). Prakriyākaumudī: "The preceding vocative is as if non-existent" (Pāṇini 8.1.72):
"āmantritampūrvam". As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the vocative] preceded by its qualifier [is as if non-existent]— [End of excerpt]

Some say that these substitutions do not occur when there is a vocative preceded by another vocative, provided that the [subsequent] vocative is excluded from the others. In this regard, the phrase "some say" (kecit) is inappropriate, because the stated meaning is already established by the present sūtra itself. Furthermore, as for what they have explained—that this is the meaning of the three sūtras—[that too is incorrect].
This is not so, because that [statement] does not touch upon the meaning of the third sūtra. [The sūtra is:

*pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130). [The phrase] "of its constituent part" (*tadavayavasya*) is used because of the rule: "A substitute takes the place of that which is being specifically indicated" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśāḥ*).
This is obtained through the conventional designation.
Thus ends the section on the self-controlled.

Regarding the form *agnimanth-* as in "he churns fire" (*agniṃ manthati*): this very form arises from the roots *mathnāti* and *manthate* with the suffix *kvip*. However, because [the root] begins with an *idit* vowel, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Thus: *agniman*, *agnimanthau*, *agnimanthaḥ*. [Roots] ending in *tha*.

"the syllable *ṅ*": the meaning is "due to proximity" (*āntaratamya*). Regarding "between a short vowel and a consonant": the meaning is that for a consonant, a short vowel is slightly similar, whereas a long vowel is dissimilar. And as for "it has been stated": the remainder [of the sentence] is "by the author of the Vārttika. Some, however...

Because the former [rule] already provides for the substitution of *m* with *u*, they cite the latter [rule] as an example where *m* does not become *u*. Since that was not mentioned at the beginning of the Bhāṣya, it has been disregarded.
[Prakriyākaumudī]: *uda īt* (Pāṇini 6.1.131).
"uda īt": this is an exception to [the rule regarding] the vowel *a*. [The following words] end in *c*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14): here, the phrase *adhātoḥ* is separated as an independent injunction (*yoga-vibhāga*).
By virtue of this, the prohibition applies only to that which ends in *as* immediately following [the preceding rule], and not to that which ends in *at*.
Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others [have said this]. He demonstrates that [distinction] by stating: "that which is different from a verbal root and ends in *as*.
In the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "Both [are called] *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.5).
Since the word "both" (*ubhe*) is already established by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "two" (*dve*), the explicit mention of "both" (*ubhe-grahaṇam*) [is for a specific purpose].

He explains [the phrase] "for the purpose of understanding the aggregate" as "both together. For otherwise, in the case of *nenijati*, the acute accent on the initial syllable— by the rule "the first [syllable] of reduplicated [bases]" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*)— would apply alternatively to each [syllable] individually.

Prau.ma.: *Jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.6). The word *jakṣiti* is a separate term. By the word *iti*, only *jakṣiti* itself is referred to. In the analysis *iti ādir yeṣām*, it is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*.
This is what the *bahuvrīhi* compound expresses: "the other six elements. They end in *-t*.

The root *gup* means "to protect. When the suffix *kvip* is intended, there is an absence of the *āya* augment by virtue of the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31). [These are] those ending in *p*.
Prau.ma.: *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane'kañ ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.60).

Regarding the phrase *tyadādiṣu*: what is the purpose of the condition *anālocane*? [Answer: Consider the example *tat paśyati iti taddarśaḥ* ("one who sees that"). Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*.

However, words such as *tādṛśa* and others are derived etymologically even with an unreal meaning of their constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), because they are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words. For this very reason...

The statement "from the root *dṛś* in the sense of 'not knowing'" is thus consistent. However, in the Bhāṣya, the derivation is shown in the sense of the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*): "People see him as it were"; "he sees as it were";

the meaning is that he becomes an object of knowledge. In that case, even though the function [of the root] consists merely in the attainment of the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*), [the agentive sense is still applicable].
It is consistent [with reason] because it has the meaning of "non-knowledge" (ajñāna), since it is an obscuration that prevents the object from being made an object of cognition.
*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding the rule *naśervā* (Pāṇini 8.2.63): here, the phrase *jhali api* is un-Pāṇinian; furthermore, it would lead to over-extension in cases such as *naṣṭam*.
[The forms] *nāga*, *ti*, and the six *ṣaḍagakāḥ* are as before. [The section on] the *śāntāḥ* [consonants] is concluded.
Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.3.58):
"even when there is intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, or *śar*. [The commentary continues: "By way of being *ṣṭu*.
This means that after the *ru*-substitution and the *visarjanīya* have been applied to the *s* of *san*, the letter *s* optionally remains in one alternative by virtue of the rule *vā śari*.
Therefore, when there is an intervention by a *śar* sound, the *s* of a *sup* [suffix] undergoes *ṣatva*, while the preceding [consonant] undergoes *ṣṭutva*;
however, it does not become *ṣ* by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ," because of the prohibition "apadāntasya. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).
Such being the case, since the desired result is established by the mention of *sakāra*, the purpose of mentioning *śar* must be considered.

Regarding the phrase "from the commentary": Haradatta’s statement that [the rule] is impossible should be disregarded, because its occurrence is possible in the case of *suhinsu*; this is the intended meaning. As for the rule *saṃyogānta* (Pāṇini 8.2.23): one should not suspect that when this [rule] is to be applied, the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) is invalid due to being *bahiraṅga*.

Because the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is indeed extraneous (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on the designation of a word (*pada*), how is it that it was previously stated that there is no elision of the final consonant cluster when denoting *kāvya*, *kalatra*, or *śālva*? If you ask this, the answer is no; for in those cases, there is a prohibition of the [elision of] *yaṇ* by the rule "or rather, not, because of the elision of the *jhal* [consonant]."

Since it has been determined that there is no deletion (lopa) in either of the two views, it is appropriate to adopt the principle that "the preceding is more internal" (*antaraṅga*) for the sake of uniformity; for it is clear that the status of being a word (*padatva*), which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), and the deletion conditioned by it, find their final rest in the portion of the target form (*lakṣya*) that precedes [the suffix]. But here, however—

In the first two positions, since the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is evident, it is more logical that the principle "that which depends on an external cause is *bahiraṅga*" should apply for the sake of uniformity; this is the general direction.
[Examples include] *takṣi-rakṣibhyām*, etc. As for what they say regarding those who speak of "the white wheel" (*śuklaṃ cakram*) or "the bright [wheel]" (*śukraṃ vā*):

*Kalopaḥ*, *śul*, *śuklau*, *śulbhyām*, *caḥ*, *cakrau*, *carbhyām*, *śūḥ*, *śukrau*, *śūrbhyām*, and so forth—all of this has been refuted by this [rule]. However, there is this distinction: in the case of *tagraḥ*, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is beyond dispute; yet in that [other] case, even that [elision] is difficult to obtain.

Thus: *didhak*. Regarding the form *didhak*: Naimiṣīya has stated that because the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* (by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ*) is considered asiddha (*asiddhatvāt*), the final consonant is elided by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, and then the *ḍh* undergoes *jaśtva* to become *ḍ*, resulting in *didhaḍ*. However, that is an error, because the substitution of *gh* (by the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ḍh*.
Because of being watchful. Those ending in *ṣ*.
Regarding *vidāna*: the suffix *śatṛ* (ana) is replaced by *vasu* after the root *vid*, and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap*. Regarding *sedivān*:
the suffix *kvasu* is applied according to the rule "In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffixes *kvasu* and *kta* are used] after the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*.
Regarding *seduṣaḥ*: [one might object], "But surely, when there is a mention of a term with a specific *anubandha*, that which has a different *anubandha* is not included."
By way of explanation: it is appropriate that the *samprasāraṇa* applies only to the *vasu* [of the suffix] prescribed by the rule "videḥ śaturvasuḥ," and not to the *kvasu*;

this is true. However, the inclusion of the indicatory letter *ū* (in *vasu*) is for the purpose of including the *kvasu* in a general sense, since its status as having an *uk* indicatory letter (*ugit*) is established even through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. In this case...
The *kvasu* suffix is not cited after roots such as *gam* because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*). Nevertheless, poets employ it;

for instance, in examples such as "to him who has attained all excellences" (*śreyāṃsi sarvāṇy adhijagmuṣe*) and "him standing near the city" (*taṃ tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe*). Thus, even Vedic forms occasionally occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
This may somehow be resolved by relying on the general indicative rule (*jñāpaka*) found in *māsaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.63).
[From] *prau.ma.*—*puṃso 'suṅ* (Pāṇini 7.1.89): "The suffix *asuṅ* [is applied] after *pum̐s*. [The word] *vivakṣitaḥ* [is used]; therefore, in the case of *paramapumān*, [the rule applies].
Because [the rule for] *asuṅ* applies later, once *asuṅ* has been applied, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound belongs specifically to the vowel of *asuṅ*.

However, if the locative case were interpreted as "after" (*parasaptamī*), this would not be established; for if the acute accent were applied to the vowel of the masculine stem even before the arising of the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, then in place of the consonant—which is by nature subject to elision—[the desired result could not follow].

Because that would result in the substitution of only an unaccented vowel for the stem-final. Nor can it be argued that even though the accent has been applied to the letter *u*, it will be removed because it is not final, while the suffix *asuṅ* will be applied because it is final; for when an internal operation such as accentuation is to be performed, [the external operation must wait].
The sense is that [the substitution] *asuṅ* is not established because it is *bahiraṅga*. This has been stated in accordance with Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others.
In reality, however, the view that the locative case [in the rule] refers to what follows (*parasaptamī*) is also easily justifiable, on account of the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*.

It should be noted that this is because [the rule for] *asuṅ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the technical designation of the final member (*antaṅga-paribhāṣā*). Now, one might object: even in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), once *asuṅ* has been applied, the accent of the suffix would be superseded by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), which is "later taught" (*satiśiṣṭa*);
consequently, *asuṅ* itself would become acute, whereas it is desired that the vowel *ū* be acute—as in *pumān*, *pumāṃsam*.
If it is argued that this is because the reading is exactly the same in cases such as *paripāṭu*, that is true;
however, Haradatta and others maintain that by the force of making the suffix *ḍumsun* marked with the *ṇi*-sign (*nit*), the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) does not apply.
But is this not incorrect? For the rule "phiṣaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.7] applies only to those forms where the division between base and suffix is absent.
If it is argued that this is because of the application [of the rule], that is true; however, in certain cases where there is partial application (*sakhaṇḍa*), this is an indicator (*liṅga*).

Although this is already established by the principle "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*), nevertheless, the inclusion of the marker *n* is intended to indicate the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*.

The conclusion is: [the term *uṅ*] is for the purpose of pronunciation. The intention is that what was stated by the ancients—that it is "for the sake of *uṅ*"—and what was explained by his grandson—that the letter *u* is for the sake of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) of *uṅ*—is inconsistent.
[In the example] "he pumann," there is no long vowel because of the rule stating "except in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*). [In the example] "puṃsu."

When there is elision of a final conjunct (saṃyogāntalopa), the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ" applies; however, because this refers specifically to the *anusvāra* that replaces *num*, the rule "num-visarjanīya" does not cause the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding the phrase "in the vocative singular" (*asya sambuddhau*), this is based on an explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). As for what Haradatta and others [have said]...

They say: since it has been made known that in certain instances *anaṅ* alone is heard by the rule stating "when *sU* is to be expressed, *anaṅ* [is substituted] for [the final phoneme of the stem]," this [result] is established; however, that has already been refuted previously.
Alternatively, it may be resolved by means of the maxim regarding operations within a complex formation (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.107). Now, one might object: let only the vowel *au* be prescribed for *su*, since the form *asau* is already established through the substitution of *tyadādyatva*; what is the purpose of prescribing the elision (*lopa*) of *su*? Do not say so, for [without it] we would have *asakau*.

In the case of *strī*, if the suffix *ṭāp* were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ī* by the rule *pratyayasthāt*. Regarding *asuka*: in the absence of the substitution of *āṬ*, the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems occurs, followed by the substitution of *s* for *u*. Thus, *amuka* is incorrect, because the substitution of *m* (by *amu*) would subvert the substitution of *s*. Similarly, forms such as *amukī* and *amukaśarmā* are likewise incorrect.
Because it is only logical [to interpret the name] as beginning with *asukā*, *adakaḥ*, and *śarma*.
[From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "eta īd bahuvacane" (Pāṇini 7.3.103). If one were to take "bahuvacane" here in its technical sense...]

Even if [the forms] beginning with *amībhiḥ* were established by this rule, the form *amī* would not be established in the nominative plural (*jas*), because here the vowel *e* is not followed by a word in the plural number; therefore, he explains: "when expressing a plurality. [Prakriyākaumudī: *na mu ne* (Pāṇini 8.2.3)].

"na mu ne" || He says that *ne* is a locative case indicating the object (*viṣayasaptamī*)—meaning "when *nā* is to be applied. The implication is that otherwise, because the condition of being followed by a *ghi*-stem would be absent, the substitution of *nā* would not occur. [Objection: Even if *nā* has been applied in this way, would there not be lengthening by the rule "supi ca"? Regarding that lengthening...

Since the substitution of *m* for *n* (*mutva*) is not established [as a valid operation], he says: "And when [the substitution] has been made. Alternatively, the matter may be resolved by means of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Here, this should be noted: whereas one ought to say "amunā" just as one says "adhunā," the statement "na mu ne" is intended to provide a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule). By that means, forms such as *rāmaḥ* and *rāmebhyaḥ* are established.
[The rule] is established. Otherwise, how could the designation *it* and its subsequent elision apply to the letter *u* due to the non-establishment (*asiddhatā*) of *ru*?
Nor should it be argued that the designation *it* and its elision are not subject to non-establishment by virtue of the force of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) notation;
for [the rule] "ato roḥ" was stated to exclude the application of "haśi ca" in cases such as *tarumūlam*.

In this case, since the purpose [of the rule] is fulfilled by the mention of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) itself, one might argue: "Let there be no nasalization in the rule *ato roḥ*, as the desired result can be achieved simply by taking the word-form as it is explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*). However, even so, in the example *deva ruhī*, the application of the rule from the root *rudh* would be unavoidable. Rāma.

In such cases as well, since the hearing of the nasalized *r* (anunāsika) is being brought about [as a result], it can easily be said that the rule has its purpose fulfilled. And thus, when the *sthānivat* sūtra also applies, the visarga is obtained because of the status of being a *pada*. Furthermore, the mention of *aś* in the rule for *yatva* (the substitution of *y*) is here [justified] by such indications as "pratyayaḥ" and "paraśca."
"Liṅga" is the direction [for further elaboration].
Thus end the masculine stems ending in consonants.
Prakriyā-mañjarī: *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34). It was not stated simply as *naḥ* [for *dhaḥ*];
for if that were the case, in the word *naddham*, there would be the substitution of *na* by the rule *radābhyām* (8.2.42), and the application of *jhaṣastathoḥ* (8.2.40) would not occur.

In this regard, the following should be noted: regarding the example *svanaḍvāhī* cited for the *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there are good oxen," that is to be questioned, because it contradicts the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from what is not a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*). As for *gīḥ*: the root *gṝ* is used in the senses of swallowing and sound; [the suffix] *kvip* [is applied], and by the rule "ending in *a*" (*añta-*)...

In *it*, there is the substitution of *it* [for the vowel]. In *pūri*, there is lengthening by the rule *rvor upadhāyāḥ*. The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling. In *pūri*, there is the substitution of *ut* by the rule *ud oṣṭhyapūrvasya*. In *āśiṣau*, the substitution of *it* for the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *āśāsaḥ kvāv upasaṃkhyānam*.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs in the forms *śāsi* and *vasi*. Thus end the feminine nouns ending in consonants.

Regarding the term *anvādeśa*, the commentators explain it as "this very [word] again. They state that even though it is elided by *luk*, the designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies here by virtue of the power of the explicit statement (*vacana*). However, in reality, this should have been stated in the sūtra itself; forms such as *enam* and *enau* are established through the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class pronouns. In the neuter, before the case-ending *am*:

Even when the suffix *luk* has been elided, the substitution of *enad* occurs by virtue of the power of the pronunciation of the letter *t*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that substitution in the case of *etac-chritaḥ*, because [the rule for *enad*] is already fulfilled by its application to the internal *su* and *am* (locative and nominative singular) suffixes— which depend on a single word— whereas the compound-level *luk* is external.
Because that [rule] does not apply there. [Prakriyākaumudī:

*ro'supi* (Pāṇini 8.2.69)—as in *ahar bhāti*. However, the introduction of the form *ahan* by the Easterners (*prācām*) is inappropriate here; for how could it serve as the basis for forms such as *ahobhyām*?

The word *cidyojyam* [is used]; as for the word *asṛk*, this is clear in the work of Kṣīrasvāmin. Regarding *bahūrji* and *antayāt*, these are based on direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*). And thus says the Vārttika: "In *bahūrji*..."

Regarding the prohibition [of *num*], some hold that "the *num* comes before the final letter. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the first *vārttika* is rejected by adopting the meaning that "*num* applies to that which ends in a *jhal* consonant following a vowel (*ac*). But even so, for roots such as *urda* (in the sense of measuring) and *garha* (in the sense of censuring), when they take the *kvip* suffix, there would still be no *num*.
It must indeed be cultivated—this is because the authority of the sages increases progressively; such is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "of the elision" (*allopasya*):

the rule "that which is elided before *kva* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*" is not relied upon here, because that rule applies only in specific instances (*kvācitkatva*). It is precisely the rule "before *kva*, with respect to an operation (*vidhi*), [the elided element] is not *sthānivadbhūta*" that is intended.
"Because it is universal" is stated clearly in the original source (*ākara*).
Regarding "become horses and eyes": the meaning is five hundred and twenty-seven. To explain:
there are eighteen from doubling the final of the nine *sau* [forms]; and among the four *āṅ* forms, those used in the sense of worship...

In the case of the three [cases] ending in *ñ* and *t*, there are seven forms; however, the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form does not exist because it is *pragṛhya*. In the *jas* [case], there are twelve due to the optionality of both the doubling of *ñ* and the nasalization. By summation, there are thirty-seven. The same applies to the second [case]. In the *ṭā* [case], there are fourteen. In the *bhyām* [case]...

Forty-eight [forms], because *bha*, *pra*, *ag*, *varṇa*, *ya*, and *mān* are doubled. In the *bhis* case, there are twenty-four. In the *ṅi* case, seven. But there is no nasalized (*anunāsika*) form, because a single vowel (*ekāc*) is not *anaṇ*. In the *bhyas* case, it is like the *bhyām* case. In the *ṅsi* case—and in the group of five beginning with *ṅs*—there are fourteen. In the *sup* case, there are three for the meaning of "going."

By doubling the *k* and *ṣ*, and by nasalizing the *u*, there are twenty-four forms. Thus, in the *kuk* alternative, by doubling the six instances of *ṅ* and *ṣ* and nasalizing them, there are forty-eight.
In the absence of *kuk*, by doubling the three instances of *ṅ* and nasalizing them, there are twelve. [The total is] 18 + 7 = 25.
jas 12, am 18, āṬ 7, śas 12, ṭā 14, bhyām 48, bhis 24, ReĀ 7, bhyām 48, bhyas 48, ṅsi 14, bhyām 48, bhyas 48, ṅs, os, ām, ṅi, os, and sup each 14; thus sup totals 48.
Here, this is to be noted: when the augment *num* is applied to *jas* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), [the following occurs].

In the case of the two optional forms, there are six forms including the three *ñakāra*s; likewise for *śa* as well, so by summation there are twelve. And thus it is said: "The form is called 'graha-agni' (539) and 'bhūta'";
this refers to the view distinct from the Bhāṣya—such is the direction [of the argument]. As for what they say:
"In this manner, by means of the options of [repeated] duality and the omission of [repeated] duality, there is an increase from fifty-eight to one hundred and seventy-three.
This is to be considered; for the repeated duality lacks authoritative basis and leads to the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of forms.
And because there is no possibility of occurrence when [the suffix] *vṛddhi* is added to the forty-eight [forms], such is the direction [of the argument].

Regarding *tiraścī*: because it is a *bha*-stem, there is elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) by the rule "after an *ac*" (*acaḥ*). Because of the statement "elision of the *al*," there is the substitution of *tiri*.
*Suvāpī*: This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a lake (*saras*) in which the waters (*āpaḥ*) are beautiful (*śobhanāḥ*). Although the rule "ṛkpūḥ...

would have required the addition of the suffix *a* at the end of the compound, there is a prohibition by the rule "na pūjanāt. As for what the ancient commentators stated—that it occurs because [the rule] is not universal—that is merely a mistake. Furthermore, the rule "dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ... does not apply here.

In this regard, it will be stated that *apaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in a compound-affix (*samāsānta*). As for *supumāṃsi*: according to the view of the ancient [grammarians] who explain the word *suṭ* in the rule *puṃso 'suṅ*, this would not be established in the case of the *śas* [ending], and there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the [dative/ablative] ending *auṅ*. However, in our [view]...
The intention is that for those who state "in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*" exactly as prescribed by the sūtra, all desired results are achieved.
Thus end the neuter gender stems ending in consonants.
Now begins the section on indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Prau.ma.: *svarādinipātamavyayam* (Pāṇini 1.1.37). The compound *svarādinipāta* is a collective dvandva meaning "the words beginning with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*). *Svar* means heaven or the other world; *antar* means in the middle.

*Prātaḥ* means at dawn. *Punar* means again or in a special sense. *Sunutar* means in concealment. The five particles beginning with *svar* and ending with *repha* [are indeclinables]. *Uccais* means in a loud voice or greatly. *Nīcais* means in a low voice or slightly.
*Śanais* means slowness of action. *Ṛdhak* means truly.

Others [are used] in the senses of separation, speed, proximity, and lightness; *ṛte* is used in the sense of exclusion; *yugapat* means at one time; *ārāt* means at a distance or in the vicinity; *pṛthak* means separate or distinct; *hyas* refers to the past day; *divā* means during the day; *rātrau* means at night; and *sāyam* means at the beginning of night.
*Ciram* means for a long time; *manāk* and *īṣat* mean slightly; *imau* (in this context) mean small; *joṣam* means in happiness or silence;
*tūṣṇīm* means in silence; *bahiḥ* and *avaḥ* mean external; *samayā* means near or in the middle; *nikaṣā* means in the vicinity; *svayam* means by oneself; *vṛthā* means in vain.

*naktam* means "at night. *nañ* is used in the sense of negation. *hetau* means "in the sense of a cause" or "on account of. *iddhā* signifies "manifestness. *addhā* denotes both "clarity" and "certainty," though some say it refers to "reality" and "excellence. *sāmīpya* signifies "proximity" and "disgust. *vat* is the suffix *vati* prescribed by rules such as "that which is equal to that" (*tena tulyam*).
The suffix *pratyaya*—specifically that which is prescribed by the rule "upasargāddhātvarthe"—is not intended here [in the definition of *nipāta*], as seen in the example:

*yad udvato nivato yāsi*. The words *san* and *sanat* are eternal (*nitya*). The word *upadha* is used in the sense of distinction. *Tiras* is used in the senses of disappearance, horizontal direction, and contempt. *Antara* is used in the sense of the middle.

*Vinā* is used in the sense of "without. *Antareṇa* is used in the sense of exclusion. *Jyok* is used for time, abundance, questioning, swiftness, and the sense of "presently. *Kam* is used for water, the head, censure, and happiness. *Śam* means happiness. *Sahasā* is used for the sudden and the lack of reflection. *Vinā* is used in the sense of exclusion.

*nānā* is used in the senses of "many" and "without. *Svasti* is used for auspiciousness. *Svadhā* is used in offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). *Alam* is used in the senses of ornament, sufficiency, capability, prohibition, and negation. *Vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *śrauṣaṭ*—these are used in the offering of oblations (*haviḥ*). *Anyat* is used in the sense of "other. *Asti* is used in the sense of existence.

*Upāṃśu* denotes that which is uttered inaudibly or kept secret; *kṣamā*, forbearance; *vihāyas*, the sky or space; *doṣā*, the night; *mṛṣā* and *mithyā*, both meaning false or untrue; *mudhā*, in vain; *purā*, in the sense of not yet ceased, long past, or imminent future; and *mathas* and *mithas*.

These two [words] are used in the senses of "secret" and "meaning. *Prāyas* is used in the sense of "mostly" (*bāhulye*). *Mahus* is used in the sense of "again" (*punararthe*). *Pravāhukam* is used in the sense of "simultaneously" (*samakāle*) and "accomplished purpose" (*siddhārthe*). *Pravāhikā* is an alternative reading. *Āryahalam* is used in the sense of "force" (*balātkāre*). Śākaṭāyana, however, [states that] *ārya* is used in the sense of "obstruction" (*pratibandhe*), and *hala*...

He says: "In the case of prohibition and dispute. *Ābhīkṣṇya* means repetition. *Sākam* and *sārdham* have the sense of "together" (*saha*). *Namaḥ* is used in the sense of bowing. *Hiruk* is used in the sense of exclusion. *Dhik* is used in the sense of censure, contempt, and reproach. *Am* is used in the sense of haste and smallness. *Ām* is used in the sense of acceptance.

Some maintain that the suffix prescribed by the rules *kimettiṅavyaya* and *kāspratyayāt*, etc., is also included here. [Examples are: *papācatarām* (he cooked better) and *kārayāmāsa* (he caused to do).

*Pratām* is used in the sense of exhaustion (*glānau*); *praśān* has the same meaning as *samān*; *pratān* is used in the sense of expansion (*vistāre*). *Mā* and *māṅ* are these two [prohibitive particles].
Regarding "doubt" (śaṅkā) and "prohibition" (niṣedha):
it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Therefore, others should also be understood [as included]. For instance: *kāmaṃ* is used in the sense of "according to one's own will";
*prakāmam* in the sense of "excessively"; *bhūyaḥ* in the sense of "again"; and *sāmpratam* in the sense of "properly" or "rightly."

*param* means "but" (*kiṃtu*); *sākṣāt* means "directly" (*pratyakṣe*); *sāci* means "obliquely" (*tiryagarthe*); *satyam* means "partial acceptance" (*ardhāṅgīkāre*); *maṅkṣu* and *āśu*—these two mean "speedily" (*śaighrye*); *samvat* means "in the year" (*varṣe*); *avaśyam* means "certainly" (*niścaye*); *sapadi* means "speedily" (*śaighrye*); *balavat* means "excessively" (*atiśaye*); *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ*.

Thus in the *Prakāśa*: *aniśam*, *nityam*, *nityadā*, *ajasram*, and *santatam*—these denote continuity. *Uṣā* means at night. *Rodasī* signifies heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). *Ai* is used for acceptance and for Brahman. *Bhūḥ* refers to the earth. *Bhuvaḥ* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). *Jhagiti*, *jhaṭiti*, and *tarasā* mean instantly.

*Śairghye* (in slowness/delay); *suṣṭhu* in the sense of excellent praise; *duṣṭhu* in the sense of difficulty or hardship; *su* in the sense of worship or excellence; *aha* in the sense of wonder; *ku* in the sense of reproach and slight; *añjasā* in the sense of truth and speed; *mithu* in the sense of "two"; *bhājak* in the sense of slowness; *cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*.

*ciram*, *cirāt*, and *cireṇa*—these have the sense of "long. *astam* signifies destruction. *ānuṣak* signifies succession. *anuṣak* signifies following after. *amnás* signifies the past and the present. *stāne* is used in the sense of "fittingly" or "appropriately. *varam* is used when something is said to be "slightly" so. *sudi* refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). *vadi* refers to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
And so forth.

*Vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like; "vā syādvikalpopamayorevārthe'pi samuccaye" (vā may be used in the sense of option, comparison, the meaning of *eva*, and also in conjunction).
*Ha* is used in the sense of renown (*prasiddhi*). *Aha* is used in the sense of reverence (*pūjā*).

*eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and for impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). *evam* is used for referring back to what has been said (*uktaparāmarśa*). *nūnam* is used for certainty (*niścaya*) and for reasoning (*tarka*). *śaśvat* is used for repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), for the eternal (*nitya*), and for the sense of "together with" (*sahārtha*). *yugapat* is used for simultaneity (*aikakālya*). *bhūyas* is used for the sense of "again" (*punarartha*) and for excess (*ādhikya*). *kūpat* is used for inquiry (*praśna*).

And in the sense of praise. *Kuvit* is used in the sense of prosperity and in praise. *Ned* is used in the senses of apprehension, prohibition, deliberation, and conjunction. *Cet* is used in the sense of "if. *Caṇ*—this has the augment *ṇ* when it means "if," but when used for conjunction and so forth, it is without an indicatory marker (*an-anubandha*). *Kaccit* is used in an inquiry regarding something desired.

The particle *yatra* is used in the senses of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), intolerance (*amarṣa*), censure (*garhā*), and wonder (*āścarya*). For example: "I do not believe, I do not tolerate, I censure, or I am amazed that you would cause a *vṛṣala* to perform a sacrifice. The particle *na hi* is used in the sense of a counter-argument (*pratyārambha*). The particle *hanta* is used in joy (*harṣa*), dejection (*viṣāda*), compassion (*anukampā*), and at the beginning of a sentence. [The particles] *mākiḥ* and *mākiṃ*...
The three words *nakiḥ*, *mā*, and *nañ* are used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

While *mā* and *nañ* are mentioned among the *svarādi* (particles beginning with *svara*) [in Pāṇini 1.1.37], their inclusion here is for the purpose of establishing their status as *nipāta* (indeclinables). On this basis, the ancients maintain that their initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) is thereby established; however, this view is to be considered doubtful.

Since the desired result is achieved even by means of the *phiṭ-svara* accent, that which they say—that the inclusion [of these words] in the list beginning with *svar-ādi* is for the purpose of granting the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) even to those denoting substantial entities (*satva-vacana*)—is also to be considered. For otherwise, the word *mā*, when denoting the goddess Lakṣmī, would undesirably incur the status of an indeclinable. Therefore, the purpose of its inclusion in both lists must be examined.

In all these cases, *yāvat* and *tāvat* function as particles of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Regarding totality: "As much work as there is, so much has been done. Regarding limit: "Stay for as long as there is to be traveled.
Regarding measure: "As much as was given, so much was eaten. Regarding restriction: "Invite as many Brahmins as there are vessels."

*tvai* is used for emphasis (*viśeṣa*) and deliberation (*vitarka*). *Dvai* is used for deliberation (*vitarka*). *Nvai* is an alternative reading. *Rai* is used in the sense of giving (*dāna*) and disregard (*anādara*). *Rai* in *rai karoti* means "he gives. [Example: *tvaṃ rai kiṃ kariṣyasi* ("What will you give?").
*Śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are used in the offering of oblations (*havirdāna*). *Svāhā* is used in the offering to the deities (*devatābhyo dāne*). *Svadha*... [is used in the offering to ancestors].

To the ancestors. The multiple readings of *śrauṣaṭ* and the others in both places are for the sake of distinguishing their accents. *Tuṃ* means the sound *tuṅ*. Having uttered a grave sound—i.e., having uttered *huṅ*. For instance, as in the illustration. *Khalu* is used in the sense of prohibition, sentence ornamentation, or certainty. *Kila*...

[The particle] *vā* [is used] in the senses of news (*vārtā*) and falsehood (*alīka*). Now, *atha* is used in the senses of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), immediately after (*anantara*), commencement (*ārambha*), inquiry (*praśna*), entirety (*kārtsnya*), authority (*adhikāra*), promise (*pratijñā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

This [particle] also belongs to the class beginning with *svar*. Therefore, although it denotes auspiciousness, it retains its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it possesses the nature of a particle (*satvārthatva*).
And so it is said by Śrī Harṣa: "Then,
having lifted the golden jars onto the interior of the altar-platform, which possessed the lovely splendor of a fourfold courtyard,
the group of matrons bathed the king’s daughter according to the family tradition."
For here, the phrase *snapayāmbabhūva* means "he performed an auspicious bathing.

The particle (*smā*), however, is auspicious by its very form, like the sound of a drum; it is read with a distinct modulation of the voice for the sake of clarity. The word *sma* denotes the past tense and serves as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*).
The word *ādaha* is used in the senses of beginning, injury, and reproach.
Regarding *avadatam*: here, because it is not a preposition (*upasarga*), the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* does not apply.
*Aham* is a substitute for a case-inflected form (*subanta*). By this [explanation], [the objection] that [the word] *kena* in the verse *geye kena vinītau vām* [is incorrect] is refuted.

This has been explained. For the word *vām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) used in the sense of "you two. The word *asti* is a substitute for a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). Similarly, *asmi* is used in the sense of "I.
*Tvām asmi vacmi* means "I speak to you. *Āha* means "he said" (*uvāca*). *Āsa* means "he was" (*babhūva*), and so forth.
*a* is used for addressing, censuring, and prohibition; *ā* for sentences and recollection; *i* for addressing, disgust, and wonder; *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *āṬ* for addressing;
*paśu* in the sense of "properly" (as in *paśu manyamānāḥ*, "regarding as proper"); and *śukam* in the sense of "speedily."

*yathākathāca* is used in the sense of disregard. *pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *he*, *hai*, and *bho*—these are used for address. *dyai* is used in the senses of "thus," "indeed," "contrariety," and "verse-filling. *viṣu* is used in the sense of "variously. *ekapade* is used in the sense of "suddenly" or "all at once. *yut* is used in the sense of "censure" and "cause. *ātaḥ* is used in the sense of "even from this" or "also from this."

It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). For example: *yat* and *tat* are used in the sense of cause (*hetu*); *āhosvit* in the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*); *sima* in the sense of totality (*sarvatobhāva*); *kaṃ* for filling out a verse (*pādapūraṇa*); *sukam* in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*); *anukaṃ* in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*); *śamvaṭ* in the sense of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and facing toward (*ābhimukhya*); *va* for filling out a verse and in the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*); *diṣṭyā*.

Thus: *ānande* (in joy); *cuṭua* and *cāṭua* (in endearing speech); *hum* (in reproach); *iva* (in similarity); *adyatve* (in the sense of "now" or "at this time"), and so forth. Here, this should be noted: although there is no distinction between the *svarādi* and *cādi* groups in that they are both *ākṛtigaṇas* (open-ended classes), [only those...]

The accent of particles (*nipāta*) is seen among those beginning with *ca* (Cādi), while others are among those beginning with *svara* (Svarādi). Those that possess both accents should be understood as belonging to both groups. For example, the word *uta* is among the Svarādis because of its usage as an oxytone in the verse "ṭhīḍaḷe nūtanairuta. As for the word *uta*:

Having stated that [the word] begins with a vowel (*svarādi*), they attempted to resolve the objection regarding its accent by resorting to the rule for *nipāta*s ending in an acute accent (*antodātta*); however, this was done hastily, because it does not begin with a vowel and because the designation as a *nipāta* ending in an acute accent would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Furthermore, as it has been stated in the *Kāśikā*:

The statements that *svar*, *śanais*, *ṛdhak*, *divā*, *vṛthā*, *naktam*, and so forth are oxytone (antodātta), and that *sanat*, *sanāt*, and so forth are proparoxytone (ādyudātta), are all merely due to negligence (*prāmādika*), because they contradict the observed usage (*lakṣya*) and lack any authoritative basis (*nirmūlatva*). Thus it is stated in the *Śabdakaustubha*.
This has been explained. *Prakriyā-pradīpa*: "And a taddhita [suffix] is *asarvavibhakti*" (Pāṇini 1.1.38).

Regarding the word *sarva*: it means consisting of all three numbers (*vacana*). Regarding *na* (not): the sense is that only the singular number (*ekavacana*) is produced. Why [is it specified as] a *taddhita*? [Consider: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *trayaḥ*.

What is the meaning of "asarva" and so forth? [The answer is: *aupagavaḥ*. [From] Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.39: *kṛnmejantaḥ* ("A word ending in a suffix beginning with *m* that is derived from a *kṛt* suffix is indeclinable"). [Example: *jīvase*. [In this case,] the suffix *ase* is applied according to [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.9]: *tumarthe sesen*.
Regarding the form *pibaddhyai*: the suffix *śadhyai* is added by the rule *tenaiva śadhyai*, and the substitution of *piba-* for *pā-* occurs by the rule *pāghrā*.

As for what they say—that [the suffix] *śap* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*)—that is due to haste; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes denote the action (*bhāve*). The inclusion of the word "final" (*antagrahaṇam*) is for the purpose of indicating that [the substitution applies only when the suffix is directly taught as such]; therefore, it does not apply here.

[This rule applies] to the suffixes *ādhaya* and *cikīrṣu*. This [sūtra] is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of these two, so that they may be established by both the *lakṣaṇa-pratipadokta-paribhāṣā* and the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. (Prau.ma.: Pāṇini 1.1.40:
*ktvā-tosun-kasunaḥ*).

Regarding *ktvātosunkasunaḥ*: *udetoḥ* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut*, with the suffix *tosun* added according to the rule "the suffix *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *iṇ*, *kṛ*, *vad*, *car*, *hu*, *mi*, and *jan* when indicating a characteristic mark of an action. Regarding *visṛpaḥ*, it is formed with the suffix *kasun* according to the rule "the suffix *kasun* is applied after the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*."

Regarding the mention of *āp*: likewise, the Vārttika states—"The prescription of elision (*luk*) of *āp* after an indeclinable is purposeless because of the absence of gender. However, the possibility of such a statement in the Sūtra should be understood by adopting the position that [the word] in the rule "striyām" is in apposition with "feminine" (*strī*). As for the lack of gender...
Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the scriptural statements found in the *Atharva-vidyā*, he says: "similarly" (*sadṛśam*).
Regarding the phrase "liṅga-kāraka," the sense is that the words "vibhakti" (case) and "vacana" (number) refer respectively to grammatical relation (*kāraka*) and number (*saṃkhyā*).
As for the example "as by speech" (*yathā vācā*), some say this is an exhaustive enumeration, while others say it is merely an illustration.
Regarding the term *vagāha*: only the initial vowel *a* is elided, not the final one, due to its association with the particle *api*. Thus end the indeclinables.
Now, the feminine suffixes.
Regarding *khaṭvā*: [it is derived] by the rule *aśū-pruṣi-kuṣi-khaṭi-kaṇi-viśibhyaḥ kvan*. Regarding *pañcājī*:
one should not say that the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply simply because of the absence of the rule for "application after a final element" (*tadantavidhi*).

This is because, among feminine suffixes, there is the mention of "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahatpūrvagrahaṇena*) and the governing rule of "not being a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanādhikāreṇa*).

This is because it indicates that the rule applies to the end of the preceding element (*tadanta-vidhi*). Regarding the word *mūṣikā*: under the governing rule *vṛścikṛṣoḥ kikan*, the form *mūṣika* is derived from the root *muṣ* with the suffix *kikan*, which causes the lengthening of the vowel; thus, the word *mūṣika* has the letter *i* in its middle.

As for the word *mūṣaka*, it is derived from the root *mūṣ* (meaning "to steal") with a long vowel in the penultimate syllable, followed by the suffix *kvun* in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Mādhava has stated that this [suffix] is also *ṭāp*; however, the distinction is that there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule "pratyayasthāt. As for the claim that this [word] ends in *kvun* and does not employ the reading in the *ajādi* group [of suffixes], they say that this is because its purpose is to trigger the application of *ṅīṣ* by the rule defining *jāti*, and because a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is not a *jāti*.
That is to be considered; for even though [the term *bhastrāphalā*] is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) like *vyāghrī* and others, its status as a genus (*jāti*) is not lost.

Regarding *bhastrāphalā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose fruits are like a bellows. This is established in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *phala* (meaning "to ripen") in the rule *ṅyāpoḥ*. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is generally...

It should indeed be read as *dīrgha* [with a long vowel], namely *pratyakpuṣpa*. This was stated after a thorough examination of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika on the sūtra beginning with *pākakarṇa*. Therefore, the reading *satprākkāṇḍa* is not to be respected.

"And *śūdrā*": if it denotes a caste (*jāti*), the word *śūdra* takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. However, this does not apply when preceded by the word *mahat*. Here too, the condition "if it denotes a caste" is connected [to the previous rule]. Regarding "but in the case of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)": there is no restriction that "connection with a male" must consist solely of the relationship of husband and wife; rather, it also includes the relationship of progenitor and progeny. Therefore—

Thus it is established that "from a Kṣatriya father, on a Vaiśya and a Śūdra mother, the two sons remembered [by tradition] are the Māhiṣya and the Ugra. Regarding the term *mahāśūdrī*: Amarasimha states, "The word *ābhīra* is identical to *mahāśūdrī* in both its generic sense and its application to a male."

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the *ajādi* (ajādigaṇa) list, the reading should simply be "śūdrā"; the inclusion of the word "jāti" (caste/species) is redundant. Since the primary meaning is understood in grammatical operations, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed by the rule for denoting a caste (*jāti*)—will itself be blocked [by the subsequent rule]. For when there is a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the application is secondary (*gauṇī vṛtti*). Furthermore, the phrase "not [denoting] *mahat*" and so forth is also redundant, because the word *mahāśūdra*...

For [the word *śūdra*] exists as a distinct [denotation] within a different class (*jātyantara*). In that case, since the constituent part [of the compound] would be meaningless, there is no possibility at all for the application of the suffix *ṭāp*, because the feminine gender (*strītva*) is not inherent in the meaning of the word *śūdra*. However, in the case of a "great Śūdra woman," the form *mahāśūdrā* is indeed intended. [The examples] beginning with *kruñcā*—these three [are the illustrations].
Some maintain that [the suffixes] end in *hal*. However, by citing examples such as "ṭhkruñcānālabheta" and "uṣṇihakakubhau," the *Bhāṣya* accepts that they may also end in *a*.
Regarding the phrase "even in the sense of relation to a male (*puṃyoga*)": when words such as *jyeṣṭhā* refer to one who is born first and so forth, then...

Since the word ends in a non-dental consonant (*adanta*), the suffix *ṭāp* is already established. However, when there is a desire to express "the wife of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya strī*) and so forth, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which applies by virtue of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—would otherwise be required; the word *api* is used to indicate that this [suffix] is superseded by the present rule.

[The suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after a word ending in *mūla* that follows a negative particle (*nañ*). Why [is it said] "after a negative particle"? [Consider] *śatamūlī*; [here] *amūlā* [does not take ṅīṣ]. This is a genus of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhijāti*). [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*:
"And after a word ending in an *ugit*" (Pāṇini 4.1.6). It is "bhavatī" (she who exists); in the list of *sarvādi* words, *bhavat* is recited as having an *udit* vowel.

It is also derived [by the rule] *ṭhbhāterḍavatuḥ*. However, from the present participle ending in *śatṛ*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, the augment *num* is obligatory by the rule *śapśyanoḥ*.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.7: *vano ra ca*.

Regarding the rule *vano ra ca*: in the word *śrutvānam*, the suffix *vanip* is applied to the root *śru*. Although the vowel *u* is followed by a letter ending in *ha* (*n*) after the *guṇa* substitution has taken place, the prohibition of the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* does not apply here, because the suffix was not prescribed after a stem ending in *ha*. Regarding the form *avāvaḥ*, the author of the Nyāsa states that this prohibition is merely general; therefore, he says the form is *avāvarī*. It is not [the case that the prohibition is absolute].

This is seen in the Bhāṣya and other works. Regarding the rule "ḍāp in the case of *pakṣa*": the sense is that in the dual number, there arise three forms—*bahudhīvaryau*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīve*. [Prakriyākaumudī: Ṭāpṛci (Pāṇini 4.1.9)]

*ṭāb ṛci*: This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅīp* suffix obtained by the preceding rule. [The phrase] "because it is not established" (*asiddhatvāt*) is stated according to the view that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is applied at the time the operation is to take effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*). However, if the designation "six" (*ṣaṭsaṃjñā*) is applied according to the view that names are applied at the time of their enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), or if the explanation is that the term "ending in ṣ or n" (*ṣṇānta*) applies at the time of its initial teaching (*upadeśakāla*), then the description regarding its being "not established" would be inappropriate.
They say that it is not applicable;

however, in reality, even under the *yathoddeśa* view, its status as unestablished (*asiddhatva*) is indeed applicable, for the rule regarding "that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛta*) is recited in the *sthānivadādeśa* sūtra.

By virtue of the mention of the term "substitute" (ādeśa), one may rely on the principle that "all substitutes replace the entire original word," and thus explain that even an inferred substitute is like its original (sthānivat). However, in either case, this does not apply in the case of a rule concerning an *al* (vowel or consonant). This is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

Regarding the term *bahuyajvānau*: because of the prohibition "not after a conjunct consonant" (*na saṃyogāt*), this [word] does not undergo elision of the penultimate vowel; therefore, the rule "of that which has elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*) does not apply.
[The sūtra] *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.13) [is relevant].

Regarding the rule *ḍābubhābhyām*: [An objection is raised: "But surely, because of the force of the explicit statement of both the prohibition (*niṣedha*) and the suffix *ḍāp*, their alternation (*paryāya*) is established. True. However, the rule is divided by means of the phrase *anyatarasyām*. In that [division], the word *manaḥ* is excluded. Thus, after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *an*, the suffix *ḍāp* may optionally be applied, along with the suffix *ṅīp*.

This [sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an option. However, the sūtra *ana upadhālopinaḥ* is for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the option which applies to a word ending in *an* applies only when there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*). Thus, in cases such as *suparvā*, where there is no elision of the penultimate vowel, this [sūtra] serves to prohibit [the application of the previous rule]. But in cases such as *bahurājñī*, [the application follows] from the rule *ṛnnebhyaḥ*.

Thus, the suffix *ṅīp* is indeed applied. By this, the form *bahudhīvarī* is established. For, in the rule "ṛnnebhyaḥ," the suffix *ṅīp* is restated (*anūdya*), and the letter *r* is prescribed as being in conjunction with it (*tatsanniyogena*). If *ṅīp* were applied by virtue of another section [of the grammar], the desired form would not be established. Now, one might object that the rule "vano ra ca" itself provides both the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ra*.

If it is argued that [the suffix] should be prescribed, we say no, because prescribing both would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, even in this case, once the *ṅīp* suffix is prohibited, the *raḥ* suffix would also be difficult to obtain, because they are taught as being mutually dependent (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*). However, in the Bhāṣya, this is resolved by breaking up the rule (*sūtrabhanga*). It is as follows: "After a *bahu-vrīhi* compound ending in *an*, [the suffix *raḥ* is applied]."
Let the sūtra *upadhālopino vā* follow immediately after this [sūtra];
let the sūtra located in another place, such as *ana upadhā*, and the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the ḍāp-sūtra, not be required.

Prakriyāmañjarī: Regarding the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28), the term *bahuvrīheḥ* is carried over from the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, and the suffix *ṅīp* is carried over from the rule *saṃkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*. With this intention, he says: [the following].

Regarding "annantādityādi" and so forth: it has been stated that this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Nor should it be said that, since the option (*vikalpa*) is already established by the preceding rule, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* here is redundant; for if that [term] were absent, this would be a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) for the sake of obligatoriness, rather than a restriction.
*Prakriyākaumudī*: "pratyayasthātkāt pūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.44).

Regarding the rule "pratyayasthātkāt pūrvasya": the letter *k* in *kāt* is for the sake of pronunciation; it is intended to signify the consonant alone. If, however, the specific letter were intended, then in forms such as *etikāś caranti*, the substitution would not occur when *akac* is applied.

With this intention, he says: "from the letter *ka*. For the suffix *-kāra* is prescribed when indicating a phoneme (*varṇa*). The point is that its occasional use as a whole [word], such as in the formulation "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is indeed higher," is achieved through a specific effort in the form of grammatical instruction. Regarding the phrase "even before *ā*": this refers to the vowel *a*.

This is the qualification. In that context, by virtue of the underlying meaning (*sāmarthya*), the substitution occurs even when there is an intervention by the letters *ka* and *ā*, but not in cases such as *rathakaṭalya* where there is an intervention of three or four letters and so on. For this very reason, it does not occur for the initial *ā* in words such as *sarvikā*. This has been stated: "The letter *i* should replace the letter *ā* when *āp* follows."
Thus [it is said]. However, if the intention were to qualify the letter *k*, he would have stated "of the *at* preceding the letter *k* that follows an *āp*.
As for what the ancients say—that the term *āpi* qualifies the letter *k*, and that in cases such as *sarvikā*, [the rule applies] to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)—[that is incorrect].

[Objection: "Even when there is an intervention by the letter *a*, [the rule] will apply by virtue of the power of the specific statement, because of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

[Response: That is not so, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rathakaṭalya*; for even when there is an intervention, the status of being "subsequent" (*paratva*) is not lost. Nor can one find a solution through the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, because [that rule applies only] in the case of an original enunciation (*anuvāda*).

Because the paribhāṣā [regarding the non-application of a rule] does not apply here; for its meaning is that it applies to the qualifiers of what is being referred to (anūdyamāna). And in this regard, the mention of the word *sthāne* in the sūtra "udīcām ātaḥ" is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The result, however, is the establishment of forms such as *śālīya*, because the paribhāṣā concerning *ik* does not apply in the context of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "vṛddha."

As for what they say—that *āpi* is a qualifier of that which is being prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*)—that is quite gross. Furthermore, it is not even to be suspected that *āpi* is a qualifier of the *aṅga*, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rathakaṭyā* and *putrakāmyā*. [The word] *śaka* [is derived with] the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). The mention of *stha*...
This is for the sake of clarity; for since there is no suffix consisting of the letter *k* alone, the property of being situated therein (*tātsthya*) is obtained by default.

Why [mention] the preceding [word]? [To ensure that] in examples such as *sarvikā*, the rule "of what follows after that" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*) prevents the substitution from applying to the *k* that follows [the word-final *ka*], thereby overriding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *ṭāp*. As for [the following]:

Even the *paribhāṣā* "that which is taught after a vowel [is stronger]" (A 1.1.56) is rendered useless. In reality, however, the locative indication "in a suffix containing *i*" (*pratyayastheki*) alone would be appropriate; furthermore, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) could easily be omitted. What is the purpose of the *tapara* marker in *ataḥ*? [Consider: "The suffix *ka* is added after roots ending in *dhā*, *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kali*. [Resulting form: *dhākā*.

*Rākā*: [The form] *māmikā* is derived by the rule "kevalamāmaka... etc., which restricts [the application of the suffix] to names and Vedic meters; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. Regarding the rule *tyaktyapoḥ*: this is an exception to the optional rule [stated as] "udīcāmātaḥ sthāne". *Dākṣiṇātyikā*: [derived from] *dakṣiṇā*, meaning "not far from the south."

The analysis is *ājantaḥ dakṣiṇā bhavā* ("that which ends in the suffix *āc*, [namely] *dakṣiṇā*, is *bhavā*"). As for the analysis provided by the Easterners (*prāc*)—*dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi bhavā* ("situated in the southern direction")—that is not correct; because in the rule prescribing the suffix *tyap*, the word *dakṣiṇā* ending in *āc* is understood specifically due to its association with indeclinables (*avyaya*). Otherwise, the rule "in all formations involving a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)," etc., would apply.

And because the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would [otherwise] apply; as for the claim that the masculine form applies only in a compound, that will be refuted later. After *tyak*, there is the augment *vṛddhi* by the rule "kiti ca," and then the suffix *ṭāp*. Then, in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, the suffix *ka* is added. By the rule "ke'ṇaḥ," there is the shortening of the vowel, and then *ṭāp*. Thus we have *ihatyikā*. [The suffix] *tyap* follows after an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

*na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45). Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāsa* states: "Since the option [to substitute] *ā* for the final vowel of *yā* is already established by the rule *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne*, this present sūtra serves as a prohibition (*niṣedha*). That is not correct, because [the word *sthāne*] refers to the substitution of *ā*.

Because that specific portion is absent here, he says "of *yat* and *tat*" with the intention that this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the pronouns *yā* and *sā*. He provides an example of the result when the actual form is not intended to be expressed: *yakām*, *takām*. This is done by omitting the term *yāsayoḥ*.
It would be more appropriate to say simply *yatadaḥ*. Regarding *upatyakā*:

according to the rule "the suffix *tyakan* is added after *upa* and *adhi* in the sense of 'near' and 'ascended,' respectively," [the form is derived]. The phrase "and in the case of *kṣipakā* and others" follows, with the word "not" (*na*) understood from the previous context.

Regarding *kṣipakā*: the suffix *ka* is added to the root *kṣip* by virtue of its having a vowel in the *ig-upadhā* (penultimate) position; then, another *ka* is added in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth. The root *caṭ* means "to split."

[The suffix] *ac* is applied after roots beginning with *pac*; from that, [the suffix] *ka*. Regarding *tāraka*: [it is derived] from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. It refers both to a star (a celestial body) and the pupil of the eye. *Varṇakā* is a specific type of woven cloth (*prāvāpa*). *Tāntava* is a derivative of threads; [it is formed] by the suffix *añ* after [the word] *otu*. Elsewhere, it is *varṇikā*, which is a commentary on a specific text.

And [the word] *stotrakartrī* means "one who performs praise.
