If it is argued that, since the meaning is already established by the rule for the indirect object (*gopaniṣṭhā preraṇā*), the sūtra "akathitaṃ ca" is therefore redundant,
it is replied: when there is a desire to express the object as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), as in "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇāmaśnīyāt*).
Thus, as in the aforementioned example, the genitive case would have applied; this sūtra is intended to set that aside.
Consequently, it is established here that the meaning of the accusative is merely "relation," just like the genitive.
However, when there is a desire to express only the status of being the *apādāna* (ablative), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) alone is used. But when the cow is intended as a qualifier of the milk—
The genitive case [is used]. Therefore, the usage *goḥ payo dogdhi* ("he milks the cow's milk") is indeed correct.
This should be inferred for subsequent cases as well. As for what was stated by the ancients:

"The object of the verbs *duh* (to milk), *aci* (to ask), *rudh* (to obstruct), *pracch* (to ask), *ci* (to gather), *brū* (to speak), *śās* (to instruct), *ji* (to win/conquer), and *muc* (to release) [is treated as the agent when these verbs have an instrumental of cause]."

"nī-hṛ-kṛṣ-manth-vah-daṇḍ-grah-muṣ-pac share the property of having two objects. Regarding this, the following must be said: the inclusion of *grah* (to seize) [in this list] is without foundation; even the example "he seized Indra on the tree" (*jagrāha dyautaruṃ śakram*) is incorrect. As for the others, although they possess the property of having two objects—

Nevertheless, the textual integrity remains authoritative; for instance, after listing the roots beginning with *duh* (to milk) and those ending in *ad* (to eat) in two distinct groups here, and then, at the conclusion of the section on the formation of verbal nouns (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*), there arises the inquiry:

"In the case of roots with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), do the suffixes *la*, the *kṛtya* suffixes, the *kta* suffix, and those having the sense of *khal* apply to the primary object (*mukhya-karman*) or to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*)?"

He himself has stated: "Verbs beginning with *nī* (to lead), when followed by a causative suffix (*ṇic*) and meaning 'motion' without an external object, take the suffix [denoting the agent] in the sense of their primary object;
those beginning with *duh* (to milk) do so in the sense of their secondary object; others, however, according to their preference."

And in this way, [the principle] would apply even to the cases of *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) and *manthin* as well; and thus it would contradict the Bhāṣya statement: "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred. For here, the hundred is the primary element, not the Gargas, according to the supplementary passage:
"Kings become desirous of gold. And here, *daṇḍin*...
The purpose is for inclusion, not for exclusion; for this very reason, it would apply even to *manthi* when it is primary, yet it is desired [to apply] when it is secondary. And so says Bhāravi:
"By whom the ocean was churned, its waters cast forth, revealing the abodes of the serpents..."
"The gods and asuras churned the ocean for nectar.
In this [verse], "nectar" (amṛta) is primary because it is the intended object, whereas "the ocean" (ambunidhi) is secondary.
Furthermore, as for what the commentators have said—that among verbs governing two objects, the reading with the root *pac* ("to cook") is unauthoritative—[this is incorrect].

This is because of its forcefulness; for instance, in the sūtra *karmavat karmaṇā*, in the vārttika *duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*, and in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), the two-object nature (*dvikarmakatā*) of the root *pac* (to cook) is obtained.
This has been made clear by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta in that very place. Mādhava also says [the same] regarding the root *ji* (to conquer).
[The examples] beginning with *karṣati*, *manthi*, *muṣ*, *gaṇḍayati*, and *pac* were cited; for instance, he gave the example: "He cooks rice into porridge" (*taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati*).
As for what was stated by Haradatta regarding the rule *akathitaṃ ca*: the word *akathita*...

If the non-primary meaning were to be taken [as the basis for the application of the karmasañjñā], then in the case of "he milks milk into a bronze vessel with his hand" (*pāṇinā kāṃsyapātryāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the designation would apply to both the hand and the bronze vessel as well.

However, if the instrumental (*karaṇa*) and locative (*adhikaraṇa*) meanings are intended, then verbs such as *pacati* ("he cooks") have their scope; for there is no possibility of this [karmasañjñā] applying there, because of the restriction to the specific enumeration of roots beginning with *duh*.

This is according to the intention of that particular school of thought; otherwise, there would be contradictions with the examples from one's own and others' treatises. Let this matter rest for now. Regarding the expression *śataṃ jayati* ("he wins a hundred"): the root *ji* means "to overcome" (*abhibhave*).

As for its being explained as "to conquer" (*jaye*), that is not correct, because that [meaning] is intransitive (*akarmakatvāt*). Although roots such as *jayati* are not listed in the *Mahābhāṣya*, nevertheless—
Kaiyaṭa states that [these] are included by means of the letter *ca*.

Regarding the phrase "based on meaning": it does not depend on the formal nature [of the word], as is seen in the commentary on the *Tad-rāja* sūtra where even the root *cud*, which is a synonym for *pṛcch*, is mentioned in the statement: "I too shall raise this objection which ought not to be raised."
The meaning is that this is because [the root *vad*] is observed to take two objects (*dvikarmaka*). And so says Bhaṭṭi:
"With a smiling face, he spoke these words of great significance loudly to Mārīca, who stood firm in battle.
Kālidāsa also [says]:
Even the mountain, as if out of great affection, spoke that very same matter loudly to the protector of the earth;
and Bhāravi [says]:
"The noble-minded king was addressed by Dvaipāyana with these noble words."
In this way, many verbs such as *nāth* and others should be understood as taking two objects (*dvikarmaka*).

Regarding the word *deśa*: only [places] such as Kuru and Pañcāla are intended; therefore, rules such as *adhiśīṅsthāsām* (Pāṇini 1.4.46) are not rendered redundant. Regarding *godoha*: its establishment here is not due to its being a measure of time (*kāla*), for in common usage...

Because only those things well-known as time, such as months and the like, are understood [by this rule], expressions such as *ghaṭam āste* ("he sits for a jar") do not occur. As for what was stated by the ancients— that some say "when used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the second case ending is applied to words denoting place, time, distance, and path"— examples such as *nadīm āste* ("he sits by the river") are given.

In this regard, the following must be said: since the designation of "object" (*karman*) has not been explicitly stated here, the *l*-affixes and others would not apply to the object, as in the example *māsa āsyate* ("the month is sat through"). Furthermore, the view of "some" (*kecit*) is also inconsistent; for a "country" (*deśa*) consists of a collection of villages, fields, and so forth, and not merely a portion thereof. Therefore, [one says] *grāmam*...

[The rule] "it does not occur in the case of *svapiti*" is stated in the original source (*ākara*). Furthermore, the mention of *adhvan* (road/path) [in the rule] is insufficient, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the suffix *kvip* would apply] in the sense of "he sleeps on the road. For this very reason, in the original source, *adhvan* is specified as "that which is to be traversed.
It is explained that [this refers to] a distance such as a *krośa*, which is well-known as something to be traversed and has a fixed duration.

Prau.ma.: "The agent of the root when it is in the *aṇ* [causative] state becomes the object (*karman*) when the root has the sense of motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or has sound as its object (*śabdakarman*), or is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.52). "Motion and cognition": *pratyavasāna* means eating. "Having sound as their object": this refers to roots whose object is sound.

The meaning is: "of those for whom [the word] *karman* functions as a *kāraka*. However, in this context, the word *karman* does not refer to an action (*kriyā*), as it does in the rule "kartari karmavyatihāre"; for the understanding of an effect (*kārya*) applies to the technical term (*kṛtrima*), and because of the force of the mention of *karman* itself. Otherwise...

He would have simply said: "Of [verbs] meaning motion, cognition, consumption, sound, and those having an object as their meaning. The ancient masters maintain that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction: if the agent [of the causative] is to be designated as the object (*karman*) by virtue of being intended by the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then it applies only to [verbs] meaning motion and so forth. Therefore, [in the case of] *pācayati devadattaḥ*...

In the case of *yajñadattena*, since the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the prompted agent (*prayojya*) with respect to the meaning of the root remains uncontradicted, the third case ending is established. And it has been said:
"Because of independence (*svātantrya*) in the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), [the agent] attains the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the act of instigation (*preraṇe*)."
"By rule, because of the designation 'object' (karman), it is expressed by its own case-ending (svadharma).

This means that the agent [of the causative] is expressed by its own case-ending, namely the third case (instrumental). Now, one might object: since the status of being an agent with respect to the meaning of the root (prakṛti) is established by its very priority over the status of being an object with respect to the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇic), [there is no need for this rule].

And because it is internal (*antaraṅga*): for an action qualified by its own factors (*kāraka*) is connected with the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), since the causative suffix is prescribed in the sense of "one who possesses a motive" (*hetumat*), and the one who prompts the agent is the motive (*hetu*). For this very reason, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is also dependent upon [the causative]. And thus—

If it is argued: "Let the status of agent belong to the one being employed (the prayojya), because of its priority, its being internal (antaraṅga), and also because it is that upon which [the other] depends; thus, the designation of 'motion' (gati) and so forth is appropriate according to the rule";
if this is so, let it be so, for there is no contradiction with the linguistic usage (lakṣya). But what is the purpose of the treatises stating that "this is a restrictive rule" (niyama-sūtra)?

If it is argued that [the *kāraka*] is the "goal" (*gati*)? Listen: by prioritizing the verbal primacy of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) at all, because the designation "object" (*karman*)—which conforms to the primary sense—is more powerful; for even though [the *gati*] is internal (*antaraṅga*) and its subsistence is required, this does not entail superiority with respect to the primary sense.

With this intention, the possibility of such statements in the texts arises; however, it should be noted that when the primacy of the meaning is prioritized, it is more appropriate to regard [the word] as being injunctive (*vidhāyaka*).
Regarding the word *śatrūn* ("enemies"): it is conducive to that movement which has heaven as its object and the enemies as its locus.
The meaning is that whatever activity culminates in [him], Śrī Hari is my goal (*gati*). Now, one might object: "How can heaven (*svarga*) be the object (*karman*) here?

For an object is that which is most desired by the agent (*kartṛ*), and the enemies are not the agents; rather, they [the enemies] are the objects according to the rule *gaty-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.52). This is not so, for regarding the designation of an object (*karma-saṃjñā*)...

The mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) is an indication of independence (svātantrya). And independence consists precisely in being the substratum of the activity conveyed by the verbal root. Furthermore, this [independence] exists in the prompted agent even when the prompter is present. Nor is there a lack of evidence for its being an indication.

For the author of the Bhāṣya himself is the authority on this point, having stated: "In the case of roots with two objects, they say that the *l*-affixes [the passive] are used when the principal object is to be expressed;

in the case of roots such as *duh* (to milk), they are used for the non-principal object"; and he further states: "[The passive suffixes] are used for the agent and the object in the case of causative (*ṇic*) verbs. Indeed, without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the passive would not apply] to causative forms.
The status of having two objects (dvikarmakatā) is obtained, whereby the rule "the agent of the causative (*ṇyanta*) [is called the object]" would have its scope.
If it is asked, "How can there be a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which is conventionally established (*saṅketita*) in its primary sense? [the answer is:

in that which is conventionally established as being unqualified by another technical name (*sañjñā*), [there is indication] in the mere primary sense itself, which is common to both that qualified state and the unqualified state.
Understand this:
regarding the roots *nī* and *vah*, although their meaning is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and not "giving" (*dā*), nevertheless,
since "going" (*gati*) also enters into the meaning of "causing to reach" as a subordinate factor, one considers them to include that [meaning of giving] on that basis alone.

The prohibition has been stated. Regarding "niyantṛ" (the driver): it means one who impels the animal, and not merely a charioteer; by this, the expression “he makes the oxen carry [the grain]” is established. Regarding "aniṣedha" (non-prohibition):
the resulting meaning is that it should be stated that the person being employed is the object (*karman*). Regarding "sūta" (charioteer): [this refers to a specific type of driver].

*niyantā*, *prājitā*, *yantā*, *sūtaḥ*, *kṣattā*, and *sārathiḥ*. [The root] *ādayati* takes the *parasmaipada* ending because, according to the rule "In the case of a result not intended for the agent, after all [roots]," the *parasmaipada* is used. However, when the result is intended for the agent, by the rule "And after a causative (*ṇic*)," only the *ātmanepada* would apply; [the following] is an exception to that.

Because of the prohibition [of the *ṇic* suffix] by the rule "nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca" through the statement "there is a prohibition for roots beginning with *ad*," [the form] *sasyam* [is used]. For *sasyam*, one should understand the injury (*hiṃsā*) to barley standing in the field while being eaten, since they possess sentience (*cetanatva*) in that state. As for the statement "it causes to remember" (*smārayati*), [it refers to the rule] "ṇeraṇau... [Pāṇini 1.3.67].

Thus, in the Sūtra, the example "the thicket of forest bushes itself causes him to remember" (ṭhsmarayatyenaṃ vanagulmaḥ svayameva) is cited; in that case, the status of the object (karmatva) is to be understood from the usage in the Bhāṣya itself. Regarding the root *śabdāyati*:
in the sense of "he makes a sound," the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "śabdavaira... and so forth, followed by the causative *ṇic*.

Regarding the phrase *dhātvarthe* (in the sense of the root-meaning): by this, those who employ an object [as a suffix] in the example *śabdāyayati sainikair ipūn* ("he causes the enemies to sound by means of his soldiers") are refuted. As for what was stated by the ancients—that there is no [suffix application] after the roots *krand*, *śabdāya*, and *hvē*—therein, the mention of *ayati* is entirely baseless. However, as for *krand* and *hvē*:
The possibility of [the object] being reached is based merely on the fact that it is an action involving sound; however, it has already been stated that this is not actually the meaning of the sūtra.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that [the object of] the verbs *śru*, *grah*, and *dṛś* becomes the object (*karma*), the inclusion of *dṛś* there—
This is indeed authoritative. As for the verb *śru* (to hear), its status as having two objects is established because it has sound as its object.

Although the status of *grah* (to seize) as having two objects is accepted by Sudhākara and others, it is nevertheless not accepted by many. For this very reason, [the author of the Mahābhārata] said: "Janaka seized that bow."
They explained that he "learned" (ajigrahat) the employment of the root *bhañj* in the sense of "he caused [him] to understand. Likewise:
"The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter, for He did not ask for her."
In this context, "to cause to grasp" means to make one understand by way of marriage.
And this is logical; for since the root *grah* takes two objects, in the phrase *jāyāpratigrāhitagandhamālyām*, the cow—the prompted agent—is denoted by the past passive participle (*kta*).

This would be so, because of the rule stating, "In the case of a causative ending in ṇic, [the agent of the causative is treated as the object] of the action. Consequently, one would have to say, *jāyayā gandhamālye pratigrāhitām* ("having caused the wife to receive the perfume and garlands"). However, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), the analysis (*vigraha*) is *pratigrāhite gandhamālye yayā* ("by whom the perfume and garlands were caused to be received"). This refers to that [wife] who became the object of the instigation residing in the wife, having the perfume and garlands as its object.

The meaning is that the act of receiving (*pratigrahaṇa*) is the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated precisely through the inclusion of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) and by reversing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
Regarding the rule *abhivādidṛśoḥ*: [the suffix is applied] because it was not applicable after the root *abhivādayati*, but was applicable after the root *dṛś*.
This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule). [From] *Prau.ma.*—*abhiniviśaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.47): "and *abhiniviś*.
Regarding the necessity of placing *abhi-* first because it has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*), [the following applies].

He states that the reversed pronunciation is for the purpose of intending such a collective form, saying "of that which is preceded by a compound. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *niviśate yadi śūkaśikhā pade*. [The rule] "in some cases not" [is stated].
The usage in the commentary, "eṣvartheṣvabhiniviṣṭānām," serves as the authority here.
He states the case-governing rule for the secondary word (*upapada*) with the words beginning "ubhasarvatasoḥ.

The meaning is that when there is a connection with words ending in *ubha* and *sarva* followed by the suffixes *-tas* and *-tra* (i.e., *ubhayataḥ*, *sarvataḥ*, etc.), the second case (*dvitīyā*) must be employed. In this regard:
The Easterners (Prāñcaḥ) say that by the word *ubha*, the word *ubhaya* is indicated (*lakṣyate*), because otherwise the suffix *tas* would be impossible;
however, in reality, even though *ayac* is applied in the context of a compound formation (*vṛtti*), the suffix *tas* is prescribed after the word *ubha*.

The view that "it indeed exists up to the end [of the word]" is correct according to the literal text. The ancients maintain that *dhik* is an indeclinable citation, just like *gavityayamāha*. That is not so; for if that were the case, then just as in the example [the elision] by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* applies because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatayā*), so too in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntike*) would the substitution of *jaś* [for *c*] apply.

Because it would otherwise follow that [the word] does not function as a linguistic item (*apravṛtti-prasaṅgāt*). Nor should one be deluded into thinking that this [word *dhik*] ends in the letter *ga*, for then the example *dhakit* in the rule *kasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.36) would result in being incoherent. Therefore, *dhik* is indeed a form ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*). By the extended application (*atideśa*) "an imitation [of a word] is like its original form" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), the case-suffix (*sup*)...
"Luk | 'ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇam' (on both sides of Kṛṣṇa). This means on both sides of Kṛṣṇa.

The suffix *tasi* is used here according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*. The second case (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). In this way, it should be understood everywhere regarding the case-endings of subordinate words (*upapada*).
"In all sentences, the relationship of a noun is established in only two ways."
It may occur either through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) or, in some cases, even by means of the genitive case.
Thus, when the Elder [Vopadeva] stated [the rule], the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its apodotic case as well.

The statement "in two ways" (*dvidhā*) is to be understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), or alternatively, by taking the genitive and its apodosis as a single category. [An example is: "Fie on the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa! (*dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam*). Of that...

The meaning is "he should be censured. How so? [In the phrase] "Fie, you fool! Since it has already been stated that a vocative word must connect with a verb, there is an absence of connection with the word *dhik* (fie). Furthermore, whether a verbal form is explicitly heard or merely implied is another matter. Thus, [the sentence] has "fool" as its object of address.
The meaning of the sentence is that the performance of prohibited acts and so forth is censured. By this, expressions such as "Alas, father! and "Alas, Queen! Be firm! are explained.
As for what they say—"the case-ending denoting a kāraka (syntactic relation) is stronger than the case-ending of an upapada (a word forming a compound)"—that is weak.
"It is only the nominative case that occurs in the vocative, because the vocative word denotes the agent (*kartṛ*) kāraka";

this is weak, because if the vocative word were the agent kāraka, there would be no possibility of such an utterance. In cases such as "O King, be gracious," from the perspective of the actual state of affairs (*vastugatyā*), [the vocative is not the agent].

If it is argued that "the Lord alone is the agent," one does not thereby obtain the status of being a case of the agentive (kartṛ) kāraka. Furthermore, in such instances as "O Lord, I worship you" (*deva tvāṃ bhaje*) or "they worship you" (*tvāṃ bhajanti*), even though the person being addressed is real, he does not possess agency; let this matter rest for now. Regarding the expression "higher and higher" (*uparyupari*): how then [is it to be explained]?
[Question: "Do the cognitions of the Lord move above and above the cognitions? [Answer:

It is said that the meaning is that they move above the cognitions of those who possess higher cognitions or even those who do not possess such cognitions. And thus, because there is no repetition (*āmreḍita*), the accusative case is not used. Alternatively, according to the rule for the specific mention of "upari," "adhi," and "adhas" [Pāṇini 1.4.90]...

The rule "sāmīpye" (Pāṇini 8.1.7) refers here to that which has already undergone reduplication; therefore, it does not apply when reduplication occurs for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). It was stated that [the suffix *tas*] is seen elsewhere as well, and he demonstrates this with the examples "abhitaḥ" and "paritaḥ.
Regarding the word "pratibhāti": this prefix *prati* is an upasarga because it qualifies the action.
But it is not a *karmapravacanīya* [as in the example] "antarā tvāṃ mām" ("between you and me"), which means "in the middle of you and me.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the semantic force" (*sāmarthyāt*): for this very reason, even the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is an object within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
The sense is that [the relation] is accepted.

Regarding the expression *nadīm anv* (along the river): the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is "relation" (*sambandha*). And here, since that [relation] takes the form of accompaniment (*sāhitya*), it is indicated by the prefix *anu*.
Prau.ma.: *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyānabhāgavīpsāsu pratiparyanavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.90).
Regarding *lakṣaṇettham*: "vṛkṣaṃ prati. The meaning is the indication of a connection with the tree.
And since that connection consists in the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), the words beginning with *prati* indicate this. [Example: *bhakto viṣṇuṃ*.
In *pratīti*, the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) between Viṣṇu and his devotee is indicated by the prefix *prati*.
In *lakṣmīḥ*, the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) between the portion in the form of Lakṣmī and Hari is indicated.
In the expression *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam* ("tree after tree"), the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated solely by the reduplication; however, the prefix *pari-* is indicated by the verbal action.

It is connected [to the following]. The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*). Because the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* subordinates the designation *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṣ* (for *s*) does not occur. It is explained in the original treatise (*ākara*) that "starting points" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are mentioned as the objects [of these prepositions] precisely for this reason. However, the rule "the fifth case ending [is used] with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" does not apply here.

Because of its association with the word *apeta* in the sense of "avoiding," [the root *as* here means] "may it come to me" (*mām abhiṣyāt*), which means "may it be my portion. The ancient grammarians also cite *mām abhiṣyāt* as a counter-example; in that case, it means "may it reach me. [This change occurs] due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*) on the root *as*.

Because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the word *mām* takes the second case (*dvitīyā*); furthermore, since the meaning here culminates in "my portion," the designation of *abhāga* as a *karmapravacanīya* is precluded,
and thus the rule "upasargaprādurbhyām" applies, resulting in the cerebral *ṣ* sound.
"And in the case of worship (*pūjā*). From the preceding rule, *suḥ pūjāyām*, the mention of "worship" (*pūjā*) is drawn over here.
[Prakriyākaumudī: *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5)]

*kālādhvanoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). *Atyantaḥ* means that which has transcended the end (*anta*), i.e., cessation (*virāma*); and that is a *saṃyoga*, meaning uninterrupted proximity. It should take the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). Because [the word] is explicitly heard [in the sūtra], [the rule applies] only to those denoting time and distance. As in *māsasya*. [This occurs] when there is usage with words having the sense of *kṛtvas*.

Some say that the genitive case here is by the rule "kāle 'dhikaraṇe," but that is incorrect; for in that rule, due to the continued application of the term *śeṣa* (remainder), the result is simply the non-application of a compound with a *kṛt*-derived word, as in the example "dvirahno bhojanam. Therefore, the truth is that the genitive in this instance is governed solely by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe."
Thus ends the second [chapter].

Prau.ma.: "The independent agent" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.54). Independence (*svātantrya*) consists in being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root that has become the primary factor.
And it is said:
"When the action is not explicitly stated by the verbal root, the *kartṛ* (agent) is always intended to be the *kāraka* [in that role]. — *Prakriyākaumudī*.

"The most effective means is the *karaṇa* (instrument). — *Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.42*. Regarding the word "most effective" (*prakṛṣṭa*): it refers to that whose operation immediately follows [and results in the accomplishment of the action].
The accomplishment of the action is its excellence. And it has been said:
"When, in a particular instance, that whose operation immediately precedes the complete accomplishment of the action is intended [as such], it is then remembered as the instrument (*karaṇa*)."

By the phrase "it is intended to be expressed" (vivakṣyate), he indicates that even things such as a cooking pot possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) depending on the speaker's intention. And he says:
"In reality, that [agency] is indefinable, for a real entity is not fixed [in one status];
since we observe the intended meaning (vivakṣā) expressed as 'the pot cooks'.
This is the sense: the state of being a factor (kārakatva), as well as its six sub-divisions such as agency (kartṛtva) and so forth, reside in a particular real entity.

It does not remain fixed in the same way as the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified. For it cannot be rightly said that "a qualifier is always a qualifier," just as one cannot say that "a cow is a cow for everyone, but is not a non-cow with respect to something.
And thus, when a meaning is presented by a particular verbal root-form (*dhātuvyakti*), [one must determine] what its agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth are.

In the context of verbal action (*praśna*), the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended as the substratum of the operation (*vyāpāra*) that is to be undertaken by the primary individual (*prakṛtavyakti*); the object (*karman*) is the substratum of the result (*phala*) which resides in a locus different from the operation;
and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum through a relationship mediated by the agent and the object. [This applies to] the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook).

And activity (*vyāpāra*) is of many kinds. Thus, when the verb *pacati* (he cooks) has as its primary intention (*tātparya*) the acts of placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring rice, and bringing fuel, then Devadatta, who is the locus of those acts, is the agent (*kartṛ*). When its primary intention is the act of flaming, then the fuels (*edhas*) are the agents.

When the focus is on the holding of the rice and so forth, the pot is the agent; when the focus is on the separation of the parts and so forth, the grains of rice are the agents. In the expression "he cooks with a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*), although the pot is the locus of the operation expressed by the instrumental case, it is merely an instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the agent (*kartṛ*), for [the status of agent belongs to] the operation of Devadatta and others alone.

Because it is included within that verbal root (*dhātu*). Likewise: when an object is expressed by roots such as *ad* (to eat) and *khād* (to eat), the agent (*kartṛ*) is the grammatical participant (*prayojya*); in that very same sense, when expressed by the root *bhakṣ* (to eat), the object (*karman*) is the participant. When an object is expressed by roots such as *śī* (to lie down) preceded by *adhi*, the locus (*ādhāra*) is the object; when expressed by those [roots] alone, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the participant, and so forth. By this, [the status] of cognition...

The objection that there is a contradiction between the agent and the object in the case of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) and so forth is refuted, because agency and the like— being conditioned by specific adjuncts such as words— are not possible to express in perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge.
By this, [the definition] that "objecthood" (*karmatva*) consists in possessing a fruit produced by an action inherent in another is also [refuted].

Even those who, fearing that the definition would fail to cover the case of the ablative (*apādāna*), refined the definition by stating that "the object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root" have been refuted; for [their definition] fails to apply to the mover in examples such as *grāmaṃ gamayati devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to go to the village"),
even though in their view the act of going is the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*).
Because that [definition] lacks the property of being a non-delimiter (anavacchedaka). In that case, the suffix *ṇic* would have the meaning of "operation" (*vyāpāra*), but not the base (*prakṛti*).
Or, even if that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) in examples such as *pācayati*.
Therefore, by the force of the statement, the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) status of "object" (*karmatva*) useful for the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) [is established].
If you argue that [the designation] is established [by the subsequent rule], then understand that it does not exist even in the case of the *apādāna* (ablative),

because within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for a single designation, the one with no scope (*anavakāśā*) sublates the one with scope (*sāvakāśā*). For this very reason, in examples such as "he kills himself by himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*), the subsequent designation of *kartṛ* (agent) [sublates the others].

Anticipating the objection that this would contradict the technical designation of "action" (*karman*), the Bhāṣya provides a solution by relying on the distinction between the Self as qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.
Regarding the word "by Rāma" (*rāmeṇa*): although here, with respect to the action, the case-factors (*kāraka*) are presented by their case-endings...

Nevertheless, while [the action] is indeed a qualifier, that which is presented by the verbal suffix (*kṛt*) is the qualificand, because it is said that "nouns have substance as their primary meaning. Furthermore, even in the case of the result and the operation presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*), when they are used in conjunction with a transitive verb (*karman-kartṛ*), there is a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualificand. And thus:

The meaning of the sentence is: Vālī is the locus of the separation of life, which is to be accomplished by the operation of the arrow, which in turn is the object of the operation [of Rāma] that is most desired by Rāma.

As for what was stated by the Mīmāṃsakas in the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice— that even the expression "cooking with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pākaḥ*) would be possible— that is refuted by the admission of our own position. This is because the rules such as *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("the agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix in various instances") and *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* ("the agent and the object [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix") establish the connection of the *kāraka*s with the meaning of the base of the *kṛt*-suffix.

The wise should reflect that there is simply no possibility for the occurrence of *vinokti* (the figure of speech based on absence) here. What is an example of [the suffix] when not expressed (*anabhihite*)? *hariḥ karoti* ("Hari does"). *jīvanaḥ* ("one who lives by this") and *śābdikaḥ* ("a grammarian") [are examples].

[In the latter case], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "he makes his living by means of words" (*śabdadūraṃ karoti*). *kṛtaviśvaḥ* ("by whom the universe was made")—[in these cases, the agent is not expressed by the primary suffix].

The meaning is "the locus of the activity of Viśvakarman"; for in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a non-sixth-case (*a-ṣaṣṭhy-artha*) [meaning], another derivation is accepted. How this is so will be explained later. Regarding the rule *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*, this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); therefore, examples such as "by name he is Sutīkṣṇa, by conduct he is self-controlled" (*nāmnā sutīkṣṇaścaritena dāntaḥ*) are included.
The object [of the action] is as follows: the combination of two *droṇas* is *dvidroṇa*.
Because it belongs to the class beginning with *pātra*, it lacks the feminine gender. The meaning is "grain related to two *droṇas*.

Regarding the word *ca* ("and"): by the recurrence of the term *karaṇa* (instrument), [the rule] "in the case of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the instrument is] the recipient (*sampradāna*)" [is understood].

Thus, since the option (*anyatarasyām*) from the subsequent rule has been brought back [to this point], the particle *ca* serves to ensure the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the two designations (*saṃjñā*). Consequently, in the example *manasādevaḥ*, both the suffix *aṇ* (by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*) and the instrumental case ending for the instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*) are established; furthermore, there is no elision (*aluk*) by the rule *manasaḥ saṃjñāyām*.

Furthermore, regarding the example *kiṃ cākṣi devadattena yajñadattena*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the agent of the causative (*ṇi*) does not become the object;

nor, by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*, is there the substitution of the *parasmaipada* ending. As for what the ancient commentators explained—that it might optionally be designated as an object—[that is incorrect].

This should be disregarded because it contradicts the form [of the word]. It might be argued as follows: there is scope for the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) in "the dice are for playing" (*devanā akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument; whereas there is scope for the designation *karman* (object) in "the dice are being played with" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of an object. Thus, in the case of "he plays with the dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), when there is a conflict between the two operations occasioned by the two designations, [the latter prevails] due to its higher status (*paratvāt*).

If it is argued that [the accusative] must be the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and not the second (*dvitīyā*), they reply here: according to the view that the application of grammatical rules occurs at the time the word is used (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the rule "the second case-ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) has no scope of application [in such cases], and thus the second case-ending is employed. Now, one might object: even in the example *dīvyante akṣāḥ* ("the dice play"), although the object is already expressed [by the verbal suffix],...

Since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not expressed [by the suffix], the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would [otherwise] apply; likewise, in the example "the dice are the means of gambling" (*devanā akṣāḥ*), even though the instrument is expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would apply because the object (*karman*) is not expressed?
Not so; for here there is only one single power (*śakti*) which is associated with two designations. And thus:

In both cases, there is indeed expression (*abhidhāna*), and not non-expression (*anabhihitatva*). [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*]: "When joined with *saha*, that which is subordinate... [Pāṇini 2.3.19]. Regarding "putreṇa": here, the father's connection to the action is verbal (*śābda*), whereas the son's...

The word *atha* (now/then) indicates its lack of predominance (*aprādhānya*). It would have been possible to omit the mention of "non-predominance" [in the rule]. Nor does this result in the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) for the father (*pitṛ*) as well; for in that case, because it pertains merely to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), the nominative (*prathamā*) arises due to its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), as in the example "the father's arrival" (*pituḥ āgamanam*).

And because the case-ending denoting the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is stronger [than the genitive]. From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "By that which there is a modification of a limb" (*yenāṅgavikāraḥ*, Pāṇini 2.3.20). The word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *aC* added after the class beginning with *arśas*; thus he says—"[of] the possessor of the limb" (*aṅginaḥ*).
By the pronoun "by which" (*yena*), only the constituent part (*avayava*) that constitutes the primary meaning of the base is grasped, due to its proximity.
And that [part] is necessarily modified, for a modification of the body is not possible through an unmodified part. This is what he states: "by whichever limb is modified."

Regarding the form *saṃjānīte*: the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix is applied by the rule *sampratibhyāmanādhyāne*. Since the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) takes precedence when used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix, one says *pitussaṃjñātā* ("the mother known by the father"). As for what Haradatta stated—that because it refers to longing (*ādhyāna*), the genitive is applied by the rule *adhāgartha* due to its higher priority, as in *mātuḥ saṃjānāti*—that is not correct, because in that case...
This is because of the governing context of what remains [to be discussed].
Regarding "substance and so forth," it has been stated:
"The cause (hetu) whose object is substance and so forth is the instrument (karaṇa), which performs its specific function."
"But when the operation [of the cause] is not dependent [on an intermediate action], it is accepted as a *nimitta* (efficient cause).
And: "The result also [is such]. This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *pratyaya*.

Thus, this third case (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used alongside the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*). For example: *adhyayanāya vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study"). This...

However, the distinction is as follows: with respect to the fruit (*phala*), there is a relation of identity (*abheda*) with study; with respect to being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*), however, there is a relation of characterization (*nirūpakatā*). Regarding the term "implied" (*gamyamāna*): the sense is that there is no insistence that [the word] must be explicitly heard (*śrūyamāṇa*). Regarding "means" (*sādhana*): the sense is that it refers to the meaning of the stem portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) in the word *sādhya*. *Mā*...
In the phrase "cāpalāyeti gaṇān vyanaiṣīt," however, the word "yatadhvam" (strive) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the term "aśiṣṭa" (unrefined), this is made known by the rule: "dāṇaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe" (and after the root dāṇ, that [suffix] occurs when it has the sense of the dative).
Thus ends the third [chapter].

He says "of giving" (dānasya) by the force of a designation that accords with its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). The intention is that, by this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *ajāṃ nayati grāmam* ("he leads the goat to the village") or *hastaṃ nidadhāti vṛkṣe* ("he places his hand on the tree"). Furthermore, giving (*dāna*) consists in the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership, for the purpose of non-reacquisition. Precisely for this reason...
In cases such as "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*ṭhrajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), [the designation of recipient does] not occur; for there, the verb *dadāti* ("gives") is used figuratively.

This is the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti. However, according to the Bhāṣya, there is no insistence on the literal meaning [of the term], because of the usage: "The teacher Khaṇḍika gives a slap to his pupil" (*khaṇḍikopādhyāyaḥ śiṣyāya capeṭāṃ dadāti*).

However, the statement "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*ṭhrajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) should be understood as being intended to express the status of [the recipient] as a *śeṣa* (subordinate element). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) in the case of "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*), because by the expression "whom he intends" (*yam abhipraiti*), the status of the primary element (*śeṣitva*) is obtained for that which is indicated by "whom" (*yam*), and the status of the subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is obtained for the object (*karman*).

The village has no status as a residual possessor (*śeṣitva*) with respect to the goat. [In the expression] *dānīya*, the suffix *anīyar* is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
[This is illustrated by] Pāṇini’s sūtra: *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.33).

*rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (A 1.4.33). The root *prīñ* means "to satisfy"; from this, the present participle (*laṭ*) is formed in the passive sense. In the example *haraye rocate*, the meaning is "he pleases Hari. Since the designation of "object" (*karman*) would otherwise apply here, this rule is stated as an exception. Why specify "being pleased" (*prīyamāṇaḥ*)? Consider: *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ pathi*. Here, [the designation of object does not apply to] the path (*pathaḥ*).
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.34: *ślāghahuṅsthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ*.
*Ślāgh* means praise (*stuti*). [Examples: *kṛṣṇāya ślāghate* (he praises Kṛṣṇa); *kṛṣṇaṃ...* [ślāghate].

The meaning is "he praises. Others, however, say: the meaning is that he speaks of himself or another as praiseworthy, [saying] "to Kṛṣṇa. In that regard, in the first alternative, since [Kṛṣṇa] would have attained the status of an object (*karman*), and in the second, since it would have attained the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to being a residual factor (*kāraka-śeṣa*), this rule is stated. [The example is] *hanute* (she hides), [meaning] from her co-wives (*sapatnībhyaḥ*).

The meaning is that she informs Kṛṣṇa of that very matter by whispering into his ear; or alternatively, it means she whispers to anyone at all. Regarding the form *tiṣṭhate*: the meaning is that she makes her intention known through her standing [in a certain posture].
The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix is applied according to the rule: "Also in the senses of manifesting and designating a place of assembly."
Prau.ma.: *dhārer uttamarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.35).
Regarding the rule *dhārer uttamarṇaḥ*: this is a statement [intended] when the sixth case ending would otherwise have applied.
Prau.ma.: *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.36).

Regarding the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ*: because it is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī], it prevails; thus forms such as *paraspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham* and *spṛhaṇīyaguṇair mahātmabhiḥ* are established. However, when there is an intention to express the remaining relationship (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive case is used. Therefore—
"Like maidens, they both tremble with fear and yearn for their beloved"—this is established. All of this has been stated according to the system of Haradatta and others;
however, in the *Vākyapadīya* and the work of Helārāja, it is stated that [the object] receives the designation of *karman* when used in connection with the verb *spṛhayati*.
It is established that this designation of "recipient" (sampradāna) supersedes the remaining genitive case.

According to that view, in the expression *spṛhaṇīyam*, a kṛtya suffix is used in the sense of the recipient, just as in the word *dānīya*. However, in the expression *kumārya iva*, one should explain it by changing the case-ending as "longing for a lover" (*kāntāya spṛhayanti*).

Prau.ma.- *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.37). The sūtra begins with *krudhadruha*. *Krudh* means "to be angry," *druh* means "to bear malice," and *īrṣya* means "to envy. *Asūya* is derived from the *kaṇḍvādigaṇa* root *asūy* with the suffix *ya*. The meaning is: those verbal roots whose sense is similar to the senses of these [four roots]. Among them—

*Krodha* is anger; *droha* is malice or injury; *īrṣyā* is intolerance; whereas *asūyā* is the attribution of faults to those who possess virtues. Since *krudh* and *druh* are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is applicable when they are used with these objects; since the other two are transitive (*sakarmaka*), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is applicable.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding the rule *rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.39): the term "kāraka" [in the commentary] refers to the "object-kāraka" (*karma-kāraka*). However, the claim of the ancients that it refers to the "object" (*karman*) is an error, because of the governing heading *ekasaṃjñādhikāra*. Nor is it intended merely to indicate the first application [of the designation].

The designation as an object (*karmatva*) is not appropriate, because by accepting the meaning "he reflects upon the auspicious and inauspicious deeds related to Kṛṣṇa," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone would be required.
[Pradīpa on Pāṇini 1.4.40]: *anupratigṛṇaśca*.

"And [the word] *anupratigṛṇaḥ*. The genitive case in *gṛṇaḥ* is used because it is an imitation of a form ending in the suffix *śnā*. [The word] *hotre* [is used] when [the status of] object (*karman*) would otherwise have been expected.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.44: "In the context of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the recipient] is optionally [designated as] the recipient (*sampradāna*)."

Regarding the term *parikrayaṇe*: *kraya* means the absolute acquisition [of ownership] by the surrender of wealth and so forth; the prefix *pari-* denotes that which is proximate to this. And he explains that this [proximity] consists in being for a fixed period, because it is less than that [absolute acquisition]; thus he says: *niyata-*. *Bhṛtyā* means by wages and so forth. Regarding *tādarthye*: for the sake of that.

"For the sake of this" (*tadartham*) means for the purpose of that effect; "the state of being for that purpose" (*tādarthyam*). By the suffix *ṣyañ*, a relationship characterized by being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is expressed, according to the established principle: "From *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, and compounds, the notion of a relationship is conveyed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). This [benefactor-ship] is...

And [this rule] applies in many ways. Therefore, it occurs even in cases such as *brāhmaṇāya dadhi* ("curd for the Brahmin"). In *bhaktir jñānāya* ("devotion for the sake of knowledge"), the meaning is that it transforms into the nature of knowledge.

When there is an intention to express a distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), the fourth case ending is used after the word denoting the modification. However, when there is an intention to express non-distinction, the nominative case alone is used because it is the subsequent rule.

"Devotion transforms into knowledge. However, when one intends to express that devotion is the *apādāna* (point of departure) according to the rule "janikartuḥ," then, because knowledge has its agency already expressed (*abhihita-kartṛtva*), only the nominative case is used: "Knowledge is transformed from devotion" (*bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpate*). With the intention that the root *klṛp* is taken here in its general sense, he says "it becomes" (*sampadyate*), etc. Regarding the word "by a portent" (*utpātena*): [The following is the continuation of the commentary: A portent is a phenomenon occurring in the sky or on earth that indicates future good or evil fortune. It is of two kinds: celestial and terrestrial. Among these, celestial portents are of three types: those arising from the elements (*bhūta-ja*), those arising from the constellations (*nakṣatra-ja*), and those arising from the planets (*graha-ja*). Terrestrial portents are likewise of three types: those arising from the earth itself (*bhūmi-ja*), those arising from trees (*vṛkṣa-ja*), and those arising from animals (*paśu-ja*). Examples of these have been described by the ancients. A portent is defined as a sign indicating the arrival of something else; it is not merely a cause, for a cause does not necessarily indicate a specific result. For instance, the conjunction of the moon and Jupiter is a cause of rain, yet it does not necessarily indicate rain. Therefore, a portent is a specific kind of cause, namely one that indicates a future event. It is said: "A portent is a sign of the arrival of another thing; it is not a mere cause, for a cause does not necessarily indicate a specific result. Thus, the meaning is that the transformation of devotion into knowledge occurs through such a portent. This is stated in the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*: "A portent is a sign of the arrival of another thing.
