An *utpāta* (portent) is a modification of natural elements that indicates the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of living beings; the meaning is that the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used for the object signified by such a portent. Regarding *vātāya*: the meaning is "that which indicates the wind. Regarding *hitā*:
the sense is that this is known from the rule prescribing the formation of the compound. The same applies when joined with *sukha*.

The object of attainment (*bodhyam*). With the intention that, by the power of the rule *tumuṇvulau kriyāyām*, an accompanying word (*upapada*) denoting an action results in being expressive of an action itself, he says: "action. [It is] that which has action as its fruit.
The meaning is that [the word] has a verbal root as its base (*kriyāvācaprakṛtika*). The mention of *tumun* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *ṇvul*.

This is because there is no obstacle to explaining "he goes for fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*) as "one who brings fruits" (*phalānyāharakaḥ*). Regarding the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*): the intention is that this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).

As for the explanation offered by the predecessors— that the sūtra is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama) so that [the designation *karma-kāraka*] may apply only to an action not [otherwise] employed, and not to one that is employed— that is incorrect, because a restriction cannot apply to what has not been established [by another rule]. Nor is there establishment [of the designation] by the rule "tādarthye" (Pāṇini 5.1.12), for that [designation] does not pertain to the fruit (*phala*).
The action of "going" (yāna) has the purpose of "bringing" (āharaṇa); however, that bringing has "fruit" (phala) as its object—this is another matter.

Since the suffix *tumun* is prescribed only for the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), it is already established that its meaning denotes a state; nevertheless, he states "by this rule" (*iti sūtreṇa*) to indicate that the mention of the word "being" (*bhava*) is intended to include a specific type of sūtra.

Nor should it be suspected that the meaning [of the suffix] is already conveyed by the word *tādarthye* (in the sense of being for that purpose) alone; for since the sense of being for that purpose is indicated precisely by the verbal noun (*bhāvavacana*)—just as it is by the suffix *-tumun*—there would otherwise follow the undesirable application of the first case ending (*prathamā*) when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).
As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the suffix is used] only after a verbal noun so that one might say, "The cook goes" (*pācako vrajati*)—[that is not the case here].

"It is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha) so that [the suffix] *ṇvul* does not occur after [a word ending in] *ṇvul*; but that is not correct, because in a word ending in *ṇvul*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is primary, and there is no sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) toward the agent,
and furthermore, because the vehicle (*yāna*), having become a *du* compound, cannot be construed with the meaning of the case-ending."

One might object: "Why [is it] 'the sixth case' (genitive) as well? Let there simply be the genitive; let the word *alam* be understood only in the sense of 'sufficiency' or 'enough'. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It prevails over that" (*tasmai prabhavati*), and so on, including "not even a blade of grass for you" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇam*). Now, one might further object: "In the alternative view, just as with words like 'grass' (*tṛṇa*), from the word *yuṣmad* [the genitive]..."

The fourth case [the dative] should be used. Not so; for in the rule "ṭhanādare" (Pāṇini 1.4.93), the word *karman* (object) is a qualifier—meaning, that object which indicates disregard. Such an object is indeed the grass, and not the referent of *yuṣmad* (you).
Thus ends the fourth [section].

Prau.ma.: *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.24). Regarding the word *dhruvam*: the root *dhru* means "to go" and "to be steady"; from this root belonging to the *kuṭādi* class, the suffix *ac* is applied [to form *dhruva*]. Alternatively, if the reading is *dhruva* in the sense of "steadiness," then the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. Thus, *dhruvam* means "steady."
[Ablative] is that which, while not being included within the action denoted by the root under discussion, is the substratum for the separation (*vibhāga*) produced by that [action].
And since that [separation] necessarily has a limit (*avadhi*), he says: "that which has become the limit. Regarding the word "running":
here, even though the horse is qualified by the action [of running], it does not serve as the limit with respect to the action denoted by the root under discussion.

[This] is contradicted. However, in the case of "the two rams move away from each other" (*parasparasmān meṣāv apasarataḥ*), since the root *sṛ* denotes both movements, the status of the one as the point of departure (*apādāna*) with respect to the movement residing in the other is not contradicted. And it has been said:
That which is indifferent toward a departure, whether it be moving or unmoving,
is called the *apādāna* (ablative) precisely because it remains fixed and is not entered by the action.
Since the horse certainly falls from the pillar, and that pillar likewise certainly falls from the horse,
the falling of that horse is also necessarily admitted.
"The status of being a limit (avadhitva) for the two rams is distinct and distinct, depending respectively on the action of the other ram;
and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct and distinct, depending on their own respective actions.
However, in the case of "He falls from the horse falling from the mountain,"...

The meaning is that the horse is the locus of the falling delimited by the mountain, and the falling residing in Devadatta and others is delimited by that [horse]. In the sense of the ablative case (pañcamī), the referent of the base (prakṛti) is a qualifier of the delimited [object] through the relation of identity; however, the referent of the suffix is [a qualifier] of the action, and that is the substratum (dharmin), not [the action itself].

It is merely the property (*dharma-mātra*), because there is no dispute regarding the fact that a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with the sense of a case ending has as its referent the substratum (*dharmin*) [of that property]. For in the example "a pot from which rice has been removed" (*uddhṛtaudana sthālī*), the meaning is "that which serves as the limit for the removal whose object is the rice. As for the word "disgust" (*jugupsā*), the author of the Bhāṣya, however...

They state that the accomplishment [of the meaning] is established by the Sūtra by relying on the fact that words such as *jugupsā* (disgust) indicate a cessation preceded by that [fear]. This is likewise the case in the subsequent Sūtras as well.
[Pradīpa]: "The cause of fear for those [roots] whose meaning is fear" (Pāṇini 1.4.25).

"Bhītrā. How then is one to explain the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "Whom do even the gods fear when he has become enraged in battle"? On this point, they say: it is [the genitive] "kasya saṃyuge" (in whose battle). And it is not thus [that the rule is violated].
In the case of *saṃyuga* (battle), there is indeed the application of the technical term *apādāna*, because it is not sublated by the subsequent technical term *adhikaraṇa*.
However, when the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the desired result follows. Regarding the example *adhyayanāt*:
the meaning is "fatigue related to study."
Prau.ma.: *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30).

"The source (*prakṛti*) of that which is the agent of birth (*janikartṛ*). Birth (*jani*) means production or origination (*utpatti*). The suffix *iñ* is applied to the root *jan* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the rule *ṭhiñādibhyaḥ*; alternatively, the suffix *iṇ* is applied by the Uṇādi sūtra *janighasibhyāmiṇ*.

By the rule *janivadhyośca*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*. The compound [in *janikartṛ*] is formed with a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "the agent of that [birth]. Thus, it occurs even when joined with another verbal root, as in: *aṅgādaṅgāt saṃbhavasi*. This is what he expresses by the words *jāyamānasya*. By this, [the suffixes] *ik* and *śtip* [are also accounted for].

The sense is that the authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*, relying on the view that this [reference] in the rule for the designation of roots (*dhātunirdeśa*) is by means of the vowel *i*, have resolved the objections raised— namely, the contingency of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) according to the rule *gamahana*, the lack of semantic connection, and the impossibility of forming a compound. In this sūtra, there is the mention of the base form (*prakṛti*).

The author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that [the sūtra] refers only to the cause (*hetumātraparam*), citing "joy arises from a son" as an example. However, the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa is that it refers only to the material cause (*upādānamātraparam*).
He provides an example common to both views: "of Brahmā. Here, Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha; and he...

It is only the cause (*hetu*), not the material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, Brahman qualified by *māyā* is the material cause of all effects; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of our school.
[Prakriyā-pradīpa: *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.31)]

*bhuvaḥ*. *Bhū* means "becoming" (*bhavanam*); the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because it belongs to the *sampad-ādi* group. He says—"*of the agent of becoming*" (*bhū-kartuḥ*)—because the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*), although specified in a compound in the preceding rule, is carried over here due to its being marked as *svarita*. "*Prabhavaḥ*" means that from which something originates; this involves the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that because the form ending in the suffix *lyap* has its meaning already implied, it is not employed. Regarding "yataśca":

the meaning is "from that," referring to that which is resorted to as a limit (*avadhi*) for the purpose of establishing or delimiting a path or time. By means of that, through the sense conveyed by the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), [the connection is established] via the object.
The first and seventh case endings occur after words denoting time when they are joined with [the suffix] *ni* in the sense of being produced or measured. Regarding the word *kalāt*:
it is expected that this refers to something joined with that [suffix].
It is for the sake of elaboration; and it is not the case that "the other [word *itara*] is used in the senses of 'other' and 'inferior'."

It should not be argued that this [term] is taken here because it has the meaning of "low" (*nīca*) according to Amara’s statement; for, as in examples such as "higher than this" (*asmāt-tāraḥ*) or "lower than this" (*mandraḥ*), the rule is already established by *Pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42).
As for the claim that the word *itara* is used only when it refers to a correlate (*pratiyogin*) being explicitly indicated—as in "Caitra..."—[that is incorrect].

"One is a hero, the other is a coward"—therefore, this [word *ṛte*] does not have another meaning. That is weak, because the expectancy for a correlative (*pratiyogi*) is equal in both cases, and because it contradicts the cited lexicon. As for "except for Kṛṣṇa" (*ṛte kṛṣṇāt*), how then is the expression "without the propitiation of the Person" (*puruṣārādhanam ṛte*) to be explained?

Some say this is an error. Others, however, maintain that because of the inclusion of the root *dṛś* in the rule "ubhasarvatasoḥ," the accusative case is also valid when used with *ṛte*, just as in examples such as "caitraṃ yāvacchītam"; and this is correct, according to the Cāndra sūtra: "ṛte dvitīyā ca."

Regarding the phrase "in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti*": this means "in connection with words whose meaning is that of *prabhṛti*" (i.e., "starting from"). Accordingly, while commenting on the Bhāṣya passage "from the full moon of Kārttika" (*kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti*), Kaiyaṭa employed the explanation: "the meaning is 'beginning from that' (*tata ārabhya*)."

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of *vacana*": by implication, only the limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed; the sense is that the qualifying portion, namely "without that," is not [intended]. Alternatively, it is called *maryādāvacana* because the word *maryādā* is mentioned therein—referring to the rule "āṅ is used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*)."
Regarding the sūtra: the meaning is that the prefix *ā* seen therein is designated as "stated" (*uktasaṃjña*).

Regarding *parihara*: according to the vārttika, "the statement [of the rule] is optional when *pari* has the sense of exclusion," there is an absence of reduplication in one alternative. Regarding *pariratra*: here, in the prescription of the ablative case, [the word *pari*] is used with the sense of exclusion by means of *apa*.

The meaning is "due to concomitance. [From] *Prauḍhamanoramā*: "And with regard to that from which there is a substitute or a counter-gift" (*pratinidhipratidāne ca*); by this very indication, when used in conjunction with these two [words], [the fifth case ending is employed].

They say [the word *pañcamī*] refers to the fifth case ending. When the primary object is absent, that which is substituted for it is called a *pratinidhi* (substitute). The repayment of what has been given is *pratidāna*.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.11]: "The fifth case ending is used for the creditor, provided it is not the agent."
"In the sense of 'other than the agent' (akartari)": the fifth case (pañcamī) should occur. This is an exception to the third case (tṛtīyā). Regarding the example *śatena*:

here, a hundred (*śata*) is a debt (*ṛṇa*) because it is being held by the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "that which prompts [an action] is both the cause (*hetu*) and [the agent]," the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is also applied.

Regarding the phrase "due to the division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgāt*): this is clear in the commentary of Haradatta on the sūtra *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "and in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*): the mention of the Vārttika, "The diversity [of suffixes] is due to the limited observation of the base forms," is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in this context.

*Prakriyā-kaumudī*: Regarding the rule *pṛthagvinānānābhistṛtīyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.32), the phrase "for the purpose of conjunction" (*samuccayārtham*) means that particles have multiple meanings; this is the intended sense.

As for the mention of the "fifth case" (*pañcamī*), the fifth case is understood there by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) [from a previous rule], while the second case (*dvitīyā*) is already present [by the preceding sūtra].

[The forms] are *dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*. Here, the locative (*saptamī*) will also be mentioned. Furthermore, because the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.34) is carried forward into the subsequent sections, these [words] take four case-endings even when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is what is to be understood. And thus it is applied: "mūtram dūrād āvasathāt" (urine [is to be discarded] far from the dwelling).
The meaning is "far from the dwelling. Regarding the term *asatva* (non-substance): its status as denoting a non-substance consists in its having that [substance] as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
In this way, by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that which has the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) as its qualificand is excluded. Thus he says:

The phrase "dūraḥ panthāḥ" (the distant path) explains the commentary of the ancients on the rule *karaṇe ca stoka* ("and [the word] *stoka* when used in the sense of an instrument"): "What is the purpose of [mentioning] *karaṇe*? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply to an accusative that qualifies an action—such as *stokaṃ pacati* ('he cooks slightly')—because an action is not a substance (*dravya*). Regarding that [commentary], having restated it... the action's...

They said that it must be considered because substancehood (*dravyatva*) necessarily follows from being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); however, that very point is what must be considered, since it is well-known in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*) is of a non-substantial nature (*asatvarūpa*). Nor is its status as a qualificand untenable.

This is because such [usage] is established merely by the lack of connection with gender, number, and so forth, similar to the state expressed by a *kṛt* suffix. Although in the *Mahābhāṣya* the connection with number is accepted in examples such as "the beds where people have been killed lie" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*),
and the connection with agency or objecthood is accepted in examples such as "he cooks and [the action] comes to be" (*pacati bhavati*), nevertheless, regarding gender—
Furthermore, the absence of any other grammatical factor (kāraka) is indeed a contradiction. And it has been said:
"An action is not joined with gender, nor with the factors of action that do not serve as the substratum for the action;
its nature is non-substantiality—this alone should be understood."
Thus ends the fifth [chapter].

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs after the subordinate element alone, because the meaning of the suffix (the person) is subordinate with respect to the meaning of the base (the king). Furthermore, that meaning [of the suffix] serves as a qualifier for the "man. The genitive does not occur after the principal element, because that would contradict the aforementioned logic and because there is no status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*). For the word "man," according to the circumstances...

When [the word] denotes merely the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) or functions as a *kāraka*, then [the rule does not apply]. However, when it is not so, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) indeed occurs even after the word *puruṣa*. As for the claim that "the subordinate is the *śeṣa*," that is not correct;
for in cases such as "a white jar" (*śuklo ghaṭaḥ*), where there is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) within the mere meaning of the nominal stem, [the genitive would otherwise be required].

Because of the contingency of the sixth case [genitive]. Nor is there sublation by the first case (nominative), since that [first case] has fulfilled its purpose in expressing predominance (*prādhānya*). Regarding "of the object and so forth" (*karmādīnām api*): just as one uses the form "rūpavān" (possessing color) when the specific [quality] is not intended to be expressed, but when that [specificity] is intended to be expressed, one employs forms such as "nīlaḥ" (blue) or "pītaḥ" (yellow).
The sense is that this [rule] is also established by logic.

Regarding the phrase "of existing things" (satām): thus, the readings found in the works of the ancients—namely, "when used in connection with a *kta*-suffix in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and when there is a desire to express the status of being a 'remainder' (*śeṣa*)," and "the sixth case is optionally used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) of roots meaning 'to satisfy'"—are also supported.

The sense is that this is not a statement of something previously unknown. Regarding the word *sarpiṣaḥ*: [these are the examples for] the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.51), *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (2.3.52), *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* (2.3.53), *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ* (2.3.54), *āśiṣi nāthaḥ* (2.3.55), and *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ* (2.3.56).

Regarding the eight sūtras beginning with *hiṃsāyām*, *vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*, and *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe*, they are not explained here because their purpose is to preclude the formation of compounds (*samāsa*). For instance, in those rules, the term *śeṣa* (the "remainder") is understood to carry over.

And when the *karaṇa* (instrument) and other such factors are intended to be expressed as a *śeṣa* (remainder), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is already established. Therefore, this is the meaning: here, only the genitive occurs and there is no elision (*luk*) of it; thus, the very compound (*samāsa*) which would be the cause for that elision does not even exist. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "The genitive prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not [elided]," and so forth.
And Hari said:
"Furthermore, when the action is heard [directly] and is designated by its factors (kārakas),
the genitive case is prescribed for every word to prevent compounding."

Therefore, when the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*) is intended to be expressed, forms such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee") and *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembering of the mother") are correct only in their uncompounded state. However, in cases such as *harismaraṇam* ("the remembering of Hari"), it should be understood that when the remaining relation is intended, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) resulting from connection with a *kṛt*-suffix (a primary derivative) undergoes compounding. And in that regard:

Because [the compound] is preceded by a *kāraka*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the *kṛt*-derivative applies. However, if it were a compound with a genitive of the "remainder" (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), there would be an udātta accent on the final syllable, which is undesirable. Thus, the ultimate conclusion is that these eight sūtras are for the sake of the accent. Furthermore, in cases such as *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered from the mother"), even the absence of compounding [is accounted for].
The result [is not expressed by the genitive]. For in that case, the genitive of the agent (kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī) is not permitted, due to the prohibition in the rule "na loka...".
And it has been said:
"In the case of a past passive participle (niṣṭhā), the genitive referring to the object (karman) is also prohibited."
"In that case, a compound with a genitive case ending [expressing] a residual characteristic (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*) is not desired.

This being the established position, whatever examples or counter-examples are seen here in this section in Vṛtti and other numerous treatises that contain non-finite verbs (*atiṅanta*), all of those are intended as mere illustrations (*upalakṣaṇatayā*).
"Hari, Haradata, and others say that this [rule] does not apply.
Prau.ma.: *sarvanāmnas tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27). Here, *sarvanāmnaḥ* is in the genitive case; thus he says: "of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*)."

Regarding the word *prayoge*: the intention is that if [the rule were applied] with the ablative case (*pañcamī*), then the genitive and instrumental cases would not occur after a word meaning "cause" (*hetu*). Regarding the phrase *nimittaparyāya*: he illustrates the purpose of including the term *paryāya* (synonym) with the words beginning with *evam*. However, the older commentators have cited *kimartham* as an example.

In that case, how is the neuter gender of *kimaḥ* difficult to justify? It may somehow be explained by resorting to the neuter gender for general categories (*sāmānya*) and to compound formation (*samāsa*). As for the rule *asarvanāmnaḥ*, although the Vārttika—*"In the case of words signifying cause, motive, or reason, all [case endings] are generally seen"*—was indeed stated here by the author of the Vṛtti, [it does not apply here].

Nevertheless, the author of the Bhāṣya has read the word *hetau* (in the sense of cause) here; therefore, it applies even when no pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is used. However, because of the inclusion of the term *prāyaḥ* (mostly), the meaning there is that it occurs only in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth. Vardhamāna, however, maintains that it also occurs in the nominative (*prathamā*).
Prakriyāmañjarī: Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30), [the word] "pañcamyāḥ" [is understood]. How then is the form *tataḥ paścāt* justified?
It is because of the usage in the Bhāṣya: *tataḥ paścāt sraṃsyate dhvaṃsyate ca*, which shows that [the suffix *tasi*] is used in connection with words such as *paścāt*.

The fifth [case ending] also [is used]. The inclusion of the term *pratyaya* [in the rule] has an uncertain purpose. [From the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "With words ending in *ena*, the second case is used. How then [is it explained] in the case of *tatrāgāram*?
"Is it 'to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth is our own'?

It should be understood that "uttareṇa" (in the third case-ending) is in grammatical apposition with "toraṇena" (by means of the archway). [Prakriyākaumudī]: With words meaning "far" or "near," the sixth case is optionally used. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.34)

"With words meaning 'far' or 'near'" (dūrāntikārthaiḥ). The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). By this, the ablative (*pañcamī*)—even though it is not explicitly mentioned—is also conjoined, according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*), but not the genitive, accusative, or instrumental cases. This is what he states: "and the ablative."
*Prauḍhamanoramā*: Regarding the rule *divastadarthasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.58): by the word *tat* (that), the two roots *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ* are referred to.

These two were included in the preceding sūtra as having the same meaning [as *div*] in the context of gambling (*dyūta*) and in the context of trade involving buying and selling (*krayavikrayavyavahāra*).

With this intention, he says: "in gambling" (*dyaūte*) and "in an action" (*karmaṇi*). The point is that here the term "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*) is not connected [to the rule], because of the commencement of the two subsequent sūtras. For this very reason, he provides an example of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) within these three sūtras: "he plays for a hundred" (*śatasya dīvyati*).

Prau.ma.: Regarding the rule *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsampradāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.34): the term *preṣya* refers to the second person singular imperative of the root *iṣ*, which belongs to the *adādi* class and has the meaning of "going"; by association with that, *bruvi* is also understood [to refer to the same form].
It is grasped exactly as it is. For this very reason, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is not connected here, because a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is never applicable.
(Prau.ma.: *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65]).

"Of the agent and the object, when a *kṛt* suffix follows. Regarding "guṇe": it has been said—"The genitive case is fixed for the principal [action], but for the subordinate [action] it may be either way. As for "kṛtapūrvī": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one by whom something was done previously" (*kṛtaṃ pūrvamanena*). The meaning is "one who has done it before."

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because the action is not intended to have an object (*avivakṣitakarmaka*). The compound is formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. The suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by the rules *pūrvādiniḥ* and *sapūrvācca*, since the word *anena* is understood from the rule *śrāddhamanena* which governs that formation. Now, how is it that [the word] *dhāyaiḥ* is used in the phrase *dhāyairāmodamuttamam*?

Bhaṭṭi? Regarding this, they say: this [rule] is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), because of the indication [in Pāṇini’s rule] "tadarham" (P. 5.1.117). As for the phrase "of the two feminine suffixes": how then is the commentary on the sūtra *suṭtithoḥ* (P.
6.1.192) to be explained, which states, "there is no sublation of *sūyuṭ* by *suṭ*"? It is because the instrumental case is used here with the intention of expressing the instrument (*karaṇatva*).
Take it! [From] *Prakriyākaumudī*:

"Not with *loka*, *avyaya*, *niṣṭhā*, *khalartha*, or *tṛn*" (Pāṇini 2.3.69). The analysis of the compound is: *u* and *uka* are *ūk*; *la* and the two *ūks* are *lauk*. Thus, the analysis is: *la* and *ūkau*.

Because of the qualification made by the letter *u*, there is the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*); thus he says: "desirous of seeing Hari, or wishing to adorn him. As for the phrase "the genitive is used in the remaining cases," this explains [the following]: "Indeed, even for the Lord of Speech, words difficult to utter are possible when the success regarding a goal hard to attain for the Ikṣvākus depends upon you."

The passage beginning with "tadvidadhīta vismayam" has been explained. Alternatively, the construction is "the successes of the Ikṣvākus," and not "unattainable for the Ikṣvākus"; likewise, the construction is "astonishment for the Lord of Speech," and not "difficult to speak by the Lord of Speech."

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "With words having the sense of *tulya* (equal), except for *atula* and *upamā*, the third case ending is optionally used" (Pāṇini 2.3.72). Regarding the phrase "tulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsasā" by Kālidāsa, and "sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā" by Māgha—how is this to be explained? It is said in reply: [The answer follows: In these instances, the word *tulya* is understood through ellipsis (*ākṣepa*). Since the sense of equality is present, the third case is employed as an alternative to the sixth case. Alternatively, one may consider that the word *tulya* is implied by the very presence of the comparison, and thus the third case is justified. Furthermore, in the case of *tulām ārohati*, the word *tulā* denotes the standard of comparison; since it is a word denoting a measure (*māna*), the third case is applied according to Pāṇini 2.3.18 (*tadarham*). As for *sphuṭopamam*, the word *upamā* here functions as a synonym for *tulya*; however, because it is explicitly mentioned in the sūtra alongside *atula* and *upamā*, it is excluded from the scope of this optional rule, and thus the sixth case is used. Or, one may interpret it as a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a clear comparison," where the sense of equality is inherent. Thus, there is no contradiction with the grammatical rule.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used according to the rule *sahayukte'pradhāne* ("when joined with *saha*, the subordinate [element takes the third case]"). This is as in the example: *svabālabhārasya taduktamāṅgajaiḥ samaṃ camaryeva tulābhilāṣiṇaḥ* ("desiring to weigh its own burden of hair against those born from her limbs, like a yak-cow"). For it has been stated: "the third case occurs even without connection to that [conjunction]."

"Because of the explanation": the word *artha* in the sūtra is also a separate cause [for the compound]. Thus, it is indeed a *dvandva*; the intention is that it is not a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *artha*.
Thus ends the section on the sixth case.
"The locus (ādhāra) is threefold"—this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *saṃhitāyām*.

"Four [types]"—the intention is that these occur when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, since the rule *dūrāntika* is also carried over here, these should be understood as occurring in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as well. "Of the *kta* suffix"—[the suffix] *in*.

The meaning is: "that which has an internal sound as its object and the ground for its manifestation. Regarding the rule "the third case [is used] in the sense of cause," it should also be understood that the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*). As for the passage beginning with *sīmā*, this was stated by Kulacandra in his *Durgavākyaprabodha*. The author of the *Medinī* also says:
"In the fields situated at the boundary-crossings and in the testicles of a woman. And:
"Furthermore, *puṣkalaka* refers to a musk deer and to two types of boundary-piles (*kīla*).
However, Haradatta and others state that *puṣkalaka* is a stake (*śaṅku*) driven or fixed into the boundary for the purpose of knowing the boundary.
They say it is "planted.
[Prakriyākaumudī]—*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37): "And of that whose... An action whose time is well-known serves as the indicator for an action whose time is not well-known.

Because it delimits time, it is a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator). This locative case (*saptamī*) expresses the agent and the object which serve as its substrata. Among these, "he went while the Brāhmaṇas were studying" is an example [of the locative] with respect to the agent. Regarding the object, he says: "in the cows. Here, [the locative is used] for the Brāhmaṇas who are studying and for the cows who are being milked.
And the status of being an indicator through implication (pratīyamāna-lakṣakatva) rests upon the two actions of studying and milking, which have become qualifiers.
"Only a distinction" means that there is no superimposition of a generic form conveyed by another word; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding "māthurāḥ" (the people of Mathurā): here, as in the case of "gavāṃ kṛṣṇā" (the black among cows) and so forth, there is no relation of general and particular; rather, there is simply a contradiction between the two properties conveyed by the words.
Regarding "nipuṇo rājñaḥ" (skilled in [dealing with] the king): when using a correct word (*sādhu-śabda*), the locative case occurs even without [the presence of] honor (*arcā*).
It is indeed so, according to the Vārttika: "And [the suffix *ka* is used] in connection with the words *sādhu* and *asādhu*.

Regarding *prasita*: Amara states that *tatpara*, *prasita*, and *āsakta* are synonyms. Regarding *mūlena*: by the rule "time joined with a lunar mansion [takes the suffix] *aṇ*," the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule "there is elision (*lup*) when there is no distinction [of time]," the suffix is elided.

"By way of alternative [explanations]" (paryāyeṇa): the word *īśvara* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). One interpretation is that it refers to the state of being a lord (*īśvaratva*) belonging to a master; here, "of whom" (*yasya*) points to the master. Another interpretation is that it refers to the state of being a lord belonging to a property (*sva*); here, "of whom" (*yasya*) points to the property. Thus, due to these different interpretations, there is an alternation.
The case ending (*vibhakti*). And that [case ending] follows from the qualifier, just as in the genitive; such is the sense.
Thus ends the seventh [chapter].
Thus ends the section on *kāraka* (case-relations) in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now, the avyayībhāva compound.
"Dependent on a capable [word]" (*samarthāśrita*): the sense is that in the Sūtra, the word *samartha* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).

"To some extent" (*katipaya*): although the author of the Vārttika has stated in the section on obligatory compounds (*nityādhikāra*) that there is a compound of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) with another finite verb denoting an action similar to it (*udātavat*) or one denoting motion (*gatimat*), nevertheless, this is not mandatory, as in the example "he brought [it] here" (*tyānayat*).

Because [the formation of] compounds is not observed in examples such as *ṭhabhiprabharadhṛṣata*, for this very reason the author of the Bhāṣya established this by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) starting with the word *saha*. The intention is that the authority of the sages increases in successive order. As for the phrase "and that," this too is solely for the purpose of establishing the desired result through *yogavibhāga*.
This is clearly stated in the *Padamañjarī* on the rule concerning the technical designation *sampradāna*.

For if this were also the case in common usage (*loka*), then in examples such as *abhipraiti*, suffixes like *su* (the nominative case-ending) would arise from the compound, just as they do in *pacatikalpam* and similar forms derived from primary derivatives (*taddhita*). And yet, [this is not the case].

The resolution [of the objection] by accepting the neuter gender for the universal term *liṅga* is untenable, because in forms such as *prakurute*, a short vowel would result, and in *prakurvīran*, the elision of the *n* would occur.
As for the phrase "because of the specific mention": otherwise, even though there is no distinction in being mentioned in the nominative case, [the rule would apply indiscriminately].

The intention is that, because the technical designation *upasarjana* (subordinate member) is based on its actual meaning (*anvartha*), the word *pūrva* itself would necessarily be placed first in the compound.
Regarding the rule "with *iva*" (*ivena*): this compound also, like the previous one, occurs only in certain instances. Therefore, [we find] "like a cloud" (*jīmūtasyeva*).
In such instances as these, the Taittirīyas read the words separately; thus, even the separate usage in "udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ" and similar examples becomes consistent.
[Prakriyākaumudī: *go-striyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.48)]

Regarding the rule *gostriyoḥ*: [the term] *upasarjanam* refers to that which ends in *go*. As for what was stated by the ancients—that it refers to the two *upasarjana*s ending in *go* and a feminine suffix—that is not correct;
for in examples such as *citraguḥ*, although the word *go* is an *upasarjana*, the entire compound ending in it (*citragu*) is not.

Furthermore, there would be an over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *gaurīpatiḥ*. If it is asked, "How then [is the shortening applied] in *sugokulam* and *rājakumārīputraḥ*?"—listen: because an *upasarjana* (secondary member) is by nature relational, with respect to the meaning of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for which the shortening is prescribed, [the rule applies].
The shortening occurs only when the two members [of the compound] have become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) as the final members. Regarding "diśayoḥ":
even if the analysis is made with the consonant-ending form *diśoḥ*, the resulting form remains the same; for the word *diś* takes the suffix *ṭac* because it belongs to the *śarad-ādi* group.

"By virtue of the force of the statement": for by the word "vibhakti" (case-ending), only that case-ending which forms part of the *subanta* (inflected nominal) with which the compound is formed is understood, due to proximity (*sannidhāna*).
The intention is that the particle *adhi* signifies the meaning of that [case-ending]. However, in the *Parishishta*, this [compound] is [formed] with a nominative (*prathamā*)-ending [word].

There are two established positions: that the compound is formed with a word ending in the genitive case, or otherwise. As for what was stated by the ancients—that in the analysis (*vigraha*) "having referred to Hari" (*harim adhikṛtya*), the form "harau adhikṛtya" results—this is not correct, because an analysis is impossible in the case of an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). As they say: "An obligatory compound is one that lacks an analysis."

[Objection: But surely even a compound whose analysis does not contain its own constituent members is accepted, as in "he makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*). Let this [term *adhikṛtya*] be likewise, since the form ending in the suffix *lyap* (i.e., *adhikṛtya*) exists even when it has not entered into the compound.
[Response: No, because that [form] is used in the analysis (*vigraha*) without conveying even a trace of the meaning of the compound.
Because entry itself is impossible.
As for what they [the commentators] explained: "The term *vigraha* is like a *vigraha*; it is merely an explanation of the meaning.
Therefore, since there is no actual analysis (*avigrahatva*), its status as a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*) is not contradictory. For this very reason...

He shows another non-worldly sentence that serves as the basis for the compound: "it stands as 'harau adhīti'. Here, this must be said: [the claim] that "it is like a *vigraha*" is inconsistent, because a *vigraha* is precisely a sentence used for explaining the meaning; therefore...

Because there is no difference [between the two cases]. Nor can it be said that [the example] is merely a statement of the meaning, for the suffix -lyap does not touch upon the meaning of the compound. As for what was stated—that *hari adhī* is ungrammatical (*alaukika*)—that too is incorrect, because in that case only *hari ṅ* enters [into the formation], according to the rule "even those operations which are internal... (*antaraṅgān api*).
This follows from logical necessity (*nyāya*); otherwise, the vowel *i* in the word *hari* would be difficult to obtain within the compound.

As for what they [the commentators] have explained—that even though the locative sense is already expressed by the word *adhi*, the seventh case ending still occurs because it is "extraordinary" (*alaukika*), for otherwise it would not occur due to the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed")—that too is merely superficial.

For "extraordinariness" (alaukikatva) indeed consists in not being finalized by virtue of being the object of another obligatory rule; however, it is not easily established that the locative case, which is itself untaught [by Pāṇini], enters into that definition merely on this basis.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As for what was explained by his grandson—

that because of the restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇanā*) "by means of verbal suffixes, *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, and compounds," the locative case occurs even when [the sense] is already expressed by the prefix *adhi*— that is not correct, because such an enumeration is not found in the original treatise (*ākara*).

Because [the use of the accusative] has been rejected, because it was stated by the author himself in the very same manner in the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā*, and because it would contradict usage such as *ṭhkramādamuṃ nārada ityabodhi saḥ* and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of the second and the fifth": this is clear in the *Rakṣi* commentary. As for what they say—that in cases such as *caitrasya vanād ārāt*, because the compound would be precluded by the requirement of expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), and because its purpose is already served there, there is no capacity for the rule to apply—this is to be considered doubtful, since it concerns an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*).
For if [the compound] were logically valid, the employment of qualifiers such as "of Caitra" and so forth would be impossible.

Indeed, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "There is no connection with qualifiers for that which has already undergone compounding (*vṛta*). If it is objected that it is also stated in the Bhāṣya that "there is no compounding for those possessing qualifiers," that is true; however, that refers to the domain of non-permanent compounds (*anitya-samāsa*).

Since the *nitya-samāsa* (invariable compound) does not apply when qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) are present, cases such as *mahataḥ kumbhasya upa* would otherwise result. As for what the ancients stated— namely, "of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasyopa*)— and what the commentators explained,
saying "when such an analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) is established," both of these are merely due to oversight (*prāmādika*), according to the reasoning previously stated.

"Now, *samprati*—the indeclinable *samprati* means 'now. As Amarasimha states: 'In this sense [are used] *etarhi*, *samprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, and *sāmpratam*. Furthermore, because it primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it is fit to be construed only with a verbal action. The negation as well—"
It belongs to the action itself;

thus he says: "it is joined" (*yujyate*). "Not currently perceived" (*asamprati*): however, in a compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*), the action of joining is included, just as the action of sprinkling is [included] in the expression "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*). As for that which...

It has been stated by some: "Non-present" (asamprati) means the absence of the present. By this, it is intended that only the present time of the object to be enjoyed is negated. That is not correct, because the logical connection of the substratum as the counter-positive (pratiyogin) with respect to the negation is contrary to all systems of tenets. For indeed...
Some maintain that by the statement "there is no jar on the ground," the ground itself is negated;

however, this is not tenable, so let that matter rest for now. As for the phrase *iti harau*: there is a compound of the word *iti*, which has the sense of "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), with the word *hari* ending in the genitive case, which refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Regarding the word *pratiśabdasya*: as for what they say—that in the case of *grāmasya vṛkṣaṃ prati*, the prescription of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) has its own scope because a compound is precluded due to the state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*)—that has already been refuted. Haradatta, however, says that even the sentence *arthamarthaṃ prati* is correct, based on the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya.

Alternatively, the indeclinable here does not function as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); rather, because it is a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits a relationship. As for the distributive repetition, however, it is indicated by reduplication.
Regarding the example *sahapūrvāhṇam*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of totality (*sākalya*). Regarding the phrase "even when [the time] is subordinate": if...

The meaning is that if it were not stated as "sādṛśye" (in the sense of similarity), then [the compound] would occur only where similarity is the predominant factor; for in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the predominance of the indeclinable's meaning is the general rule (*autsargikatva*). Regarding the word "anta" (end):
it refers to the delimitation of a specific extent of text, such that one thinks, "Now, this much portion is to be studied."

In this context, "end" (anta) is intended to mean completion relative to that [study]. And since that [completion] occurs even when the study is incomplete, it is mentioned separately from "completeness" (sākalya). The word *agni* refers to the treatise concerning its subject matter;
that word, ending in the third case, is compounded. Although the expression *agninā saha* (together with Agni) would indeed be appropriate for usage, [it is not used here].
Nevertheless, it is so when there is mere proximity (*sāhityamātre*). However, when the intention is to express "finality" (*antatva*), the compound is obligatory.

For this very reason, the analysis (*vigraha*) *agnigrantham* is shown as one where the words are not in apposition (*asvapadavigraha*). As for the claim that the analysis is either with a nominative case ending—*agniranto 'syeti*—or with a genitive case ending expressing Agni’s finality—*agnerantatvam iti*—the former [is incorrect].

Or [it might be argued] that there is a compound with a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*); but that is not so, because the word *saha* does not denote an "end" (*anta*), and because an "end-ness" is even more impossible to obtain. Furthermore, it would lack syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the act of study (*adhyayana*). Moreover, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) when joined with *saha* is the logical rule, as in the expression *satṛṇam atītya*, where it signifies completeness (*sākalya*).

In the case of *sāgni*, since even the state of being "ending in" (*antatva*) is expressed by the co-occurrence (*sāhitya*), one accepts a compound there with a word ending in the third case; therefore, its abandonment here [in the present rule] is without foundation. Regarding *yāvac-chlokam*: the indeclinable *yāvat* is compounded. However, the analytical statement (*vigraha*) is as follows:

By the term *taddhita*, it should be understood that there is no co-occurrence within the same word (*asvapadatva*). [From] the *Prakriyākaumudī*: "Optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). This refers to the following: this is an indication of a principle (*liṅgadarśana*) regarding a matter already established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*).

Since the designation *samāsa* (compound), like the designations *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so forth, is always applicable, there can be no optionality for these designations either—just as there is none for other rules—unless there is an explicit statement to that effect. It might be argued: "In that case, *sup-supā* would also be obligatory. But this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Because it would result in a contradiction with established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). To explain: in the *vṛtti* on the *caraṭ-sūtra*, the author stated that *bhūtapūrvaḥ* means "formerly been," and that this is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*. Likewise, regarding the *śākala-sūtra*, in the statement "there is a prohibition of the *śākala* [substitution] in the case of a *sin* [suffix] and in obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*)," there is no purpose in the inclusion of the term "obligatory" (*nitya*), for this [case] is also...
Regarding the *bhāṣya* statement, "The compound *vāpyaśvaḥ* (a horse for a pond) is established as *vāpya-aśvaḥ*," Kaiyaṭa explained:

"'*Vāpyaśvaḥ*' is a compound formed by the rule *sup-supā*. Since the compound [by the rule] *saṃjñāyām* is obligatory, the prohibition [of the accent] is established. Likewise, [he says] "anudātam..."

This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on such rules as "padamekavarjam" and "asiddhavadatra. Therefore, he says: "By means of *sup supā*, [the compound] is established"; that is, "the compound. Since the compound is already established by the very act of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the fact that it is prescribed again by subsequent rules indicates that the former [rule] applies only occasionally (*kvācitkatā*). And thus...

Since the compound with *iva* is also only occasional (*kvācitkatva*), forms such as *udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ* are established. Although the Vārttika *ivena* is recited under the rule *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), Kaiyaṭa maintains that it is merely a reminder (*smārita*) of the same principle already present under *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) within the context of the compulsory (*nitya*) section. This being the case:

Those who assume that the compound [in *jīmūtena*] is Vedic have been refuted; for although the Bahvṛcas accept the compound in *jīmūtasyeva*, the Taittirīyas read it as an uncompounded form— this is the general direction of the argument.

Prau.ma.: *apa-pari-bahirañca-vaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12). From this very [sūtra] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed in connection with *bahiḥ*. That which is established by an indicator does not apply everywhere. By this, the form *karasya karabho bahiḥ* ("the cub is outside the trunk") is established.

Regarding the phrase "down to children" (*ābālam*): as for the expression "from the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) up to the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*)" used in the *Kiraṇāvalī*, that is a mere error, because the use of the particle *ca* within a compound is impossible.
The correct reading, however, is "up to the terrestrial globe" (*ābhūgolakāt*).

Regarding the phrase *yaṃ padārtham*: in the sūtra, the word *yat* is neuter because it denotes a general category (*sāmānya*). Since this is already established by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* ("an indeclinable [is used] for case-endings"), the present sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). Consequently, as an alternative, one may cite *vanasyānu*.

Regarding the term *anugaṅgam*: here, both length (*āyāma*) and the state of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) are indicated by the prefix *anu*. However, the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is the meaning of the compound. For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "the length of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgādairghya*). [The word] *vārāṇasī* [is derived as follows]: that which is both excellent (*vara*) and not perishable (*ana*) is *varāna*.
*Śreṣṭhodaka* means "situated not far from that [excellent water]. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *adūrabhavaśca*. There is vṛddhi of the first vowel.

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. Because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. [This is governed by] Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.7: *nadībhiśca*.

"And by [the word] 'nadībhiḥ' (by rivers)": here, there is no inclusion of the *svarūpa* (the word-form itself), the technical name (*saṃjñā*), or the river itself, because of the indication by the plural number; rather, it refers to the meaning. Nor does that meaning constitute a technical name (*saṃjñā*) through composition.
Therefore, this compound applies to those words which denote that meaning. And these are not merely specific terms, but also—
Even a general term [is included].

"It is always a compound" (nityasamāsaḥ); this is clear from the commentary (*vṛtti*). Kaiyaṭa’s own intention regarding the *Śākala-sūtra* is also thus. But, if this is so, then by parity of reasoning, the same would apply to the *bahuvrīhi* as well.
If it is argued that this would result in the word being an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), it is not so;

for through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words such as *yasya* ("of whom"), there is the cognition of an external referent (*anyapadārtha*). For this very reason, it is stated [in the Vārttika] that "the name is not understood," rather than saying "the external referent is not understood. Regarding the name:
What [is the example]? The region called Śīghragaṅga.
Now, he states the uncommon suffixes for compounds (samāsāntas) in the case of avyayībhāva: "avyayī... [and so on]. Regarding the term "samāsānta":
it means the final member of the compound, or the final member of the word that constitutes the latter part of the compound's meaning.

By this [rule], the feminine suffix *ām* (ām) in *upaśaradam* is established by the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*, and the suffix *ṅīp* in *dvipurī* and similar forms is established by the rule *dvigoḥ*. Regarding *jarāyāḥ*: this is a *gaṇasūtra* (a supplementary rule for the list).
Regarding *pratipara*: the phrase *akṣṇaḥ param* means "beyond the scope"; that is, the word *akṣi* is not within the domain of the *vṛtti* (compound formation).
[The compound] refers solely to the sense organ (*indriya*). Regarding the term *samakṣam*: it is that which is suitable for the eye (*akṣi*).

[In the rule for] *nadī*, here there is the inclusion of the actual form itself and not the technical name (*saṃjñā*), because *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* are mentioned separately. In *upanadī*, there is the absence of the suffix *ṭac*.

The neuter short [vowel] [is used]. However, this should be noted: it was stated under the rule *nadībhiśca* that there is no evidence for the inclusion of the actual forms (*svarūpa*) of the [names of] rivers, as there is for the inclusion of their specific [sub-classes], such as *viśeṣāṇām*. By this, the form *pañcanadam* is established. And in this case—
It is eternal. As it has been said:
"If [the word] follows after the number *godāvarī* and the word *nadī*.
And this is established by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) into *ac* from the rule "ac-prati-anv-ava... (Pāṇini 6.2.192).

The phrase "for the sake of worship" (pūjārtham) is used because the mention of "either one" (anyatarasyām) is understood from the context; this is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds.
[Repeated pattern of vertical bars]
Now begins the section on technical rules (paribhāṣā).
(Praunmukhi-Īkāra-Pada-Sūtra 1.1.3):

*iko guṇavṛddhī*. [The word] "by the two words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*" means that, having carried forward (*anuvartya*) the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding sūtras, [the meaning is] "those which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*."

It is obtained through application; therefore, it does not apply here in cases such as *dyauḥ* (from *diva āṬt*, Pāṇini 7.1.84), *saḥ* (from *tyadādīnāmaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.2.102), or *imam*. As for the term "ending in the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhaḷntam*):

because the word in the sūtra is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in the sixth case, it refers to the formal shape of the word itself (*śabdasvarūpaparatayā*), and thus the elision of *su* occurs after a neuter [word].

The word *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding the word *padam*: that [term] is applicable when coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, and it is connected in the sequence beginning with "of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *iṭ* vowel," and so forth. However, in rules such as "the *guṇa* of *mid*" (*miderguṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.3.82) and "the *guṇa* of *mid*" (*miderguṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.2.114), etc.,...
Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, the word *ika* is connected with the parts of the roots *midi* and *mṛdaj*.

As for the explanation given by the ancients that "the two [substitutes] exist in the place of *ika* alone," and what the commentator on that work stated— that this [rule] is for the sake of restriction where there would otherwise be a lack of restriction— all of that...

It should be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya; for they say that after refuting the view that [the suffix] is a remainder of that [word], the Bhāṣya supports only the view that it is the presentation of the word itself. Furthermore, the rebuttal of objections even against the view that it is a remainder of that has been clearly set forth by us in the Śabdakaustubha.

[Prakriyākaumudī 1.1.47]: "In the midst of vowels. As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the augment] follows the final vowel—that is not correct, because in rules such as *śemucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59), the final vowel is impossible [as the base would end in a consonant].

It is an internal part (*antāvayava*) of that very [stem]. By this, in forms such as *trapūṇi*, the lengthening of the vowel is established because the stem (*aṅga*) ends in *n*. If [the suffix] were initial (*parādi*), that would not be established. However, if it were not a separate element (*abhakta*), then in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*—where the suffix *khaś* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.32 (*vahābhre lihaḥ*)—the rule Pāṇini 6.2.32 (*arurdviṣad...*) would apply.

The anusvāra should not occur after *mum*, because it would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*). As for the objection that if it were not a part of the suffix (*abhakta*), the long vowel would not occur, that has already been effectively refuted by the vārttika on the rule defining the technical term *aṅga*: "The mention of 'beginning with that' (*tadādi*) would be for the sake of [including] the *num* augment."
*Pradīpa*:

"In connection with *sthāne*" (*sthāneyoga*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a connection (*yoga*) by way of position (*sthāna*). The change to *e* [from *yoga*] occurs by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). "Of many kinds" means it is produced by position, meaning, quality (*guṇa*), and measure (*pramāṇa*).
"Because it is stronger. The meaning is that, in the case of *cetā stota*, there is no internal vowel (*āntaryavān*) [of the same class] for the letter *a* on the basis of the authoritative evidence.
(Prakriyākaumudī 1.1.76)
The word *tasmin* is an imitation (anukaraṇa) ending in the locative case. The prefix *niḥ* signifies "immediacy" (*nairantarya*).

The root *diś-* denotes the action of utterance. When it is stated that "yaṇ occurs in place of iK before aC," since [the rule] would apply whether there is an intervening element or not, the restriction is made that it applies only when there is no intervention; and since [the rule] would apply to both the preceding and the following [vowels], the restriction is made that it applies only to the preceding one.

It is restricted [to the following]. However, the phrase "of that which is not separated" is a statement of the resulting meaning. Regarding the rule "the first letter of the subsequent [element] after 'tasmāt'," it was not formulated as a separate sūtra.

Because the portion [of the rule] beginning with "ādeḥ" would result in subverting the status of being a substitute for the whole; however, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), it will be stated immediately below that the status of being a substitute for the whole is the subverter due to its higher priority.
Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|1|25:

"That which has more than one letter [is called anekāl]. An example of a *śit* suffix is "idama iś" (Pāṇini 5.3.3). As for the example given by the author of the Vṛtti, "jaśśasoḥ śiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.20), that is not correct.
Because the status of being *śit* (having *ś* as its marker) is not obtained prior to [the application of] the replacement of the whole (*sarvādeśatā*), for in that case,
the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the status of being a replacement of the whole occurs by this very rule through sequential order (*ānupūrvyā*), just as in the case of *ḍāṇal*.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) includes, by the word "etcetera," the rule "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9).

Regarding the phrase "because it is subsequent": for this very reason, it has been stated that [the rule] *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) is treated separately. As for the portion *utarasya*, however, it indeed applies even to the [suffixes] *auṭ* and *śas*.
As for what was said by the ancient commentator while explaining the sūtra *ādeḥ*:

It has been stated [by some] that [the rule] is by way of a *pañcamī* (ablative) designation, and it is quite clear that this is irrelevant. Regarding the principle *paranitya* ("the subsequent and the obligatory"): as in *tudati* and *ruṇaddhi*, the augment *num* [is applied] by the rule *radhijabhoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.61), overriding even the subsequent *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate short vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Nor is there...
It must also be stated that this [term] is non-eternal because it undergoes the acquisition of another form;

for in some cases, even by the mere application of the rule regarding what has been done and what has not been done (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅga*), eternality is accepted. An example of an internal (*antaraṅga*) [rule] is: *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ* (both gods and humans). Here, although the rule *prathamacarama-* (Pāṇini 1.1.33) is subsequent...

Having set aside the alternative interpretation, the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun) by the rule *sarvādīni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27) applies because it is *antaraṅga* (inherently internal) due to its independence from case endings (*vibhakti*). Even an exception (*apavāda*) is indeed sublated by that which is *antaraṅga*, provided that the exception has its own scope elsewhere. For example: *ayaje indram*.
In this village, all things are thus. Here, the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel-lengthening of homogeneous vowels) is superseded by the internal *guṇa*.
Although that [internal *guṇa*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to both *yaṇ* [substitution] and *guṇa*, it nevertheless finds its application when the locus (*āśraya*) is identical.
Thus states the Vārttika: "The *guṇa* of *iṇ*, *śī*, and *nā* [is applied] because of the *savarṇadīrgha*."
Regarding the statement *asiddham iti*: because of this, in examples such as *pacāvedam*, the substitution of *e* for *ai* does not occur.

Regarding the rule *akṛtavyūhāḥ*: although another paribhāṣā is recited which states that "even an operation already performed may be set aside," and its result is the same, nevertheless, [the rule] is stated simply as *akṛta*.
The sense is that this follows the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. (Laghu)
"They do not perform [the action]" means that, for example, in cases such as *niṣeduṣīm*,

although the augment *iṭ* would have applied to the suffix *kvasu* because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), they do not apply it, considering that the status of being preceded by a consonant (*valāditva*) will be destroyed by the forthcoming *samprasāraṇa*. This is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on general rules (paribhāṣā).

In *ehi kṛṣṇa*, the [protracted vowel] is elided by Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.2.84, *dūrād dhūte ca*. As for what the Easterners (*prāc*) have stated—namely, *kṛṣṇā3 ehi*—that is incorrect; because in rules such as 8.2.84, *dūrād dhūte ca*, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) from 8.2.82, *vākyasya ṭeḥ*, applies. In the example *cakryatra*: here...

The elision of *v* by the rule *skoḥ—* (Pāṇini 8.2.29) does not occur here. This is because, under the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that rules apply at the time the operation is to take effect), the elision is rendered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding external operations), and also due to the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, the restriction "that which is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it does not [apply]" does not hold here, for there is a specific exception to that rule: "there is a fault in that [restriction]."
The elision of *saṃyoga* and so forth has been stated previously.

Prau.ma.: Regarding the rule *dūrād dhūte ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.84), the word *dhūta* means "calling" (*hūtam āhvānam*), and intending that this is an indication for mere address (*sambodhana-mātra*), he says: "in address from a distance" (*dūrāt sambodhane*).
He illustrates the result of the explanation by way of an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) with the example beginning "Drink the barley-meal" (saktūn piba), and so forth.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "Of a heavy vowel (*guru*) that is not *ṛ*, even if it is not final, [there is *pluti*] for each one individually, according to the Easterners" (Pāṇini 8.2.86). Regarding the term "of a heavy vowel": the word "also" (*api*) is intended to include both a heavy vowel and a non-heavy vowel (*aguru*) when they are final (*ṭi*). For example: *devadatta ehi* ("O Devadatta, come here"), and so forth. It is the same in the following cases as well. "Every *pluta*" means that such is the case. And thus:

Regarding the sūtra *agnītpreṣaṇe parasya ca*, the Bhāṣya states: "Every protracted vowel (*pluta*) must be applied optionally (*vibhāṣā*), even by one who does not desire to take liberties. Haradatta explains that "taking liberties" (*sāhasam*) means the abandonment of the grammatical treatise; thus, "even by one who does not desire it" means even by one who follows the treatise.

Others maintain that the meaning is: even though the performance of optional rites results in an abundance of merit, one does not desire them because they involve the hardship of practice and are impossible [to perform completely].
By this, the *Bhāgavata* passage—"Dvaipāyana, distressed by separation, called out 'O son!'"—is explained.

Because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is optional; furthermore, it can easily be argued that here the word *putra* does not stand at the end of a sentence, since it is possible for a word to be an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) even when it precedes a verb. Moreover, let there be the protracted vowel, but let the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) not occur, as it is also optional. And thus: "ī" [etc.]

Regarding the phrase "of Cākravarmaṇa," the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra states: "There is no purpose in the inclusion of the vowel *ī*, as in the case of *vaśā* and *iyaṃ vaśeyam*. Indeed, every instance of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) after a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is difficult to find, because of the Sūtra "aplutavad upasthite. That which is called *upasthita* is non-Vedic.

The meaning of that [sūtra] is indeed: "the word *iti*, when followed by another [word], shall be protracted (*pluta*) as if it were not protracted. Thus, since the explanation in these four ways is clear, the statement by Śrīdhara—that it is an archaic usage (*ārṣa-prayoga*)—is not to be respected.

Regarding the term *dvivacanam* ("dual ending"): the intention is that by the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending") in the rule *suptiṅntam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), it is indicated that "in a rule prescribing a technical name (*sañjñā*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix. Therefore, it does not apply here; for example, *kumāryagāram* ("the house of two maidens" or "of two young wives").

Regarding the term *vadhvagāram*: this is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources. The claim that a dual-form ending in [e] or [o] should be *pragṛhya* is merely the error of the ancients. In the example *harī etau*, there is no application of the Śākala rule; as stated, this is because the word *nitya* was included in the sūtra *plutapragṛhyā-ac-...* (Pāṇini 6.1.125). Here—

The author of the *Vṛtti*, having read the rule as "the prohibition for those who maintain [the view that] *maṇi* [is indeclinable] must be stated," cited examples such as *maṇīva*, *rodasīva*, *dampatīva*, and *jampatīva*. However, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that this is not authoritative because it was not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). This being the case—
"Like two jewels hanging from a camel's neck, my two dear calves hang down."
Thus he justifies the usage in the *Bhārata*: "the sense of 'as it were' (*iva*). Regarding the word "va":
according to the *Medinī*, "one should know that *vaṃ* is used for the wise (or *pracetasa*) and is an indeclinable in the sense of 'as it were' (*iva*)."

The meaning is that this is because, on the occasion of explaining the Amarakośa entry "va vā yathā tathaivaivaṃ sāmye," learned scholars cited the usage by Kālidāsa, "śātravaṃ va papuryaśaḥ" (or they filled with fame the enemy's [domain]),
and because such examples as "kādambakhaṇḍitadalāni va paṅkajāni" (like lotuses whose petals have been torn by geese) are observed.

As for the alternative reading, "vadvā yathā tathā," and so forth, that is incorrect; for in the context of a treatise on names and genders (*nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*), the suffix *vat* is inappropriate, and furthermore, suffixes such as *aṇ*, *phiñ*, and *vuñ* are not mentioned among the synonyms for "offspring" (*apatya*), "collection" (*samūha*), and the like.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: "After *adas*, [the final phoneme] is *m*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.12). Intending to show that the vowel *e* does not carry over here because its occurrence is impossible, he says: "*īdūt-au*. Now, one might object: the carry-over of the vowel *u* is redundant, as in the case of "two women" (*striyau*).

In the case of *phale vā amū āsāte*, since the result is already established by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇaiva*), even though the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the form would still end in *e*; therefore, he says *rāmakṛṣṇau*. The intention is that in the masculine, the result is not established by the preceding rule, because [the base] ends in *au*. [This applies to] *adaso*...

With respect to the sūtra *māt* (Pāṇini 1.1.12), the status of being a *tumun* suffix and the substitution of *ī* are not established as *asiddha*, due to the force of its specific formulation. "The vowel *e* also [is not *asiddha*]"—the sense is that the inclusion of the term *māt* has the purpose of making it understood that the vowel *e* does not carry over [from the preceding rule]. In this regard, the following...

This is worthy of consideration: why was it not simply formulated as "īdūt-saptamy-arthe pragṛhyam, adasaḥ, ec-ca dvivacanam"? For in this way, the mention of *īdūt* in the preceding sūtra and the mention of *māt* in the present sūtra would be unnecessary; furthermore, there would be no difficulty regarding the burden of partial recurrence (*ekadeśānuvṛtti*).
*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding the rule *śe* (Pāṇini 1.1.13): this [mention of the word *śe*] is stated for the sake of clarifying the context, even though it is Vedic;
however, in reality, since it serves as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), it is indeed possible for it to have a worldly meaning as well, as in the example *tve rāyo me*.

In cases such as *rāya* and so forth, there is no purpose for the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of *tve* or *me*. As for *asme*, it means "to us" (*asmabhyam*). The substitution of *śe* for the dative plural ending (*bhyas*) is according to Pāṇini 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk*);
the elision [of the final vowel] is according to Pāṇini 7.2.90 (*śeṣe lopaḥ*).

*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14), since the form *aj* (a vowel) is already understood as a *nipāta* by the very exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *āṅ*, the inclusion of the term *nipāta* is for the sake of what follows; it is placed here specifically for clarity. For example: *ā evam iti*. This refers to something previously introduced.

This particle *ākāra* indicates a change in the meaning of the sentence; its sense is: "Previously you thought thus, but now you think otherwise. [In the phrase] *ā evaṃ kila*, this particle *ākāra* indicates recollection.
Regarding the passage beginning with *vākya* and so forth, the Bhāṣya states as follows:

"One should know that *aṅ* has the marker *ṅ* when it signifies slightness (*īṣadartha*), connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), limit (*maryādā*), or inclusion (*abhividhi*); [and] *aṅ* has the marker *ṅ* in the sense of a sentence (*vākya*) or recollection (*smaraṇa*).
Here, the intention is solely to define the technical name *aṅ*, because of parsimony; the fact that the others have the marker *ṅ* is established by the meaning itself.

The rule beginning with *īṣadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.7), however, is a restatement by way of partial extraction (*avayutyānuvāda*). And thus, in the example *abhra āṅ apaḥ*, since the vowel *ā*—which functions here in the sense of the locative case—is also an *iṅ* vowel, the rule *āṅe 'nunāsikaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.126) applies; this is the intended meaning.
Prakriyā-mañjarī: *ot* (Pāṇini 1.1.15).
What is the purpose of the term *nipātaḥ* [in this sūtra]? [Consider: *devo'si* ("You are a god") and *vāyavāyāhi* ("O Vāyu, come hither").
Prakriyā-mañjarī: *sambuddhau śākalyasyetāvanārṣe* (Pāṇini 1.1.16). [This rule applies] when there is a vocative (*sambuddhi*), according to Śākalya, provided it is not a Vedic (*anārṣa*) context.

Regarding the vocative (*sambuddhau*): the *ṛṣi* is the Veda, because it is seen so in such passages as "that was said by the *ṛṣi*. With this intention, he says "non-Vedic" (*avaidika*). Why [is the term] "vocative" used? [Consider] "aho. Here, let there not be an option due to the subsequent rule. As for the fact that [the word] "not" (*na*) is carried over from "ot" and is present here as well...
The counter-example for the inclusion of the term *saṃbuddhi* is stated in the *Vṛtti* and other works as *gavityayamāha*.

That is not correct, because even though the designation *pragṛhya* applies there, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not result. For it is clear from the commentary on Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.127 (*iko'savarṇe*) that the mention of "the end of a word" (*padānta*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

And thus, in the rule *plutapragṛhyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.125), its connection is necessary. Furthermore, *gavi* is not a word (*pada*), because, due to the intended non-distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there is an absence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), and consequently, no case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises.
Prakriyāmañjarī on *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17):
Regarding the rule *uñaḥ*, since the designation *nipāta* would have applied by the rule *nipāta ekāj* (Pāṇini 1.1.14), this [rule] provides an option (*vibhāṣā*).
[Prakriyākaumudī]—Regarding the sūtra *āṣ* (Pāṇini 1.1.18): [the word] *anunāsika* [is used]. Therefore, when this [āṣ] follows, [the rule] *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) applies.
[This is] an alternative view. As for what you read as *tanūṃ* or *tanūḥ*, [the rule] states that "this is long," and so forth.
It is precisely for this purpose that the mention of the nasal (*anunāsika*) occurs there; otherwise, he would have simply stated *yaro ñami ñam vā*.
Prau.ma.: *maya uño vo vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.33).

Regarding *maya uño vo vā*: [the meaning is] "of that which follows *may-*. However, the claim of the Easterners (*prācām*) that it means "after [the letter *m*]" is an error, because according to the Bhāṣya—"substitutes are prescribed for that which is indicated by the genitive case"—in the rule prescribing a substitute, [the genitive must refer to the element following the preceding one].

Furthermore, it is logical that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) belongs to the substituendum (*sthānin*). Regarding the phrase "because it is not established" (*asiddhatvāt*): for this very reason, this substitution of *vat* is prescribed in the Tripādī section. For if its purpose were merely to subvert the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), he would have stated "or *uṅ* after *mayaḥ*" immediately after "yaṇ for *ik*" (Pāṇini 6.1.77). [He would not have needed to mention] the *yaṇ* [substitution].
And he would have applied [the rule]. Here, in the presence of *it* following *maya* and *uñ*, there are twenty-eight forms. To illustrate:

in the case of *uñ* being treated as a *pragṛhya* by the rule "uñaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.17)—*kimu iti*; in the alternative view of *vatva* (the substitution of *u* for *o*)—*kimviti*; and in the case of the *ūṅ* substitute—*kimūṅ iti*. By virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of the substitute being like the original) of that *ūṅ* substitute, the rule "maya uñaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.33) applies.

In the case of the nasalized *v* (anunāsika), which constitutes an exception to the rule of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) due to its closest similarity (*āntaratamya*), we have the example *kimviṃti*.

In the alternative where there is substitution of *va* for *vat*, there are eight [phonemes] including *rūpa*; in its absence, there are two, making ten in total.

In the alternative where the technical terms *pragraha* and *gṛhya* are not applied, because the substitution of *va* for *vat* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), only the *yaṇ* substitution (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies, and of that—

In the form *sidhdatvam*, when the anusvāra is replaced by the following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) according to Pāṇini 8.4.59 (*vā padāntasya*), there arises the eleventh form, which consists of two *va*s— one nasalized and one non-nasalized. When the nasalized *va* is doubled according to Pāṇini 8.4.64 (*halo yamām...*), [the twelfth form results].
Because the *laṇ* [saṃdhi] is optional, there are three forms when it is not applied, resulting in twelve forms.
In the alternative where there is no *parasavarṇa*, because the *anusvāra* is subject to doubling, there are two optional doubled forms.
By adding these together, there are fourteen. This applies to the vowel *i* in the word *iti*.
