Due to the optional nasalization prescribed by the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), there are twenty-eight [forms].
Thus ends the section on vowel sandhi (ac-saṃdhi).
*Prakriyākaumudī-manoramā*: An Elaborate Explanation of the *Prakriyākaumudī*. **Auspicious Invocation**:
Meditating again and again upon the Supreme Brahman, and repeatedly recollecting the words of my Guru...
We compose the *Prakriyā-prakāśa*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, known as the *Prauḍhamanoramā*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*, *Imāḥ Sūtrāṇi*:

*ha ya va ra ṭ*. The instruction of the letter *ha* (*hakāropadeśaḥ*) is for the purpose of including *ha* in the rules concerning *aṭ*, *ś*, and *ṣi*. [Example: *arheṇa*; here, by the rule "*aḍ-vyavāye'pi*", there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. [Example: *devā hasanti*.
The substitution of *u* [for *i*] occurs by the rule *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114). Thus we have *lilihidhve* and *lilihidhve*;
the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.79).
*Prau.ma.imā.sū.*:

*ha l* || This sūtra is for the purpose of including the letter *h* among the *val*, *rjhal*, and *śal* [categories]. [Examples are: *rudihi*, *svapihi*; [the suffix *hi* is added] by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76), which characterizes it as beginning with a *val*.
*iṭ*: having become affectionate (*snehitvā*, *snehitvā*); here there is optionally the status of being *kit* by the rule "ralo vyupadhāt" (Pāṇini 1.2.26).
*adāgdhām*: here there is the elision of the *s* by the rule "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26).
*alikṣat*: here there is the suffix *ksa* by the rule "śala igupadhāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.45).

The rule *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3) means "the final [element] in a *hal*-containing [string]. The sense is that in the analysis *hali antyam*, the compound is formed either by the *yogavibhāga* ("separation of rules") known as *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), or by the general rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4).

Alternatively, this may be a genitive tatpuruṣa compound. It might be argued that let there be one of the options for *ekaśeṣa*—namely, *tantra*, repetition (*āvṛtti*), or *ekaśeṣa* itself—regarding the rule *hal*. And it will be explained as *hasya l* ("of *ha*, *l*").
The meaning of the genitive case here is proximity (*sāmīpya*). Or rather, let there be no *tantra* and so forth; let it be a collective dvandva compound: *hal*.

And as for the [objection] beginning with "ca l ceti"—if it is argued that there is the elision of the final *l* of the *saṃyogānta* (consonant cluster ending in *l*) by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, do not say so; for in the first case, the compound would be strained (*kliṣṭa*). Indeed, in examples such as "brāhmaṇakambala," a blanket belonging to someone other than the one near the Brāhmaṇa is not understood, nor is it [the case here].

From the word *citragu*, a tree or other object situated near the cows of Citragu is understood. For this very reason, it is clearly stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that there is no compound formation with words such as *anantara* (immediate), because they are not so prescribed. Furthermore, much more could be said:
even the analytical usage (*vyasta-prayoga*), such as "the blanket of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇasya kambalaḥ*) or "his cows are brindled" (*citragāvo 'sya*), is undesirable in those cases.
Even in the second case, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is difficult to achieve, because of the commencement of the prohibition regarding *yaṇ* sounds.
Even on the view that this [prohibition] is rejected, [the rule] from "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26) [applies].

Furthermore, because the elision of *jhal* is prescribed by extracting the mention of *jhal*, and because the understanding of the meaning of a sentence is impossible without the understanding of the meaning of its constituent words— therefore, since it would follow that the meaning of this sūtra could not be understood prior to the establishment of the *hal-pratyāhāra*,
this effort is made for the sake of rescuing [the system]. And in this state, while the meaning of the word *hal* remains unestablished, [the objection stands].

A copulative compound (*dvandva*) is indeed impossible because the desire to express [the members] together cannot occur; therefore, that which has been stated above alone is logical. (Prau.ma.i.1.1.71)

Regarding the term "of those situated in the middle": the whole collection is implied by its two constituent parts, the beginning and the end. Since it is impossible for that [collection] to be applied simultaneously to the entire object of designation (*lakṣya*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) descending upon its constituents comes to rest upon those situated in the middle, and not upon the beginning and the end, because those two are included within the very nature of the name itself.

The sense is: "because of the determination [of the word] for the sake of another. Regarding the phrase "and its own," this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "its own form" (*svarūpam*).
And "its own form" is understood as belonging only to the first [word], not to any other;
for the mention of the third case in the word "by the last" (*antena*) indicates it is subordinate. This is because pronouns (*sarvanāman*) generally [refer to what precedes].
Because it refers to the primary [element].

(Prau.ma.i.1.3.2) "The first utterance" means that, although it is explained through the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) as "that by which something is taught," [it is actually the object].

Although it is explained in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other works that "śāstra" means "instruction" (*upadeśa*), this is nevertheless merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is because the suffix *ghañ* is difficult to obtain in this sense, as it is superseded by the suffix *lyuṭ*.
Nor can the suffix *gha* apply, because [the word] is not a technical term (*asaṃjñā*), given that the rule for *gha* is generally explained as applying only to technical names (*saṃjñā*).

Because it is afflicted (*kliṣṭatvāt*), and because the author of the Bhāṣya has shown disregard for it by stating, "for a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) cannot itself be a limiting adjunct," and so forth. For this very reason, even the suffix *ghañ*—as in the rule *hal-śca*—is not applied here. The notion of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*) is a resort only when there is no other way out. For this same reason, [the word *prakṛti*] is explained as "those by which words are derived" (*prakriyante śabdā yābhiḥ*).
The derivation based on the sense of instrument (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) is also refuted; thus, the *Vārttika* states:

"In the case of *strī*, *khala*, and *na*, [the suffixes] *añ* and *ap* [are applied], while for *strī* [the suffixes] *kha* and *lañ* [are applied] by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*). Therefore, the point is that it is only logical that the suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*).

Regarding what they recite beginning with "In the Dhātusūtra," and what they explain: "The status of being an *upadeśa* belongs to those [terms] mentioned in the first half [of the work] by way of the instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*), whereas for the *āgamas* and so forth, it is by way of the objective derivation (*karmavyutpatti*).
Since the *uṇādi* [list], the *liṅga-anuśāsana*, and the *sūtras* are already established as such, their separate mention [is for a specific purpose]."

[The objection continues: "By the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalivardanyāya*), since [the term *dhātu*] is already established as a class (*gaṇa*) by this very fact, [it follows that] 'of the verbal root (*dhātu*) also'...
and so forth. Here, this must be said: Is this the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of these [roots], or is it merely a conventional usage (*yoga*)?
Not the first, because the author of the treatise has not stated such a designation; and since it is not a technical designation, the suffix *gha* does not apply.

And because it is stated in the Bhāṣya; and because if a technical name (saṃjñā) created by ourselves were to establish the system of the grammar, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For it is not the case that *ām*—from which the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) has been dropped—is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), such that it would not possess the property of being *mit*. Furthermore, in this way, regarding the rule for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), [the use of] the ablative case...

If it were assumed that the sixth case [of *san*] functions as a determiner (*prakalpakatva*), one might suspect that the substitute for *san* should be *san* itself; however, this would contradict what is stated in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, namely that because there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply. Furthermore, [the question arises]: "What is the purpose of mentioning 'root' (*dhātu*)? [Consider the example: *lūñ*..."

The *Bhāṣya* states, "lavitā, pūñ, pavitā," and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary— which intends to show that the designation of a verbal root (*dhātusaṃjñā*) occurs only after the elision of the suffix has been performed— would otherwise be contradicted. Furthermore,
in the rule "ghvasoreddhau" (Pāṇini 6.4.119), the term "lopaśca" contains two *ś* sounds.

The explanation [of the rule] would also contradict the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, and other works regarding the rule *al-ontya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), which states that the second *śakāra* is *it*. It cannot be the second alternative either; for if the *yoga* itself were prioritized, the enumeration (*parigaṇana*) would be rendered useless. Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency: the derivation based on the sense of instrument (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*) would apply to roots (*dhātu*) and so forth, but not to augments (*āgama*) and the like.
Furthermore, because [the definition] would be difficult to establish;

and because it would contradict your own text, which states that the meaning is "the final consonant (*hal*) of a collection [of sounds] delimited by adventitious properties (*upādhi*) such as 'being a verbal root' (*dhātutva*), which serve as the basis for being a designation (*upadeśatā*). This applies to both positions regarding the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*).
Because it would not serve the purpose of the present context, and because the rule *lopaś ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) does not include the letter ś;

furthermore, because it is universally accepted that in rules such as *ādeca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 6.1.45) and *upadeśe 'tvataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.62), the term "upadeśa" refers exclusively to the initial enunciation [of a sound]. This is the general direction [of the argument].
Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|3|2:

"In grammatical instruction, a non-vowel [consonant] with a nasal mark (anunāsika) is [called] *it*. Although, due to its status as a prerequisite, it would have been more appropriate to state the technical term *anunāsika* first, nevertheless, by following the etymological derivation (*yoga*) "that which follows the nose" (*nāsikām anugata*), [the definition is established].

Since its purpose has already been explained, the sūtra defining the technical term *anunāsika* (nasalized vowel) is of little utility; this is what [the author] intends to suggest by not citing it here. [Question: What is the purpose of the word *upadeśe* (in the instruction)? [Example: *ababhra āṅ apaḥ*. Although one might easily argue that the substitution of *it* does not occur here due to the force of the specific rule, as in the case of *uñaḥ* in Pāṇini 1.1.17–18, [the word *upadeśe* is necessary].

Nevertheless, the inclusion of the term *upadeśa* right here has been made for the sake of clarity, so that it must necessarily be understood as referring to the subsequent purpose. Why [is this necessary]? So that [the substitution] does not apply to the *makāra* of *manin*. That which is promised (*pratijñāyate*) is a *pratijñā*.
[The suffix] *aṅ* is applied in the sense of an object according to Pāṇini 3.3.106: *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, it is a *pratijñā*.

The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom there is nasality" (ānunāsikya). Thus, one need not resort to the laborious explanation that "the word *pratijñā* [in the term *prātiśākhyam*] has a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to what is understood through the *pratijñā*," because the meaning can be established without any figurative sense, just as in expressions such as "grammar is the discovery (*upajña*) of Pāṇini."

The sense is this: although the nasalized reading (anunāsika-pāṭha) composed by the author of the Sūtras has now been lost, nevertheless, on the strength of the usage of the authors of the Vṛttis and others, it is inferred that it existed previously according to its function.
One might object that the rule "of *ra* and *la*" (*ralayoḥ*) is deficient because the letter *ṭa* is also situated between them; therefore, he says:

"in the *pratyāhāras*. Regarding the word "are used" (*vyavahriyante*): it is derived from the sense "wherein letters are brought back" (*pratyāhriyante*) or "abbreviated" (*saṃkṣipyante*), with the suffix *ghañ* in the locative sense according to the rule of frequent usage (*bāhulaka*).

Although the mere application of etymological derivation (*yoga*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakta*) regarding the designations *akāra* and so forth, the intended meaning is that it is a case of "etymological-technical" (*yogarūḍhi*) designation.
Furthermore, the ancients maintain that there are forty-one *pratyāhāras*;
these are formed by the *hal* and *it* markers found in the fourteen *sūtras* and are employed within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

The meaning of that [statement] is "forty-one. Therefore, they say that the term *su-p* (the *su*-pratyāhāra) and *tiṅ* etc., as well as the *rapratyāhāra*, the expression "the second [consonants] are *ca*" (*cayo dvitīyāḥ*), and the *ñam* in the rule "only one [nasal] is desired after *yam*, *ram*, and *man* when followed by *aniṭ*" (*yamirñamaniteṣvaniḍeka iṣyate*)—all these were employed by the author of the Vārttika; however, this is a statement made in haste.

Because the first [rule] belongs to the *uṇādi* sūtras and the second is found in the *kārikās* of Vyāghrabhūti; let this matter rest for now. Furthermore, this restriction regarding the number [of suffixes] is not of much practical utility, and thus it has been disregarded.
*Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|1|37*:

*ūkālo’c*. This is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), and "protracted" (*pluta*). The masculine gender is used according to the rule of the *sūtra*. The phrase "like their time" (*vāṃ kāla iva*) is a statement of the resultant meaning; however, the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is "the time of them" (*vaḥ kālo*).
The word *yasya* is to be understood [as the subject]. By the word *ū*, its own time of pronunciation (*uccāraṇakāla*) is indicated. Regarding *āye*:

according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* 12 (Pāda 4), "particles (*nipātāḥ*) have the acute accent (*udātāḥ*) on their first syllable," the vowel *a* is acute; however, the word *yat* is [acute] by the *Phiṭ-sūtra*. As for *ṅ*: the vowel *a* is grave (*anudātaḥ*).
(Prakriyākaumudī, Īpāda Sūtra 1.2.32):

*tasyāditaḥ* (of that, from the beginning). Regarding *atantram*: the meaning is that, as in the case of the prefix (*upasarga*) in the word *upeyivān*, it is not intended to be significant. [Objection: But in that [context], there is the phrase *īyivāṃsam atisridhaḥ*.

If you argue that non-intentionality [of the grammatical operation] may be accepted based on the observation of such usages as these, then what is the proof for non-intentionality in this present case? To this, understand that the proof consists in the observation of the actual linguistic data (lakṣya) as well as the Prātiśākhya and other treatises.
For instance, in the word *yerāḥ*, the vowel *e* occurs; and in the word-pāṭha (*padapāṭha*) of *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpatim*, [the same applies].
It is well-established among all the Bahvṛcas that [the two syllables] beginning with *ū* are udātta when followed by *ardha*.

In the case of the words *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati*, once the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied to the initial syllables of both the preceding and following members according to Pāṇini 6.2.140— "In the case of *vanaspati* and others, both [members take the acute accent] simultaneously"— then [the remaining syllables become] *anudātta*.
By the rule "padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), there is the elision of the accent on the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*).
Regarding the two preceding words, *snūṣā* and *śacī*, it is stated in the Prātiśākhya that the final syllable of each may optionally be *svarita*.
"Or, as in *jātyavat*, the two [preceding sounds] remain as they were, with *tanū* and *śacī* being the first two";
likewise, regarding the acute (*udātta*) nature of the half of a circumflex (*svarita*), the Prātiśākhya also states:
"When there is the coalescence of single syllables, the accent of the first two is circumflex (*svarita*)."
Of that [vowel], compared to one that is more exalted (udātatarodātāt), the duration is half a mātrā, or indeed even half of that.

"Something is called udātta (high-pitched), or else the following syllable is svarita (circumflex). The meaning of this is: when the preceding qualities of udātta and anudātta (low-pitched) coexist in one [syllable], it should be understood as svarita. Of that svarita...

It should be understood that the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is more acute (*udāttatara*) than an independent acute (*udātta*). The example "kva vo'śvāḥ" and others intend a short vowel (*hrasva*), whereas "ardhaṃ vā" intends a long vowel (*dīrgha*). Since this very [rule] includes even the short vowel and is thus all-encompassing (*vyāpaka*), this alone should be respected.

The particle *eva* is used for the purpose of restriction. The statement beginning with "anudāttaḥ" (the anudātta [is used]) is an exposition of a meaning established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

That *śeṣa* (the remaining [vowel]) would have the quality of being heard as udātta. Is this without distinction? No, he says: "na cet" and so forth. The meaning is: excepting that which is followed by an udātta or a svarita. Śākalya also said:

"But that which is non-ordinary (aprākṛta) *svāra* is preceded by a *svarita* or an *udātta*; having raised its first half, they then strike the remainder as tremulous (*kampita*). [The commentary explains: "Having raised" means having made it *udātta*. By the word "half-short" (*ardha-hrasva*), a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is indicated.

The works of Haradatta and others, however, must be interpreted in some way as being intent upon other views. Regarding *kvā*: from the root *kim*, the suffix *at* is applied; it is *svarita*. Regarding *vā*: because of the governing rule "everything [is] *anudātta* except at the beginning of a *pāda*" (Pāṇini 8.1.18), it is *anudātta*. Regarding *aśvāḥ*: from the root *aś*, the suffix *kvun* is applied.
By its own accent, *adya* is acute (*udātta*). However, in *saṃhitā*, the vowel *o* is acute according to Pāṇini 8.2.25: "A single substitute [for an acute and a non-acute] is acute.
In *ye arāḥ*, both words are acute at the end by the Phiṭ-sūtras. But the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is optionally circumflex (*svarita*). [Pāṇini 8.2.6: "The circumflex..."
This is because of the rule "or [the first syllable is] unaccented at the beginning of a word" (Pāṇini 8.2.6).

Furthermore, in the analysis of the compound *mukhaṃ ca nāsikā ca* ("mouth and nose"), since it denotes a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), it undergoes singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.2.42.
It might be thought that [the term] should be *mukhanāsikaṃ*; therefore, he says *mukhasahitā* (accompanied by the mouth).
Intending [the rule] *śarīrāvayavādyat* ("the suffix *yat* occurs after words denoting parts of the body"), he says *tālvādī* (beginning with the palate).
"Internal" (ābhyantara). This is understood from the force of the word *pra* [in the sūtra]. What is meant by "having the same place of articulation" (*tulyāsya*)? Example: *tarptā*.
Here, when *ta* follows *pa*, the elision [of the former] by Pāṇini 8.4.65, "a *jhara* is elided before a *jhara*," shall not take place.
Why is the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) included? Example: *vāk ścotati*. Here, there is no elision of *ś*.

Regarding the statement *ṇamaṅṇanānām iti*: by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *ṭhnāsikā ca*, the respective points of articulation such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth are conjoined with each of their own classes. The *Prātiśākhya* of the Taittirīyas states: "The *anusvāra* and the final [consonants of each class] are nasalized (*anunāsika*). Furthermore: "The nose is the place of articulation for the *yamas*, the *anusvāra*, and the nasals (*nāsikya*)."

"The last [consonants] of each class are nasalized," according to the *Kātyāyana-prātiśākhya*. Its commentary states: "The last [consonants] of each class—*ñ*, *m*, *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *n*—are nasalized; by the word 'and' (*ca*), the meaning is that they possess the nose as their second place of articulation, without abandoning their own original places. [And regarding the rule] "of *e* and *ai*..."
In such instances, the use of the *t* as a marker (*taparatva*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, and not for the purpose of including sounds of that specific duration;
therefore, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is also included.

"pūrvatrāsiddham. If this were an independent rule (*svatantra-vidhi*), then one would only obtain the meaning: "the Tripādī is asiddha with respect to what precedes it"; however, [it would not follow that] a subsequent rule belonging to the Tripādī is not asiddha with respect to what precedes it.

Therefore, he says: "This is an *adhikāra* (heading/rule governing). If it were intended here that [the subsequent rule] is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, then in examples such as *manorathaḥ*, the substitution of *u* would not occur, because the rule *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14) would apply due to its being subsequent. And thus, [it is said]: "When a preceding rule is not established..."

Otherwise, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—namely, "there is no conflict because of the absence of the other"—would be contradicted, and forms such as *amū* and *amī* would not be established; therefore, he says: "the three chapters" and "the subsequent treatise.
By this, the statement of the ancient commentators (*prācām granthaḥ*) that "an operation prescribed in the three chapters [is superseded]" and so forth is refuted.

"They open the throat" means that their effort (*prayatna*) is expansion (*vivāra*). "Those belonging to the classes and the *yamas*" means those belonging to the classes (*varga*) and those belonging to the *yamas*. "Beginning with *ka*" refers to the consonants starting from *ka*.
This [rule] is based on the reading well-known in the world, because it is impossible for [the visarga] to be the final element in the fourteen sūtras.
Regarding "ardhavisarga": similarity should be understood both in pronunciation and in writing. (Prakriyākaumudī Vārtika)

Regarding the rule *ṛlṛvṇayoḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "ā and ā are *ralau* (the letters *r* and *l*); those two and the phonemes (*varṇau*) [make up the compound]," or alternatively, "u and ul are *ṛlau*; of those two, of the phonemes *ṛ* and *l*. This is because of the established principle that the analysis may be performed using either the nominative case or a fully inflected form. [This refers to the rule] *ṛtyakaḥ*.

By this [rule] (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.128), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). According to the *Prakriyākaumudī* (Sūtra 1.1.10), it is "accompanied by the vowel *ā*. And here [the rule] "at the times of *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.167) applies.

These and other such indications are evidence for *praśleṣa* (the insertion of an elided vowel). Furthermore, even in cases such as *yiyā3so*, where there is a *pluta* vowel according to Pāṇini 8.2.86 (*guroranṛtaḥ*), the rule for changing the *s* of the suffix *san* to *ṣ* after an *a*-vowel does not apply.

It must be said that this is indeed the case; for in the compound *āś-ca āś-ca*, by means of the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*), [the vowel] following the long one is understood to be elided even after a protracted (*pluta*) vowel—so it is explained. Regarding the phrase "yaṇ and so forth": in the word *śītala*, the long vowel resulting from *savarṇadīrgha* is the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādiśabda*).

Regarding the word *atre*: the meaning is "in this very [context]. Regarding the phrase *yadyapi* ("even though"): the sense is that the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the technical rules for listing phonemes) has not yet been finalized.
The rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31) is an illustration; [it implies] the substitution of *ṣ* in *ramāsu*.

In the case of *vāg-aśīḥ*, it should be understood that the substitution of *gh* for the vowel *ā*—as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.4.62 (*jhayo haḥ*)—does not apply; nor does the substitution of *gh* for the initial *d* in *dāsī-ṣṭa* and similar forms, as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.2.32 (*dādeḥ*).

However, if one maintains the connection of the word *īṣat* from the rule concerning the sibilants (*ūṣman*) being slightly open (*vivṛta*) to the rule concerning vowels (*svarāṇāṃ ca*), [then the following applies].
If it is explained that the distinction between [the effort of] vowels and consonants is set aside, then it is established in the Bhāṣya that the rule *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10) need not exist.
(Prakriyākaumudī, Introduction, Pāda 1, Sūtra 1.1.1)
The rule *vṛddhir ādaic* [Pāṇini 1.1.1] states that *ai* and *au* are indeed two-mora (*dvimātra*) only when followed by *t* (the augment *t*);
therefore, in the case of *kṛṣṇaikatvam*, it is not three-mora (*trimātra*). The same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well;
thus, in cases such as *gaṅgodakam*, it is not three-mora.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.1: *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. "Bhū" and "vā" form a *dvandva* compound.
The two words "ādi" (beginning) undergo *ekaśeṣa*, as they both denote the manner of arrangement. Thus, "bhūvau" are the "ādī" (beginnings).

The term *yeṣām* is a bahuvrīhi compound. [It refers to] *bhū* and so forth, which are similar to *vas*. Intending that this similarity is with respect to a word expressing action (*kriyāvācaka*), he says: "of those expressing action. Why "expressing action"? [So that] in examples such as *yāḥ paśyasi*, there may not be the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*). For if that were present, [the rule] "āto... [would apply].

[The suffix *ghañ*] would apply by [Pāṇini 6.4.140]: "after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Why [specify] "beginning with *bhū*"? [So that it does not apply] to words such as *hiruk* and *pṛthak*, nor to forms ending in a *tiṅ* suffix that express a state of being (*bhāva*), such as *śiśye*. The status of those [words] listed in the Sūtras as roots is established by the fact that [the roots] beginning with *stambh* are marked with the indicatory letter *u*.
It is thus made known. As for roots such as *culumpa* and others, they are included by means of the *gaṇa*-sūtra: "This illustration is manifold."

Prau.ma.ipā.sū.1|4|57: *cādayaḥ* (The particles beginning with *ca*). [Question: Why specify "not denoting a substance" (*adravyārthāḥ*)? [Answer: [To exclude] *paśuḥ* (an animal). A substance (*dravya*) is that which is endowed with gender and number. But in this case, it would indeed apply: *lodhaṃ naśyanti paśu manyamānāḥ* ("Those who consider the Lodha tree to be an animal perish"). Here, *paśu* is used in the sense of "correctly."

(Prakriyākaumudī, I Pāda, Sūtra 59): *Upasargāḥ*. The forms *nis* and *dur* end in *s*, as established in the section on the *ayogavāha*s without distinction by the specific mention in the rule "nisastapatau" (Pāṇini 8.3.102).

This is stated by citing *duṣkṛtam*, following the remark of the author of the Bhāṣya: "The *visarjanīya* that follows a *sakāra* which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter. Vāmana also says the same in the rule *upasargasyāyatau* (Pāṇini 8.2.19). Furthermore, there are the rules *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.46) and *suduroradhikaraṇe*.
Haradatta states in that very same sūtra that [the term] also includes those ending in *r*, because of the explicit mention [in the rule].
Thus ends the section on designations.
Now, the feminine suffixes.

Regarding *khaṭvā*: [it is derived] by the rule "aśū-pruṣi-kuṭi-khaṭi-kaṇi-viśibhyaḥ kvan". Regarding *pañcājī*: one should not say that the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply here simply because of the absence of the rule for "application to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*).

This is because, with respect to feminine suffixes, there is the mention of the condition "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahatpūrvagrahaṇa*) and the governing rule regarding "non-subordinate elements" (*anupasarjanādhikāra*).

This is because it indicates that the rule applies to the end of the word (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding *mūṣikā*: under the governing rule *ṭhvṛścikṛṣoḥ kikan*, by the specific rule *muṣerdīrghaśca*, the word *mūṣika* is formed with the suffix *kikan*, having the vowel *i* in the middle.
As for the word *mūṣaka*, it is derived from the root *mūṣa* (meaning "to steal") with a long vowel in the penultimate syllable, using the suffix *kvun* in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Mādhava has stated that this [suffix] is also *ṭāp*; however, the distinction is that there is *itva* (the substitution of *i*) by the rule "pratyayasthāt. As for the claim that this [word] ending in *kvun* does not employ the reading in the *ajādi* group [of suffixes], they say that this is because its purpose is to provide for the application of *ṅīṣ* by the rule defining *jāti* (generic class), and because a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is not a *jāti*.
That is to be considered; for even though it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) like *vyāghrī* and so on, its status as a genus (*jāti*) is not lost.

Regarding *bhastraphalā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose fruits are like a bellows. As for the rule *ṅyāp-*, this is established in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *phala* (meaning "to ripen"); however, in the Bhāṣya, it is generally...

It should indeed be read as *dīrgha* (long vowel), namely *pratyakpuṣpa*. This was stated after a thorough examination of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika on the sūtra beginning with *pākakarṇa*. Therefore, the reading *satprākkāṇḍa* is not to be respected.

"And *śūdrā*": the word *śūdra* takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp* if it denotes a caste (*jāti*). However, it does not do so when preceded by the word *mahat*. The phrase "if it denotes a caste" is connected here as well. Regarding "but in the case of connection with a male" (*puṃyoge tu*):
there is no restriction that "connection with a male" must consist solely of the relationship of husband and wife; rather, it also includes the relationship of progenitor and progeny. Therefore—

It is established by the rule: "From a Kṣatriya man, however, a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman give birth to two sons, known as the Māhiṣya and the Ugra. Regarding the term *mahāśūdrī*, Amarasimha states: "The word *ābhīra* is identical [in form] to *mahāśūdrī* in both its generic sense and when used in connection with a male."

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the *ajādi* (ajādigaṇa) list, the reading should simply be "śūdrā"; the inclusion of "jāti" (jātiḥ) is redundant. Since the primary sense of the word is understood, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed for the [denotation of] a genus (*jāti*)—will itself be barred [from applying]. For when there is a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the application is figurative (*gauṇī vṛtti*). Furthermore, the restriction "not when preceded by *mahat*" (*amahat*) and so forth is also redundant; for the word *mahāśūdra*...

For [the word *śūdra*] exists as a distinct entity within a different class [of beings]. In that case, since the constituent part [the suffix] would be meaningless, and because there is an absence of femininity inherent in the meaning of the word *śūdra*, there is no possibility at all for the application of the suffix *ṭāp*. However, where there is a "great Śūdra woman," the form *mahāśūdrā* is indeed desired. As for *kruñcā* and so forth—these three...

Some maintain that [the suffixes] end in a consonant (*halantāḥ*). However, by citing examples such as *kruñcān ālabheta* and *uṣṇihakakubhau*, the fact that they also end in the vowel *a* is accepted in the *Bhāṣya*.
Regarding the phrase "also in the sense of relation to a male" (*puṃyoge 'pi*): when words such as *jyeṣṭhā* refer to those born first and so forth, then...

The suffix *ṭāp* is established precisely because [the stem] ends in a non-dental consonant (*adanta*). However, when there is a desire to express "the wife of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya strī*) and so forth, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which applies by virtue of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—would otherwise be applicable; the word *api* is used to indicate that this [suffix] is superseded by the present rule.
[The rule] "Not after *mūla* and *nañ*" [is stated]. Why mention *nañ*? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *śatamūlī*. [In the case of] *amūlā*, this is a genus of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhijāti*).
[From] Pāṇini 4.1.6: "And after that which has the *ugit* designation. It exists; it is listed as having the vowel *u* among the *sarvādi* group in the sense of "being."
It is also derived [by the rule] *ṭhbhāterḍavatuḥ*. However, when the suffix *śatṛ* is present, the augment *num* is obligatory by the rule *śapśyanoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.81].
[The rule] *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7) [applies here].

Regarding *vano ra ca*: in the word *śrutvānam*, the suffix *vanip* is added to the root *śru*. Although the rule for the prohibition of *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* applies because [the suffix] follows a stem ending in a consonant (*haśantāt*), the prohibition does not take effect here because the suffix is not prescribed after a stem ending in a consonant (*haśantāt*). Regarding *avāva*: the author of the *Nyāsa* states that this prohibition is merely general (*prāyika*), and therefore he says *avāvarī*. It is not [absolutely so].

This is seen in the Bhāṣya and other works. Regarding the rule *pakṣe ḍāp* [Pāṇini 4.1.8], the point is that in the dual number, there arise three forms: *bahudhīvaryau*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīve*. [Prakriyākaumudī: *ṭābṛci* (Pāṇini 4.1.9)]
*ṭāb ṛci*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅīp* suffix that would otherwise be obtained by the preceding rule. Regarding the phrase "because it is not established" (*asiddhatvāt*):

this is according to the view that the rules apply at the time the operation takes effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*). However, if the designation *ṣaṭ* is determined according to its original enunciation (*yathoddeśa*), or if the explanation is given that the condition "ending in ṣ or n" (*ṣṇānta*) applies at the time of the initial instruction (*upadeśakāla*), then the description of its being "not established" is unnecessary.
They say that it is not applicable;

however, in reality, even under the *yathoddeśa* view, its status as unestablished (*asiddhatva*) is indeed applicable, for the rule "the addition of [the treatment of] that which has undergone a partial modification" (*ekadeśavikṛtasyopasaṃkhyānam*) is recited in the *sthānivadādeśa* sūtra.

By virtue of the mention of "substitute" (ādeśa), and by relying on the principle that "all substitutes take the place of all words," it is explained that even an inferred substitute is like its original (sthānivat). In either case, however, this does not apply in the case of a rule concerning an *al* (vowel or consonant). This is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

Regarding the term *bahuyajvānau*: because of the prohibition "not after a conjunct consonant" (*na saṃyogāt*), this [word] does not undergo elision of the penultimate vowel; therefore, the rule "of that which has elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*) does not apply.
[The sūtra] *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.13) [is relevant].

*ḍābubhābhyām*. Now, one might object: since the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] and the rule for *ḍāp* are established by the force of the specific wording, their alternation (*paryāya*) is already proven. True; however, the rule is divided by the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*). In that [division], the word "manaḥ" is no longer operative. Thus, after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *an*, *ḍāp* may optionally be applied, along with *ṅīp*.
This [sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an option. However, the sūtra *ana upadhālopinaḥ* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*):

namely, that the option which applies to a stem ending in *an* applies only when there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*). Thus, in cases such as *suparvā*, where there is no elision of the penultimate vowel, this [sūtra] serves to prohibit [the application of the previous rule]. But in cases such as *bahurājñī*, the [application of the previous rule] is governed by *ṛnnebhyaḥ*.

Thus, the suffix *ṅīp* is indeed applied; by this, the form *bahudhīvarī* is established. For, in the rule "ṛnnebhyaḥ," the suffix *ṅīp* is restated, and the letter *r* is prescribed as being in conjunction with it. If *ṅīp* were applied by virtue of another rule [such as "vana-ra ca"], the desired form would not be established. One might object: "But surely the rule 'vana-ra ca' itself prescribes both *ṅīp* and *ra*."

If it is argued that [the suffix] should be prescribed [for both], we say no, because prescribing both would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, even in this case, once the *ṅīp* suffix is prohibited, the *raḥ* suffix would also be difficult to obtain, because they are taught as being mutually dependent (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*). However, in the Bhāṣya, this is resolved by breaking up the rule (*sūtrabhanga*). It is as follows: "After a *bahu-vrīhi* ending in *an*... [Pāṇini 5.4.103].
Let the sūtra *upadhālopino vā* follow immediately after this [sūtra];
let the sūtra located in another place, such as *ana upadhā*, and the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the *ḍāp*-sūtra, not be required.

Prakriyāmañjarī: Regarding the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28), [the author] says with the intention that the term *bahuvrīheḥ* is carried over from the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, and the suffix *ṅīp* is carried over from the rule *saṃkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*.
*Ana upadhā...* [The remainder of the sūtra follows]. From the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is understood;
and from the rule *saṃkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*, the suffix *ṅīp* is understood—this is the intended meaning. Thus he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with *annantādityādi*, it has been stated that this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Nor should it be argued that, since the option (*vikalpa*) is already established by the preceding rule, the mention of *anyatarasyām* here is redundant; for if that were absent, this would be a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) for the obligatory case, rather than a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
**Prau.ma.:** *pratyayasthātkāt pūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.44).

Regarding the phrase *pratyayasthātkāt pūrvasya*: the letter *ka* [in *kāt*] is for the sake of pronunciation; what is intended is the consonant alone. If one were to intend a specific [vowel], then in forms such as *etikāś caranti*, the substitution would not occur when *akac* is applied.
With this intention, he says: "from the letter *ka*. For the suffix *-kāra* is prescribed when there is a mention of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

The point is that its occasional usage from a whole word (samudāya), as in the mention "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance [is] higher," is achieved through effort. Regarding "before *āp*"—and this refers to the vowel *a*.

This is a qualification. In this context, by virtue of the underlying meaning (*sāmarthya*), the change occurs even when there is an intervention by the letters *ka* and *ā*, but not in cases such as *rathakaṭalyā* where there is an intervention of three or four letters and so on. For this very reason, it does not occur for the initial *ā* in words such as *sarvikā*. This has been stated: "The letter *i* should replace the letter *ā* when followed by *āp*."
Thus [it is said]. However, if the intention were to qualify the letter *ka*, he would have stated "of the *at* preceding the letter *ka* after an *āp*" (*āpparātkakārāt pūrvasyātaḥ*).

As for what the ancients [said]—that "after an *āp*" (*āpi*) is a qualifier of the letter *ka*—in cases such as *sarvikā*, this refers to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of the *ā* of *āp* and the *i* of *ika*].

[Objection: "Even when there is an intervention by the letter *a*, [the rule] will apply by virtue of the power of the specific statement, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

[Response: That is not so, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rathakaṭaḷa*; for even when [an element] is intervened by another, its status as "following" (*paratva*) is not lost. Nor can one find a solution through the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, because [that rule applies only] to an original enunciation (*anuvāda*).

Because the paribhāṣā [regarding the non-application of a rule] does not apply here; for its meaning is that it applies to the qualifiers of what is being referred to (anūdyamāna). And in this regard, the mention of the word *sthāne* in the sūtra "udīcām ātaḥ" is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The result, however, is the establishment of forms such as *śālīya*, because the paribhāṣā concerning the short vowel *i* (*ikparibhāṣā*) does not apply when the designation *vṛddha* is in force.
As for what they say—that "āpi" is a qualifier of that which is being prescribed—this is quite crude.

Furthermore, it is not even to be suspected that "āpi" is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (the base), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rathakaṭyā* and *putrakāmyā*. [The form] *śaka* is derived from the root with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). The mention of *stha*...
This is for the sake of clarity, because the suffix *ka* alone is absent [in the examples], and thus the property of being situated in that [suffix] (*tātsthya*) is obtained by default.

Why [mention] the preceding [word]? [To prevent the rule from applying] in cases such as *sarvikā*, where—despite the fact that the single-substitute *ekādeśa* of *ṭāp* [and *i*] would block it—the substitution of *kā* for what follows [the word ending in *ṭāp*] might otherwise occur, according to the paribhāṣā: "That which is taught after [a certain element applies] to what follows that [element]. As for [the objection]:...

This is because even the *paribhāṣā* "ṭhvārṇādāṅgam" (an internal operation [āṅga] takes precedence over one based on a phoneme [ṭhvārṇa]) would be rendered useless. In reality, however, the locative indication (*saptamī-nirdeśa*) in "pratyayastheki" is more appropriate; furthermore, the mention of "pūrva" (preceding) could easily be omitted. What is the purpose of the *tapara* (the *t* in "ataḥ")? [Consider: "The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kali*. [Resulting in] *dhākā*.

*Rākā* | *Māmikā*: By the rule "only [the suffix] *āmaka*," etc., because of the restriction that this applies only to words ending in a technical name (*sājñā*) or a Vedic meter (*chandas*), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. Regarding *tyak-tyap-au*: this is an exception to the optional rule "for those of the Northern Grammarians, [the substitution of] *ā* in place of *āt*" (*udīcām ātaḥ sthāne*). *Dākṣiṇātyikā*: [The suffix *tyap* is applied] after *dakṣiṇā*, meaning "not far from the south."

The analysis is *ājantaḥ dakṣiṇā bhavā* ("that which ends in the suffix *āc*, [namely] *dakṣiṇā*, becomes *bhavā*"). As for the analysis provided by the ancients—*dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi bhavā* ("existing in the southern direction")—that is not correct; because in the rule prescribing the substitution (*tyagvidhi*), the word *dakṣiṇā* ending in *āc* is understood due to its association with indeclinables (*avyaya*). Otherwise, the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre* ("in all compound formations involving a pronoun... would apply.

And because the substitution of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) would result [in an error]. As for the claim that the masculine form applies only in a compound, that will be refuted later. After the suffix *tyak*, there is the augment *vṛddhi* by the rule "kiti ca," and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Then, in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, the suffix *ka* is added. By the rule "ke'ṇaḥ," the short vowel is substituted, and then *ṭāp* again. Thus we have *ihatyikā*. [In the case of] *avyayībhāva*, the suffix *tyap* is applied.
*Prakriyākaumudī*:

*na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.45). Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāsa* states: "Since the substitution [of *ai*] for the vowel *ā* of the root *yā* is optionally prescribed by the rule *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne*, this [sūtra] is a prohibition"; however, that is not correct, because [the rule *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne* applies only to] the place of *ā*.

Because that specific portion is absent here, the author intends *yā sā* as an illustration for both *yad* and *tad*, and thus says "of *yad* and *tad*. He provides an example of the result when the actual form is not intended: *yakām* and *takām*. This is done by omitting *yāsayoḥ*.

It would be more appropriate to say simply *yatadoḥ*. Regarding *upatyakā*: [it is derived] by the rule "from *upa* and *adhi*, the suffix *tyakan* is added in the sense of 'near' and 'ascended' respectively. From the rule "and in the case of *kṣipakā* etc.," the word *na* (not) is understood to carry over. As for *kṣipakā*: from the root *kṣip*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots with an *iṅ* vowel as an *upadhā*. Then, the suffix *ka* is added again in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth. [The root] *caṭ* means "to split."

[The suffix] *ac* is applied after [the root] *pac* and others; from that, [the suffix] *ka*. Regarding *tāraka*: [it is derived from] *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. It refers to a luminous body or a constellation, as well as the pupil of the eye. *Varṇakā* is a specific type of woven cloth. *Tāntava* is a derivative of threads; [it is formed] by the suffix *añ* after [the word ending in] *u*. Elsewhere, it is *varṇikā*, which is a commentary on a specific treatise.

And [the word] *stotrakartṛ* means "one who composes hymns. In the case of *vartakā*, meaning "a bird," there is optionally the shortening of the vowel (*itvam*); elsewhere, it is always [long]. "The ancestors" (*pitaraḥ*) and "those deities" (*devatāḥ*) constitute "the ancestral deities" (*pitṛdevatāḥ*); the ritual for their sake is *pitṛdevatyam*. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "after a word ending in *devatā*, the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of 'for the purpose of'. They eat.

The *aṣṭakā* is that [rite] on which Brahmins [are fed]. From the roots *sthā* and *śib*, the suffix *takan* is applied, resulting in *aṣṭikānī*. Since its measure (*parimāṇa*) is eight, the suffix *kan* is added according to the rule "after a numeral ending in *ati* or *śat*, [the suffix] *kan* [is applied]. Having superimposed the feminine gender inherent in the meaning onto the form [of the word], the rule "when preceded by *ya* or *ka*" [applies].

This is a designation in the feminine gender. With the intention that a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is thereby obtained, he says: "of the form of the feminine suffix. Regarding *sāṅkāśyikā*: [the city] *Sāṅkāśya* is "produced by Saṅkāśa"; the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule "vuñ-chaṇ-... etc., from the group beginning with *saṅkāśa*.

Then, regarding the sense of "born there" (*bhava*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *dhan* or having *ya* as its penultimate letter," and the substitution of *a* occurs. Since that [suffix] would also optionally cause the shortening of the vowel *ā* in a feminine form such as *sāṅkāśyā*, the expression "of an *ā*" (*ātaḥ*) was stated [in the rule].
Now, one might object: just as this [substituted] *a* is not in the place of an *ā*, so too it should not be in the place of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).

This [definition] is deficient in two parts. Regarding this, they say: for if *ātaḥ* exists, then by the force of the feminine gender indication, it is understood that the vowel *ā* which denotes a female is indeed a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).
But if that [word *ātaḥ*] were absent, only this much would be understood: "that which is the vowel *a* of a word denoting a female. From that...

"In this case too, [the designation] 'sāṅkāśyikī' would result. To this, the following must be said: since the word *sthāne* is present in the rule "in place of that which has *ya* or *ka* preceding it," how can there be a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)?

Let it remain as it is; nor should it be said that this [suffix] stands in the place of *vuñ*, for although the aggregate form *ak* is so, the constituent form *akāra* is not. Furthermore, because *vuñ* is not preceded by *ya* or *ka*, the elision by the rule "yasya" does not apply in that state either.

It is obtained. Furthermore, if a feminine suffix were obtained by its specific mention (*pratipadokta*), there would be no possibility at all for *vuñ* and other suffixes prescribed in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*). Therefore, the rule *ātaḥ* is indeed for the sake of clarity. As for *aśvakī*:
the followers of Kumāra, however, read the word *aśva* even in the list beginning with *bhastrā*, and thus [they derive it] from this as well.

They maintain that there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). *Śubham* is a particle ending in the suffix *mān*. That which has a good method (*sunaya*) is called *sunayā*. From that [word], the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule:
*bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānañpūrvāṇām api* (Pāṇini 7.3.47).
"Bhastraiṣā" || [The word] "tadantā" [is used]; the intention is that [the rule] applies because of its being an auxiliary (aṅga). And thus [it is said]:
Haradatta has stated—here, the expression "of the substitute for /at/" is a qualifier of the word "itself" (sva-śabda).
For in that case, both possibility and deviation exist when the crow and the palm tree are present.
"There is no possibility of [the application of] two [terms], nor is there deviation elsewhere;
therefore, this rule would not apply to a pronoun that is its own word. Thus [it is said].

Here, it should be understood that the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied immediately after the phrase "of its own word" (*svaśabdasya*). This has also been indicated in the root text itself. And thus: "The *haṃsa* residing within the body, moving about like the mental activity of a sage within his own [body]..."

Thus, the sense is that those who explain the verse by Śrī Harṣa as "bhastraiṣā" (*bhastraiṣā*)—claiming that the *it* (the shortening of the vowel) is optional—are to be disregarded. Regarding the word *ātmīyāyām*: the sense is that in the case of one's own self, kinsmen, or wealth, the feminine gender simply does not exist [as a primary referent]. As for the forms *svakā* and *svikā* used for "kinsman" and "wealth": [these are explained as follows].

They say that two forms, *svakā* and *svikā*, exist in the source [the *Śiṣyahitā*]; however, this is to be reconsidered, because such a source is unestablished and it contradicts the rules of gender instruction (*liṅgānuśāsana*). As for what is cited in the *Kāśikā*—namely, *svakā* and *svikā*—that pertains to the domain of technical names (*saṃjñā*), and not...

[The suffix] refers to the *jñāti* [group]. As for the claim that "sometimes *svārthika* suffixes deviate from the gender and number of the base (*prakṛti*)," that too must be considered; for even if the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were possible after a word ending in the suffix *kap* according to the aforementioned method, since the base itself is not feminine, [the rule] "in place of *āt*" [would not apply].

Because this portion [of the rule] is difficult to justify, he states counter-examples and then provides examples, beginning with *nirbhastrikā*. *Nirbhastā* means "gone out from a bellows" (*niṣkrāntā bhastrāyāḥ*). There is shortening of the penultimate vowel due to its being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and the suffix *ṭāp*. Then, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of "unknown" and so forth. Regarding the phrase *kṛtaṣatve*: in the sūtra, there is a mention of a modified form.

The intended scope is not merely illustrative—as in the rule *na yāsayoḥ*—but rather definitive; this is the sense. Because of the feminine gender indication (*strīliṅga-nirdeśāt*), only those [words] such as *ajā* that are feminine in gender are included. Therefore, it does not apply here: *śubhrājikā*, meaning "she whose goat (*aja*) is white. [Similarly: *jñaḥ* means "one who knows"; *priyajñā*, meaning "she whose knower (*jña*) is dear."
Regarding the term *priyajñikā*:

according to the rule *abhāṣitapuṃskācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.48), it is explained by taking "that which has no corresponding masculine form" (*abhāṣitapuṃska*) as a qualifier of the suffix that is prescribed.
He states the result: "of the bahuvrīhi.

Regarding the word "nityam" (always): the meaning is that since this optional rule does not apply, the general rule (*utsarga*) "pratyayasthāt" alone operates. The intention is that if [the final vowel] were a qualifier of the subsequent element (*paraviśeṣaṇatve*), this option would indeed occur.

The term *bahuvrīheḥ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the status of being a secondary member (*upasarjana*). Therefore, even in cases such as *atikhaṭvikā* and *niḥkhaṭvikā*, the suffix *kā* is applied invariably. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the diminutive suffix *kaP*," the intention is that this applies when there is the short vowel [ā] in the alternative option provided by the rule "āpo 'nyatarasyām."

"Pervading" (abhivyāpya). For this very reason, regarding the example *bahuyuvā śālā* ("a house with many young men"), the ancient grammarians say that the suffix *ti* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.79 as] *yūnastiḥ* does not apply because [the word *yuvan*] is an *upasarjana*. Prau.ma.: [The feminine suffixes are applied after stems ending in] *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇ*, *añ*, *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, *mātraC*, *tayaP*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhaÑ*, *khaÑ*, *kvarap*.

Regarding the rule *ṭiḍḍhā* (Pāṇini 4.1.15): here, the author of the Vṛtti has inserted the suffix *khyun* into the sūtra. [The example is] *āutsī*. [It means] "one who exists on a hill (*utsa*)," formed by the rule *utsāgadibhyo 'ñ*. And it is not formed by the *ṅīn* suffix according to the rule *śārṅgaravādyaña*.

It should be stated that this [rule] is established; therein, the word "jāteḥ" (of a genus) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Otherwise, it would apply even in the case of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). By this, the statement of the ancient commentators—that the mention of *añ* here is for the sake of clarity—is refuted. Here there are several sentences; therein, the term *anupasarjana* (not being a subordinate member) applies to *aṇ*.

Because of the explanation that [the suffix] follows what ends in the letter *a*, it does not apply here in the case of *āpiśalam adhīte* (she studies the Āpiśala grammar) or *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī* (an Āpiśala Brahmin woman). For in this instance, the suffix *aṇ*—which conveys the sense of "taught by"—is subordinate (*upasarjana*), while the suffix *adhyetraṇ* has been elided; since the primary element is the phoneme (*varṇa*), there is no application of the rule regarding the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and thus only the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs. [The phrase] "in the case of those expressing habitual character" (*tācchīlike*)...

This is the derivation: regarding the suffix *ṇa* in the word *śīla*, the operation of *aṇ* applies by the rule "chatrādibhyo ṇaḥ," as indicated by the statement "kārmastācchīlye. For it is by this [rule] that the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in order to override the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) which would otherwise be enjoined by the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, we have *caurī*.
*curā* is her character (*śīla*).

[From] *prau.ma.*—*halastaddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.150). Regarding the phrase "of that which has become the penultimate (*upadhā*)": one might object, "But does not [the rule] *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) apply here?"

Once the elision of the vowel *a* has been performed, the letter *y* indeed follows the vowel *ī*; so what is the purpose of the continued application of the rule regarding the penultimate (*upadhā*)? Nor can the elision of *a* be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), because that is prohibited in the case of *yalopa*.
Do not say so, for [the prohibition applies] when the operation of *yalopa* is to be performed.

Because the elision (*allop*) is *asiddha* due to its being *ābhīya*. Regarding the term *anapatya*: although there is a Vārttika stating that "the mention of *apatya* (offspring) must be made," even so, that refers only to [suffixes] prescribed under the governing rule for offspring (*apatyādhikāra*).
And such [a suffix] is only *yañ* from the *gargādi* group, not *yañ* from the *devādi* group; for the latter does not fall under the governing rule for offspring.

This is even more evident from the recitation [of the sūtras]. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya has elided the vowel *a* in the rules "ṭhañ-kañ-kvarapa-ayañ-iñaś-ca" and "gargādibhyo yañ. The same applies to the rule "yaskādibhyo gotre 'yañañoś-ca."

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.17). Regarding the mention of "taddhita" [in the sūtra], it is for the purpose of establishing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Now, one might object: even without that [designation], the suffix *ṅīṣ* will certainly occur by the very power of the marker *ṣ*. If this is so, then...

The mention of *taddhita* indicates that the suffix *ṣpha* occurs even after a word ending in *iñ* in certain instances; for although the desired form could be established by the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of similar vowels) in a word ending in *yañ*, the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "of that which [ends in i or u]" would not be necessary. By this, the upcoming statement, "the addition of [the suffix] is required for *āsuri*," is justified.

Prau.ma.: *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ phaḍhakhacchaghāṃ pratyayādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.2). [The sūtra continues with] *āyane*. The letter *ph* in *phakārādiṣu* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). There is no substitution of *n* for the *n* of *āyan* and *īn*, due to the force of the designation *nit* applied to the suffix *phin*.
*Prakriyākaumudī*: "And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *kauravya* and *māṇḍūkya*" (Pāṇini 4.1.19).
Regarding *kauravya*: how then is one to explain Bhaṭṭi’s usage: "O Māṇḍūka of the well, if you have such pride"?
On this point, they say: due to its association with *kauravya*, [the word here refers to] only that which ends in a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*).
In this case, there is the inclusion of *maṇḍūaka*. However, in the phrase "this is the wife of Maṇḍūaka," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to him").
As for the word *kumārī*, it denotes specifically the first stage of life and is not used merely on account of being unmarried.

The term *vṛddhakumārī* (old maiden) is a figurative usage. Regarding *tryanīkā*: it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of three armies; here, because [the word] belongs to the class of words beginning with *ajādi*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, according to the Mīmāṃsakas in their discussion on the *tryanīkā*.

Regarding "pañcāśva": one might object that here the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not apply by the rule "dvigoḥ," yet it would surely apply because the word ends in *ṭhak*. This is not so, because the interpretation is that [the suffix applies] to the *akāra* which follows *ṭhak*. As for "dvibistā," Amarasimha states: "suvarṇa and bista are measures of gold; ten bhāras make an ācita."

Regarding *dvikambalyā*: it means "bought for two *kambalyas*. A *kambalya* is one hundred *palas* of wool. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule "after *kambala*, when it is a name. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ* which has the sense of "bought. Regarding *dvyāḍhakī*: it means "she who cooks two *āḍhakas*," [by the rule] "after *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*... [the suffix *kan* is applied].

In the case of *anyatarasyām*, by the rules "dvigor lug anapatye" and "dvigoḥ ṣṭhaś ca," when the suffixes *kha* and *ṭhan* are optionally excluded, the suffix *ṭhañ* belonging to the *prāgvatīya* group applies; its *luk* elision occurs. By this, *dvyācitā* is explained.
[Prau.ma.: From a word ending in *kāṇḍa*, when referring to a field (*kṣetra*). (Pāṇini 4.1.23)

"From the end of a *kāṇḍa* [comes the suffix] when [the word refers to] a field. A staff (*daṇḍa*) measuring sixteen cubits is a *kāṇḍa*. Although the rule of reference to what follows (*tadantavidhi*) is established by the qualifying term itself, nevertheless, if the word "end" (*anta*) were not used, then because the word "field" (*kṣetre*) is directly heard in the rule, it would qualify the *kāṇḍa* alone and not that which ends in *kāṇḍa*. Consequently, even in this case [the suffix would not apply].

It would occur in cases such as *dvikāṇḍī vaḍavā* ("a mare bought for two *kāṇḍas*"), where the fields are measured by two *kāṇḍas*. However, it would not occur here in *dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ* ("a field-division consisting of two *kāṇḍas*").
Therefore, the mention of *anta-* [in the rule] is necessary. Regarding the suffix *mātrac*: as for what was stated previously—that there is elision (*luk*) of *dvayasac*—that is not correct.

"According to my view, the first and the second [parts] are considered when measuring upwards"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus, [the compound] *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope of two sections") is formed. Now, one might object that here there would be a prohibition by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.2.37], "after a word ending in a measure," because the word *kāṇḍa* refers to length (*āyāma*).

Because it has an immeasurable object. That by which something is measured on all sides—both in height and in circumference—is indeed a measure (*parimāṇa*), such as an *āḍhaka* or a *kuḍava*; it is not merely any kind of delimiting factor whatsoever. As they say:
"Unmāna is indeed measurement by height; parimāṇa is measurement from all sides; pramāṇa would be measurement by length; and saṃkhyā is external measurement in every respect. Thus [it is said].

For this very reason, there is no application of the suffix *ṅīp* in the case of *dvihastā bhittiḥ* ("a wall two cubits long"). On this point, they say: this [rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that the prohibition may apply only to the case of a field (*kṣetra*). Therefore, the result of the rule is that in the case of *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope two sections long"), the suffix *ṅīp* indeed occurs.
Prau.ma.: *puruṣāt pramāṇe 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.37).

Regarding the rule *puruṣāt pramāṇe*: although the word *puruṣa* denotes a genus (*jāti*), nevertheless, in the sentence *dvau puruṣau pramāṇam asyāḥ* ("two men are her measure"), it indeed functions in the sense of a measure (*pramāṇa*).

This is because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*). In the case of the *vṛtti*, however, it is due to its very nature. Thus says the *Śulbasūtra*: "A man is five *aratnis* long. Regarding the term *dvipuruṣī*, the author of the *Nyāsa* states that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *dvayasaC* by the rule "In the sense of a measure, *lo* [is substituted] after a *dvigu* compound, invariably."

That is not so; because the word *puruṣa* does not denote a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the rule from the *Ślokavārttika*, "the suffix *lo* [is applied] when a means of valid cognition is expressed," does not apply there. For that rule applies only to those things well-known as means of valid cognition, such as tranquility (*śama*) and the like, but not even to the word *puruṣa*. Otherwise, [it would follow that...].

In the case of *puruṣadvayasa-* as well, there would be elision (*luk*). This is clear from the commentary on the rule *puruṣahastibhyāmaṇ ca* in the *Padamañjarī*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the suffixes *-dvayasaC* and *-daghnaC* would also not occur after this [word *puruṣa*]; for those two [suffixes] are intended when measuring height (*ūrdhvamāne*).

This is because of the statement "mama. Likewise, the application of the rule *puruṣāt pramāṇe* occurs by the very force of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*). As for what Haradatta stated regarding that very sūtra, taking up the commentary (*vṛtti*) which says "the elision (*luk*) of *dvigu* is compulsory," that "therefore, the elision is prescribed here precisely where it was not [otherwise] applicable."
This too is to be considered: for the statement that there is an injunction [of elision] not mentioned by the three sages (the *Munitraya*) is contradictory.

Furthermore, as for what was said by those explaining the ancient grammatical system—that there is elision (*luk*) based on another *vārttika* read under the rule *puruṣahastibhyām*—that is merely a rash assertion.
Let us leave it at that for now, as this cited sūtra has not been touched upon by either the author of the Bhāṣya or the author of the Vārttika.

In reality, however, in the sūtra *puruṣāt pramāṇe*, the phrase *dvigor lug anapatye* is understood to carry over; by its force, elision (*luk*) is also implied. This is also the statement of Haradatta.
How this is so should be understood by those with refined discernment (*sahṛdaya*) through its very application to such cases. What is the authority?
A cow bought for two men is called *dvipuruṣā*; this is simply due to the elision of the secondary suffix (*taddhitaluk*). In the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), it is *pañcapuruṣī*.

Prau.ma.-ūdhaso'naṅ (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.131): Regarding the rule "ūdhaso'naṅ," although [the desired form] could have been established by the substitution of the vowel *ā* alone, the employment of the suffix *anaṅ* is for the sake of the rule "dhanuṣaśca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.132).
Prau.ma.: Regarding the rule *dāmahāyanāntācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.27):
since the word *dāman* is already established [as taking the suffix] by virtue of being a qualifier of a *bahuvrīhi*, the inclusion of the term *anta* (ending in) is for the sake of clarity.

As for the phrase *saṃkhyādeḥ* (beginning with a numeral), the intention is that only the portion [of the previous rule] starting from *saṃkhyā* carries over by the force of its being marked as *svarita*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.30: [The suffix *cha* is applied after the following words to form adjectives meaning "made by": *kevala*, *āmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *ārya*, *kṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, and *bheṣaja*.

Regarding the passage beginning with “*kevalamāmaka*”: “In this my own body (*tanū*), which is the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa, let there be wretched bodies that are not to be cultivated; and the Maghavan has conquered all enemies. Our intention (*ākūti*) is as one, [our] noble action (*āryakṛtī*) is as one.”
"Sumaṅgalī! This bride is auspicious; she is the auspicious healer of Rudra.

As for the counter-example provided by the ancients—"antarvatī," "pativatī"—the sense is that this is incorrect. If it is asked, "How [is it applied] when the words are separate? as was stated by the ancients...

The notion that "the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) applies to the whole [compound]" has been described; the sense is that this is erroneous. *Prakriyākaumudī*: "In the case of *pūtakratu*, there is also *ai*. (*pā.sū. 4.1.36*). The substitution is the vowel *ai*, not a suffix (*pratyaya*), as is clear from the following rule regarding the acute accent (*udātta*).

Because of this statement [of the Vṛttikāra]. But not so—otherwise, the word *vṛṣākapi* would have its middle syllable acute by virtue of the rule "the heavy [syllable] at the end of a polysyllabic word, or when there are two [heavy syllables], is acute," which prescribes acuteness for the middle [syllable]. Regarding the three words beginning with *agni*, the [correct form] is established simply by the rule "the most similar in place [is substituted]. Such is the position in the treatises of the ancients.
The sense is that [the rules] would be contradicted.

Regarding the statement "the vowel *e* is udātta": for the word *manu* has its initial vowel as udātta, because in the rule prescribing the suffix *u* for the root *man*—namely, *śṛsvṛsnih...* and so forth—the governing heading *dhānye nit* applies.
This concise statement demonstrates that the term *udātta*, which is understood as continuing from the previous rule,
connects only with the vowel *ai* due to the continuity of its grammatical relationship, and not with the vowel *au* as well. Consequently,
what was stated by the ancient authorities— that the vowels *ai* and *au* are both acute (*udātta*)— should be disregarded.

The sense is that this is because it contradicts the *Vṛtti*, the *Padamañjarī*, and other works. Regarding *manāyī*: it has the middle syllable as udātta (accented); the other two have the first syllable as udātta.
*Etā* means brindled (*karburā*). Regarding "of colors": *etaḥ*, *śoṇaḥ*, *śitiḥ*, *pṛśniḥ*, *pṛṣat*.

These are the examples. Regarding *tryeṇyā*: the point here is that although the final member of the compound is an *upasarjana*, the entire compound is not an *upasarjana*. Alternatively, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs because it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*). Regarding "some [read] *knam*" (*knameke*): since the *Bhāṣya* states "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) in this context, in common usage (*loke*), we find: "The troop of the *asiknikās* has gone quickly."

The ancient commentators maintain that such usages as these are due to negligence (*prāmādika*). However, in reality, because of the connection [of the rule] with the words "in Vedic [usage], some" (*cchandasyeke*), the intention of the Bhāṣya is that [the rule applies] even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Otherwise, he would not have included the word "some" (*eka*).
For indeed, in Vedic usage, there are no such usages as *paliknīr idyauvatayaḥ*.
Someone might object: [the word *avadāta*] denotes purity, because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) that "the root *daip* means to purify.
However, the point is that its usage in the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "white, fair, *avadāta*" is based on the common property of being pure (*viśuddhatva*).

Regarding the rule *laghāv*: when there is one light syllable (*laghu*) at the end, or two light syllables following [the penultimate], a heavy syllable (*guru*) belonging to a word with many vowels (*bahvaṣ*—*aṣ* being an ancient designation for vowels) shall be acute (*udātta*). In the example *kṛṣṇā*:
the suffix *na* is applied by the rule *kṛṣeśca*, and the suffix *ilac* is applied by the rule *kapeśca* to the root *kap* mentioned in the Sūtra (Uṇādi).

And [the words] *kṛṣṇa* and *kapila* end in long vowels. [Pāṇini 4.1.41 states: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after [stems ending in] *ṣit* and after *gaura* etc. Here, the word *śvan* is recited [in that list]. Consequently, [the rule] "ṅīp is applied after stems ending in *ṛt* and *n*" [applies].
Regarding this, that which was cited by the earlier [author] as *śunī* is incorrect. As for what others explain—
that in the sense of "he describes a dog" (*śvānam ācaṣṭe*) or "he behaves like a dog" (*śva ivācarati*), there is either a causative suffix (*ṇic*) or a *kvip* suffix,

and since it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in the *kvip* formation, the *ṅīṣ* is absent and instead *ṅīp* applies, just as in *niḥśunī*— that is not correct, because in the case of the causative (*ṇic*)...

The form stated [for *āpavana*] is difficult to obtain according to the primary opinion due to the occurrence of *samprasāraṇa* and the elision of the *ṭi* suffix; however, in other views, it may somehow be established.
Regarding "if it is *āpavana*": that in which grain (*dhānya*) is sown (*opyate*), that is, deposited. Regarding "goṇānyā":...

That which has an arbitrary name is "unartificial" (*akṛtrimā*). For example: "This is that very spot where you were being sought. Regarding "artificial" (*kṛtrimā*): it is prepared by a person. For example:
"They collect water from the *sthali* (an artificial reservoir). "Boiled" (*śrāṇā*) means cooked. Regarding "an iron product": [it refers to] a plowshare (*phāla*).
Thus it is well known. Regarding the term *kuśāni*: the Chāndogas (chanters of the Sāmaveda) use the word *kuśā* to refer to stakes made of Udumbara wood used for counting the *stotriya* hymns.

This is seen in the rule *Pāṇini 8.3.46* (*ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa...*) and in the *Vyāsasūtra* (*Brahmasūtra* 3.3.26) which states, "But [the reward] is the taking up [of what was previously given], as in the case of the *kuśā*s," where it says, "O *kuśā*s, you who belong to the trees, stand firm..."
This [meaning] is indeed well-known in the Vedic revelation (śruti) as "pāta.
Regarding the term "pativara": the sense is that this word is an adjective denoting a quality, because it expresses the longing for the taking of the hand in marriage.

*Prakriyākaumudī*: "And from *bahu* and others" (*bahvādibhyaśca*, Pāṇini 4.1.45). Since the word *bahu* denotes a quality (*guṇavācin*), its inclusion is already established by the preceding rule; they say that its mention here is for the sake of subsequent rules. In reality, however, the word *bahu* [is intended] for the subsequent sūtra, "Always in the Veda" (*nityaṃ chandasi*).
Thus, both [the suffixes] are indeed redundant, because all grammatical options are established in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Regarding the phrase "due to connection with a male" (*puṃyogāt*): the implication is that this is a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛttiḥ*). However, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*) based on the primary meaning, then the form is simply "gopī."

Some maintain that "union with a male" (puṃyoga) here refers exclusively to the state of being husband and wife; however, in reality, since there is no evidence for such a restriction, the relationship of progenitor and progeny is also included. Thus says Bhaṭṭi:
"Rāma was easily conceived by Kausalyā, and subsequently Bharata was born from Kekayī."

Thus: *kekayasya duhitā* means "the daughter of Kekaya. If the patronymic suffix *añ* were applied according to the rule *janapadaśabdāt*, the form would be *kaikeyī*; however, its elision (*luk*) by the rule *ataśca* does not occur here, because of the prohibition in the rule *na prācyabhargādi*. Accordingly, Kālidāsa [wrote]: "O Kaikeyī, [your] desires..."
"...have ripened for you. By this, Devakī is explained.
[The term] *yavānī* is "bad barley" (*duṣṭo yavaḥ*). By this, a different species (*jātyantara*) is denoted.
This is its very defect: that even in the absence of the stated genus of being barley (*yavatva*), there is an imitation of its form. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is to be expressed.
Thus it is stated; and this point is established in the third [section] of the Bhāṣya under the rule *iṅśca*. How so?

As for what they say—that by the force of the long vowel [in *ānuk*], the word is divided as *ā anuk*, whereby *indra* and the others are already established by the suffix *ānuk* alone—[that is incorrect].
By the force of the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā* for [the final vowel], it is inferred that in some cases the substitution occurs even from other sources;

thus, the form *brahmāṇī* is established. This, however, is questionable, because if the short vowel were substituted, the rule *ato guṇe* would result in the application of the single-substitute (pararūpa) form. [Objection: But surely, by the force of the actual pronunciation of the long vowel *ā*, the long vowel [is maintained].

If it is argued that [the *k*] will indeed come into being, for otherwise one would simply perform the elision (*luk*)? No, because [the rule] "allopo 'naḥ" has its purpose fulfilled by being superseded. Just as in the case of "patyurno," when a substitute (*ādeśa*) is to be applied, the elision (*al-lopa*) will not occur precisely due to the force of pronouncing the letter *k*, which serves as an indicatory mark (*liṅga*) for the augment (*āgama*).
If one asks why? It is not so, because the letter *ka* in the word *śarva* has its own purposeful function.

Indeed, there is no elision (*lopa*) there, due to the prohibition in the rule "not after a conjunct consonant" (*na saṃyogāt*). Therefore, the lack of functional capacity between the letter *ka* and the vowel *a* is for the sake of subverting the rule for the single-substitute form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*).

The long vowel pronunciation is necessary; by this, Haradatta’s statement—that for the sake of brevity one should simply state *anuk* with a short vowel—is refuted. [In the case of] *karmaṇyaṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; from that which ends in it, the suffix *ṅīp* is added.
By the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām," the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.

Regarding the term *vastrakrītī*: in the state where [the compound] is formed as *vastraiḥ krītā*, because it ends in /ā/ before the addition of the case-ending (*sup*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule for compounds ending in /a/. Regarding the phrase "not in some cases": because of the inclusion of the word *bahulam* (diversely) in the sūtra *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*, in some instances there is a compound with a word ending in a case-ending (*subanta*). And in that case, [there is the elision] of the case-ending (*sup*).
The intention is that the suffix *ṭāp* applies first because it is antaranga (internal); consequently, since the word no longer ends in an *a*-vowel, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply.
Thus, we have *bahvī*. The underlying principle is as follows: [the rule] "bahornañvadutarapadabhūmni" and "nañsubhyām."
The rules prescribing that the final syllable is udātta— namely, *jātikālasukhādibhyo 'nācchādanāt ktokṛtamitapratipannāḥ*—
state that the word *jāti* comes first; by this, it follows as a matter of course that words preceded by *bahu* and so forth are excluded.

Since it will be stated later that the suffix applies optionally when the first member is not a word denoting a limb of the body (*asvāṅga-pūrvapada*), he says here "ūrubhinnī" (one whose thighs are split) as an example specifically of one where the first member is a word denoting a limb (*svāṅga-pūrvapada*). Regarding the phrase "from a word ending in *jāta*":
