just as [the rule] "after *varman*, provided it is anudātta," so too [here] it is simply "after a *bahuvrīhi* that is udātta."

The mention of the term *anta* (end) in the rule *siddhe* is for the purpose of establishing its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). However, the intention is that in the case of *vā jāte*, the acute accent (*udātta*) is optional and not obligatory. As in the example *sumukhā śālā*; thus, it pertains both to the result (*phalamukhī*) and to the cause (*kāraṇamukhī*).
It should be understood that usages such as *cāvanastha* and others are due to negligence (*prāmādika*). Regarding *uraḥ-kroḍā*, Haradatta and others maintain that this word is feminine.
In that case, once the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply because the stem ends in *ā*. However, Amara [states]— "not... [and so on].

He states that *kroḍa* means "the space between the arms" (the chest). Ratnamati, however, asserts its masculine gender. Furthermore, the author of the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* reads only the nominal stem *kroḍa* in the list [of the *gaṇa*], and not the form ending in *ṭā*. Thus, since there is no distinction, it serves as an example for all three genders.

Regarding the word *bodhya*: Mādhava, however, states under the root *kruḍa* (meaning "to immerse") in the *tudādigaṇa* that *kroḍaḥ* [is derived from it]. [The suffix] *ghañ* [is applied]. *Kroḍā* means the chest of horses. This word ending in *ṭāp* is by its very nature restricted to specific objects, because it is read with the *ṭāp*-ending only in the lists beginning with *kroḍā*.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is conditioned by the word being a part of the body (*svāṅga*)—does indeed occur for the word *kroḍa*, which has as its scope only the region between the arms. Thus, one finds both *kalyāṇakroḍī* and *kalyāṇakroḍā mayūrī*.
This is because *ṅīṣ* is replaced by *ṅī*; [the rule] "from that which has a directional word as its prior member" (*dikpūrvapadāt*) prescribes *ṅīṣ* by means of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).

The intended meaning is that the genitive case is substituted for the nominative. However, if the suffix *ṅīp* were independent (i.e., not part of a compound), it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *prāg-gulka*.

To avoid this, there would be the disadvantage of having to carry over either the previously mentioned exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or the prohibitions (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). This is the underlying point.

Regarding "vṛṣalī": the point is that once the status of being a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) has been stated with respect to a single individual, it is easily understood—even without explicitly stating it—with respect to their offspring, siblings, and so forth. Regarding "aupagavī":
this [suffix] supersedes the *ṅīp* prescribed by the characteristic of ending in *aṇ*, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. And thus, in the section on offspring (*apatya-adhikāra*)...

The sense is that those who, taking *āṬpagavī* as the illustrative example (*pratīka*), explain it by saying "the suffix *ṅīp* [is applied] by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*," are to be disregarded. Regarding the word *brāhmaṇī*: the implication is that, in this way, the example of *ṅīṣ* cited by the Eastern grammarians (*prācī*) is based on a mere error (*prāmādika*).
In the *Prakriyākaumudī*,

regarding the forms *kurūḥ* and *kurūḥ* [from *kuru*], the case endings (*svādayaḥ*) are applied because of the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) by means of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning gender-distinctive forms). However, the author of the *Prācīna* (Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita),
having cited the rule "ṭhantādivacca" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), stated that the case endings are applied due to the treatment as being like the beginning of the word (*ādivadbhāva*).

In this regard, the following must be said: the state of being "like that" (tadvat) is prescribed with respect to another [element]. And thus, because of the prohibition "not a suffix" (apratyaya), there would be only a negation here, and not the application of the case-endings (svādayaḥ). As for what they have explained—namely, that "ādi" means "prior to ūṅ," i.e., the nominal stem (prātipadika)—it is because of the state of being like that.

"Because it is perceived as a constituent part of that [word], it exists just like the preceding [part]," so it is said; however, that too is convoluted and contradicts the texts of both our own and other schools. For, according to the method already stated, even in cases such as *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍaḷe*, the suffix *su* would apply by the general rule "the singular number is the default. To prevent that—
Furthermore, if one accepts that *apratyaya* is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), there is a fault in the present context;

moreover, in the case of *śvaśrūḥ*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not apply, the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender) is necessarily required. As for the argument that [the rule applies] there because of the mention of *svādayaḥ* in the rule "śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā," [that is incorrect].
That is not so, because the grammatical instruction (nirdeśa) refers to the word-form itself, as in the rules "viparābhyāṃ jeḥ" and "ReĀryaḥ.

Regarding the form *śvaśrūḥ*: when the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply by virtue of her connection with a male (puṃyoga), the suffix *ūṅ* is applied instead; and the elision (*lopa*) prescribed in conjunction with that [suffix] applies only to the final vowel *a*, due to its proximity, and not to the initial one.
Furthermore, this statement is intended merely to explain the meaning established by the rule *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*; therefore, one should not suspect that there is an elision of the first vowel *a*.

[The term] "the preceding member expresses the object of comparison" applies here; however, in the case of the example *dhātrīkarābhyāṃ karabhopamoruḥ* ("her thighs are like the forearms of a nurse"),...

No, because even though the word *karabha* expresses a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it lacks the status of being a prior member of a compound (*pūrvapada*). Regarding "the two hooves" (*śaphau khurau*): although Amara states that "the word *śapha* is neuter and *khura* is masculine," nevertheless, the masculine gender of the word *śapha* is also widely accepted, as seen in the Vedic scripture: *śaphāviva jarbhurāṇā*.

Because of its frequent usage in the *Nyāsa*, *Haradatta*’s works, and other treatises such as the *Vācaspatya* at the occasion of commenting on the sūtra "in the case of herds of domestic animals," and because of the *Mahābhāṣya* statement,
"Gender is not to be taught, for gender depends upon common usage," [the word] *śapha*...

This is because the word *bhuja* is listed in the *kroḍādi* group in the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi*—along with *guda* and *ghoṇā*—and because Hemacandra’s lexicon (*Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*) states: "The word *śapha* refers to the hoof of cattle and the like, as well as the root of trees.
Furthermore, the *Viśvakośa* declares it to be both masculine and neuter. [Thus, the compound means] "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are beautiful (*vāmau*)."

[This is] the analysis [of the rule]. Here, because there is no possibility [of the application of the rule] anywhere due to the absence of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), this is an injunction for what has not otherwise been obtained. How then is it that Kumārasambhava says, "The thick-thighed one drinks as if [he were] a peacock"? This is simply an error. Some say that because it is preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), the *guṇa* substitution in the vocative does not occur. [The rule continues: "With *hitena* and *saha*"—[the word] *sama* optionally [governs the same].

The word *sahita*, derived from the rule "hitatatayoḥ," is not accepted here; the point is that [the desired form] is established simply by the mention of *saṃhita*, since it is a modification of a single part [of that term].
Regarding the phrase "the letter *y* after *añ*": why is *akāra* (the letter *a*) a qualifier for *añ*? [Consider the example: *śūrasenī*.
From the word *janapada*, by the rule *ataśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.173), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ*; then, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for generic names (*jāti*).

Regarding *śārṅgaravī*: from the word *śṛṅgaru*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of offspring. Regarding *nṛnarayoḥ*: from the word *nṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṛnnebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.5); whereas from the word *nara*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable by the rule for generic names.
[This is] the statement. But surely, in the word *nara*, there would be vṛddhi of the final vowel [by P. 7.2.116]? As for what they say:

because the final [vowel] is removed by the elision [of the suffix] according to P. 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), the vṛddhi occurs for the non-final *a* as well, due to proximity (*āntaratamya*). However, "in the case of *guṇa*, an unjustifiable assumption [of such a rule] is improper."
[The opponent argues: "Thus, it is more logical that the subsequent rule (*antyaparibhāṣā*) itself be set aside. [The author replies: That is not so;

for since the *vṛddhi* substitution, which is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix (*pratyaya*), is an *antaranga* operation, it is proper that it takes effect even by setting aside the subsequent elision (*lopa*) governed by the rule "yasyeti ca. Furthermore, even if the elision were to somehow occur, [the following would apply].
The *vṛddhi* substitution would apply to the letter *r* alone and not to the letter *a*,
because the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the final phoneme) takes precedence over the *antaratamaparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the most similar substitute). Furthermore,
the *antaratamaparibhāṣā* excludes a substitute that is dissimilar, but it does not exclude the original element (*sthānin*).

[The rule] prescribes [the substitution]; how then can there be an exclusion of the status of the *repha* as the locus (*sthānitva*)? Furthermore, the citation of the maxim "but in the case of *guṇa*, it is improper" is quite gross, because there can be no mutual relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) between two *paribhāṣās*.

Herein lies the truth: "nara" is an imitation of the form ending in *ra* with the vowel *a* elided, [thus] *naraḥ aḥ naraḥ*. It should be explained as "of *nā* and *nara*. Alternatively, *naraḥ* is *nara-sya aḥ*, following the rule for the single substitute form (*pararūpa*) as in the case of *katanta*; thus it refers to "of *nṛ* and *nara*" (*nṛnarayoḥ*). And in the case of *nara*, it is the very first vowel, *a*.

Only the first [meaning] is accepted, and not the second, due to the force of the phonetic combination (*praśleṣa*). This should be understood in detail from the *Śabdakaustubha*. Here, the word *putrī* is read; for example: *śailaputrī* ("daughter of the mountain"), and "she spreads joy in the heart like a daughter" (*putrīva harṣaṃ hṛdaye tanoti*), and "I shall do all this, O daughter of the lord of the earth" (*kurve tadurvīpatiputri sarvam*). Nor is the word *putra* used for a daughter.

One should not be deluded by thinking [these terms] do not exist; for the *Amara-kośa* states: "These—*ātmaja*, *tanaya*, *sūnu*, *suta*, and *putra*—are all said to denote a son, while [the term] *striyam* refers to a daughter."

For this very reason, the *vārttika* "optionally for *sūtakā*, *putrikā*, and *vṛndāraka*" (*vā sūtakāputrikāvṛndārakāṇām*) and its commentary (*bhāṣya*) and so forth, which fall within the section on the substitution of *ī* by "pratyayasthāt," are consistent [with this view]. As for what was stated here by Haradatta— that the word *putra* alone does not [denote] a woman— [that is incorrect].

The claim that "it occurs" is to be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya and other such works, and because it contradicts one's own text situated within the section on *it* (the substitution of *i*).
However, this must be considered regarding the rule "kāre satyāgadasya": [what is the intended meaning?]

What is the purpose of the *vārttika* rule: "After the words *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhojaka*, and *meru*, the suffix [ṅīṣ] is applied to the daughter (*duhitṛ*) as if it were a son (*putra*)"? As for the claim that it is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), that is not correct; because the suffix is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, when *ṅīp* is applied, even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word ending in an acute-accented *ṅīp*, the accent is determined by the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara* (the accent that replaces the original low tone).
Since there is no difference in accent because [the compound] is necessarily oxytone by the accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*),
even the claim that the word *putra* has been interpolated into the *śārṅgarava* group and is not traditional is incorrect;
for that would contradict the usage cited in the Vārttika, "or *sūtakā*" and so forth.
Furthermore, because it would contradict the elision of the vowel *a* as established by Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others, let us leave the matter at that for now.

Regarding *āmbaṣṭhyā*: the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to the rule "vṛddhetkosalāt. Regarding *kārīṣagandhyā*: [the compound] *karīṣagandhiḥ* means "one whose scent is like that of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*)," according to the rule "upamānācca."

In the word *gandhī*, there is the substitution of *id* for the final vowel. The feminine descendant of that [lineage] is formed with the suffix *aṇ*. By the rule "aṇiñoḥ," this is replaced by *ṣyaṅ*. Although this [suffix] is prescribed only for the feminine, nevertheless, by the force of the addition of the marker *ṅ*, the suffix *cāp* is applied even after a stem ending in that [suffix]. Thus: *pautimāṣyā*.

The word *pūtimāṣa* belongs to the *gargādi* group. [From] *Prauḍhamanoramā*: "Taddhitāḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.76). The plural number is used for the purpose of including those suffixes not explicitly mentioned that are to be added as supplements.

And the designation "taddhita" is applied to those suffixes following the *prayoga* (the actual formation) in order to ensure they possess their etymological meaning—that they are "beneficial to" (*hita*) the base.
By this, they shall function exactly according to their names. It might be argued: "Let this governing rule (*adhikāra*) apply prior to the suffix *ṭāp*;
let there be no mention of 'taddhita' in the rule for *ṣpha*, and no mention of *īt* in the rule for the elision of *yasya*."

Not so; for in the word *paṭvī*, there would be the undesirable application of the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *o*. [The form] is derived from a stem ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*; this is because of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "one who joins" (*yauti*) or "one who mixes" (*miśrīkaroti*), i.e., a husband (*patyā*). Some, however, state that the suffix *katip* is an *auṇādika* (primary) suffix added to the root *yu* by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). In either case, [the same result follows].

The collective group of young women is *yauvatam*. However, because of the rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) when the suffix *aṇ* follows the suffix *tyap*, it is simply *yauvanam*. The statement in the *Vṛtti* that it does not undergo *puṃvadbhāva* due to the force of its inclusion in the *bhikṣādi* list is contrary to the *Bhāṣya*, since that reading is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*; such is the direction [of the argument].
Thus end the feminine suffixes.
Now follows the section on the euphonic combination of *s* and *v* sounds (*svādi-saṃdhi*).

Prau.ma.: *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.66). The term *padaḥ*, which is understood [from the previous rule], is qualified by *sasajuṣbhyām*; because of this qualification, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application to that which ends with the specified element) applies. Furthermore, regarding the portion of the word *sajūḥ*, [the rule] does not apply to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is accompanied by a suffix (*grahaṇavatā*).

One should not suspect the prohibition "there is no rule for the final element of that [preceding word]," because that [prohibition] applies specifically to the domain of rules prescribing suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*). The meaning is: "for a word (*pada*) ending in *s* or the word *sajuṣ*, there shall be *ru*, and that [substitution] occurs for the final letter. This being established, he states the resulting conclusion: "of the word-final" (*padāntasya*).

Regarding the phrase "of the word *sajuṣ*": the meaning is "of a word ending in that [suffix]"; by this, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *sajuṣaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that there is non-application (avyāpti) in the case of *sajūḥ*, because of the prohibition: "The treatment of a thing as being like itself does not apply when a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*) is involved."
This is because [the objection] was refuted in the *Śabdakaustubha* under the sūtra "yena vidhiḥ";

furthermore, both paribhāṣās— "vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena" and "grahaṇavatā— "— pertain specifically to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), as stated in the sūtra "diva ut."

Furthermore, because this has been stated by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta, forms such as *paramasajūrbhyām* are also established without objection. This being the case, it should be noted that the statement of the ancients— that there is no *tadantavidhi* (extension of a rule to what ends with the word) for the term *sajuṣ* in this context— is merely superficial.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *bho-bhago-ago-a-pūrvasya yo 'ci* (Pāṇini 8.3.17), [the commentary states] "the non-sandhi is due to the sūtra. This means that the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) resulting from the combination of the vowel *o* in the words *bhago* and *agho* with a following vowel does not occur because it is prescribed by a Vedic sūtra (*sautratvāt*). However, if [one considers] *bhos*, *bhagos*,...

If one explains *aghoṣ* as having an *s*-final or an *r*-final, and then applies the rule "for the three beginning with *bho*, let there be *y* for the final vowel, provided it is not preceded by *r*," then the absence of sandhi (*asandhi*) is indeed logical.
And this is appropriate; otherwise, [forms such as] *vibhor idam* and *suprabhā* would not be possible.

[The form] *suprabhagoridaṃ* [is derived from] *suprabhaguḥ*, which means "one who has a beautiful wife" (*gaurī yasya saḥ*). In the case of *raghoridam* as well, the substitution of *ya* would apply because this *ru* occurs after the word *bhoḥ* when preceded by something else. Nor is there non-application here due to the fact that the word *bhoḥ* is *lākṣaṇika* (derived/metaphorical), because [the rule] "vibhāṣā... [applies].

Since the words *bhoḥ* and others— derived from bases such as *bhavat*, *bhagavat*, and *aghavat* by means of the Vārttika rule "bhavadbhagavadaghavatām occāvasya"— are likewise characterized as *lākṣaṇika* (metalinguistic),
their lack of meaning (*anarthakatva*) is equal in both cases; for it is only those [words] qualified by a specific phonetic form (*rūpa*) that possess meaning.
One might object: since the letter *r* in *roru* is an *anubandha*, only the letter *r* would be the substitute for the *visarga*;

and thus, by the rule "analvidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.56), the status of being a *sthānin* would not apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For this [is not so]," just as in the case of *agrahīt*, where the substitution of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) by the rule "graho 'liṭi" (Pāṇini 7.2.37) [does indeed take place].

The intention is that because [the substitute] possesses the property of *iṭ* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the rule "iṭa īṭi" (Pāṇini 6.1.104) applies; likewise here as well, since the visarga has become *ru*, the substitution of *yatva* would apply. Accordingly, the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivat* sūtra states: "For this [substitute] relies upon a specific non-verbal element called *iṭ*."
For this reason as well, it should be understood that the enumeration beginning with *dhātvaṅga* is incorrect.

Regarding the term *nipātāḥ*: those [particles] specified in the rule *bho-bhago-* (Pāṇini 8.3.17) are to be understood there because the group beginning with *ca* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. And thus, regarding the rule *vibhāṣā*...

The Vārttika "bhavadbhagavat—" should not be resorted to; for otherwise, although forms such as *bho hare* would be established by the rule for the singular masculine alone, forms such as *bho hariharau*, *bho vadadvṛnda*, and *bho gaṅge* would not be established—this is the intended meaning. And this...

This was stated according to the opinion of Haradatta and others; however, according to the natural drift (*svarasa*) of the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika beginning with "vabhāṣā—" ought indeed to have been initiated. But since there is also a particle (*nipāta*) "bhoḥ," there is no fault regarding the dual number and so forth, nor in the case of the feminine and neuter genders. And this [latter view] is more appropriate. He [Bhartṛhari says]: "He..."

Since the usage of "he bho" is also desired—just like the usage of "bhavan"—and since that [usage] is established by the very commencement of the Vārttika; [this refers to] the particles (nipāta) denoting address mentioned by Amara in the verse: "syuḥ pyāṭ pāṭ aṅga hai he bhoḥ."

Because simultaneous application [of two particles] is not possible. Furthermore, just as in the case of *bhavān hariḥ tatrabhavān*, forms such as *tatra bhoḥ* and so forth are established only when the *vārttika* exists;
for by the rule *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 5.3.14), the suffixes *atra-* and *-tas* are seen following words such as *bhavat* after all case endings.
Because it is intended [as such]. Furthermore, if it were not an *āmantrita* (vocative), there would be the elision of the eighth case-ending (*aṣṭamika-nighāta*) for what follows a word;

the rule "the preceding *āmantrita*—" (*Pāṇini 8.1.72*) would apply the status of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*), and the rule "after *āma*, separated by one interval—" (*Pāṇini 8.1.55*) would be the injunction [to apply the vocative accent].

The doubling [of the word] occurs by the rule *vākyāderāmantritasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.8), and its status as being like a subsequent member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) occurs by the rule *subāmantrite* (Pāṇini 2.1.2); thus everything is established, and not otherwise—this is the general direction. Furthermore, if the particles *bhago* and *agho* [are also treated in this way]...

Let it be granted, then, that these two [rules] are authoritative; however, the accomplishment of the operation for the vocative case-ending must proceed solely on the basis of the Vārttika—this is what should be understood by the wise. As for what they say—that the Bhāṣya assumes these particles to end in /s/ and applies the rules for *rutva* (the substitution of /r/) and *autva* (the substitution of /au/) accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "when [the vocative] has been rejected," this is due to excessive haste. It might be argued: "If the particles (*nipāta*) are accepted, then only those [particles] would be included in the rule for *yatva* (the substitution of *y* for *i*), because they are *pratipadokta* (stated explicitly), whereas the forms ending in the vocative case-suffix (*sambuddhi*) would not, as they are *lākṣaṇika* (derived through grammatical rules). This is not so.

In the rule *svaritenādhikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.11), by adopting the explanation that *adhikaḥ kāraḥ* means *adhikāraḥ* (an extended application), and by relying on the state of being *svarita* according to the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), both [the preceding and following] are included;
this is why the term *mahāvyāhṛti* is explicitly mentioned in the rule *bhuvaśca mahāvyāhṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.71).

This is because Haradatta and others have stated that it is for the purpose of making known the non-eternality [of the rule] by means of the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which is taught as a specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*).
Furthermore, even with this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *prabhoḥ*, because— by virtue of mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*)—
only those [words] mentioned in the Vārttika, namely *narapāt* and so on, are included, while others are not.
*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: Regarding *vyor laghuprayatnataraḥ śākaṭāyanasya yaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.11):

"Of *v* and *y*, [there is] that which has a lighter effort. "Lighter effort" means easier articulation. And because of the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*), he says "of *v* and *y*" (*vayau*), meaning that for *v* there is *v* and for *y* there is *y*.
Prakriyā-mañjarī: *oto gārgyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.20).

Regarding the word "from *o*" (*okārāt*), the explanation given by the ancients—that it means "from a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *o*"—is incorrect. This is because a "stem" (*aṅga*) has not been introduced in this context, and furthermore, such an interpretation is impossible.

For in the examples [cited], there is no member ending in the vowel *u*. [Pradīpa on Pāṇini 8.3.22: "In the presence of a consonant (*hal*), for all [grammarians]. Regarding the mention of *yakāra*, as for *vakāra*...

It does not apply [to the case of *v*], because it is impossible for [the *v*] to be preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, or *agho*. Although it is possible for it to be unpreceded—as in *vṛkṣav karoti*—nevertheless, there is no occasion for elision (*lopa*) in that instance, because the word *aśi* (in the locative) is carried over [from the previous rule] and serves as a qualifier for the consonant (*hal*). As for examples such as *vṛkṣav hasati*, however...
They say that [the form] is incorrect because it is not so prescribed. However, in the case of *gavyam*, there is no status as a word-final (*padānta*);

and in the case of *gavyūti*, it has been stated that there is no elision of *v* due to the inclusion of the letter *v* (*vakārapraśleṣa*). But surely, in cases such as *devā namyāḥ*, the result is established by the rule "lopo vyoḥ—" (Pāṇini 6.1.76) alone?

It is not so, because [the rule] is unestablished with respect to that [word], and because in the case of *devā yānti*, there is an absence of the condition of being followed by *val*. Regarding *ahorātra*: the masculine gender is applied by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.29). Regarding *aharādīnām*: in both instances, the word *ādi* signifies "type" (*prakāra*). By this, [it includes words such as] *svarcakṣas*.
One should include [the examples] such as *rathinaḥ satyaśuṣmaḥ* and *vipraḥ kaviḥ kāvyena svarcanā*.

Regarding *tṛḍhaḥ* and *vṛḍhaḥ*: because [the roots] end in an *u*-vowel, they optionally take the augment *iṭ*; however, by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), the augment *iṭ* is not applied in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix.

The substitutions of *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha* [apply here]. As for the counter-example cited by the Easterners (*prācām*) regarding the word *dṛḍha*, that is incorrect; for in that case, there is no elision of *ḍha* at all. To explain: according to the rule *dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.20), there is the elision of both the *na*- and *ha*-sounds of the root *o-hṛ*.
The substitution of *ḍha* for *ta* is prescribed by way of *nipātana* (irregular derivation), but the rule for *ḍha* belonging to the section on unestablished forms does not apply here,

because it is superseded by the rule "of a root beginning with *da*, [substitute *gh*]" (Pāṇini 8.2.32). Nor can it be argued that let the absence of *iṭ* and the substitution of *ḍha* be prescribed by *nipātana*,
while the substitution of *dha*, the substitution of *ṭhu*, and the elision of *ḍha* will simply occur as a matter of course.
This must be stated; for if that were the case, in the word *paridṛḍhayya*, the substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇiC* (by Pāṇini 6.4.56,
*lyapi laghupūrvāt*) would not occur, and in the word *paridṛḍhī kanyā*, the feminine suffix *ṣyaṅ* (by Pāṇini 4.1.78, *aṇiñoḥ*) would also apply.

It is established in the Bhāṣya that because the elision of *ḍha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the vowel following the heavy syllable (*gurūpottama*) condition applies. As for the explanation given by the ancients—that this is a specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*) only for the root *oṇ*, while *dṛha* in the sense of "growth" is a different root, and that due to the non-eternality of rules regarding augments, there is an absence of *iṭ* in its past participle (*niṣṭhā*)—[the view is as follows]: "Or... [and so on].

Regarding the rule *druhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.33), it is argued that because of the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) by the word "optionally" (*vā*), this counter-example should be understood as occurring when, in one alternative, there is an absence of the substitution of *gha* and the elision of *ḍha*. That is not correct, because both [the substitution of *gha* and the elision of *ḍha*] are accepted as being prescribed. Thus Vāmana said: "Now, *dṛhi* is another root."
This is its elision, with the exception of the elision of *n*. And this is logical; otherwise, the suffix *ṇe* would not be replaced by *ay*, and *ṣyaṅ* would instead apply.
[The rule] "only the substitution of *u" [applies], because established and unestablished [operations] do not possess equal strength. In the case of a prohibition of *va*:

The meaning is that since the rule *paraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.2) does not apply, there is no counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), and thus only the substitution of *u* occurs. As it has been said: "When a preceding rule is not established [for the subsequent], there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) because of the absence of the subsequent. By this, the operation of the case-ending (*vibhakti-kārya*) [is established] first.
The passage beginning with "paścād utvamatve" has been explained.

He states that in the sūtra, *su* is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided: "yaḥ suḥ etatadoḥ. This means: of that *su* which expresses the number inherent in *eta* and *tad*. [The phrase] "vihitaḥ etatadoḥ" means "prescribed after *eta* and *tad*."
In the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), however, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *paramas dadāti* or *paramaiṣa dadāti*.
It should be understood that the evidence for resorting to a relationship mediated by the meaning (*arthadvāraka*) is the mention of "in a compound with *nañ*" (*ṭhanañsamāse*).

[The question] "Why [specify] 'of *ak* and *au*? (*akoḥ kim iti*) is a question based on the fact that there is no possibility [of the rule applying] to forms containing the augment *k* (*sākackayoḥ*), because they are different words (*śabdāntaratvāt*). [The example given is] *eṣaka*.

Thus, the very prohibition [stated] as "of *ṭhak* and *ka*" indicates the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "that which falls in the middle of [an element] is included by the mention of that [element]. This is the intended meaning.
Regarding the mention of *bahula*: for this very reason, even when filling out a verse-quarter (*pāda-pūraṇa*), [the suffix may be applied] without elision (*lopa*).
In some cases it occurs as *sāsmā aram* and *saḥ asmai*; the analysis (*chēda*) is *sā asmai*. Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of *svādi* (the nominative and other case endings).
Thus ends the section on the five junctures.
Now, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) of the *visarga*.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule beginning with *satva* (Pāṇini 8.3.36). For if it were stated simply as "not when followed by a *śar* [consonant] followed by a *par* [vowel]," then...

Even when the [substitution of] *s* for *t* has been negated in the case of a *satva* (the substitution of *s*), the substitutions of *k* and *p* for *kup* (the letters *k* and *p*) would still occur;

as in *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*. With the intention that the mention of *visarjanīya* serves to exclude the letter *v* alone, he says: "but not anything else. He clarifies this very point with the words: "here," etc.

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: "So'padādau" (Pāṇini 8.3.38). [The word] "apadādyoḥ" [is used]; however, in the sūtra, the singular number is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). If, on the other hand, *kha* is qualified as "in a non-initial position within a word" (*apadādau khari*), then it is correct according to the literal reading. However...
The difficulty arises from the fact that the phrase "before a *khar* consonant" (*ṭhkhari*) must be brought over [from a previous rule] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*) [method].

Furthermore, there is no necessity for it to recur in subsequent rules either; since a visarga is difficult to find except before a *khar*, its recurrence would be fruitless. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "In the case of *pāśa*, *kalpaka*, and *kāmya*."

This is a demonstration of possibility, not an exhaustive enumeration, because nothing else is possible. Regarding the phrase "the morning ritual" (*prātaḥkalpam*): although the word *prātaḥ* primarily denotes the locus (time), in this context of a compound, it refers to that which possesses the power (the ritual). This is similar to expressions such as "the day became night" (*doṣābhūtam ahaḥ*) or "the night became day" (*divābhūtā rātriḥ*). [The word] *gīḥ*.

Regarding the form *kāmyati*: here, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] by Pāṇini 8.3.39, "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ," does not apply, because the rule "kāmye roreva" (only after *r*, in the context of the suffix *kāmya*) is understood to carry over there as well. However, if this were read in that very same place [Pāṇini 8.3.39], then even if the substitution of *ṣ* were prohibited, the substitution of *s* would still occur by the preceding rule [8.3.59].

*Prakriyā-mañjarī*: *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.39). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Both this sūtra and the one beginning with *saḥ* are carried forward (*anuvartate*) into subsequent rules. The distinction is that, as far as possible, *ṣa* replaces a *s* following the root *iṇ*, while *sa* replaces any other *s*.

"‘The city (purah) is to be entered. [This is derived as follows: from the root *pṛ*, meaning ‘to protect’ and ‘to fill,’ the suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.177 (*bhrājabhās...* etc.).
From that form ending in *kvip*, the nominative singular case-ending (*jas*) is added. To make clear that it ends in *jas*, the form ‘pūḥ parā’ has been presented."
*Prakriyākaumudī*: Regarding *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41):

"of that [cluster] which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate (*upadhā*), [the *visarjanīya*] which is a member (*avayava*) thereof" is a relationship of different grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). As for the phrase "not being a suffix" (*apratyayasya*), however...

The term "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*) is connected with "visarga. This is because when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is improper to assume a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Nor should it be argued that the status of the visarga as a suffix is unestablished; for its status as a suffix is established through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) in cases such as *agniḥ karoti*. Not...

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the Tripādī is non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to rules of extension (*atideśa*), because its existence is made known precisely by the prohibition in the rule *apratyayasya*. For this very reason, the substitution of *visarga* for *ru* in forms such as *agniḥ* is established;
otherwise, it would not occur because [the *r*] would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*). However, the rule for *visarga* applies in cases such as *punar*.

[The rule] has already achieved its purpose; furthermore, an indicator (jñāpaka) depends upon a specific [context]. Therefore, the rule "acaḥ parasmin—" (Pāṇini 1.1.57) does not apply within the Tripādī. And thus, the established conclusion (siddhānta) that "in a case where a preceding element is not established, there is no substitution by virtue of the original place" (na sthānivat) is based on the reasoning already stated, and not [on anything else].

This has been explained by us at length in the *Śabdakaustubha*. If it is objected that, in this case, there would be the substitution of *ṣ* in forms such as *mātuḥ kāryam*, we reply: no; because the word *bhrātuṣputra* is listed among the *kaska-* group, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for a letter following the *u* of the genitive and locative endings (*ṅsi* and *ṅs*).

Because it serves to indicate [the rule]. And thus, what Haradatta stated—that even the phrase "of the suffix *ṭha*" (*ṭhapratyayasya*) is indeed a case of different grammatical coreference (*vyadhikaraṇa*)—is not to be taken too seriously.
Regarding the word *mātuḥ*: for here, by the rule "after *ṛ*, *u* is substituted" (*ṛta ut*, Pāṇini 8.2.111), the rule for single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [prevents] the *visarga*.

The indirect cause [of the fault] is through a traditional succession. However, in the original source (*ākara*), the prevalent reading is "ekādeśaśāstranimittāt. In that context, the meaning is: "from that *u*-vowel for which the rule of single-substitution (*ekādeśa-śāstra*) is the cause."

Regarding *muhuḥ kāma*: here the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau* (Pāṇini 8.3.37) applies. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the reading *muhuskāma* with the letter *s* is found in some places; however, Haradatta maintains that this is an error resulting from negligence (*prāmādika*).
Prau.ma.: "dvi, tri, and catur" [are used] in the sense of "times" (kṛtvas).

(Pāṇini 8.3.43) Regarding "dvi, tri, and catur": here, due to association with the two words *dvi* and *tri* which end in the suffix *su*, the word *catur* will also be understood as ending in *su*. The mention of "in the sense of times" (*kṛtvo'rtha*)...

The indicator is that concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is not a regulator in all cases. Therefore, in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6), even though there is concomitance with verbal roots (*dhātu*), the augment *iṭ* is included.
And this option (*vibhāṣā*) applies to both [cases]. As for the word *catuḥ*:

This being the case when [the rule] *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) applies, and since it does not apply to the other two cases, one might suspect that even for those two, the desired result is established by the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44). However, this is not so, because in that rule (*isusoḥ*), only the suffix *is* and meaningful words are intended to be included. Thus we have *catuṣkapāla*.
By the rule *ṭh-id-ud-upadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41), the substitution of *ṣ* is obligatory.
"Even in the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)" means, for example, in cases such as *tiṣṭhatu sarpiṣkuṇḍikām ānaya* ("Let him stay; bring the ghee-pot").
"In the case of mutual expectancy" means, for example, in the phrase *idaṃ sarpiṣkuṇḍikāyāḥ* ("This belongs to the ghee-pot"). As for that which... [text ends]

The Pārāyaṇikas say: "The inclusion of *sarpaṣkuṇḍika* and others in the *kaskādi* group is for the sake of the *ṣatva* [substitution] even when the word is in the final member of a compound. This should be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya.
[The term is] *ayaḥ-sahita*, but not a derivative of *ayas* (iron), according to the rule *jānapada-* (Pāṇini 4.1.42).
Because of the possibility of the suffix *ṅīṣ* [applying]. Regarding *ayaskarṇī*: it means "one whose ears are like iron.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule beginning with *nāsikodarauṣṭha-* (Pāṇini 4.1.55).

Prakriyā-mañjarī: Regarding the rule *adhaḥśirasī pade* (Pāṇini 8.3.47), the word *adhaḥśirasī* [is used]. In the sūtra, however, it should be understood that the nominative case is used in place of the genitive. Thus, *adhaspadam*; this is a compound by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. Similarly, *śiraspadam*.
A genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).
Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of the visarga.
